links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Nyctimene is the Lesbian girl turned into an owl, not Nycteus's daughter; Apollodorus gives Nycteus the daughter Antiope, and Hyginus has Nycteus father Nyctimene only in another tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban regent, brother of Lycus and father of Antiope; no other names to question.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Circe as daughter of Helios and Perse (1.9.1), not Hecate. Only a late tradition makes Hecate her mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Hecate. Her parents Perses and Asteria agree with Apollodorus 1.2.4. Other Wikidata parents (Zeus, Hera, Demeter) are minor variants.
Idas son of Aphareus (or Poseidon in some versions), husband of Marpessa, brother of Lynceus, father of Cleopatra; the match is right. Poseidon as father is a known variant, so Neptune stays.
Wikidata match is the goddess Hestia, daughter of Cronus and Rhea; no other names are listed.
Pleiades matches the seven sister-nymphs, daughters of Atlas; Peleiades is just a variant spelling.
Xuthus son of Hellen and Orseis, husband of Creusa, is the right match; no other names.
Licymnius, son of Electryon, is the right match; Pausanias names his tomb at Argos as the son of Electryon. The Wikidata spouse entry is unnamed and not in this book's tree, so nothing to fix.

links.reason: Hermes is father of Polybus of Sicyon's line (Pausanias) not Polybus of Corinth; in Apollodorus Polybus of Corinth, who raised Oedipus, has no such parentage.

identity.detail: Polybus of Corinth, who raised Oedipus, matches; Merope as wife is fine.
Theras, son of Autesion and regent of Sparta who colonised Thera, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Nestor of Pylos is the right being.
Nausithous is the Phaeacian king, son of Poseidon and Periboea, father of Alcinous and Rhexenor (Odyssey 7); the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias (Olympia) names Troilus, son of Alcinous, an Elean Olympic victor. This is a different Alcinous, not the Phaeacian king.
Alcetus son of Alcinous is an Elean boy-victor statue at Olympia, so another Alcinous than the Phaeacian king.
Corcyra was mother of Phaeax by Poseidon, and Phaeax's descendants include Nausithous. Alcinous is Nausithous's son, so Corcyra is at most a grandmother's line and not his mother.
Arete was Alcinous's wife and niece, daughter of his brother Rhexenor, not his sister (Odyssey 7).

identity.detail: The match is the Phaeacian king. The Troilus and Alcetus links come from the Elean Alcinous of the Olympia statues, a namesake.
Jocasta (Epicaste) is the Theban queen, mother and wife of Oedipus; the Wikidata match is correct. Both spouse links, Laius and Oedipus, are genuine marriages, so the flag needs no change.

links.reason: Hesiod's Sicyon is not Erechtheus's son. Pausanias (2.6.5) calls Sicyon son of Marathon or Metion, and Apollodorus has Metion as Erechtheus's brother-line, so Sicyon is another man's child at most a grandson-level confusion.

identity.detail: The match is the Athenian king Erechtheus. The Erichthonius conflation is only a note on the name, not a separate being in this book.
Iris, daughter of Thaumas, is the rainbow messenger; the epithet Thaumantian (Thaumantias) refers to her father Thaumas, so the Wikidata match and the name are correct.
Phorcus is Phorcys, the sea god, son of Pontus and Gaia; the match is correct.

Daulis is the nymph of Phocis for whom the town is named; the Wikidata match fits, and Pausanias' statement that she was Cephisus' daughter agrees with Wikidata's father Cephissus, so the flag is only a naming difference.
Minos, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete, is the right match. Wikidata lists Crete as a spouse, which is not a person, but that is a Wikidata quirk and not a link in this tree.
Wikidata match is Cresphontes, son of Aristomachus and husband of Merope; all links are consistent with Pausanias.
Sinis is the Isthmian pine-bender killed by Theseus. The book's links (Polypemon and Sylea) are correct, and the Wikidata match is right.
Wikidata's Deiphobus is the Trojan prince, son of Priam and Hecuba, who married Helen after Paris died. The match is correct, and no other names are attached.

In Metamorphoses 14, Tiberinus is the Alban king, son of Capetus, who drowned in the river Albula and gave it the name Tiber. Wikidata matches him to the river god Tiberinus. They are the same figure by apotheosis. The spouse Rhea Silvia comes from a different tradition, and no spouse link is in the book's tree.
Amata is Latinus' wife and Lavinia's mother; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match Haemon, son of Creon, is the same being; no other names listed.

links.reason: Pausanias' Henioche is daughter of Creon of Corinth (father of Glauce/Creusa), a different Creon, not the Theban.
Pausanias' Pyrrha belongs to the Corinthian Creon's family; confusion of two namesakes, not the Theban.

identity.detail: Match is the Theban Creon, son of Menoeceus and brother of Jocasta; the parent flag is only a naming difference.

Carme, mother of Britomartis by Zeus and daughter of Eubulus, matches the Wikidata Carme. Pausanias 2.30.3 gives her father as Eubulus, which fits the Wikidata father Eubuleus. The Wikidata father Phoenix and mother Cassiopeia are not in this book, but nothing contradicts them, so no change is needed.

links.reason: The Odyssey text says Arete is Rhexenor's daughter and Alcinous's niece and wife, so she is not his sibling. The link probably comes from a different tradition or a mix-up.

identity.detail: Arete of Scheria matches Wikidata.
The Wikidata match is the Corinthian hero Bellerophon, and Hipponous is his own earlier name.
Wikidata's Amulius is the king of Alba Longa, the usurper brother of Numitor and son of Proca, so the match is correct. The link Proca parent_of Amulius is right and is kept.

Cyparissus, the boy beloved by Apollo who became the cypress, matches the Wikidata entry. Wikidata lists two fathers, Amycleus and Telephus, which are variant traditions, not an error. No other names are attached.

Megara, daughter of Creon of Thebes and first wife of Heracles, matches Wikidata. Creon and Kreon are the same person under different spellings. Wikidata also lists Iolaos as a spouse, but that is a separate matter and not a link in this tree.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Aphidas (Apheidas of Tegea) as father of a different Stheneboea, wife of Proetus in a variant tradition, but Iobates is the usual father; Hesiod's Stheneboea is the Lycian king's daughter, and the book has no Aphidas.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Stheneboea, wife of Proetus; no other names.
Wikidata's Clytemnestra is this same being; the names Clytaemnestra, Clytemnestra and the Ghost of Clytaemestra are all her.
Wikidata's Antaeus is the Libyan wrestler son of Poseidon and Gaia whom Heracles defeated, so the match is correct. He has no other names.

Adamas, son of Asius (son of Hyrtacus), is the Trojan warrior of Iliad 12 and 13, and the Wikidata match is this same person. The book's sentence names Asius as his father, which agrees with Wikidata, so the parent flag needs no change.

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, not a person; Apollonius makes Cyzicus their king, descended from Poseidon only loosely.
The Moliones (Eurytus and Cteatus) are twins; the Iliad names them sons of Molione, with Actor or Poseidon as father in some tradition. Treat as group of two; keep only as individuals.
Wikidata lists Tyro as spouse, but editor reads non-marriages as lovers; Tyro was seduced by Poseidon, so lover is right.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Poseidon; the epithets Earth-shaker and Sea-king are his.
Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Aeneas; the alternate names (Cytherean hero, Indiges, Trojan) all refer to him.
Telephus matches the son of Heracles and Auge, king of Mysia.
Wikidata match is Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus and Iole, the Heraclid grandson of Heracles. This fits Apollodorus, who has Aristomachus as his son.
The Wikidata match is the Sirens as a group, which suits the book's plural 'Sirens'. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Hyrmina is a place in Elis, and Pausanias's Hyrmina is the daughter of Epeius, king of Elis, a different Epeius (son of Endymion) from the Trojan horse builder.
Anaxiroe was the wife of the Elean Epeius, son of Endymion, not the son of Panopeus.

identity.detail: Epeius, son of Panopeus and builder of the Wooden Horse, is the right match.
Wikidata's Adonis is the right being. Hesiod's parentage (Phoenix and Alphesiboea) is one of several traditions, alongside Theias/Myrrha and Cinyras/Metharme, and is correct for this book.

Metope is the Arcadian naiad daughter of Ladon who married the river god Asopus. Apollodorus (3.12.6) gives her as Asopus' wife and the mother of Ismenus, Pelasgus and twenty daughters, including Thebe and Aegina. The Wikidata match is correct.

Wikidata's Rhacius is the Cretan son of Lebes who settled Colophon and married Manto, which matches Pausanias. The two Manto spouse links are duplicates of one real marriage, so both are right and need no fix.

links.reason: Epicasta is not named as Nestor's daughter in the Odyssey; Homer gives Polycaste as the youngest daughter. The Hesiod link makes Epicasta a mother of Homer, which belongs to a different tradition and is not a Nestor-Epicasta link in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Nestor of Pylos, correct.
Wikidata match is Teleclus, the Agiad king of Sparta, son of Archelaus and father of Alcamenes. This fits the book.

links.reason: Reversed: Pandora is Pyrrha's mother (Apollodorus, Theoi), so Pyrrha cannot be Pandora's parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion; no other names.
Wikidata match is Thrasymedes, son of Nestor of Pylos; the Nestor link is correct and no other names are attached.
Wikidata match is the king of Pisa, son of Ares, father of Hippodamia; no other names to question.
The Wikidata match is Gelon of Syracuse, the Deinomenid tyrant, and no other names are attached.
Pylades, son of Strophius of Phocis and friend of Orestes, is the right match. Electra as his wife is standard (Euripides' Electra and Orestes) and Strophius is his father, so both links are fine.

links.reason: Idomeneus is the son of Deucalion son of Minos (Cretan Deucalion), not the flood hero Deucalion son of Prometheus; the editor's decision limits Minos as parent to hesiod and odyssey.
Molus is the son of Deucalion of Crete (father of Idomeneus's line), not the son of Prometheus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Prometheus' son Deucalion, but the tree merges him with the Cretan Deucalion son of Minos (father of Idomeneus and Molus); those links belong to the other Deucalion.

links.reason: Apollodorus makes Actor a son of Phorbas or brother of Augeas only in a variant; Pausanias gives Augeas as son of Eleus, and Actor is a different figure, so the link is not supported in this book.

Agamede, wife of Mecistes in the Iliad, is a daughter of Augeas in the Iliad scholia, but Theoi's own listing does not cite her. The Iliad says only that she was Augeas' daughter, not mentioned in Pausanias; the link imports an unsupported tradition.

identity.detail: Augeias of Elis is the right being; no other names.
The Wikidata match is the Theban king Eteocles, son of Oedipus.
Wikidata's Autolaus is the illegitimate son of Arcas who raised the exposed Asclepius at Thelpusa, which matches Pausanias; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Hesione was given to Telamon as war prize after Heracles sacked Troy, mother of Teucer; a concubine, not a wife (Apollodorus). Editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse as lover.

identity.detail: Telamon, son of Aeacus and Endeis, father of Ajax and Teucer, is the right match.

The Wikipedia description is of the Egyptian son of Aegyptus, but the Pausanias character is the Thracian king Cisseus, father of Theano (and in some traditions Hecuba). The Wikidata spouse Telecleia fits the Thracian king, so the match is a namesake and the Aegyptid should not be merged with him.
Alcyone, daughter of Aeolus and Enarete and wife of Ceyx, matches Wikidata's Alcyone.

Death here is Thanatos, the personified god of Hesiod's Theogony, a child of Night and brother of Sleep. The generic Wikidata match for personified death is loose but acceptable, and no other names are involved.

links.reason: Selene is the Moon goddess; the editor ruled Zeus as parent of Selene wrong, and Hesiod's Selene child Pandia is confused with Diana's cult.
Hesiod's Homeric Hymn tradition is mixed with Selene; editor has Selene-linked relations wrong, and Pandia belongs to Selene as child of Zeus only in a hymn, unsupported here.
Thalia the Grace and Thalia the Muse are confused; the editor rules Helios's Thalia wrong and this is a duplicate merge.
A group taken for a person; the individual Muses are already linked.
A group taken for a person; the Graces are linked individually (Aglaea, Euphrosyne).
A group taken for a person.
A group taken for a person.
Opportunity (Kairos) is a personified cult figure from Pausanias, not a firm child of Zeus.
Sibyl is a title, not a person; Pausanias names her as daughter of Zeus and Lamia in one tradition only.
Pallas is the Titan or giant, or Athena's epithet, not Zeus's child.
Eetion, Andromache's father, has no Zeus parentage in the Iliad.
Xanthus the river or Trojan horse is not Zeus's son; the editor ties Xanthus to Midas.
Juno is both sister and wife of Jove; the book says she is his wife, so the sibling link should not be a spouse removal.
Wikidata and Hesiod give Metis as Zeus's first wife, but editor says only Hera/Juno is marriage, so this stays a lover.
Unsupported guess; no Iliad sentence names Truth as Zeus's child.
Macar is a Lesbian king in Pausanias, not Zeus's son.
Hermus is a river, unsupported as Zeus's son.

identity.detail: Jove, Jupiter and Zeus are the same being, matched correctly to Zeus.
Polydorus, king of Thebes and son of Cadmus and Harmonia, is the right match.

links.reason: Eurus is born of Astraeus and Aurora in Hesiod's Theogony only for the three winds Zephyrus, Boreas, Notus; Eurus is not listed there and Wikidata's claim lacks ancient support.
Phaethon, son of Aurora and Cephalus, is a Pausanias-only tradition per the editor; in other books Phaethon is the son of Helios and Clymene, so this link does not belong here.

identity.detail: Aurora is the Latin name of Eos; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Helle, daughter of Athamas and Nephele, who fell into the Hellespont. The Persians passage in Aeschylus names her as Athamas' daughter. No other names to check.

links.reason: Pausanias does not make Hyperion a child of Agamemnon; Agamemnon's children are Orestes, Electra, Iphigenia, Chrysothemis, etc. The link likely confuses a different figure or misreads a sentence.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Agamemnon, king of Mycenae.
Wikidata's Atthis is the eponymous heroine of Attica, daughter of Cranaus. Pausanias 1.2.6 matches this, and no other names are attached.

links.link: Linus, son of Apollo parent_of Pierus
links.reason: Linus is not Pierus's father; in Hesiod's tradition Pierus is father of Linus by a Muse, and the Metamorphoses gives Pierus no such parentage. Wikidata gives Makedon as his father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Macedonian king Pierus, father of the Pierides, and is correct.
Ismenis is a nymph, daughter of the river Ismenus, and the match is consistent with the book.
Wikidata match is Iamus, the seer son of Apollo and Evadne; no other names involved.

links.reason: The quoted line is Aphrodite addressing Anchises as 'son of Dardanus', which is a generic descent phrase. Anchises' father is Capys, the son of Assaracus, and Dardanus is a remote ancestor, not his father.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Anchises, the Trojan father of Aeneas.

links.reason: Pausanias reports the Cypriot claim that a Cypriot woman named Themisto was Homer's mother, which is a different Themisto from the Lapith princess, daughter of Hypseus and wife of Athamas.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Lapith princess Themisto, daughter of Hypseus and wife of Athamas. This is correct for the Ptous passage.
Wikidata match is Iris, the rainbow goddess and messenger, daughter of Thaumas. Her parentage is confirmed by Theoi and Hesiod. No other names are listed that could belong to someone else.
Wikidata match is Tereus, the Thracian king, son of Ares and Bistonis, husband of Procne. No other names are attached.
Agapenor, son of Ancaeus, leader of the Arcadians at Troy and founder of Paphos, is the same being Pausanias describes; his daughter Laodice is correctly linked.
Macris, daughter of Aristaeus, is the right match. The book's sentence names her as Aristaeus's daughter, and Theoi agrees.

Atthis is the daughter of Cranaus and Pedias, as in Apollodorus 3.14.5, where Cranaus' daughters are Cranae, Cranaechme and Atthis. The Wikidata match is the right being, and no other names are attached.
Eleutho is Pindar's name for Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Alcestis, daughter of Pelias and wife of Admetus; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Hesiod's Catalogue (and the Eugammon/Hellanicus tradition) has Telemachus marry Nestor's daughter Polycaste; she is a wife, not a lover. It is absent from the Odyssey itself, but the link comes from Hesiod.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Odysseus' son Telemachus; no other names to doubt.
Wikidata match is Protesilaus, son of Iphiclus and husband of Laodamia. Polydora is a spouse in some traditions (Hesiod's Catalogue of Women), so the spouse links are not flagged as wrong.
Latona is Leto, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus. The match is correct.

links.reason: Aethra slept with Aegeus once at Troezen and was never his wife, so by the editor's rule this is a lover link, not a marriage.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Aegeus, king of Athens. He has no other names to question.

links.reason: Pausanias gives Oeneus a father Pandion (Athenian tradition) in a variant; Iliad and Theoi/Wikidata give Porthaon (Portheus) as father, so the Pandion link is another tradition not followed here.
Editor's rule: only marriages stay spouse links; Althaea is Oeneus' wife, Periboea is read as a secondary partner (Hesiod's tradition, Apollodorus), so mark as lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Oeneus of Calydon; no other names.
The Wikidata match is Oenomaus, king of Pisa, who is the right being. The spellings Hippodameia and Hippodamia are the same daughter. No other names are in question.
Autonoe, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon, is the right match.
Wikidata Oenone is Paris's first wife, daughter of the river Cebren, as Apollodorus 3.12.6 says. The island Oenone (Aegina) is a different being, but it does not affect this match.

Wikidata's Scylla is the sea monster, which matches the book. The Great Eoiae fragment gives Phoebus and Hecate as her parents, and the book states this in its own words, so both links are right for this book.

links.reason: Duplicate spelling of Aegina, already linked as Asopus's daughter; this is the same person listed twice, so drop the duplicate node.

identity.detail: Asopus is the river god, son of Oceanus and Tethys in Apollodorus; the match is acceptable.
Wikidata's Marica is the Laurentine nymph, mother of Latinus by Faunus, as Aeneid 7 says. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Cybele is not Saturn's wife in this book; his wife is Ops (Rhea), and Cybele is a separate Phrygian goddess merely conflated with Rhea.
Cybele is a Phrygian mother goddess, not Saturn's sister. Other books may mean Rhea under that name, but this is a confusion of two beings.

identity.detail: Saturn/Cronus is the right being. Cybele is only a conflation with Rhea/Ops, not a true alias.

links.reason: The Mecisteus line (son of Mecisteus, sprung of Talaus, who fought with Diomedes) is a different Eurypylus, the Argive. The Mysian Eurypylus is the son of Telephus and Astyoche.

identity.detail: The book names two men called Eurypylus: the Mysian son of Telephus and the Argive son of Mecisteus. The Wikidata match fits only the Mysian one, so the Argive should be a separate character.
Wikidata match is Danaë, mother of Perseus; no other names to separate.
Wikidata's Archander, son of Achaeus and brother of Architeles, is the same person as Pausanias's Archander. The parent link to Achaeus matches Wikidata, so the flag is unfounded.

links.reason: Doris is Nereus' wife (daughter of Oceanus and Tethys per Hesiod); Apollodorus' link confuses her with a Nereid daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea-god Nereus; no other names to question.
Periphetes, also called Corynetes, is the club-bearing bandit killed by Theseus. The match is correct. Hephaestus as father is the standard tradition (Apollodorus), and Theoi confirms it.
Wikidata match is the goddess Harmonia, wife of Cadmus; the Theoi alternative parentage (Zeus and Electra) belongs to the Samothracian Harmonia, but Apollodorus follows Ares and Aphrodite.

links.reason: Apollodorus 1.7.5 makes Endymion son of Aethlius and Calyce; Zeus as father is a variant from Wikidata that this book does not tell (Aethlius was son of Zeus).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Endymion.

links.reason: Pausanias' Pierus is the Macedonian king who came to Thespiae and founded the Muses' cult there, and Wikidata gives Makedon as his father. Linus, the musician son of Amphiaraus or of Apollo, is another figure and is not Pierus' father.

identity.detail: Pierus of Emathia is the right match. Wikidata's father is Makedon, so the parent link from Linus comes from a confusion.

Wikidata match is the Theban seer Tiresias, son of Everes (Evereus) and Chariclo. High Seer is only a title for him in this book. Manto and Historis as daughters are variant traditions but are attested (Manto in Apollodorus, Historis in Pausanias).
Hylas, Heracles' companion, is the right match. Theiodamas is his father in Apollodorus (and Apollonius Rhodius), so the link is fine.
Bias son of Amythaon, brother of Melampus, king of Argos; the match is the same person.
Wikidata match is Ino, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, who later became Leucothea. No wrong names.

Wikidata match is Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, husband of Autonoe and father of Actaeon. Theoi's other parent listings (Ouranos and Gaia; Karystos) are variant traditions, not a different being.
Callirrhoe is the Oceanid, daughter of Ocean and Tethys, who bore Geryones to Chrysaor in Hesiod's Theogony. The Wikidata match is the same being.

links.reason: In Ovid, Iole is Dryope's sister-in-law: Dryope says her father had Dryope's mother's child by another wife, and Iole is the daughter of Eurytus. Dryope is the daughter of Eurytus's wife's line, so the book calls them half-sisters at most, and the sentence names no sibling link to Iole directly. Actually Iole calls Dryope her sister, so the book supports a half-sibling link.

identity.detail: Iole, daughter of Eurytus, matches Wikidata.
Wikidata match is Capaneus, the Argive hero of the Seven against Thebes; no other names are involved.
Hyllus son of Heracles and Deianira matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Arete is Alcinous's wife and niece, not his sibling. Odyssey 7 makes her daughter of Rhexenor, who was Alcinous's brother. Hesiod's sibling tie is a misreading.

identity.detail: Arete of Scheria, wife of Alcinous, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Pyrrha is the wife of Deucalion, son of Prometheus, the flood hero Pindar tells of in Olympian 9. The Cretan Deucalion, son of Minos, is a different man, whose wife in Wikidata is Cleopatra.

identity.detail: Pindar's Deukalion (Olympian 9) is the son of Prometheus, who survived the flood with Pyrrha. He is not the Cretan Deucalion, son of Minos and Pasiphaë, so the Wikidata match is wrong.
The Wikidata match is Hephaestus, and no other names are attached to him.

links.reason: No ancient source makes Juno the mother of Bellona. Her parentage is not given in Statius, and Wikidata's Juno link is an unsupported guess.
No ancient source makes Jupiter the father of Bellona. Statius does not say so, and this link is an unsupported guess.

identity.detail: Bellona is the Roman war goddess, and the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Titan Atlas; no other names are involved.

links.link: Berenice lover_of Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas
links.reason: Pausanias' Berenice (wife of Ptolemy I, mother of Magas and Ptolemy II) is the Berenice who loved Philip, not Berenice Phernophorus; the Macedonian Philip of Pausanias' Magas passage is an obscure commoner, not Philip II's son Amyntas line, and Philip son of Amyntas is wrongly linked.
The Wikidata Berenice Phernophorus is Ptolemy II's daughter, but Pausanias' Berenice is the wife of Ptolemy I and mother of Magas, so this father link belongs to another Berenice.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Berenice is Berenice I, wife of Ptolemy I and mother of Magas of Cyrene, not Berenice Phernophorus, the Seleucid queen and daughter of Ptolemy II.
Arion is the divine horse of Adrastus, and the Wikidata match is correct. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Aethra lay with Aegeus at Troezen but was not his wife; the rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Pirithous was the son of Ixion (or Zeus) and Dia; Aethra is his namesake confusion, not his mother.
Pausanias' Phalanthus's wife is Aethra of Taras legend, a different Aethra from Pittheus' daughter; namesake.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Pittheus' daughter, mother of Theseus; the Phalanthus wife is a separate namesake but the main identity is fine.
Melampus the Amythaonian seer is the right match: son of Amythaon, brother of Bias.
Wikidata match is the Homeric Patroclus, son of Menoetius. The two Menoetius entries are the same father under variant spellings, and the book's fragment confirms him.

links.reason: Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.948) and Apollodorus make Cyzicus son of Aeneus and Aenete; Apollo as father is an unsupported Wikidata guess.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Dolionian king Cyzicus; no other names.
Hebe matches the goddess; Juventas is her Roman counterpart, a fair alternate name.
Pammon is a son of Priam, named in Iliad 24.250 among his surviving sons; the Wikidata match is the same being.
Wikidata match is Helle, daughter of Athamas and Nephele, who fell into the Hellespont; no other names to dispute.
Wikidata's Cerberus is the hound of Hades; Apollodorus makes him the child of Typhon and Echidna (Bibliotheca 2.5.1, 2.5.12), which agrees with both links.

links.reason: Erato in the Aeneid and Argonautica is a Muse, not Zeus's daughter by that name's namesake; the Aeneid's Erato is a Muse invoked, and the Argonautica's is likely a nymph — the match mixes beings.
Selene is a daughter of Hyperion and Theia; the editor rules Zeus is not her parent, and no lover tradition is given.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus and given by Zeus; she was not his lover.
Pallas is a Titan son of Crius, or the giant; not Zeus's child. Athena's epithet is a cult title.
Sisyphus is a son of Aeolus, not Zeus.
Sibyl is a title for several prophetesses; Pausanias gives Lamia or Theodorus as parent, not Zeus.
Macar is a son of Helios or Aeolus in tradition, not Zeus.
Xanthus is not a son of Zeus; the editor gives Midas as a parent in Hesiod.
Opportunity is an abstraction, not a person with Zeus as father.
Truth is a personification with no Zeus parentage fixed by the book.
Fortune is a personification; the parentage is an unsupported guess.
Hesiod makes Eris a daughter of Night.
Hermus is a river, with no known Zeus parentage.
Eetion is the father of Andromache or a son of Iasion; not Zeus's child.

identity.detail: Zeus matches; Jove and Jupiter are the Roman equivalent and are acceptable.

links.reason: The book's sentence names Ægialeus as son of Adrastus; Adrastus was Polynices' father-in-law, not his son. Polynices' son in the book is Thersander.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Polynices, son of Oedipus.

Polyidus the seer, son of Coeranus, matches Polyeidos. The flag is not a real conflict: Pausanias also calls him son of Coeranus, and Wikidata's father is Coeranus. Euchenor is Polyidus' son in Apollodorus and Homer's tradition (killed at Troy), so that link is fine.
Pleuron, son of Aetolus and Pronoe, eponym of Pleuron in Aetolia; Wikidata match is correct.
The Wikidata match is Europa, the Phoenician princess and mother of Minos, so it is the same being.

links.reason: Hippocoon's mother is Batea (daughter of Teleboas), wife of Oebalus, per Apollodorus; Gorgophone, Perseus' daughter, is Oebalus' other wife and mother of Tyndareus, so this link confuses the two wives.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Spartan king Hippocoon; no other names to question.
Rhesus of Thrace is the right match. Apollodorus names Euterpe and Strymon as parents and notes the Calliope variant, so the tree needs no change.
Protesilaus matches the Thessalian hero, son of Iphiclus. The flagged 'two spouses' is one Polydora entered twice (once via Hesiod, once from Pausanias citing the Cyprian Poems), so nothing is wrong.
Liber/Bacchus is Dionysus; the names Bromius, Iacchus, Lenaeus, Evan and others are all his epithets, so the match holds.
Ganges is the river god of the Ganges, and the Wikidata match to the river is acceptable. In Ovid's Metamorphoses (5.47), Limnate is his daughter and the mother of Athis, so the link is right.

links.reason: Hesiod's tradition has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter, mother of Pan; this was a union, not a marriage, and only marriages count as spouse.
Mars is the son of Jupiter and Juno; Mercury is the son of Jupiter and Maia, so they are only half-brothers, and Statius does not make them siblings by mother.
Pindar's odes name no such child; Fame is a personification and no genealogy supports this link.

identity.detail: Mercury and Hermes are one being under Roman and Greek names; the Wikidata match is correct.
Helenus the Trojan seer, son of Priam and Hecuba, is correctly matched; no other names to question.
Tlepolemus, son of Heracles and leader of the Rhodians at Troy, matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata's Circe is this Circe, the daughter of Helios and Perse(is). No other names are attached to her.
Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, is the same being as the Wikidata match; no other names to correct.

Menestheus is the Athenian king, son of Peteos, who led the Athenians at Troy. The Wikidata match is correct. The link Peteos parent_of Menestheus matches Wikidata's father Peteus, which is the same name in a different spelling, so the flag is only a spelling difference.

links.reason: Editor decided Jove is not Pasithea's parent. Pasithea is a Grace in Iliad 14 and Pausanias, not Hera's child, and Theoi lists Hera as her mother only loosely, so the link is unsupported in this book.
Bellona is a Roman war goddess with no ancient tradition naming Juno as her mother, so the link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Juno matches Hera as the Roman equivalent, and the alternate names Hera and Saturnia are the same goddess.

links.reason: The Graces are children of Zeus and Eurynome; the editor already rules Helios the father of Aglaea and Thalia wrong, so the group link goes too.
Pindar says Helios 'lay with' Rhodos; only marriages count as spouse links, so this is read as a lover link.
Amalthea is the nurse of Zeus; a Helios parentage is a doubtful variant. It is unsupported in this book.

identity.detail: Helios matches the correct god. 'Sun' is just his name in translation.
Epione is the wife of Asclepius (Æsculapius); the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Philander, son of Apollo and Acacallis and brother of Phylacides, matches Pausanias' Philander.
Wikidata's Meges is Meges son of Phyleus, leader of the Dulichians and Epeans at Troy. No other names are listed that belong to someone else.

The Wikidata match is Ancaeus the Argonaut. Apollonius's Argonautica follows the Samian tradition (Poseidon and Astypalaea), so the parents differing from Wikidata's Arcadian line (Lycurgus) is a variant tradition, not an error.
Wikidata match is Tiresias, the Theban seer; the Historis link from Pausanias is a variant daughter, not an error.

links.link: Amphion, son of Antiope spouse_of Niobe
links.reason: Amphion's wife is Niobe daughter of Tantalus; Pausanias mentions both Niobes, and the Argive Niobe (daughter of Phoroneus) is a different being, so this spouse belongs to the Theban Niobe.
Chloris is the daughter of Amphion's Niobe (daughter of Tantalus), not the Argive Niobe.
Tantalus is father of the Theban Niobe turned to stone, not the Argive Niobe daughter of Phoroneus.

identity.detail: Pausanias has two Niobes under one name: Niobe daughter of Phoroneus (mother of Argus and Pelasgus by Zeus) matches Wikidata; Niobe daughter of Tantalus, wife of Amphion and mother of Chloris, is a separate person.
Xerxes I matches the king of Persia who invaded Greece; Pausanias calls him son of Darius, and the links to Darius, Atossa and Artaxerxes are consistent.

links.reason: Hesperus (the evening star) is son of Astraeus and Eos in Hesiod's Theogony only as Eosphorus; Hesperus as her son is a confusion, though Ovid/Apollonius treat Hesperus as son of Cephalus or Atlas, so unsupported here.

Pausanias gives Phaethon as son of Cephalus; Hesiod's Phaethon is son of Eos and Cephalus, so the editor's decision on Cephalus is the right link, but Aurora as parent is a variant of the same story and should be kept.

identity.detail: Aurora is the Roman Eos; match is correct.
Wikidata match is the goddess Hecate; the epithet Epipurgidia ('on the tower') is a cult title of the same goddess in Pausanias, so it is not a separate person.

links.link: Helice parent_of Ion, son of Xuthus
links.reason: Pausanias says Bura was Ion's daughter by Helice, so Helice is Ion's wife, not his parent; the link reverses the relation. The spouse link already covers her.

identity.detail: The match is the right Ion, son of Xuthus and eponym of the Ionians.
Wikidata match is Cychreus, king of Salamis, son of Poseidon and the nymph Salamis; no problem.

links.reason: Demodoce is the daughter of the Argive/Arcadian Agenor's line in other tradition; Hesiod's Agenor is not clearly the Phoenician king.
Pausanias' Crotopus is the Argive son of Agenor, son of Triopas or Phorbas, a different Agenor.
Iphidamas is the Trojan son of Antenor, a confusion with a different Agenor/Antenor.
Preugenes is the Achaean son of Agenor of Patrae, a different Agenor.
Echeclus is the Trojan son of Agenor (Iliad), a different Agenor.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Phoenician king, father of Cadmus. Namesake children from Pausanias belong to other Agenors.
Tityos is the right match. Apollodorus 1.22 makes him a son of Zeus and Elare, and both links are right for this book.
Veritas is the Roman counterpart of Pindar's Aletheia; the match is acceptable and the parent difference is only a tradition variant.
Eidyia, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys and wife of Aeetes, matches Wikidata. No other names are mixed in.
Libya, daughter of Epaphus and mother of Belus and Agenor by Poseidon, matches Apollodorus 2.1.4 and the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Pausanias names Piras as a father of Styx's namesake or a river figure; Hesiod has no such husband, and the link confuses two beings. The flag is justified for Piras only.

identity.detail: Styx the goddess and river is the correct match; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is the nymph Calypso of Ogygia; no other names are involved.
Lamedon is the king of Sicyon, son of Coronus, as Pausanias tells it. The parents match Wikidata's father Coronus, so the flag does not point to a real error.
Androdamas, son of Phlias and Chthonophyle of Sicyon, matches the Wikidata entry; the book names Phlias as his father in the Sicyon rite passage.

links.reason: Anchises' father is Capys, son of Assaracus, son of Tros; Dardanus is a distant ancestor (Iliad 20.215-240), so he is not the parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan Anchises, father of Aeneas; no names to split.

Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, is the right match. Teledamus is a son of Odysseus and Calypso in some accounts, and the Eustathius passage on the Telegony names him as a son of Odysseus and Penelope, so the alias is a different figure, but it does no harm here.

links.reason: Odyssey 12 names Neaera as mother of Helios' daughters Phaethusa and Lampetia; Apollonius' Argonautica names no mother, and Clymene (Klymene) is a different mother, mainly of Phaethon and the Heliades, so this link confuses two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Phaethusa, daughter of Helios. Do not confuse her with the Heliad of the same name.
Psamathe daughter of Crotopus of Argos, mother of Linus by Apollo, matches Wikidata; no other names to split.
The Wikidata match is Eurysaces, son of Ajax and Tecmessa. No other names are involved.
Pausanias's Chios is the son of Poseidon and a Chian nymph, citing Ion of Chios. The Wikidata match is a disambiguation of two eponyms, but the Poseidon link fits the son.
Selinus is the king of Aegialus (Aegialea) in Achaea, whom Pausanias names as father of Helice, who married Ion. The Wikidata match is the same being.
Androgeus, son of Minos, matches Wikidata; the book's sentences support both the Minos parentage and his son Alcaeus.
Wikidata matches Phocus, son of Aeacus and Psamathe, whom Peleus kills in Metamorphoses. 'Nereian youth' fits his mother Psamathe, a Nereid.
Tyndareus the Spartan king matches; no other names are given.
Ptolemy Lightning (Keraunos) is Ptolemy Ceraunus, son of Ptolemy I Soter and Eurydice, and brother of Lysandra, as Pausanias says. The match is correct.
Wikidata's Iambe is the servant of Demeter's Eleusis story. Her parentage as the daughter of Pan and Echo is the tradition Wikipedia gives, so the match is right and no other names are mixed in.
Phyleus is the Elean prince, son of Augeas and father of Meges; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias names Hyperion as a son of Aegisthus-era Orestes' line, not of Agamemnon; Hyperion is a Titan or a different figure, so this is a misreading or confusion with another being.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (daughter of Atreus) in some sources, or the wife of Nestor; Pausanias does not make her his daughter, so it is a confusion with another Anaxibia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the king of Mycenae; the names Atreid kings, Atreides and Atreus' son are epithets that also fit Menelaus, so they are not exclusive to Agamemnon.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome (or Hera); Dionysus is not her father in the Iliad or the tradition it follows. The editor rules Jove and Bromius as her parent wrong everywhere.

identity.detail: Bacchus is Dionysus, the right being; Wikidata parents Jupiter and Semele match the Iliad's passage.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses the daughter of Dryops is Dryope, whose sister is Iole, wife of Andraemon, not Eurytus' daughter Iole; Apollodorus makes Iole the daughter of Eurytus.

identity.detail: Wikidata Iole, daughter of Eurytus of Oechalia, matches this character.
Wikidata match is the Oceanid Metis, wife/consort of Zeus and mother of Athena; no other names to question.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony) and Wikidata make Themis Zeus's second wife, not merely a lover; the site's rule reads non-Hera spouses as lovers, but Themis is traditionally a wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis; no other names listed.
Merope, daughter of Oenopion and object of Orion's assault, matches the Wikidata princess; no other names are involved.

links.reason: A group label, not a person. Apollodorus names the sons Mermerus and Pheres, and the individual links cover them.
Eriopis is Jason's wife or sister in other traditions, not clearly his daughter in Apollodorus; Pausanias does not make her a child of Jason and Medea.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason, and there are no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Anchises, father of Aeneas; no other names to question.

links.reason: Harmonia is Mars's daughter and married Cadmus. Mars was not her husband.
In Statius, Venus is Mars's lover. In the Iliad Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, so she is no sibling of Ares by the same parents. The lover link already exists.
Duplicate spelling of Penthesilea, which is already listed as Mars's child. Merge the two.

Mercury is the son of Jupiter and Maia. He is called 'brother' in Statius only as a half-brother, but Mars's mother is Juno, so the tie is a loose half-sibling. Keep the sentence as the book's own phrasing.

identity.detail: Mars and Ares are the same being. Gradivus and Mavors are Roman epithets of Mars. The Wikidata spouse is Aphrodite, treated as a lover per the editor's rule.
Autonoë is Cadmus and Harmonia's daughter, wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon (Hesiod, Theogony 977 ff.). The Wikidata match is the same being.
The Wikidata match is Polydorus, son of Priam, who is the Trojan prince killed by Polymestor in Thrace in the Aeneid. All of the listed links fit.

pindar-odes/apollo.name: Apollo
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Loxias, Phoebus, Apollo

links.reason: Apollo's twin is Artemis; the Moon (Selene) is a different being, a Diana/Selene conflation in Metamorphoses. The editor has also ruled that Selene is not Apollo's relative.
Several figures are named Kyknos; the Wikidata link is unsupported in this book and likely belongs to a different Kyknos (Ares's son in Pindar).
Scylla is the daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis (Phorbas or Hecate in other versions); Apollo as father is a mix-up with another Scylla, Nisus's daughter, or a misreading in Hesiod's fragments.
Pindar describes a bridal bed and 'common wedlock' for Apollo and Kyrene, so it is a marriage.
Same figure as Kyrene; Pindar describes wedlock, and the duplicate spelling should be merged.

identity.detail: Loxias, Phoebus and Apollo are all names of the same god, so the match is correct.
Polybius the historian, son of Lycortas of Megalopolis, matches Pausanias' statue references; Wikidata match is correct.

The Eubulus in Pausanias 2.30.3 is the Cretan son of Carmanor and father of Carme. He is a different person from Eubuleus of Eleusis, the Orphic and mystery god (son of Dysaules, or of Trochilus and Eleusis, or of Demeter). The Wikidata match to Eubuleus is a namesake mix-up, and the Eleusinian parents (Dysaules, Trochilus) do not belong to the Cretan Eubulus.

links.reason: Alcinous is son of Nausithous (Odyssey); in Apollonius Corcyra is the island nymph loved by Poseidon, whose son was Phaeax by tradition, not Alcinous.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right being: Corcyra, naiad daughter of Asopus and Metope.

links.reason: Hermes's son Polybus is a different man (Pausanias' Polybus of Sicyon context); the Odyssey's Polybus is father of Eurymachus (Ithacan), with no Hermes parentage in the book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Ithacan Polybus, father of Eurymachus; no other names are mixed in.
Wikidata's Zelus is the same being as Hesiod's Zelos, the child of Pallas and Styx, and 'Emulation' is simply the English rendering of his name.

links.reason: Electra here is the Pleiad who bore Harmonia to Zeus, or the Samothracian Electra, and she is not a daughter of Agenor. Pausanias links her to Cadmus only through Samothrace, which confuses the two Electras.

Metamorphoses uses Hermione as another name for Harmonia, Cadmus's wife; the tree has made a separate person out of it. Hermione, daughter of Menelaus, is a different figure, so the link duplicates Harmonia.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Cadmus the founder of Thebes. Hermione is not a separate wife but a duplicate of Harmonia.
Helicaon son of Antenor and Theano, husband of Laodice, is the same being as the Wikidata match; no other names to check.
Wikidata match Aegisthus is the right figure, the son of Thyestes who killed Agamemnon; the spelling Ægisthus is just a variant.
Amphion of Thebes, husband of Niobe and son of Jupiter (Zeus) and Antiope, is the correct match. The flagged spouse links both name Niobe, who was his wife, so they are fine.
Wikidata match is Alexander the Great, the Macedonian king; no other names to question.

links.reason: Rhadamanthys married Alcmena only in a late tradition (after Heracles' death, per Apollodorus/Pherecydes); Hesiod doesn't say it, and the editor's rule reads non-primary spouses as lovers.

identity.detail: Alkmene is the correct match for Alcmena; Alcmene is just a spelling variant.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, is said in the Thesprotian tradition (Eugammon's Telegony) to have married Odysseus after his wanderings, which makes her a marriage in that tradition. But the editor's rule is that only the Penelope marriage counts, so any other spouse link is read as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Odysseus, king of Ithaca. The other names Laertes' son, Laertes' seed and Ulysses all refer to him.
Deianeira, daughter of Oeneus and Althaea, wife of Heracles, matches Deianira. Macaria is traditionally her daughter by Heracles (Pausanias), so that link stands.
Leaena matches the hetaera and mistress of Aristogiton in Pausanias; the lover link is correct as stated in the book.

links.reason: Mausolus' wife was Artemisia II of Caria, his sister; Artemisia I (Xerxes' ally at Salamis, Herodotus 7.99) was daughter of Lygdamis, a generation earlier, so the link belongs to the namesake.

identity.detail: Pausanias mentions Artemisia of Halicarnassus, who fought at Salamis, so the match with Artemisia I is plausible; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Pausanias' Spartan hero-chapel concerns a different Ægeus, son of Œolycus (a Theban/Spartan Aegeid line), not the Athenian king, son of Pandion.
Æthra lay with Ægeus (and Poseidon) in one night at Troezen; she was not his wife, only a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian king, but the Spartan hero Ægeus, son of Œolycus, is a different person who is merged under this name.
Athena matches the Wikidata goddess; Athene, Pallas Athene and Tritogeneia are all epithets or names of the same goddess. Metis as mother is Hesiod's own account in Theogony 886-900, 924.

links.reason: The Daughters of Pelias (the Peliades) are a group, not one person. They should be individual links to Alcestis, Asteropea, Antinoe and others, not a single group node.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Pelias is the king of Iolcus, son of Poseidon and Tyro, so the match is correct.
The Wikidata match is Adonis, the beloved of Aphrodite, and there are no other names to check.
Wikidata match is Hector, the Trojan prince, son of Priam and Hecuba and husband of Andromache. No other names are attached to him.
Themistocles the Athenian general, son of Neocles, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed.
Death here is Thanatos, the personification who is Sleep's brother in the Iliad (Book 14). The Wikidata match is a generic personification of death, which is acceptable for this being.

links.reason: Pausanias's Acusilaus is the Rhodian boxer, son of Diagoras of Rhodes, not the Argive logographer, son of Cabas or Scabras.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Acusilaus of Argos, the logographer. Pausanias means the Rhodian Olympic victor, son of Diagoras and brother of Damagetus, so this is a different person.
Wikidata's Osiris is the Egyptian god, the same being; Isis as his wife is correct.
The Wikidata match is Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Bacchus (Dionysus) by Jove (Zeus). Nothing else is wrong.

links.reason: This is a different Stheneboea, the Arcadian daughter of Aphidas and sister of Aleus, who also married Proetus in the book's Arcadian genealogy. The Lycian queen Stheneboea (Antia) is the daughter of Iobates or Amphianax, so the two are conflated under one name.

identity.detail: The Arcadian Stheneboea, daughter of Aphidas and sister of Aleus, has been merged with the Lycian Stheneboea (Antia), daughter of Iobates. Apollodorus names both as wives of Proetus, but they are separate figures in his text. The Wikidata match is right for the Lycian one. The Aphidas link belongs to the other being.

Wikidata match is Lampetia, daughter of Helios, who herds the cattle on Thrinacia. Her mother Neaera is attested in Homer's Odyssey, and the Argonautica names only Helios as her parent. Wikidata also lists Klymene as mother, which is a tradition variant, not a confusion of beings.
Alexanor, son of Machaon and grandson of Asclepius, matches the book; Pausanias names Sphyrus and Polemocrates as his brothers, which fits.
Wikidata match is Eriphyle, wife of Amphiaraus; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Cadmus's sister Electra is a different Electra (Pausanias), a daughter of Atlas or Agenor's line; Aeschylus' Electra is Agamemnon's daughter and has no brother Cadmus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Agamemnon's daughter Electra; the Cadmus sibling link comes from a different Electra.
Wikidata's Learchus is the son of Athamas and Ino, the same being Ovid describes in Metamorphoses. No other names are attached.
Phaethon, son of Helios and Clymene, is the right match. In the Aeneid he appears as the youth whose fall the Heliades mourn, and no other name is attached to him.

links.reason: Hercyna is a nymph of Lebadea; Pausanias (9.39.2-4) calls her a girl who played with Core, not a daughter of Trophonius, so the link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right being, the hero of Lebadea.

links.reason: Anubis is an Egyptian god (child of Osiris/Nephthys or Set); no Greek source makes Typhon his father, only a late Wikidata association with Set-Typhon.

Hesiod Theogony 304-325 has Echidna bear Typhon's children as his mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse; the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers, but this is a standard pairing, so keep as spouse.

identity.detail: Typhœus is Typhon; the Wikidata match is correct.

Wikidata's Protesilaus is the Thessalian hero, son of Iphiclus, and husband of Polydora (daughter of Meleager), as the Cypria fragment in this book says. The two spouse links are the same marriage listed twice, so there is no conflict.
Wikidata's Aegyptus is the king of Egypt, brother of Danaus and son of Belus, so the match is right.
Thoas, king of Lemnos, son of Dionysus and Ariadne, father of Hypsipyle and Sicinus; the Wikidata match is correct.
Celæno in the Aeneid is the Harpy, daughter of Thaumas and Electra (an Oceanid), which matches the Wikidata parents. The Wikipedia description is generic, but the match is the Harpy Celaeno.

links.reason: Sciron is the son-in-law of Pylas in tradition (Pylas gave his daughter to Pandion; Sciron is separate). Plutarch and Pausanias make Sciron a Megarian, but Pylas as father of Sciron is not supported; Pausanias does not state this.

identity.detail: Pylas/Pylon of Megara matches; Cleson is Pausanias's spelling for Cteson, a variant, not a different person.
Wikidata's Antenor is the Trojan counselor, husband of Theano, and he matches this being. No other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Tantalus, the king punished in Tartarus; no other names are listed, so nothing to split.
Argalus is the eldest son of Amyclas who succeeded him as king of Sparta (Pausanias 3.2.2); the Wikidata match is the same person.

Wikidata's Procne, daughter of Pandion I and wife of Tereus, is the Progne of Ovid's Metamorphoses. The flagged parent difference is only the mother Zeuxippe, whom Ovid does not name. That is not an error.
Xanthus is the Trojan river god, also called Scamander; the Wikidata match is the same being.
Wikidata match is Polites, son of Priam and Hecuba, the swift Trojan watchman in the Iliad; no other names are involved.
Taygete the Pleiad, daughter of Atlas and Pleione, mother of Lacedaemon by Zeus; the Wikidata match is correct.

Aristaios is Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, husband of Autonoe, father of Actaeon. Agreus and Nomios are his cult epithets in Pindar, so they are the same being. Theoi's extra listings (Ouranos and Gaia, and Karystos) are variant traditions, not a different person.
Wikidata match is Telephus, son of Heracles and Auge. Wikidata's second father, Corythus, is a variant tradition, not a different being.
Wikidata match is Machaon, son of Asclepius; the alias 'Aglaia's son' is a matronymic for him (Aglaia as mother in Quintus Smyrnaeus), not another being.
Wikidata's Ceto is the sea goddess, daughter of Pontus and Gaia and wife of Phorcys; no other names are involved.
Gorgythion is Priam's son by Castianeira of Aisyme (Iliad 8.302-308); the Wikidata match is correct.
Pamphylus, son of Aegimius and brother of Dymas, is the Dorian hero in Pausanias (2.28.7: Orsobia, daughter of Deiphontes, was later married to Pamphylus). The Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Calydonian hero Meleager; no other names need splitting.
Menestratus is the Thespian who died fighting the dragon to save his lover Cleostratus (Pausanias 9.26); the Wikidata match is the same man.

Wikidata's Arne is Melanippe/Arne, daughter of Aeolus and mother by Poseidon of Aeolus and Boeotus. In Pausanias she is the Boeotian Arne, so the match is right. The link to Hellen (the son called Aeolus) is a known tradition, so I keep it.

links.reason: Cercopes line names Theia and Ocean as parents, but Ocean's wife is Tethys; per editor's rule, other spouse links read as lovers.
A chorus is a group, not a person; the individual Oceanids are already listed.

identity.detail: Oceanus match is correct.
Labotas (Leobotes), Agiad king of Sparta, son of Echestratus and father of Doryssus, matches Wikidata; no mismatched names.
Wikidata Plouto is the Oceanid in Hesiod Theogony 355 and Homeric Hymn 2; this matches the book.
Wikidata's Iasion is this same being, the lover of Demeter (Ceres) and son of Zeus and Electra. He has no other names to question.
Iodama in Pausanias (9.34.2) is the priestess of Athena Itonia, daughter of Itonus, who was turned to stone by seeing Athena's Gorgon-head. She matches Iodame, daughter of Itonus; nothing to fix.

Wikidata's Picus is the Latin king, son of Saturn, as in Aeneid 7.48. Its father Mars differs from the book, but the Aeneid names Saturn and that link is kept. Canens as wife of Picus comes from Ovid and is fine.
Wikidata match is the Muse Polyhymnia, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne in Hesiod's Theogony. No other names are attached.
Hephaestus matches the Greek god (Roman Vulcan). Both spouse links stand: Aphrodite is his wife per the editor's decision, and Charis is his wife in Homer's Iliad 18.
Almus/Olmus is Sisyphus' son, the Corinthian prince who founded Halmones near Orchomenus, matching the Wikidata entry. Olmus is only a spelling variant of the same name.

links.reason: Hesiod's Gaia/Uranus descent is not Ovid's. Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night (Nyx), so this link follows a different tradition from the book.
Hesiod's Uranus descent is not Ovid's. Metamorphoses 4.453 calls the Furies daughters of Night (Nyx), so this link follows a different tradition from the book.

identity.detail: Tisiphone is the right match for this Fury. Erinnys is a generic name for the Furies, but Ovid uses it for Tisiphone in Metamorphoses 4.
Wikidata match is the hound Cerberus; Typhon and Echidna are his standard parents, so no change is needed.

Wikidata's Eris is the goddess of strife. Parentage differs by tradition: Hesiod gives Nyx alone, Wikidata gives Erebos and Nyx, and Iliad 4.441 and Quintus Smyrnaeus 10.51 give Zeus and Hera. Theoi sources the Zeus and Hera tradition, so it is not unsupported, and Quintus is the poet of this book, so it is right for it. Ares as brother matches the Iliad.

links.reason: In the Aeneid (2.340) Dymas is a Trojan warrior who fights beside Aeneas and is killed in the night battle; he is not the Phrygian king Dymas, Hecuba's father in some traditions.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Phrygian king Dymas, father of Hecuba. The Aeneid's Dymas is a different man, a Trojan fighter who dies in the sack of Troy.
Autesion, Theban king, son of Tisamenus (son of Thersander), father of Theras per Pausanias; Wikidata match is correct and the parent link agrees with Wikidata.

links.reason: Pausanias's Aethra wife of Phalanthus is a Spartan/Tarentine Aethra, daughter of Oebalus? a different woman from Pittheus's daughter, the mother of Theseus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Aethra daughter of Pittheus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Apollodorus (3.12.3) makes Tithonus a son of Laomedon; the Cephalus link confuses him with Cephalus's son Phaethon, whom Eos also carried off, and rests on a Wikidata conflation.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Tithonus, the Trojan prince and lover of Eos.
Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, mother of Arcas by Zeus, matches the Wikidata entry. Hesiod follows the Lycaon tradition, so the Ceteus and Nycteus variants do not apply here.
Oncius (Oncus), son of Apollo and ruler at Onceum near Thelpusa in Arcadia, matches the Wikidata entry; no names belong to anyone else.
The Wikidata match is the Danaid Amymone, daughter of Danaus; she is the mother of Nauplius by Poseidon. No other names are involved.
Wikidata Hyacinth is the Spartan youth loved by Apollo; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Dexamenus of Olenus is father of a different Eurypylus (Heracles' kin, Pausanias 7.19); the Iliad's Thessalian Eurypylus is son of Euaemon (Iliad 2.736), so the two Eurypyluses are confused.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Thessalian Eurypylus son of Euaemon, matching the Iliad.
Wikidata's Leto is the Titaness, mother of Apollo and Artemis; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: In Aeneid, Latinus is son of Faunus (and Marica), and Faunus is the Roman counterpart, not Pan himself; the link confuses Pan with Faunus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Pan; no other names listed.
Wikidata match is Hestia, the goddess of the hearth, daughter of Cronus and Rhea. No other names are attached.
Aeolus son of Hellen, as in Apollodorus 1.7.3; the Wikidata match fits. The Wikidata spouse Iphis is likely a different figure, but no spouse link is in this book's tree to correct.

Proteus, the Old Man of the Sea (the Carpathian prophet of Ovid), matches Wikidata's Proteus. Poseidon (Neptune) as his father is confirmed by Theoi (Apollodorus, Lycophron), so the parents flag is not a real conflict.

Aglaea is the Grace Aglaia, the same being. Hesiod (Theogony) gives her as a daughter of Zeus and Eurynome. The Theoi listing also gives Eunomia as a mother in another tradition, but that is a variant and not a fault. The Hephaestus marriage in Wikidata is not in this tree.
Wikidata match is Perseus, the hero son of Zeus and Danae; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Pindar's 'Hermes' daughter Fame' (Olympian 8) is a poetic personification of Angelia, the messenger. It is a figure of speech and not a mythic child.
Hesiod has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter, mother of Pan, with no marriage. Under the editor's rule, any non-listed spouse link is a lover.

identity.detail: Hermes matches the Olympian god. Mercury is his Roman equivalent.

The Wikidata match is the generic concept of death and its Grim Reaper personification. Pausanias' Death is Thanatos, the Greek son of Night and brother of Sleep, so the match should be changed to Thanatos.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses 14, Hersilia is the wife of Romulus (Quirinus), and the book never calls her Tatius's daughter; the tradition making her his daughter is a rare one. Plutarch and Livy more often tie her to the Sabine women or to Hostus Hostilius, so the link is not supported by this book.

identity.detail: Tatius is Titus Tatius, the Sabine king, so the match is right.
Eros and Cupid are the same figure, so the match and the alias are fine.
Wikidata's Philoctetes is the right hero. Poias is a spelling variant of Poeas, so it is a duplicate node, not a different person.

links.reason: Telegonus marrying Penelope is a late sequel tradition (Telegony; Hesiod's Catalogue has Circe's sons), not Pausanias' account, but it is a real marriage after Odysseus' death, not a lover link; keep as a marriage only from hesiod, not here.</br>

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Odysseus' wife Penelope, daughter of Icarius.
Wikidata match is Polyxena, daughter of Priam and Hecuba; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Calliope the Muse, mother of Orpheus; no other names are mixed in.
Archegetes is a cult title, and Aulonian, Cotylean and Gortynian are local epithets of Asclepius, not other persons. The Wikidata match is correct.
Acastus, son of Pelias and Anaxibia (or Philomache), who sailed with the Argonauts and hunted the Calydonian Boar, matches the Wikidata entry. The tree's only link, Pelias as his father, is correct.
Dropion is the Paeonian king; Pausanias calls his father Deon, while Wikidata gives Leon, probably a variant spelling of the same name. The book's sentence supports the link, so keep it.

links.reason: Apollodorus (1.9.13) makes Bias the husband of Pero, and Talaus is the son of Bias and Pero in tradition; but the link is listed as parent_of Talaus, which is actually correct, so this is not wrong.

identity.detail: Pero, daughter of Neleus and Chloris, wife of Bias, is the right match.

links.reason: Morn is Pindar's word for Dawn (Eos), a common noun for the goddess, not a separate person; the passage means Eos, so this is a duplicate of Eos as mother, not a distinct parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Memnon, king of Aethiopia, son of Tithonus and Eos, is the right being.

links.reason: Callisto is the Arcadian nymph who became the Bear and mother of Arcas; she is not Faunus's mother. Wikidata and tradition (Virgil) give Faunus as son of Picus and Canens, and the Metamorphoses never makes Callisto his mother.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Roman god Faunus, so the identity is correct and there are no other names to split off.
Eileithyia is the right match; Eulinus is an epithet of Ilithyia that Pausanias reports, not a separate person.

links.reason: Nessus the centaur is the son of Ixion and the cloud Nephele, the Ixion figure, not the Nephele who bore Phrixus and Helle (Athamas's wife).
Oceanus as father is attached to the Athamas Nephele by Wikidata, but Theoi lists no such parentage and the Ixion cloud was shaped by Zeus; the link is unsupported and mixes the two figures.

identity.detail: Wikidata/Wikipedia merge two figures: the cloud Nephele shaped by Zeus for Ixion (mother of Centaurs/Nessus) and Athamas's wife, mother of Phrixus and Helle. Keep Phrixus and Helle with the Athamas Nephele; Nessus belongs to the Ixion cloud.

links.reason: Metanira's son Demophon is the Eleusinian child nursed by Demeter; Hesiod's Demophon is the son of Theseus, so the link belongs to a namesake.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Demophon, king of Elaeus in Thrace, which is not clearly the son of Theseus in this book. The Eleusinian Demophon, son of Metanira, is a third being. The names should be kept apart.

links.reason: Pausanias' Polydorus son of Alcamenes is the Spartan king, not the Theban son of Cadmus.
Eurycrates son of Polydorus belongs to the Spartan king Polydorus, not the Theban.

identity.detail: The tree joins two men named Polydorus: the Theban son of Cadmus (father of Labdacus) and the Spartan king son of Alcamenes (father of Eurycrates). The Wikidata match is the Theban one, so the Spartan links need a separate node.

links.reason: Hesiod's Demodoce, daughter of an Agenor, belongs to a different Agenor (a Calydonian or Argive figure), not the son of Poseidon and Libya.
Pausanias's Crotopus is the son of Agenor of Argos, a descendant of Phoroneus, not the Phoenician king.
Iphidamas is the son of the Trojan Antenor, a different figure whose name is close to Agenor.
Preugenes belongs to the Argive Agenor, father of Crotopus in Pausanias's Achaean line.
Echeclus, son of Agenor, is the Trojan Echeclus killed by Achilles, from a different Agenor.

identity.detail: The match is the Phoenician king Agenor, son of Poseidon and Libya.

links.reason: Calus (Talos/Perdix) is Daedalus's nephew, the son of his sister, not his sibling; the link is unsupported by Pausanias.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian craftsman Daedalus; Palamaon as father is the book's own variant and is right for this book.

Aganippe the Naiad of the Boeotian spring matches Wikidata. Termesus (Termessus) is the same river-god as Wikidata's father, and Pausanias says so in his own words, so the flag is only a spelling difference.
Ida is the Cretan nurse of the infant Zeus, daughter of Melisseus per Apollodorus, and the Wikidata match fits. Pausanias mentions Ida only in passing, so nothing contradicts the link.
Erato is the Muse, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne in Hesiod's Theogony; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Hesiod's Menoetius is the Titan, son of Iapetus and brother of Atlas, not Patroclus' father, who is Menoetius son of Actor. It also duplicates the correct Menoetius link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Patroclus, the companion of Achilles; no other names listed.

In Apollodorus this Podarces is Priam's original name, the son of Laomedon and brother of Hesione, ransomed by her and so renamed Priam. The Wikidata match is Podarces son of Iphiclus, brother of Protesilaus, of Phylace, who is a different person. The Laomedon and Hesione links are right for the Trojan Podarces, so the mismatch lies in the Wikidata match and not in the links.
Porphyrion the Giant, son of Gaia and Uranus per Apollodorus 1.34; the Wikidata match is correct. The Theoi Erebos and Nyx listing, which has no citation, likely belongs to a different Porphyrion.
Messene, daughter of Triopas and wife of Polycaon, matches Wikidata. The alias Zancle is the old name of the Sicilian city Messina, not a separate person, but it does not conflict with this identity.
Wikidata match is the pretender Andriscus (Pseudo-Philip), the same person Pausanias names.
Wikidata's Tanagra is this nymph, eponym of the Boeotian city. Graia is her other name in Pausanias, so the names are fine.

Wikidata's Aeacus is the king of Aegina, son of Zeus and Aegina. The Theoi listing of Zeus and Europa is a different tradition, perhaps a confusion with Aeacus the judge of the dead, and not a mismatch.
Wikidata match is the Boeotian king Athamas, son of Aeolus; the Minyas father is a variant tradition.

links.reason: Pausanias (6.9) makes Pantias of Chios the pupil of his father Sostratus, a sculptor of Chios, not Sostratus of Dyme, the beloved of Heracles; the sentence does not concern the Dyme figure.

identity.detail: Sostratus of Dyme (Heracles' beloved) is joined with the Chian sculptor Sostratus, father of Pantias. Acrochersites is a separate name: Pausanias gives it as the epithet of the Dyme Sostratus, so it stays with him, but the sculptor is another person.
Wikidata match is Pythagoras of Samos, the philosopher Ovid presents in Metamorphoses 15; no other names.
Dorieus, son of Diagoras of Rhodes, is the Rhodian athlete and naval commander the book describes. The Wikidata match is correct, and the book's parent link agrees with Wikidata's father.

links.reason: Pausanias makes Triptolemus a daughter-of-Cercyon's kin (Cercyon's daughter Alope's line) only in his own telling; Apollodorus never links them, and Cercyon the Eleusinian wrestler is not Apollodorus's sibling for Triptolemus, so the link is imported from another book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the same Eleusinian hero Triptolemus.
The match is Admetus, king of Pherae, and he has no other names listed. His marriage to Alcestis is well attested, so the link is right.
Tantalus the Lydian king, father of Pelops and Niobe, is the right match.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links. Glauce (Creusa) is Jason's later bride in Apollodorus, not a wife in this book, so she is read as a lover.
This is a group, not a person. The sons are already listed by name (Mermerus, Pheres, etc.), so the group node duplicates them.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason; the name 'Aeson's son' is just a patronymic for him.
Wikidata match is Amphion, son of Antiope and twin of Zethus, who married Niobe; the identity is correct. The two Niobe spouse links are genuine marriages, so there is nothing to fix.

metamorphoses/io.name: Io
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Io, Isis

links.reason: Anubis is the child of Osiris/Nephthys in Egyptian myth; this comes from the Isis match, not from Ovid's Io, whose only child is Epaphus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match joins Io with the Egyptian goddess Isis. Ovid does hint at Io's later identification with Isis, but Isis (child of Geb and Nut, wife of Osiris) is a separate being, so her family should not be merged into Io's. The Isis match should be dropped and 'Isis' removed from Io's names.
Wikidata match is the nymph Egeria, consort of Numa Pompilius; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: In the Odyssey (3.282) Phrontis is Menelaus' helmsman, son of Onetor, not the Argonautic son of Phrixus and Chalciope.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Phrontis son of Phrixus, but the Odyssey's Phrontis is Menelaus' helmsman, son of Onetor.
Minerva is the Roman counterpart of Athena; the match and the alias are the same being.

links.reason: Hesiod has no Aidos child of Prometheus; unsupported, likely a misread of Hesiod's Aidos.
Pausanias' Aetnaeus is not a son of Prometheus in the tradition; unsupported.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus; no other names to question.

links.reason: This is a group label (the children Medea killed), not a person. The sons are already named individually as Mermerus and Pheres.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Medea is the Colchian princess, daughter of Aeetes. 'Aeaean Medea' is an epithet, not a different person.
The Wikidata match is the right Ceyx, husband of Alcyone and son of Lucifer (Phosphorus).

Pirithous of the Lapiths, son of Ixion (or Zeus) and Dia, husband of Hippodamia, is the right match. Iliad 12.129 names him as the father of Polypoetes. Hippodame is a variant spelling of Hippodamia, not a different person.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 306-325) and Apollodorus make Echidna Typhon's mate and the mother of his monstrous brood; Wikidata also lists her as his spouse, so she was a mate rather than a mere lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Typhon. Typho and Typhoeus are the same being.

links.reason: Endeis, Peleus' mother (daughter of Chiron or Sciron), is not Thetis' sister. Thetis' sisters are the Nereids, daughters of Nereus and Doris.
Phocus son of Aeacus was Peleus' half-brother, whom Peleus killed. His mother was Psamathe, a different Nereid. He is not Thetis' son.

identity.detail: Thetis matches the Nereid, daughter of Nereus and Doris, wife of Peleus and mother of Achilles. The Wikidata spouse Neptune is only a rumored suitor, not a marriage; the Peleus link is right.
The Wikidata match is Acamas, son of Antenor and Theano, the Trojan leader in the Iliad. The Thracian Acamas, son of Eussorus, is a separate person, but no link here confuses the two.

links.reason: Pausanias does not name Evander as her son. Echemus and Timandra's son is Laodocus in the tradition; the Arcadian Evander is son of Hermes and a nymph (Carmenta/Themis), so this is a confusion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Spartan Timandra, daughter of Tyndareus, who married Echemus; this is the right being.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive taken as concubine by Aias (Sophocles' Ajax), not a wife; the editor's rule treats non-marriage links as lover.

identity.detail: Ajax the Great (son of Telamon, Salamis) is the right match; Eriboia is Periboea under another name.
Wikidata match is the Hesperides, the nymphs of the golden apple garden, and the character has no other names.
Wikidata's Calypso is the nymph of Ogygia; Hesiod's Oceanid Calypso is the same being under a different genealogy. No other names to split.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros but was not a marriage; the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Helen's union with Achilles is a post-death tradition on Leuke (Pausanias) and not a marriage; the editor reads it as a lover link.

links.link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus of Epirus is a historical king who claimed descent from Achilles; the mythic Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, already linked as his son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis.
Wikidata match is Assaracus, king of Dardania, son of Tros and father of Capys, as Iliad 20 states. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Hyrieus is son of Poseidon and Alcyone (Pleiad) in the usual tradition; Learchus (son of Athamas) is a confusion, not his father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Boeotian Hyrieus, father of Orion; no names to split.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children, not a person; the individual sons are the proper links.

identity.detail: Heracles is the correct match for Hercules; Alcides and Tirynthian are his epithets.

links.reason: Gaia is not Poseidon's lover in any cited source; unsupported guess.
Editor: Aegeus and Aethra are Theseus's parents only in Pausanias; for Pindar the tree keeps Poseidon only in tradition, but not confirmed here.
Editor ruled wrong everywhere.
Editor ruled wrong everywhere.
Sarpedon the Lycian is son of Zeus; Poseidon's son Sarpedon of Thrace is a different person (namesake).
The Doliones are a people, not a person; group taken for a person.
Moliones are the twin sons of Molione; the Iliad is cited, the twins' father is Actor or Poseidon, a variant.
Cteatus is son of Actor/Molione, with Poseidon only a variant paternity.
Wikidata lists Tyro as a spouse, though the myth makes her a lover.

identity.detail: Poseidon matches; the epithets are all his.
Wikidata Thaumas is the sea god, son of Pontus and Gaia, and the match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias' Thalpius son of Eurytus belongs to Eurytus son of Actor (a Molionid, Eurytus of Elis), not Eurytus of Oechalia.
Pausanias' Theraphone, wife of Eurytus, belongs to the Molionid Eurytus, not the king of Oechalia.

identity.detail: Eurytus of Oechalia, the archer whose bow Odysseus carries, is the right match. Only the Pausanias links (Thalpius and Theraphone) belong to a different Eurytus.

links.reason: Ixion's father is Phlegyas (or Antion/Leonteus/Aeton in other versions); Ares as father is an unsupported guess, and Metamorphoses gives no father for him.

Nessus is a centaur, one of the offspring of Ixion and the cloud in some versions, but Metamorphoses names no parent for him, and the tradition usually treats him as a son of Centaurus or Ixion only loosely; the link is unsupported here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lapith king Ixion; no other names involved.
Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite; no other names are given.

links.link: Urania parent_of Linus, son of Urania
links.reason: Two different Linuses are joined under one name: Hesiod's Linus son of Urania and Pausanias' Linus son of Apollo are distinct traditions; the Linus son of Apollo link should be tied to a different mother (Psamathe or Calliope in other tellings), not Urania.

links.link: Urania parent_of Linus, son of Apollo
links.reason: Pausanias gives Linus as son of Apollo by Psamathe (Argive Linus) and Urania appears as his mother only in the separate Hesiodic Linus; the two Linuses are confused.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Urania. The alias 'Mnemonian maids' is a collective term for the Muses, not Urania alone, but it is harmless as an epithet.

Opheltes is the Nemean infant, also called Archemorus; the match is correct. Apollodorus 3.6.4 names Lycurgus and Eurydice as parents, which agrees with Wikidata, so the flag does not show a real conflict.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony) makes Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule only turns spouse links into lovers for Zeus and Hera or Juno, so Themis stays a wife.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis, and she has no other names to question.
Panthus (Panthous), Trojan elder and priest of Apollo, is the same person as Wikidata's Panthous, father of Euphorbus, Polydamas and Hyperenor. In the Aeneid he appears as Othrys' son, which matches.
Wikidata match is Orestes, son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the seer Melampus, son of Amythaon; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Anchises' father is Capys, son of Assaracus, son of Tros; Dardanus is a more distant ancestor (great-great-grandfather), not his parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan Anchises, father of Aeneas by Venus; no other names to check.

links.reason: Pausanias' Diophanes, son of Diaeus, is the Achaean League's Diophanes of Megalopolis (earlier, 3rd–2nd c. BC, father of a different man), while Diaeus of Megalopolis was the last strategos in 150–146 BC. The Diaeus who fathered Diophanes is a different, earlier man of the same name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Diaeus of Megalopolis, the 2nd-century BC Achaean strategos. The Diaeus named in this passage is the father of Diophanes, the Achaean League's earlier leader, so he is a different man with the same name.

links.reason: Anius's daughters are a group, not a single person. Metamorphoses 13 has Anius say he fathered five children (a son and four daughters, the Oenotropae), so the link is plausible but cannot be a person node.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Anius, king of Delos and priest of Apollo. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Parthenopaeus was son of Atalanta with Melanion or Meleager (Apollodorus 3.9.2), or Ares; the cited Pausanias sentence about Asphodicus's tomb says nothing of Talaus. Talaus' sons were Adrastus, Parthenopaeus is sometimes given as Talaus' son in Aeschylus/Euripides? No, mainstream is Atalanta's son.

Aristomachus son of Talaus is a rare variant not stated in Hesiod's text; Aristomachus is usually son of Talaus only in Apollodorus 1.9.13 as a brother of Adrastus, so keep is arguable, but the book gives no support.

identity.detail: Talaus, king of Argos and Argonaut, son of Bias and Pero, is the right being.

Eudorus is the Myrmidon commander, son of Polymele and Hermes (Mercury) in Iliad 16. The Wikidata match is correct. The link to Mercury agrees with the book and with Wikidata, so the flag is a false alarm.

links.reason: Ares as father of Ixion is a doubtful Wikidata entry among five candidates; Pindar (Pythian 2) gives no father, and the usual tradition names Phlegyas (or Antion/Peirithous's line), not Ares.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lapith king Ixion; no other names involved.
Agenor is the Trojan son of Antenor and Theano, who confronts Achilles in the Iliad. The Wikidata match is correct and he has no other names.
