links.reason: In Argonautica, Idmon is the son of Apollo and Asteria (or Cyrene per some Wikidata claims) — the book names Aristaeus as Cyrene's son, and Apollonius gives Idmon's mother as Cyrene only in some scholia; nothing in this book supports it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Thessalian huntress Cyrene, mother of Aristaeus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, wife of Autolycus's namesake? In Ovid's Metamorphoses (8.738ff) she is Erysichthon's daughter, who shapeshifts and is sold; Hyginus later gives her as Autolycus's... no ancient marriage is in Pausanias, and the book names only Neaera as wife; the link is unsupported here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Parnassian thief Autolycus, son of Hermes and Chione; Pausanias also mentions a Daedalion-father variant, which is the book's own report.

links.reason: Aratus the poet of Sicyon was son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor: right only in Pausanias), not a child of Asclepius; this is a namesake confusion.

identity.detail: Asclepius is the right match for Æsculapius, the Roman name.

links.reason: Direction reversed: Apollodorus (and Hesiod's tradition) makes Pandora Pyrrha's mother, not her daughter; Pandora is the first woman and Pyrrha is her daughter.
Apollodorus calls Amphictyon an autochthonous king of Attica, not a son of Deucalion and Pyrrha; only Hellen, Protogeneia and others are their children.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion.
Wikidata match is Hypsipyle, queen of Lemnos, daughter of Thoas; no other names listed.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, son of Echion and Agave, matches Wikidata; no other names to dispute.

Wikidata's Coeus is the Titan son of Uranus and Gaia, husband of Phoebe, father of Leto and Asteria. The parent flag is only because Theoi lists variant parentages (Hyginus, Virgil). Hesiod's Theogony gives Heaven and Earth, so the links are right.
Wikidata match is Niobe, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, the Theban queen of Iliad 24; no other names involved.
The Wikidata match is the same Thasus; no other names are listed.
Merope, daughter of Cypselus and wife of Cresphontes, matches Wikidata. Her parentage agrees with the book and Wikidata's father, Cypselus.

links.reason: The Phaethon son of Eos is the one by Cephalus, a tradition the editor limits to Pausanias. In Hesiod, Phaethon is Eos's son by Tithonus, but Apollodorus and others use the name for Helios's son. It does not suit the Fall of Troy, where Eos's son is Memnon.

identity.detail: Eos matches the goddess of dawn. Aurora is her Roman name, so it is the same being.
The Wikidata match is Euphemus the Argonaut, son of Poseidon, which fits Pausanias' description of him as Jason's companion and Poseidon's son.

links.reason: Harmonia was wife of Cadmus; the editor's rule reads any non-marriage 'spouse' link as a lover. Ares was her father or lover per tradition, not husband; Argonautica names her as his child/lover.
Panic (Phobos/Deimos-like personification) is not a person; Theoi lists Phobos and Deimos as sons, but 'Panic' as a child is a loose personification, not a being; keep only if tied to Phobos.
Hermes is son of Zeus and Maia, so a half-brother at most; Statius' mention is not a sibling statement from Hera.

identity.detail: Wikidata Ares is the war god; Mars and War-god are the same being in Roman equation.
Pluto is Hades, the god of the underworld, son of Cronus and Rhea, husband of Persephone. The Wikidata match is correct, and the two names belong to the same being.
Wikidata's Nereids is the group of fifty sea-nymph daughters of Nereus and Doris, which matches the Iliad's chorus of Nereids (18.37ff). Both parent links are correct.
Wikidata's Pentheus is the Theban king, son of Echion and Agave, and no other name is attached to him.

links.reason: Euryphaessa is Hyperion's wife in the Homeric Hymn. Hesiod does not make her his sister. The sibling link confuses the two names (Theia and Euryphaessa).

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Hyperion. In the Odyssey the name Hyperion is used for the sun-god, which is a known epithet or patronymic usage for Helios and not a different person.
Wikidata match is the goddess Eunomia, one of the Horai; the book's passage (Pindar, Olympian 9) names Themis as her mother, which is consistent.
Phoebe the Titan, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of Coeus, is the right match; no other names to split.
Wikidata match is Astyanax, son of Hector and Andromache; the parent links are correct.

links.reason: Midas is a mortal Phrygian king, not a child of Rhea; in Ovid's Metamorphoses Rhea/Cybele is only his patron deity, so the link confuses Midas with her divine children.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match Rhea is the Titan, mother of Zeus, Poseidon and Hades, so it is correct.
Wikidata's Lysandra, daughter of Ptolemy I Soter and Eurydice, wife of Agathocles son of Lysimachus, matches the book's Lysandra.

links.link: Sisyphus parent_of Glaucus, son of Sisyphus
links.reason: This is a duplicate node for Glaucus, son of Sisyphus. In Apollodorus 2.3.1 he is the same Glaucus already linked as Sisyphus's son, so the duplicate should be removed.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Sisyphus of Corinth, and no other names are listed.
Podalirius, son of Asclepius and brother of Machaon, is the Iliad's physician-king of Tricca; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are listed.

links.reason: Polypemon is the father of Procrustes (Damastes), not Sinis; the link confuses the two bandits. Sinis's father is Poseidon or Polypemon's son Procrustes per Wikidata/Plutarch variants, not Polypemon.

identity.detail: Pityocamptes ('pine-bender') is Sinis's epithet; the Wikidata match is right.
Aeëtes, king of Colchis, son of Helios (Sun) and Perse, is the right match; Æetes is just a spelling variant.

Wikidata match is Orpheus the Thracian bard; no other names listed. The two Eurydice spouse links are duplicates of one true marriage, and Apollodorus states it (1.3.2: 'his wife Eurydice'). Oeagrus and Calliope are right, since Apollodorus gives Oeagrus 'or, nominally, Apollo' as father.
Phoenix son of Agenor, eponym of Phoenicia, is the right match; Hesiod's Phoenix is the same being.
Heliades are the daughters of Helios who weep amber for their brother Phaethon (Apollonius Rhodius 4.598); the Wikidata match is the same group.

Moirae matches the Fates, a group personified as three sisters. Parentage varies by tradition (Night in Hesiod, Zeus and Themis, Ananke in Plato), and Theoi lists Kronos and Nyx among them, so both links stand.
Corinthus, eponym of Corinth, matches Corinthos. The Zeus parentage is the local Corinthian tradition; Marathon is another tradition. No fix needed.
Wikidata's Polyxena is the daughter of Priam and Hecuba sacrificed at Achilles' tomb, which is the Polyxena in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

Electra the Oceanid, wife of Thaumas, mother of Iris and the Harpies, matches Wikidata. The Pleiad Electra, mother of Dardanus by Zeus, is a different being, but the book's Dardanus link may come from a Hesiod fragment. The two are not clearly joined under this name, so no split is needed.
Wikidata match is Atreus, son of Pelops and king of Mycenae.
Nile is the river god Nilus, son of Oceanus and Tethys (Hesiod Theogony 337); the match is correct.
Folly is Atë, daughter of Zeus (Iliad 19.91-94) and, in Hesiod, of Eris (Theogony 230); the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias quotes Chœrilus saying Cercyon's mother was a daughter of Amphictyon (Alope), and Cercyon's father was Poseidon; Amphictyon is Cercyon's grandfather, not parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Amphictyon son of Deucalion; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Hades, god of the underworld; no other names listed.
Aglaea is the youngest of the Charites in Hesiod's Theogony 907-911, where she is also Hephaestus' wife. The Wikidata match is correct.
Pausanias' Cassandra daughter of Priam, called Alexandra at Leuctra, is the Trojan prophetess; the Wikidata match is correct.
Agenor, the Trojan son of Antenor and Theano, is the right match. Homer's Iliad names him as such, and he is not the Phoenician king Agenor.

links.reason: The cited sentence is about Asphodicus' tomb and says nothing of Talaus; Talaus was father of Adrastus, and Parthenopaeus is son of Atalanta by Melanion (or Meleager/Ares).

identity.detail: Parthenopeus is the same Arcadian Seven-against-Thebes hero; no other names to question.

links.reason: In Hesiod's Theogony Earth (Gaia) is born from Chaos, before Night and Day; Day cannot be her parent, and Theoi's listing does not support it.

identity.detail: Hemera is the correct match for Day, the daughter of Erebus and Night.
Wikidata match is Semele, also called Thyone, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus. The alias Thyone is a genuine alternate name for her, so no split is needed.

links.reason: Phaethon's mother is the Oceanid Clymene wife of Merops in Ovid/Argonautica tradition, not Hesiod's Clymene wife of Iapetus; in Hesiod's book this is a different being.
The Heliades are daughters of Clymene wife of Merops (Ovid), a different Clymene from Iapetus' wife.
Apollodorus' Clymene, daughter of Minyas, is mother of Atalanta by Iasus; unrelated to the Oceanid.
This is Clymene daughter of Minyas (Scholiast on Od. xi.326), not the Oceanid; belongs with Iphiclus and Atalanta.

links.link: Clymene parent_of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus
links.reason: Iphiclus' mother is Clymene daughter of Minyas, not the Oceanid wife of Iapetus.

identity.detail: Several Clymenes are merged: the Oceanid wife of Iapetus (Hesiod), the Oceanid wife of Merops (mother of Phaethon and Heliades), and Clymene daughter of Minyas (wife of Phylacus, mother of Iphiclus and Atalanta). Wikidata match to the Iapetus' wife is fine.

links.reason: Pindar's Deinis and his father Meges are Aeginetan race winners (Nemean 7), not the Epeian Meges son of Phyleus at Troy.

identity.detail: In Pindar the Meges is a different man, the father of Deinis and an Aeginetan athletic figure. The Wikidata match is the Trojan War commander Meges Phyleides, so it is a different person.
Amyntor son of Ormenus, king of Eleon/Ormenium and father of Phoenix, is the right match.
Wikidata's Xuthus, son of Hellen and husband of Creusa, matches the Xuthus Pausanias describes. He has no other names.
Athena is the right match; the other names are cult epithets of the same goddess.
Wikidata match is the right Adonis.
Laestrygon, son of Poseidon, is the eponymous ancestor of the Laestrygonians. The Wikidata match is the same being.
Hippolytus, son of Theseus and an Amazon, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

links.reason: Metamorphoses names only Venus as Cupid's parent ("son of Venus", "Cupid, my son"); Mars as father comes only from Wikidata's variant tradition, which Ovid does not tell.

identity.detail: Wikidata Cupid is the right being. The Wikidata parents Diana and Mercury are not in Ovid, but they are not links in this tree.
Oxyartes is the Bactrian nobleman, father of Roxana, wife of Alexander the Great. The Wikidata match is correct.
The match is the right Pelops, son of Tantalus and king of Pisa.

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, not a person. Their eponym Dolion is the son of Poseidon in the tradition.
Podaleirius is the son of Asclepius in the Iliad, not of Poseidon.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Roman Neptune, which fits the Poseidon alias. Venilia and Thetis appear in Wikidata as spouses, but they are not the standard Greek tradition for Poseidon.
Hersilia is the Sabine woman, wife of Romulus, who became the goddess Hora (Ora) in Ovid's Metamorphoses. The Wikidata match fits, and the name Ora is her divine name, not a different person.

links.reason: Rhea is the mother of Zeus, Hera and their siblings, not of Enyalios; Wikidata gives Enyo as mother, and Pindar names no parent for him.
Enyalios is early on identified with Ares as an epithet or aspect (Iliad), so listing Ares as his father makes the god his own father; Wikidata's father link is a confusion of identity.

identity.detail: Enyalios is a war god identified with Ares, which is the same being as the Wikidata match Enyalius. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Aeneas's wife Creusa was a Trojan, daughter of Priam; Pausanias' Creusa is the Athenian daughter of Erechtheus, whose husband was Xuthus. The Pausanias passage names Clymene, Aristomache and others, not Aeneas as her husband. The Aeneas link belongs to the Trojan Creusa.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, which fits Pausanias. Only the Aeneas link comes from the Trojan namesake.
Wikidata match is the Spartan king Tyndareus; no other names to question.
Aegipan matches the goat-footed being, a son of Zeus in Apollodorus (he helped Zeus against Typhon). Theoi's Hermes parentage is a variant, but the Zeus link is sound.
Wikidata's Lynceus the Messenian son of Aphareus and Arene, the Argonaut, matches Pausanias' Lynceus, brother of Idas.

Wikidata's Byblis, daughter of Miletus and Cyane, is the same being as the book's Byblis. Ovid (Metamorphoses 9.446) names Cyane as mother, and the other mothers in Theoi are variants. Wikidata also lists Asterius as a father, but that is not a problem for this book.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Ulysses after his return (Eugammon's Telegony tradition); this was not a lasting marriage, and the editor reads any spouse other than Penelope as a lover.

identity.detail: Ulysses is the Latin name of Odysseus, so the Wikidata match is correct.
Nausithous is the Phaeacian king, son of Poseidon (Neptune) and Periboea, father of Alcinous and Rhexenor; the Wikidata match is correct.
Cephisus is the river god, son of Oceanus and Tethys, father of Narcissus by Liriope (Ovid, Metamorphoses) and of Eteoclus in Hesiod's account. All links fit.
Iasion, son of Zeus and Electra and brother of Dardanus, is the right match. Eetion is a genuine alternative name for him.
Wikidata's Iolaos is the Theban hero, nephew and charioteer of Heracles; the parent link to Iphicles agrees with Wikidata and with Pindar, so nothing needs changing.

links.reason: In Pausanias the river Alpheus loves Artemis but is refused and she escapes; a pursuer, not her lover, and the Argonautica tells no such story.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus and Leto. The alias 'Leto's daughter' is a patronymic epithet for her, not another being. The Demeter parentage in Aeschylus is a rare variant and is not the Argonautica's tradition.
Wikidata's Ardalus is the Troezenian son of Hephaestus in Pausanias, who founded the Muses' temple and discovered the flute. No other names are attached.

links.reason: Pausanias' Pythagoras, father of the Elean wrestler Caprus, is a different man, a Samian athlete's namesake. Pausanias also treats Pythagoras the Wise separately, as son of Mnesarchus. The philosopher is not Caprus' father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the philosopher Pythagoras of Samos, which suits the Mnesarchus passage. The Caprus passage refers to another man of the same name, which is handled in the link fix.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Pierides are daughters of a Macedonian Pierus and Evippe, who is a different man from Hesiod's Pierus, father of Oeager, so the link belongs to the other Pierus.
Evippe is the wife of the Pierus of Metamorphoses; in this book Pierus's partner is the nymph Methone.

identity.detail: The match is fine. Note that the Pierus of Ovid, father of the Pierides, is probably a separate figure from this Pierus.
Wikidata's Euphrosyne is the Charis (Grace), the same being Pausanias names; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Odyssey 7.56ff makes Alcinous the son of Nausithous, himself son of Poseidon and Periboea. Corcyra's son by Poseidon is Phaeax, so Alcinous is at most a descendant.

identity.detail: The match is the naiad Corcyra, daughter of Asopus, which is correct.

Wikidata's Aeacus is the king of Aegina, father of Peleus, Telamon and Phocus. The Theoi listing of Zeus and Europa is a different being (a Europa-born figure such as Minos or Rhadamanthys), not a conflict for Aeacus.
Wikidata's Damasichthon is the Theban king, son of Opheltes. Pausanias' Damasichthon is the Ionian son of Codrus, brother of Promethus, so the match is a namesake and should be unlinked.

links.reason: Oenone was a nymph he lived with before Helen (Apollodorus), not a formal marriage; editor's rule reads non-marriages as lovers. Hesiod does not mention her.

identity.detail: Wikidata Paris is the Trojan prince Alexandrus; the names are the same person.
Pyrrhus is the same being as Neoptolemus, son of Achilles and Deidamia, so the Wikidata match is correct and the alternate name is not someone else.

links.reason: Arete was Alcinous's niece and wife (daughter of his brother Rhexenor), not his sibling; the spouse link already covers the relationship.
Alcetus and Troilus are not children of the Phaeacian Alcinous in Odyssey or Apollodorus; the Pausanias attribution likely confuses another person of that name.
Troilus is a son of Priam or Apollo; the link confuses another figure with Alcinous.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Phaeacian king Alcinous, son of Nausithous; no other names to split.
The Wikidata match is the Athenian statesman Pericles, son of Xanthippus, which fits Pausanias's text. No other names are listed.
The Wikidata match is the poet Homer, which is right.

Wikidata's Laomedon is the Trojan king, son of Ilus and father of Priam, which matches Pausanias. The flagged parent difference is only because Pausanias names no parents, and Ilus as father is the standard tradition (Iliad).
Egyptus is Aegyptus, son of Belus and brother of Danaus; the match is correct. In Apollodorus, Egyptus's son Lynceus (husband of Hypermnestra) is stated, so the outside link is fine.
Agathocles is the son of Lysimachus, the Thracian king, and the Wikidata match fits. Pausanias also names him as husband of Lysandra, and no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Tydeus is the Aetolian hero, son of Oeneus and father of Diomedes; the name 'Oeneus' son' is just his patronymic.
Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy; no other names listed.

links.reason: Aeneas' wife Creusa, daughter of Priam, is a different person from the Athenian Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, who married Xuthus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian princess, daughter of Erechtheus and Praxithea, which is right for this book.
Wikidata's Neis is the eponym of the Neitian Gate at Thebes. Pausanias names Neis as a son of Zethus, which is a variant of the tradition that makes Neis a daughter, but it is still the same being.
Ilus, son of Tros and founder of Ilion, is the right being. In Ovid, Ilus is father of Laomedon (Met. 11.756), which matches the tree.
Wikidata match is Deiphobus, son of Priam and Hecuba. The book's sentence about Priam's strong son fits him. Nothing to correct.

links.reason: Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.948) makes Cyzicus son of Aeneus and Aenete; Apollo as father is an unsupported Wikidata addition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Dolionian king Cyzicus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Doris is Nereus' wife and the mother of the Nereids (Hesiod, Theogony), not his daughter; Doris spouse_of Nereus is the correct link.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Nereus is the sea-god of the Iliad.

Crocon, husband of Saesara, daughter of Celeus, matches Wikidata. Pausanias (1.38.0) says the Athenians report he married Saesara. Wikidata also makes Triptolemus his father, and Pausanias 1.38 supports that Crocon was a descendant of Triptolemus' line, so the link stands.

links.reason: Hesiod's Selene is the moon goddess, daughter of Hyperion; the editor ruled Zeus is not her parent, and she is not his lover.
Pandia is the daughter of Zeus and Selene only in the Homeric Hymn; the editor rejected the Selene link, so this one is unsupported.
Pallas, the Titan or giant, is confused with Athena Pallas; Athena is already listed as Minerva.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus at Zeus's order; she was not his lover.
Hermus is a river; Hesiod does not make Zeus his father.
Hesiod's Eetion is Iasion, who is already listed separately.
The Graces are a group; the individual Graces are already listed.
The Muses are a group; the individual Muses are already listed.
A group, not a person.
A group, not a person.
Opportunity (Kairos) is an abstraction; Pausanias only mentions an altar, and no father is stated.
Truth is an abstraction; Zeus is not stated as her father in this book.
Macar is not a son of Zeus in the sources; Macareus is a descendant of Aeolus, not of Zeus.
The editor says that Lamia and Theodorus are the Sibyl's parents in Pausanias, so Zeus is not her parent.
The editor rules this link wrong everywhere.

identity.detail: Zeus and Jupiter are the same character here, with Roman names mixed in.

links.reason: This is the Milesian boy boxer Antipater, son of Clinopater, not the Macedonian regent.
This is Antipater son of Cassander and Thessalonice, who killed his mother, a grandson of the regent.

links.link: Antipater sibling_of Philip, son of Cassander
links.reason: The sentence is about Cassander's sons, so the Antipater here is Cassander's son, not the regent.

identity.detail: The tree merges several men named Antipater: the Macedonian regent (father of Cassander and Eurydice), the Milesian boxer son of Clinopater, and Cassander's son who killed Thessalonice. The Wikidata father Iolas fits the regent, so the Wikidata match is fine, but the other two should be separate people.
Wikidata's Physcoa is the woman of Elis in Pausanias, mother of Narcaeus by Dionysus; no other names to doubt.

Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto, king of Arcadia, matches Wikidata. Pausanias lists Azan, Apheidas, Elatus and Autolaus as his sons, and Erato as his wife (a dryad), so the extra links are consistent. No other names are given.

Wikidata match is the same Aegisthus, son of Thyestes and Pelopeia. The links to Thyestes, to Erigone (Pausanias says she was his daughter by Clytemnestra, or Aletes's mother) and to Clytemnestra as lover are all supported.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony) and Wikidata treat Echidna as Typhon's mate, and Apollodorus has Typhon beget Orthus, the Chimera and the Sphinx on her; this is a marriage, not a mere affair.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Typhon is this same being.

links.reason: Rhadamanthus is a son of Zeus and Europa (Apollodorus); Hephaestus is not his father in any source.

identity.detail: Vulcan matches Hephaestus and Mulciber, a Roman identification of the same god. The aliases are fine.
Doris the Oceanid, wife of Nereus, matches Wikidata.
Wikidata match is the winged horse Pegasus; no other names listed.
Wikidata match is Paris, son of Priam, also called Alexander; no other names are mixed in.
Wikidata match is Tydeus, the Aetolian hero, father of Diomedes; no other names to check.
Tros, king of Troy and father of Ganymede, matches Wikidata. Erichthonius as his father, and Ilus and Assaracus as his sons, agree with Iliad 20 and Apollodorus.
Mecisteus, son of Talaus and father of Euryalus, is the right match; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Idomeneus was the son of Deucalion and so grandson of Minos (Iliad, Odyssey); Pausanias is loose here.

identity.detail: x
Lavinia, daughter of Latinus and Amata, wife of Aeneas, matches Wikidata. Silvius as her son is the tradition in Aeneid 6, where Anchises says he is born to Aeneas in his old age.
Wikidata's Atlas is the Titan son of Iapetus; no other names are attached.
Wikidata match is Neoptolemus (Pyrrhus), son of Achilles and Deidamia. Hermione was his wife, so all three links are right.
Wikidata's Theronice is the Olenian princess, daughter of Dexamenus and sister of Theraephone, as in Pausanias. No other names are attached to her.
Taygete the Pleiad, daughter of Atlas, mother of Lacedaemon by Zeus; Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias' Lycus son of Pandion is the Athenian hero of the Lyceum and the Great Goddesses, not the Theban regent.
Thrasybulus, son of Lycus, is the Athenian general, whose father was an Athenian Lycus, not the Theban king.
The sentence only mentions Phidolas' sons winning a horse race; it says nothing of a son Lycus.

identity.detail: Pausanias' text joins at least two Lycuses: the Theban regent, brother of Nycteus and husband of Dirce, and the Athenian Lycus son of Pandion. The Athenian one should be separated.
Pterelaus, king of the Taphians, son of Taphius and father of Comaetho, matches Apollodorus (2.4.5-7).
Panopeus, son of Phocus and twin of Crisus, is the right match; the book's Asius passage agrees with the Wikidata parents.
Hydna of Scione is the diver daughter of Scyllis (Scyllias) in Pausanias; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias' Asterion is a different Cretan figure (Asterion/Asterius, Minos' stepfather in tradition); Minos' son is not that Asterion in this book's tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata Minos the king of Crete matches; 'Gnossian' epithets are fine.

links.reason: Themistinoe is not known as a daughter of Ceyx of Trachis; the link appears to come from Hesiod's tree and is unsupported for Pausanias.

identity.detail: Ceyx of Trachis matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.

Phaëton is the son of Helios (the Sun) and Clymene, matching Phaethon. The Sun link and the Apollo link both point to the same father in Ovid, where Apollo is the Sun. The editor has ruled Apollo right in this book.
Wikidata match is Ganymede, the Trojan cupbearer of Zeus. Tros as father is right for this book, and Zeus as lover is the accepted tradition.
Aras is the autochthon of Phliasia who founded Arantea; the Wikidata match fits, and he has no other names.

Pausanias' Aristion is a boxer from Epidaurus, son of Theophiles, whose statue was made by Polycletus. The Wikidata match is the Athenian philosopher and tyrant Aristion (d. 86 BC), a different person. The link Theophiles parent_of Aristion is right for the boxer, so it should not be attached to the tyrant.
Pausanias names Zeno the Stoic, son of Mnaseas, teacher of Persaeus; this matches Zeno of Citium.
Wikidata match is the Minotaur (Asterion); Pasiphaë as mother is confirmed by Theoi and Ovid's Metamorphoses, so no change is needed.

links.reason: In the Iliad Ares is son of Zeus and Hera, and Aphrodite is daughter of Zeus and Dione; they are half-siblings at most, and the Odyssey makes them lovers.
Panic (Phobos/Deimos group) is the child of Ares and Aphrodite only as personified Fear; 'Panic' as a person is a group or misreading, not a distinct child.

identity.detail: Venus and Aphrodite are the same goddess in this translation; the match is fine.
Wikidata match is Philoctetes, son of Poeas, the Greek archer. Poeas and Poias are the same father under different spellings, so both links are right.

Hystaspes is the father of Darius I, satrap of Parthia and Persis, and the Wikidata match fits him. Artaphernes the satrap of Sardis was a brother of Darius and a son of Hystaspes in Herodotus. Pausanias does not name him, so the link does not conflict.
Wikidata match is the Minotaur (Asterion), son of Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull; no other names to separate.
The match is the god Dionysus. Bacchus, Bromios, Iacchos and the other names are all epithets or forms of the same god.

links.reason: Pausanias (2.18.6; 3.18.13) calls Nicostratus a son of Menelaus by a slave woman, Pieris the Aetolian, not by Helen; Hesiod's Helen has only Hermione. Helen is not his mother in this book.

identity.detail: Nicostratus son of Menelaus matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Pan as son of Callisto is not in Pausanias; the editor ruled Dryops' daughter as Pan's mother right only in Hesiod, and this link comes only from Wikidata.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Callisto is the Arcadian nymph or daughter of Lycaon followed by Pausanias. Her other fathers (Ceteus, Nycteus) are variants, not a different being.
Wikidata's Abantidas, tyrant of Sicyon, is the same person; the flagged parent difference is only the spelling Pascas versus Paseas.

links.reason: Anaxiroe is a daughter of Coronus and wife of Epeus in no standard source; Pausanias links Anaxiroe to Epeius only dubiously, and the Aeneid never mentions a wife, so the link is unsupported.
Hyrmina is a place/eponym tied to Elean Epeius (king of Elis, Endymion's son), a namesake of the Trojan horse builder, not Panopeus' son.

identity.detail: Epeius son of Panopeus matches the horse builder in the Aeneid.

links.reason: Editor ruled this wrong everywhere; Aeschylus (Suppliants 305, Prometheus Bound 566) makes Argus a son of Earth (Gaia).

identity.detail: Argus Panoptes is the right match; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Pausanias (1.2.5 area) gives Cleogenes as a son of a different Silenus figure; in Apollodorus this link has no support and Theoi lists no such child for the Dionysian Silenus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Dionysian Silenus, and he has no other names listed.

links.reason: The quoted sentence only says Hercules sided with Lycus in a battle against the king of the Bebryces; it names no Mygdon and no sibling. Mygdon appears there as a fellow king of Mysia/Phrygia and is not called Amycus' brother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Amycus, king of the Bebryces, son of Poseidon; no other names to check.
Carmenta/Carmentis is the Roman prophetic goddess and nymph, mother of Evander in Aeneid 8; the match is correct.

Mycene is the daughter of Inachus and wife of Arestor, the eponym of Mycenae. Myceneus is a different being, the son of Sparton (or Phoroneus's line) and eponym of Mycenae in another tradition, so it should not be merged under this name.

links.reason: In Fall of Troy (Quintus), 'Pallas' is the goddess Athena, whom Zeus bore from his head; the Wikidata Pallas is Athena's friend, daughter of Triton, so the Zeus link comes from mixing the two.
Clytus son of Pallas in Metamorphoses is a different Pallas (the Titan or Evander's line), not the goddess Athena, who is a virgin.
Butes son of Pallas in Metamorphoses belongs to a male Pallas, not the virgin goddess Athena.

identity.detail: In Fall of Troy, Pallas is an epithet of Athena, not the friend of Athena (daughter of Triton). The match should be Athena; the children Clytus and Butes belong to a male Pallas.

Hygiea in Pausanias is Hygieia, daughter of Asclepius; the book also names Athene Hygiea as a separate cult title, which is not a different person here. The Theoi listing of Eros and Peitho as parents is a different tradition and is not in the tree.
Wikidata's Arete is Queen Arete of Scheria, wife of Alcinous, which matches this character.
Wikidata match is Procris, daughter of Erechtheus and wife of Cephalus; this is the right being.

links.reason: Etias is unattested in the Iliad; Pausanias gives this name to a different figure, so the link is not supported for Iliad Aeneas.
Thrasybulus is unattested as Aeneas's son in the Iliad or Aeneid; it is a doubtful Pausanias-only link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite; no other names to question.
Cynurus, son of Perseus and founder of Cynuria, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Odysseus in the Thesprotis epic tradition; this was a union after Troy, not a marriage. Only Penelope is his wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Odysseus is correct; Aethon, Eperitus and Noman are aliases he uses in the book (Noman is the name he gives the Cyclops).

Moerocles is the Athenian orator of Salamis, a contemporary of Demosthenes. Pausanias names him as the father of Callippus, the Athenian commander at Thermopylae against the Gauls in 279 BC. The match is sound.

links.reason: The quoted sentence only denies that Aristomenes was a son of Hercules or Zeus. Nicomedes does not appear in it, and the book names no human father in that passage. Wikidata's father link is unconfirmed in this book, so this is probably a misread sentence.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Messenian hero Aristomenes, which is correct.

links.reason: Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived; Pausanias' Erytheia as a daughter is a confusion of place with person. Theoi lists no such child for Geryon, and Hesiod and Apollodorus give him no daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the giant Geryon, son of Chrysaor and Callirhoe.
Tyndareus the Spartan king; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are attached.
Wikidata match is Anchises, father of Aeneas. The Wikidata spouse entry is not in the Iliad tree, and Venus is correctly kept as lover.
Wikidata match is Aristotimus, tyrant of Elis (272 BC), the same man Pausanias describes. The link from Damaretus is supported by the book's sentence.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; no other names are involved.
Gelanor is the Argive king, also called Pelasgus, son of Sthenelas. In Apollodorus he is the king who yields the throne to Danaus. The Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Orthus is Echidna's son (Apollodorus: begotten by Typhon on Echidna); Hesiod's line about Orthus is misread as a union.
Typhon is Echidna's mate in Hesiod and Apollodorus, and Wikidata lists him as spouse.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the monster Echidna; no other names are involved.
Archelochus, son of Antenor and Theano, is the Trojan leader of the Dardanians in the Iliad (killed by Ajax); the Wikidata match is correct.
Dardanus, son of Zeus and Electra, founder of Dardania, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Hebe matches the goddess Hebe, daughter of Zeus (Jove) and Hera (Juno), who married Heracles (Hercules); the sibling link to Ilithyia (Eileithyia) is also right.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive concubine won in war, not a wife; the editor's rule reads non-marriage 'spouse' links as lovers.

identity.detail: Ajax the Great, son of Telamon, is the right match. Eriboia and Periboea are the same mother under different names.
Europa the Phoenician princess, mother of Minos, matches.
Wikidata match is the right Tantalus, king of Lydia and father of Niobe and Pelops.
The Wikidata match is the right Peleus. The alias 'Aeacus' son' is only a patronymic for him.
Wikidata's Medusa is the Gorgon of Apollodorus, daughter of Phorcys and Ceto; no other names are attached.
Wikidata's Melampus is the Argive seer, son of Amythaon, brother of Bias; this matches the book.
Eurybia, daughter of Pontus and Gaia, wife of Crius, is the same being in Hesiod's Theogony (Wikidata match is correct).

Charillus is the Eurypontid king of Sparta, the same being as Wikidata's Charilaus. Pausanias calls him son of Polydectes, while Wikidata gives Eunomus as father. This is the same man under a different tradition: Eunomus is Polydectes' father in Pausanias's own genealogy, and other ancient sources (Plutarch's Lycurgus) make Charillus the son of Polydectes or of Eunomus. The book's link is right, so no change is needed.
Wikidata match is the same Hyacinth, the Spartan youth loved by Apollo.

links.reason: Metamorphoses treats Moon as Diana (Artemis); the editor ruled Selene is not Apollo's sibling, so this confuses Selene with Artemis.
In the Argonautica Cyzicus is son of Aeneus and Aenete, king of the Doliones, not Apollo's son.
The quoted passage calls Caphaurus the grandson of Phoebus; Amphithemis (Garamas) is son of Acacallis and Apollo, but here Caphaurus is the grandson, so the line is misread.

identity.detail: Match is Apollo; the names Far-Darter, Leto's son and Phoebus are all Apollo.

links.reason: Phialo, daughter of Alcimedon, belongs to the Arcadian Alcimedon of Pausanias (Phigalia legend, mother of Aechmagoras by Heracles), not the Myrmidon son of Laerces in the Iliad.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Myrmidon charioteer, son of Laerces; consistent with the Iliad.
Antilochus, son of Nestor, prince of Pylos, matches the Wikidata entry; the Nestor link is correct.
Trochilus is the Argive initiating priest of Pausanias, who fled to Attica and had Eubulus and Triptolemus; the Wikidata match fits.
Wikidata match is Deianira, daughter of Oeneus and wife of Heracles; no other names to check.
Wikidata match is the Titan Coeus (Koios); no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Pallas as a son of Lycaon comes from Hesiod's tradition and is not in Apollodorus's list of Lycaon's sons; however, Pallas the Arcadian is a different figure (Evander's father), so the link is unsupported here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Arcadian king Lycaon, son of Pelasgus; no confusion found.

links.reason: Hesiod's Demodoce is a daughter of a different Agenor (the Argive/Pleuron-type figure), not the Phoenician king in Ovid.
Pausanias gives Crotopus as son of the Argive Agenor, son of Triopas, not the Phoenician king.
Iphidamas, son of Antenor in Homer, is confused with Agenor; not a child of the Phoenician king.

Pausanias names Thasus as son of Agenor in some accounts (Phoenician) but the Pausanias link is unclear; the Phoenician Agenor is usually Thasus's father or grandfather, so ambiguous; treat as other Agenor.

links.link: Theopompus, father of Agenor parent_of Agenor
links.reason: This Agenor, son of Theopompus, is a different man from Pausanias, not the Phoenician king.
Preugenes is son of the Achaean Agenor in Pausanias, not the Phoenician king.
Echeclus, son of Agenor, is a Trojan-side figure from a different Agenor, not the Phoenician king.
Dido's father is Belus (Mutto/Belus of Tyre) in Virgil, not Agenor.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Phoenician king, which fits Ovid's Agenor; the other-Agenor children came in from Pausanias and Hesiod and belong to namesakes.

Bura is the eponym of Boura in Achaea, daughter of Ion and Helice. The Wikidata match is correct. Wikidata also lists Zeus as a father, which conflicts with Pausanias and the Wikipedia description. This is a data issue in Wikidata, not in the book's tree, so no link here needs a fix.
Wikidata match is the Messenian king Aphareus, son of Perieres and Gorgophone; no name problems.
Wikidata match is Machaon, son of Asclepius; no other names involved.

links.reason: The quoted passage is about Aeneas sailing from Circe's land to the Tiber and says nothing of Faunus. Ovid's Metamorphoses does mention Latinus of Alba Longa, a later king, but that is a different man from the Latinus of the Aeneid.
Ovid's Latinus Silvius is a later Alban king. He is not the Latinus who was king in Latium in the time of Aeneas, and Amata and Lavinia belong to the earlier king.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Latinus of Latium, who is Lavinia's father. The Metamorphoses also names a later Alban king, Latinus Silvius, so the two should not be merged.

links.reason: Enceladus is a Giant, born from Gaia and the blood of Ouranos (Hesiod Theogony 183-187); no source makes Tartarus his father, and Hesiod does not say so.

identity.detail: Tartarus the primordial deity matches the Wikidata entry, which covers both the place and the god. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, who sold herself to support him (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8), and is not Autolycus' wife. Her link to Autolycus is unsupported.

Autolycus' wife was Neaera in some sources but not Pausanias; Apollodorus gives Amphithea, daughter of Pereus (Apollodorus 1.9.16, 2.4.?). Neaera is a different woman, so this link comes from a confusion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Autolycus, son of Hermes and Chione, grandfather of Odysseus. No other names to split.
Moirae is the right match for the Fates, and the other name 'The Fates' is the same being.
Philonome and Phylonome are the same woman: Cycnus' second wife and the stepmother of Tenes and Hemithea.
The Wikidata match is Alkmene, mother of Herakles; Alcmene is only a spelling variant.
Acarnan, son of Alcmaeon and Callirhoe, brother of Amphoterus, matches Pausanias's account.
Hipparchus the Athenian son of Pisistratus, killed by Harmodius and Aristogiton; the Wikidata match is right.
Wikidata Talaus, king of Argos and Argonaut, son of Bias and Pero, is the right being.
Canachus of Sicyon, the sculptor, matches the Wikidata entry; the book's sentence calls Aristocles his brother.
Laodice, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, wife of Helicaon in the Iliad (3.121-124). Wikidata also lists Telephus as a spouse, but that link is not in the book's tree, so nothing needs fixing.
Wikidata match is the Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Poseidon (Neptune) and Thoosa; the Metamorphoses (13.857) names Neptune as his father and no other names are attached.

links.reason: Adrastus was Polyneikes' father-in-law (Argia's father), not his son; Pausanias' Adrastus is a different relation. Polyneikes' son was Thersander.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Polynices is the son of Oedipus; no wrongly attached names.
Eumolpus the Thracian son of Poseidon and Chione matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.

links.reason: In Pausanias, Alpheus only pursued Artemis and failed, and she is a virgin goddess, so he was never her lover. The river is not a partner in the Bacchae.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Artemis. The alias Dian is just the Latin name Diana, so it is the same being.
The Wikidata match is the Lernaean Hydra, which is the right being. She has no other names. Echidna is her mother in Hesiod's Theogony, and Typhon is her father.

links.reason: Anaxiroe is not Epeius's wife in any source I can name; Pausanias has Anaxiroe as daughter of Coronus and wife of Epeius's namesake line is unsupported. The link looks like a confusion with another figure, so it is not a marriage here.
Hyrmina is the daughter of Epeius, son of Endymion, eponym of Hyrmine in Elis; this is a different Epeius from the Trojan horse builder.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Phocian horse builder, son of Panopeus; the Elean Epeius (son of Endymion) is a separate being, handled in the Hyrmina link.

Wikidata match is Althaea, queen of Calydon, wife of Oeneus and mother of Meleager. The Iliad names her only as Meleager's mother. Her links to Oeneus and to Deianira (by Oeneus, in Hesiod and Apollodorus) are standard tradition.
The Wikidata match is the Trojan prince Hector, son of Priam. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Pontus is Gaia's own child, and the Theogony has her bear Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and Eurybia to him. This is a union of mother and son, not a marriage, so it should be read as a lover link.

identity.detail: Pontus is the right match for the sea personification.
Creon of Thebes, son of Menoeceus and brother of Jocasta, matches Wikidata. The parent flag is only a difference in naming: Menoikeus and Menoeceus are the same man.

links.reason: Æthra is the mother of Theseus, Pirithous' friend; Pirithous' mother is Dia (wife of Ixion), so the two are confused.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lapith king Pirithous; no other names.
Zethos is the Theban twin of Amphion, son of Antiope and Zeus; the match is correct.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Phoronis is a patronymic of Io (daughter of Inachus, and Phoroneus is her brother). The Io match is acceptable, and no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is the sea monster Charybdis; no other names are listed. Parentage by Poseidon (Neptune) and Gaia (Earth) is standard, with Pontos as a Theoi variant for the father.
Wikidata match is Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis; no other names to check.

The Odyssey's Neaera is the mother of Phaethusa and Lampetie by Helios/Hyperion, as the Wikipedia description says. The Wikidata parents (Nereus and Doris) and spouse (Aeëtes) do not fit this being. They belong to a different Neaera, a Nereid, or a confusion with another figure. The parent and spouse data should be dropped for this character.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theia is the Titan sister of Ocean and wife of Hyperion; Apollodorus pairs Ocean only with Tethys, and Hyperion with Thia.

The river Xanthus (Scamander) is a son of Ocean, but the link is flagged as brought from fall-of-troy; the editor ruled Midas as Xanthus's parent only in hesiod, so this may be a different Xanthus. Not clearly wrong though.
A chorus is a group, not a person.
Apollodorus gives Acheron as a son of Gaia and Helios (or Demeter), not Ocean.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Oceanus, the Titan; no other names are confused.
Wikidata's Licymnius is the illegitimate son of Electryon and Mideia, and Apollodorus names him as the same person. The Wikidata spouse entry is not shown in the book's tree, so nothing needs fixing.

links.reason: Duplicate of the Pleiades entry; the same group of daughters is listed twice under two spellings.
Pausanias' Maera is a different Maera, the daughter of Atlas in a minor tradition; she is a confusion with the Pleiad Maia and not part of Ovid's account.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Atlas; no other names are involved. Ovid's Atlas in Metamorphoses 4 is also the Titan, though he is described there as a Mauretanian king turned into a mountain.

links.link: Thetis parent_of Phocus, son of Æacus
links.reason: Pausanias (2.29.9) says Phocus's mother was Psamathe; the Thetis here is a different woman, a sister of Endeis. She is a namesake, not the Nereid, and has no relation to Æacus's son in the Nereid's line.
The Thetis here is a different woman, Endeis's sister in the book's sentence, not the Nereid daughter of Nereus, so the link does not belong to the Nereid.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Nereid Thetis, mother of Achilles. The book's Thetis who is Endeis's sister is a different person, but the name list shows no other names.

links.reason: Anius's mother is Rhoeo in the tradition (Theoi, Diodorus, Ovid); Creusa here is a different woman, likely confused with Aeneas's wife Creusa, who is not Anius's mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Delian king and priest of Apollo, which is the Anius of Aeneid 3.
Wikidata match is Diomedes of Thrace, the Bistones' king and owner of the man-eating mares, son of Ares and Cyrene. No other names are attached.
Iophossa is Hesiod's name for Chalciope, daughter of Aeetes and wife of Phrixus, so the Wikidata match is correct.
The Wikidata match is the goddess Athena. Minerva, Pallas and the other names refer to her. 'Onca Athena' and 'Onca Pallas' are cult epithets (Onca/Onga), not different people.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Aeolus a daughter Alcyone, but Hesiod's Catalogue names only sons here, and Alcyone is usually a different figure. The link was imported from another book and the Hesiod text does not support it.

identity.detail: Aiolos, son of Hellen, matches the Hesiod fragment. The Aeolus of the Odyssey, keeper of the winds, is a different figure, but he is not mixed in here.

Hesiod's fragment concerns Pandora daughter of Deucalion, and the Wikidata match is that same Pandora; but the book's Pandora of Works and Days (first woman, made by Hephaestus) is a different being and should not be merged with this one.
The Wikidata match is Hecuba, queen of Troy and wife of Priam, so the match is correct and no other names are in play.
Copreus is Eurystheus' herald, the son of Pelops of Elis; the Wikidata match is correct and he has no other names.
Wikidata's Tegeates, the Arcadian eponym of Tegea and son of Lycaon, is the same being the book names. The Wikidata link to Catreus as a son is not contradicted by the book, so it is kept.
Phoenix son of Agenor, eponym of Phoenicia, is the right match. Pausanias's Phœnix is the same being, and Asius names Perimede as his wife.
Wikidata's Coronis is the Thessalian daughter of Phlegyas and mother of Asklepios, which is the being Pindar means in Pythian 3.
The Wikidata match is the Messenian Leucippus, son of Perieres and Gorgophone and brother of Aphareus, which fits Apollodorus.

Medus, son of Medea, matches this being. Pausanias (2.3.8) names Aegeus as the father, which matches the book's sentence. Wikidata's extra father Jason reflects another tradition, but it does not affect this book's links.
Lycaon, king of Arcadia and son of Pelasgus, matches Pausanias' Lycaon; no other names to question.

links.reason: Pausanias has Pandion as father of Aegeus and Cecrops; Oeneus is son of Porthaon (Portheus) per Iliad and Apollodorus, and this Pandion link confuses a different Oeneus, son of Pandion, with the Calydonian king.
Hesiod and Apollodorus give Periboea as Oeneus' wife (mother of Tydeus), a marriage, so it is a valid spouse link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Calydonian king Oeneus, son of Porthaon; the name Œneus is just a spelling variant.
Belus, king of Egypt, son of Poseidon and Libya, father of Danaus and Aegyptus, matches Apollodorus.
Wikidata's Aegina is the nymph, daughter of Asopos, and the book's Oinopian isle is her island, so the match is right.

links.reason: In Metamorphoses Book 8 Scylla is Nisus's daughter, who betrays Megara to Minos. Glaucus loves the other Scylla, the sea nymph of Book 13. Her parents there are Phorcys and Crataeis, or others. The link belongs to that sea-monster Scylla.

identity.detail: Scylla daughter of Nisus (also called Ciris, turned into a bird) is a different being from Scylla the sea monster loved by Glaucus. The Wikidata match to Nisus's daughter fits only the first. The Glaucus link should be moved to the other Scylla.
Marpessa, daughter of Evenus and wife of Idas, mother of Cleopatra, is the same being the Wikidata entry describes.
Romulus is the founder of Rome, and Quirinus is the name he is given after his deification (Metamorphoses 14), so the match and the alias are right.

links.reason: Statius's Hypseus is a Theban, son of Asopus (the river of Boeotia). Wikidata's Hypseus is the Lapith king, son of Peneus, so the parentage belongs to the other Hypseus.

identity.detail: Statius's Hypseus is an Argive/Theban warrior, son of the river Asopus, killed in the Thebaid. The Wikidata match is the Lapith king, son of Peneus and father of Cyrene, a different being. The Kyrene link belongs to the Lapith Hypseus, not to this character.

links.reason: Pindar's 'Fame' is a personified abstraction (Pindar's own phrasing), not a son of Hermes; the tree misreads the sentence.
Hesiod's Dryops' daughter bore Pan to Hermes but was never his wife; only marriages are spouses.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Olympian god Hermes; no other names are listed.
Itys is the son of Tereus and Procne, and the Wikidata match is the same being.

The sentence names Plato as the one who makes Myson of Chen the seventh sage, and it calls him the son of Aristo. That is the philosopher Plato, son of Ariston, so the Wikidata match is correct. The flagged parent difference is only the spelling Aristo versus Ariston, and the link is fine.
Wikidata match is the nymph Rhodos, wife of Helios; no other names are confused.
Wikidata's Tiresias is the Theban seer, the same being as Teiresias; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Mnesileus (also called Mnasinous), son of Pollux and Phoebe, is the same being as Apollodorus's Mnesileus.
Minotaur matches Wikidata; Asterius is his own name in Apollodorus, and Pasiphae as mother is right. The Cretan Bull as father agrees with Theoi, so the flag is not a real error.
Wikidata match is Agave, daughter of Cadmus and mother of Pentheus; no other names are involved.
Aleus, king of Tegea and son of Aphidas, matches Wikidata. The flag about parents is only a spelling difference (Aphidas/Apheidas) for the same father.
Rhodos matches Rhode, the nymph of Rhodes and wife of Helios; no other names to split.
Periander of Corinth, son of Cypselus, husband of Melissa; the match is correct.
Wikidata's Tydeus is the Aetolian hero, father of Diomedes and one of the Seven against Thebes. The links to Oeneus, Diomedes and Deipyle are correct.
Timalcus, son of Megareus, who went to Aphidna with the Dioscuri, matches Wikipedia's Megarian prince. The book's sentence supports the parent link, so no change is needed.
Astyanax is the son of Hector and Andromache; the Wikidata match is correct.
Turnus, king of the Rutuli, is the right match. 'Daunian chief' fits his father Daunus.

links.reason: Metamorphoses' Moon (Luna/Selene) is not Apollo's sister; the editor ruled Selene is not his sibling or child. Diana is his sister.

links.link: Apollo parent_of Linus, son of Apollo
links.reason: Linus is a separate, differently identified figure; the editor allows Amphiaraus as Linus's parent only in Pausanias, so this link belongs to another Linus.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus; Pausanias gives her no Apollo parentage, so this is an unsupported guess.

identity.detail: Apollo matches the Olympian god; Phoebus is his usual epithet-name.
Wikidata match is Europa, the Phoenician princess abducted by Zeus and mother of Minos; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Ceryx is the Eleusinian herald, son of Hermes and Aglaurus (or Eumolpus in another tradition); the match is right.
Wikidata's Vulcan is the right match. Hephaestus and Lemnian are the same god, so the names stand.
Hypsipyle is the Lemnian queen, daughter of Thoas and mother of Euneos by Jason (Pindar, Pythian 4 and Olympian 4 mention the Lemnian women). The Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata's Ino is Cadmus' daughter, who became Leucothea; the match is correct.

links.reason: Theseus abducted Helen as a girl, but she was never his wife. Only marriages count as spouse links, so this is a lover link.
Achilles and Helen met only after death on Leuke, in a late tradition, so it was not a marriage. This is a lover link.
Paris took Helen from Menelaus, who remained her husband. The editor treats non-marriage links as lover links.

identity.detail: Helen of Troy is the right match.

links.reason: Apollodorus calls it an intrigue (3.13.8); Deidamia was not a wife, so she is a lover.
Pausanias (3.19.13) has Achilles and Helen united on Leuce, an afterlife marriage; the tradition names it a marriage, though Apollodorus does not mention it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles; Ligyron is his childhood name in Apollodorus, so it is a correct alias.
Side is the first wife of Orion, cast into Hades by Hera (Apollodorus). The Wikidata match is correct, and she has no other names.
Thocnus, son of Lycaon and eponym of Thocnia in Arcadia, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.

Wikidata's Pellen is the same founder of Pellene. Pausanias gives Phorbas as father and Triopas as grandfather, which matches Wikidata's father, so the flag is only about the mother, Hyrmine, whom the book does not name.
Alcyoneus is the Giant who opposed Heracles; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names need splitting.

links.link: Apollo parent_of Coronus, son of Apollo
links.reason: The name is a descriptive label, not a person. Pausanias' Coronus is the son of Apollo only by a misread phrase, so it looks like a mislabeled entry.

links.link: Apollo parent_of Linus, son of Apollo
links.reason: The node name carries a descriptive label. The book's sentence gives Apollo and Aethusa as parents of Linus, so the link should point to plain Linus, not this labeled node.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Apollo. Epithets such as Phoebus, Far-Shooter, Iepaeon, and Delphinius all refer to him.
Wikidata's Britomartis is the Cretan goddess Pausanias describes. Aphaea and Limnaea are her own cult names (Pausanias also notes Aphaea at Aegina), so they do not point to a different person.

links.reason: Harmonia is Ares' daughter by Aphrodite in tradition (and wife of Cadmus); the editor's rule reads non-marriage 'spouse' links as lover, and this contradicts the parent link.
Aphrodite is Ares' lover, not his sibling; the Iliad calls her Zeus' daughter but Ares is not her brother in the tree's tradition.
Duplicate spelling of Penthesilea, already linked as the same person; this is a duplicate node, not a different person.
Panic is a personification, not a person; Phobos and Deimos are Ares' sons, so this should be a personification and not a person.

identity.detail: Wikidata Ares is the Greek god; Mars is his Roman counterpart and is acceptable as an alias.

links.reason: A group of children, not a single person; the sons are Mermerus and Pheres (or Thessalus), listed separately.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason; no other names.
Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths and father of Koronis in Pindar's Pythian 3, matches the Wikidata entry. He has no other names to split.
Wikidata Pan is the Greek god, correct.
Myrmidon, eponym of the Myrmidons and son of Zeus by Eurymedusa, is the right match. Apollodorus (1.7.3 and 3.12.6) has Zeus approaching Eurymedusa as an ant, so the Zeus link fits.
Wikidata match is the goddess Athena; her other names (Minerva, Pallas, Tritonis, Trito-born, Atrytone) are epithets or the Roman equivalent of the same being.
Doryssus the Spartan king, son of Labotas and father of Agesilaus I, matches the Wikidata entry and the book's text.
Oxylus, king of Elis, son of Haemon or Andraemon, matches. Theoi's parent Oreios belongs to a different Oxylus, the Hamadryad father in Athenaeus, but this is not a link in this tree.
Delphus, the eponym of Delphi, matches. Apollo as father is the tradition in Aeschylus' Eumenides setting, and Theoi confirms it.
Wikidata Briareus is the Hundred-hander, son of Uranus and Gaia. The Aegaeon parentage is a variant tradition (Homer, Ion of Chios). Hesiod makes Briareus husband of Cymopolea, so that link is fine.

links.link: Theopompus, father of Agenor parent_of Agenor
links.reason: Pausanias' Agenor son of Theopompus is a different man (an Arcadian/Argive figure), not the Phoenician son of Poseidon and Libya.
Pausanias' Crotopus is the Argive king, son of Agenor son of Triopas, not the Phoenician Agenor.
Iphidamas son of Antenor (Iliad) is a Trojan, and Pausanias' Agenor is the Trojan, not the Phoenician king.
Preugenes belongs to the Achaean Patrai line of Agenor, not the Phoenician one.
Echeclus son of Agenor (Iliad) is a Trojan, the son of Antenor's brother, not the Phoenician king.

identity.detail: Wikidata matches the Phoenician king, but several links from Pausanias belong to other men named Agenor.
Vulcan here is Hephaestus, the smith god, and the Wikidata match is fine. The book names him only as Vulcan, so no other names are affected.

Wikidata's Lepreus matches the eponymous founder of Lepreum. Pausanias names Pyrgeus as his father, so the link is right and the tree has nothing to fix. The difference from Wikidata's other parents (Poseidon, Astydameia) is only an alternative tradition.
Wikidata match is the Rhodian leader Tlepolemus, son of Heracles and Astyoche, who fought Sarpedon in the Iliad; no other names are involved.
Epicaste in the Odyssey (11.271ff) is Jocasta, mother and wife of Oedipus; the match is right. Both spouse links (Laius, Oedipus) are real marriages.
Immaradus, son of Eumolpus, slain by Erechtheus in Pausanias; the Wikidata match is the same being.

links.reason: Parthenopaeus is the son of the Arcadian Atalanta (with Melanion or Ares), not the Boeotian daughter of Schoeneus the book names.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Atalanta merges two figures: the Boeotian daughter of Schoeneus (this book) and the Arcadian daughter of Iasus and Clymene. Clymene, Iasus, Maenalus, Melanion and Parthenopaeus belong to the Arcadian one.

links.reason: In the Iliad (20.219-229) Boreas, in the shape of a stallion, sired horses on Erichthonius' mares; he was not Erichthonius' lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Boreas; no other names.

links.reason: Hesiod's Pluto is the child of Demeter and Iasion (wealth), not her sibling; the sibling link confuses him with Plutus or Hades-Pluto, and Apollodorus gives no such link.
Pausanias' Clymenus (a Hermionean cult title for Hades) is a cult title for Hades taken as a separate person; Apollodorus lists Demeter's siblings without him.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Demeter; no other names.

Phoebe the Titan, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of Coeus, mother of Leto and Asteria (Hesiod, Theogony). The Wikidata match is correct. The parent flag is only a naming difference: Heaven is Uranus and Earth is Gaia.

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, a group taken for a person (their eponym Dolion was a son of Poseidon's line, not a single child).
The Moliones are Actor's sons in the Iliad (Molione the mother); Poseidon fathering them is only a rare variant, not stated here.
Charybdis is a monster, daughter of Poseidon and Gaia in some sources, but here it is likely a misread; not stated in the Odyssey.
Machaon is Asclepius's son, not Poseidon's.
Podaleirius is Asclepius's son, not Poseidon's.

identity.detail: Neptune matched to Poseidon is the same god; Wikidata's father Saturn equals Cronus.
Io is the Argive princess loved by Zeus; Isis is her Egyptian identification, a standard equation, so the match and name are fine.

links.reason: Pindar's Fame is a personification, and Hermes is not her father in Hesiod or Theoi's listing; the link is an unsupported guess.

identity.detail: Hermes matches. The alternative names (Mercury, Cyllenian) refer to the same god.

Eunomus is the Eurypontid king of Sparta, son of Prytanis, matching the Wikipedia entry. Wikidata lists Polydectes as a father, which looks reversed, but the book's links are correct and need no change.

links.link: Danaus parent_of Chorus of the Danaids
links.reason: The Chorus of the Danaids in Aeschylus is a group, not a person; the daughters are already linked individually.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Danaus is the same being, the son of Belus and brother of Aegyptus. The parent flag is only a mismatch in how the sources list his mother.

links.reason: Ops is the Roman counterpart of Rhea, so this duplicates the Rhea link as a second wife; Metamorphoses uses Ops for Rhea.

Picus is the son of Saturn in Roman sources (Aeneid, Metamorphoses). Saturn is the Roman name for Cronos, but this link is merged from the Latin books under a different figure and is not in the Argonautica; it is a Latin-tradition father, not Greek Cronos.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Cronus is correct; Kronos and Cronus are the same being.
Ganymede is the Trojan prince, son of Tros, abducted to be Zeus's cupbearer; the Wikidata match is correct.
Epaphus is the son of Zeus and Io, and the match is correct. Libye and Libya are the same daughter, not two beings; the two spellings are variants of one name.
Wikidata's Orphne is the nymph of the underworld who bore Ascalaphus to Acheron in Ovid's account, so the match is the same being.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Lynceus son of Aphareus, brother of Idas, is the Messenian Argonaut, not the Egyptian Lynceus who married Hypermnestra; the Aphareus parent link and the Idas sibling link belong to him.
Idas's brother is Lynceus son of Aphareus, a different man from Danaus' son-in-law Lynceus.

identity.detail: Two Lynceuses are merged under one name: the son of Egyptus who married Hypermnestra and ruled Argos (the Wikidata match), and the Messenian son of Aphareus, brother of Idas. Aphareus and Idas links belong to the latter.

links.reason: Harmonia is Ares' daughter by Aphrodite (Theogony 937); the Argonautica link confuses her with a spouse, and only Hera-Zeus and Aphrodite-Hephaestus count as marriages.

In the Iliad Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, and Ares is the son of Zeus and Hera. Neither shares a mother with the other, and the poem never calls them siblings; Wikidata lists her as Ares' partner.

identity.detail: Ares and Mars are the same god in the Greek and Roman traditions, and the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Aegina, the nymph daughter of Asopus, abducted by Jove; no other names to fix.
Molurus, son of Arisbas, killed by Hyettus (Pausanias 9.36.6; Megalai Ehoiai); the Wikidata match is the same person and the parent link agrees with Wikidata, so the flag is spurious.

links.reason: In the Iliad Aphrodite is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, and Ares is the son of Zeus and Hera, so they are half-siblings at most. The book makes them lovers (Mars lover_of Venus), not siblings.

identity.detail: Venus matches Aphrodite; the alternate names are correct.

links.reason: Mars is Venus's lover in the Thebaid, not her brother. In the Iliad, Ares and Aphrodite are children of Zeus but not full siblings. Statius has Venus in Mars's embrace.
Panic (Phobos/Deimos) are sons of Ares and Aphrodite, not a singular figure 'Panic'; the link confuses a group or personification with a person.

identity.detail: Aphrodite and Venus are the same goddess; Cytherea is her epithet, so no change is needed.

The Wikidata match is the Spartan Lichas, but in Pausanias the Lichas who is Arcesilaus' son is the Olympic chariot victor, son of Arcesilaus (Lichas son of Arcesilaus, 5th c. BC). The Agathoergus Lichas who found Orestes' bones is a different Spartan. The Wikipedia description is a disambiguation-like entry, so the match is uncertain, but the link itself is stated by the book and is right.

links.reason: Pausanias (8.53) has a different Catreus, son of Tegeates' line in Arcadia? Actually Tegeates' sons include Cydon, Archedius, Gortys; the Cretan Catreus is son of Minos and Pasiphae, so this link confuses two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata Catreus, the Cretan king son of Minos, matches the main being; Pausanias also mentions an Arcadian Catreus-related link only via Tegeates, handled above.
The Wikidata match is the constellation Orion, but the character is the mythical hunter Orion, son of Poseidon and Euryale. The match should point to the hunter, not the star group.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children, not a person.
Statius' Chromis is a different, minor figure; unsupported as Hercules' son.

identity.detail: Hercules is the Roman form of Heracles; Alcides and Tirynthian hero are epithets of the same hero.
Wikidata match is Chalciope, daughter of Aeëtes and wife of Phrixus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Under the editor's rule only marriages count as spouse; Medea's union with Aegeus at Athens, which Apollodorus and Ovid tell, is read as a liaison, and Hesiod does not mention it.
This is a group of unnamed children taken as one person; the sons should be linked individually (Mermerus and Pheres), and the sentence quoted is from Pausanias, not Hesiod.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Colchian Medea, daughter of Aeetes; no other names are attached.
Pandrosos, daughter of Cecrops and Aglauros, matches Wikidata's Pandrosus; no other names to question.
Tyndareus matches the Spartan king, husband of Leda. The two Wikidata fathers (Oebalus, Perieres) reflect competing traditions and do not indicate a wrong match.
The Dryops of the Homeric Hymn to Pan is the king of Oeta or Arcadia whose daughter Hermes wed. The Wikidata match is a king of Oeta, which fits, and there are no other names to question.

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, not a person; Dolion is the eponym, a group taken for a person.
Machaon and Podaleirius are sons of Asclepius, not Neptune.
Podaleirius is a son of Asclepius, not Neptune.

identity.detail: Neptune matches Poseidon and the names are correct. The Wikidata father Saturn is consistent with Cronus.
Wikidata match is Danaë, daughter of Acrisius and mother of Perseus; no other names to check.

Brontes the Hesiodic Cyclops, son of Uranus and Gaia; the Wikidata match is the same being. The only link, Earth as parent, agrees with Wikidata's Gaia. The flag is probably only a missing Uranus link, not an error.
Wikidata's Pentheus is the Theban king, son of Echion and Agave. The links are consistent with Pausanias, Euripides' Bacchae, and Apollodorus.
Wikidata's Berossus, the Babylonian priest and writer, fits the Berosus Pausanias names as Sabbe's father (10.12.9), and the book gives no other names for him.
Wikidata's Eileithyia is the goddess of childbirth, daughter of Zeus and Hera; Eileithyia is just a spelling variant of Eilithyia.

links.reason: Pausanias says Medus was her son by Aegeus, but nothing makes her his wife in this book; under the editor's rule non-primary unions are read as lover links.
A group node, not a person; Mermerus and Pheres are already linked individually.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Colchian sorceress Medea; no other names listed.
Tityus matches Tityos, the giant punished for assaulting Leto; no other names are attached.

links.reason: In Metamorphoses Dryope is the daughter of Dryops (Andraemon's wife, sister of Iole by the same mother only); she is not Eurytus's daughter. Wikidata confuses her with Iole's sister.
Apollodorus's Actor-father Eurytus is the Molionid Eurytus, not Eurytus of Oechalia, whose father is Melaneus.
Hesiod's Eurytus son of Actor/Molione line or different Eurytus; Oechalian Eurytus's mother is not Stratonica.
Antioche is wife of a different Eurytus in Hesiod's catalogue (mother of Iole? uncertain); not confirmed for Eurytus of Oechalia, and attaches to the namesake line.
Pausanias's Theraphone and Thalpius belong to the Molionid Eurytus (Thalpius is son of Eurytus son of Actor), not Eurytus of Oechalia.
Thalpius is son of the Molionid Eurytus, per Pausanias and the Iliad.

identity.detail: Match to Eurytus of Oechalia is right, but the tree mixes in the Molionid Eurytus's relatives.
Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas, lover of Apollo and mother of Aesculapius, matches Wikidata. Coroneus as her father is a Metamorphoses variant, already handled by the editor.
Erginus the Argonaut, who took over as helmsman after Tiphys died, matches the Wikidata entry. Poseidon as father is confirmed by Theoi; Branchus is a variant father.

links.reason: Timandra is Tyndareus' daughter in Hesiod and Pausanias, but Theoi lists her only as a daughter of Leda and Tyndareus in a loose sense; in the Odyssey Leda is mother of Castor and Polydeuces and Helen is Zeus's child, so this link is unsupported by this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Leda, wife of Tyndareus and daughter of Thestius; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Acastus is the son of Pelias who sailed with the Argonauts and hunted the Calydonian Boar, so the match is correct. No other names are attached.

links.reason: Creusa, Aeneas' wife, is a daughter of Priam in the Aeneid, but her mother is not Hecuba in the tradition. Virgil gives no mother for her; Hecuba is not named as her mother.
Polyxeina is just a variant spelling of Polyxena, so the link duplicates Hecuba parent_of Polyxena and should be merged into it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan queen Hecuba; no other names to check.

links.reason: Pausanias gives Aeneas no child Etias in the Aeneid's tradition; the name is unsupported here and likely a different figure or confused with a namesake.
Thrasybulus is not a child of Aeneas in the Aeneid or in the main tradition; the Pausanias link looks like a confusion with another person.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Aeneas himself; the alternate names are all epithets of him, though 'Teucrians' is a group name and not an alias of him.
Thalia the Grace, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome per Hesiod as quoted by Pausanias; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias tells of Alpheus pursuing Artemis, who escaped him; he was never her lover, and Pindar's Ischys passage does not mention him.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the goddess Artemis. The Demeter-parent listing on Theoi is the Aeschylus/Pausanias variant, which this book does not follow.
Wikidata match is correct. Hercules is the Roman name of the same hero.
Wikidata match is the goddess Harmonia, wife of Cadmus. The Theoi listing of Zeus and Elektra (Diodorus 5.48.2) is the Samothracian variant, not another being.
Wikidata match is the Argive king Phoroneus, son of Inachus; no wrong names.
Dorus, son of Hellen and the nymph Orseis, eponymous ancestor of the Dorians, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are listed.
Wikidata match is the king of Tiryns/Mycenae, son of Sthenelus; no mismatched names.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive concubine of Ajax (Sophocles' Ajax), not a wife; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.

identity.detail: Ajax the Great (son of Telamon) matches only the Salaminian Ajax. 'Locrian Ajax' is Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus, a different hero, so that name should be split off.
Wikidata match is Stheno the Gorgon, sister of Euryale and Medusa. Her parents Phorcys and Ceto are right (Apollodorus 2.4.2 names the Gorgons as daughters of Phorcys and Ceto).
Dryops, eponym of the Dryopians, matches. Pausanias says the Asinaeans hold him to be Apollo's son, which fits the Apollo link. Wikidata also lists other fathers, but those are variant traditions.
Electryon, son of Perseus and Andromeda, king of Mycenae, matches Wikidata. Wikidata lists spouses, which are probably Anaxo and Lysidice; the book names only Anaxo.
The Wikidata match is the king Erechtheus of Athens, son of Pandion I, and the other names are fine.
Poeas, king of Meliboea and father of Philoctetes, is the right being, and the book's sentence confirms Philoctetes as his son.

links.reason: Learchus died as a child, killed by Athamas (Pausanias 1.44.7); Hyrieus is the son of Poseidon and Alcyone or Clonie, or of Thebes tradition, not of Learchus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Learchus, son of Athamas and Ino.
Hephaestus matches the right god, and Vulcan is his Roman counterpart. Cypris is Aphrodite and the editor already treats her as his spouse, so no fix is needed.

Sirens match the generic mythological siren; the plural group name is fine as a single entry. Both parent links (Achelous and Melpomene) are supported by Apollodorus and Hyginus, so nothing needs fixing.
Erginus, king of Minyan Orchomenus, son of Clymenus, matches Wikidata. The flagged parent difference is not real: Pausanias names Clymenus as his father, as Wikidata does.
Agasthenes son of Augeas, king of Elis, is the right match; no other names to question.
Perseus the son of Zeus and Danae and founder of the Perseid dynasty is the right match, and the book names no other names.
Mariandynus, eponymous hero of the Mariandyni, matches Wikidata. The book names Phineus as his father, which is one of the traditions listed, so the link is fine.

links.reason: Aratus the Sicyonian is the son of Clinias and Aristodama, per the editor's decision (right only in pausanias), so he is not Asclepius' child. Pausanias mentions Aratus only as a hero honoured at Epidaurus, not Asclepius' son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Asclepius himself, and no other names are given.

Galatea the Nereid appears in the Iliad's Nereid catalogue (18.45), and the Wikidata match is this Nereid, daughter of Nereus and Doris. The statue Galatea is a different figure, but it is not matched here.

Hippocoon, the Spartan king, son of Oebalus and Bateia, is correctly matched. His sons (Dorceus, Enaraephorus, Eumedes, Alcimus, Sebrus, Alcon and others) are attested in Pausanias and Apollodorus, so the links are fine.
Aphrodite/Venus match is correct; Cyprian is a cult epithet for the same goddess.
Aethlius, first king of Elis, is the right match. Both links are traditional: Aethlius is the father of Endymion, and Zeus is his father by Protogeneia.
Wikidata's Phorcys is the sea god, son of Pontus and Gaia, so the match is right and he has no other names.

links.reason: Aidos as a child of Prometheus is a Hesiodic-only item; the Argonautica does not say it and it is not a Prometheus tradition in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus; no other names.

Pausanias (6.24.5) describes Pyrrho, son of the Sophist Pistocrates, as a statue in Elis with great persuasiveness. The Wikidata match is Pyrrho of Elis, the founder of Pyrrhonism, and the book's text does not say this is the philosopher. Diogenes Laertius gives the philosopher's father as Pistocrates, so the match is plausible. I keep the match, with a caveat.

links.reason: Ovid's Glaucus loves the monster Scylla, the sea-nymph daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis. The Megarian princess Scylla, daughter of Nisus, betrayed him to Minos and is a different being, so the link belongs to the monster.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Megarian Scylla, daughter of Nisus, which fits Apollodorus. The parent mismatch is only Wikidata adding the mother Abrota, which does not contradict Nisus.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 304-325) makes Echidna Typhon's mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse; the lover label undersells a union that bore his monstrous offspring.

identity.detail: Typhaon is a standard variant name of Typhon, so the match is correct.
Onchestus is the Boeotian eponym and son of Poseidon; the Wikidata match is correct.
Corycia is the Parnassian naiad, and the Wikidata match is correct. She has no other names.

Briareus (Aegaeon) is the Hundred-Hander, son of Uranus and Gaia; Hesiod (Theogony 817-819) gives him Cymopolea, daughter of Poseidon, as wife. Theoi's Aigaios-and-Thalassa listing is a variant tradition (Ion of Chios) and does not contradict the links.

links.reason: Aethra lay with Aegeus once at Troezen (Plutarch, Apollodorus); no marriage, so he is a lover.
Pausanias' Phalanthus story concerns Aethra, daughter of Oceanus, in Taras, a different Aethra; Pittheus' daughter did not marry him.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Pittheus' daughter, mother of Theseus. Phalanthus link comes from a namesake.
Mnemosyne is the Titaness of memory, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, as Hesiod says. Wikidata's extra parents (Zeus, Clymene) are wrong, but the match itself is the right being.

The Wikidata match is the Sirens as a group, and the Odyssey names them as a pair. No other names are attached to them. The parentage links are traditional: Achelous is the father in most sources, and Terpsichore is named as mother by Apollonius Rhodius 4.892.
Wikidata match is the wife of Amphiaraus and daughter of Talaus; no other names listed.
Wikidata match is the right Eriphyle, wife of Amphiaraus and daughter of Talaus.

Wikidata match is the Iliad's Ascalaphus, son of Ares and Astyoche, a leader of the Minyans. Theoi's parents Acheron and Gorgyra/Orphne belong to the other Ascalaphus, the Underworld one who informed on Persephone. Wikidata's mother Pernis is a variant. No other names to correct.
Circe matches the right being; no other names.
Bromius is an epithet of Dionysus. The match is acceptable since the book uses it for Dionysus.
Wikidata's Helle is the daughter of Athamas and Nephele who fell into the Hellespont. No other names are attached to her.
Argus, son of Zeus and Niobe and king of Argos, matches Wikidata; no other names to split.
Wikidata's Thronia is the daughter of Belus and mother of Arabus by Hermes. The links match that figure. The Naiad Thronia, mother of Abderus, is a separate namesake, and no link here belongs to her.

links.reason: Editor's rule reads any non-marriage spouse link as a lover; Oeagrus is not among the listed marriages, and in Pausanias' tradition Orpheus's parentage is disputed (he says Orpheus was son of the daughter of Pierus, not Calliope), so a union is best treated as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope; no other names to check.
