Isus is Priam's son killed by Agamemnon in Iliad 11; the Wikidata match is the same being. Priam as father is correct.
Wikidata match is the right Philoctetes, son of Poeas; 'Poeas' son' is just a patronymic epithet for him.

links.reason: Pausanias' Antiope (the Amazon) is Theseus' lover; Hippolyte is the same Amazon figure, and the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Pausanias says Theseus 'married' Helen, but she was carried off as a girl and was no real wife; the editor treats non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Ægle was a lover whom Theseus abandoned for Ariadne (Hesiod); not a marriage, and not from Pausanias.
Pausanias writes Demophon, which is already a separate link; Demophoon is the same son, so this is a duplicate spelling.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Theseus; no other names listed.

Magnes in Pausanias is the son of Aeolus, father of Eioneus, while the Wikidata match is the son of Argos and Perimele. These are different traditions of the eponym of Magnesia. The Pausanias passage states the link, so it stands. The Wikidata father (Argus) is the other tradition and does not contradict the book's own tree.
Wikidata match is the Eleusinian king Celeus. Metanira and Metaneira are spelling variants of one person and should be merged.
Strymon the Thracian river-god, son of Oceanus and Tethys and father of Rhesus in Apollodorus, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Pausanias gives Anaxiroe, daughter of Coronus, as wife of Epeus of Elis, son of Endymion, not the Phocian horse-builder, son of Panopeus.
Pausanias makes Hyrmina the daughter of Epeus, king of Elis, son of Endymion, not the son of Panopeus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Epeius, the son of Panopeus who built the Wooden Horse.
Match is the Trojan prince Hector.
Wikidata's Leda is the Aetolian princess, wife of Tyndareus and mother of the Dioscuri; the match is correct.

links.reason: Hesperus is usually son of Eos and Cephalus or Astraeus; Hesiod's Eosphorus (Morning Star) is Eos's son, not Hesperus, so this confuses the morning and evening star.
Apollodorus (1.7.2) makes Boreas a son of Astraeus and Eos, but this link only comes from Wikidata; Boreas's mother is more often Eos, so keep is safer.

identity.detail: Aurora is the Latin name of Eos, so the match is the same being.
Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle, brother of Alcmaeon, is the right match.
Hyamus son of Lycorus, founder of Hyampolis, matches Wikidata; the book's links (Lycorus as father, Celæno as daughter) are right for this book.

links.reason: Sinis the pine-bender is a separate bandit, said to be a son of Poseidon (or Polypemon) in tradition, not a son of Procrustes; Apollodorus gives no such parentage for Procrustes.

identity.detail: Procrustes matches Wikidata; Polypemon, Damastes and Prokoptas are his recognized alternative names.
Neleus of Pylos, son of Tyro and Poseidon, father of Nestor and Pero, husband of Chloris; the match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias' Electra is a different figure (Electra, a Theban gate/Atlas's daughter, or Cadmus' Thebes namesake); in Apollodorus Cadmus' siblings are Europa, Phoenix, Cilix, so this joins a different Electra.
Hermione is an alternate name for Harmonia in some sources (Metamorphoses/Ovid's Harmonia), so it duplicates the spouse Harmonia and is not a separate wife; Apollodorus gives only Harmonia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban founder Cadmus; no other names to question.
Iobates, also called Amphianax, is the Lycian king and father of Philonoe and Stheneboea (also called Antea). The Wikidata match and the alternative name are correct.
Wikidata match is the Muse Euterpe; no other names are attached.
Cupid is the Roman Eros and the Wikidata match is correct; the other names (Eros, Love) refer to the same being.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages stay spouse links; Oeagrus is Calliope's partner as Orpheus' father, not a marriage the book states, so read as lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope; no other names to question.

Wikidata's Muse matches the Muses as a group of goddesses. Pausanias also mentions other Muse genealogies, such as the daughters of Pieros and the Muses of Ouranos, but the Zeus and Mnemosyne links are the standard tradition.
The Wikidata match is the Syracusan fountain nymph Arethusa. 'Alpheian Nymph' is an epithet for the same being.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive concubine taken in war (Sophocles, Ajax), not a wife; the editor's rule reads non-marriage 'spouse' links as lovers.

identity.detail: Ajax the Great, son of Telamon, is the correct match; the names given are all the same hero.
x

links.reason: Pausanias ix.5.10 (citing the Oedipodea) makes her Oedipus' wife and mother of his sons; Wikipedia and Wikidata call her his wife, so she is no mere lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Theban queen Euryganeia, wife of Oedipus, and she has no other names.
Wikidata match is Atreus, king of Mycenae, son of Pelops; no other names to question.

links.reason: Tyrrhenus in the Aeneid (Etruscan Tarchon's ally/Tyrrhenus the Etruscan warrior) is not given as Hercules' son; Wikidata's list (Heracles, Atys, Telephus) blends the eponymous Etruscan founder, son of Atys or Telephus, with a different tradition, and the book states no such parentage.

identity.detail: The Aeneid's Tyrrhenus is a minor Etruscan warrior (Aen. 11.612, a brother or companion of Tarchon's troops), not clearly the eponymous Lydian founder that Wikidata describes, so the match is doubtful.
Antilochus, son of Nestor, prince of Pylos, killed by Memnon at Troy, matches the Wikidata entry. The book's tree has no other names for him that could belong to someone else.

links.reason: Leocritus son of Polydamas in Pausanias is a different Polydamas (the Skotoussa athlete, or another); the Trojan Polydamas son of Panthous has no such son in the Iliad.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan Polydamas, son of Panthous; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Elean Endymion, son of Aethlius; no foreign names are attached.
Marpessa, daughter of Evenus and wife of Idas, mother of Cleopatra, matches Wikidata.
Hades is the right match; Aidoneus is a normal alternate name for Hades.

Capaneus, son of Hipponous, one of the Seven against Thebes, is the right match. The links are consistent with Apollodorus; the flagged parent difference only reflects Wikidata also listing Alector as a father.

links.reason: Ovid's Cygnus, son of Poseidon at Troy, is a different being from the Cycnus of Hesiod's Shield, who is a son of Ares.
The Doliones are a people, not a person; Apollonius names their king Cyzicus, who is not Poseidon's son.
The Moliones are the twin sons of Molione and Actor (or Poseidon in some versions), but the Iliad names Actor as their father; the link is a doubtful guess.
Hera is Poseidon's sister in the Iliad, but the link is a stray duplicate with no support in the tree; it is consistent with Hesiod and should stay.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the god Poseidon, and both of his other names, Dark-haired One and Earth-Shaker, are epithets of the same god.

links.reason: The Iliad (17.9, 17.40) makes Euphorbus the son of Panthous. Pausanias' Alcimachus seems to come from a confusion with another figure; the link has no support in the Iliad.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Trojan Euphorbus, son of Panthous, who wounded Patroclus and was killed by Menelaus.
Wikidata's Chiron is the centaur, son of Cronus (Saturn) and Philyra, so the match is right. He has no other names.

links.reason: Duplicate spelling of Ganyetor (Ganyctor) and the book's own link is the same; however the Wikidata Antiphus is the Myrmidon's son, and this Antiphus, son of Ganyctor who killed Hesiod, is a different person.

identity.detail: The Wikidata Antiphus is the Phthian prince, son of Myrmidon and Peisidice. Hesiod's Antiphus is the brother of Ctimenus and son of Ganyctor, who was accused of killing Hesiod, so the match is a different being.
Numa is Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome; the Wikidata match is correct. Ovid (Metamorphoses 15) calls Egeria his nymph wife, so the spouse link is right.

Itonus, son of Amphictyon and father of Boeotus, is the same being as the Wikidata match. The links to Boeotus and Amphictyon are right, and Iodame as a daughter agrees with the Wikipedia description.
Wikidata's Teucer is the son of Telamon and Hesione, the Greek archer at Troy and half-brother of Ajax, so the match is correct. No other names are listed.

Archelaus of Sparta, Agiad king, son of Agesilaus I and father of Teleclus, matches Pausanias. The flag about parents differing from Wikidata is unfounded, since Wikidata also gives Agesilaus I as father.

links.link: Thetis parent_of Phocus, son of Æacus
links.reason: Pausanias' sentence says Phocus' mother was Endeis's sister, but the nymph Psamathe is the mother in the tradition (Hesiod, Apollodorus); Thetis here is a Nereid taken for Psamathe, and the sentence reads as a quoted doubtful claim.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Phocus son of Aeacus and Psamathe; no confusion.

links.reason: The book's line calls Electryon 'the son of Perses', which is a patronymic for Perseus' son. Perses the Titan's son (Hecate's father) is a different being, so the link is a namesake. Perseus parent_of Electryon already holds the correct link.

identity.detail: Electryon, son of Perseus and Andromeda, is the right match. 'Electyron' is only a spelling variant.

links.reason: Pluto here is the nymph Plouto (daughter of Ocean and Tethys in Hesiod), not the god Pluto/Hades of the Odyssey; the editor limits her Ocean/Tethys parentage to Hesiod, and the link was brought in from Hesiod, which names her under a different identity in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Tantalus, the Odyssey's punished king in the underworld.
Aphareus the Messenian king, son of Perieres and Gorgophone, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Opportunity (Kairos) is a personification, and Pausanias gives no parentage from Zeus.
Pausanias gives Lamia, daughter of Poseidon, as the Sibyl's parent. The editor also ruled Lamia and Theodorus parents of the Sibyl, so Zeus is unsupported.
Pallas, the Titan son of Crius, is confused with Athena's epithet Pallas.

links.link: Zeus parent_of Thaleia, one of the Graces
links.reason: This is a garbled duplicate of Thaleia/Thalia that joins the Muse and the Grace in one link.
Eetion, son of Zeus, is a variant of Iasion, and the Eetion of Thebe is a different person.
Hermus is a river, and Zeus is not named as its father.
Theogony 901 says Zeus married Themis, and Wikidata lists her as a spouse.
Theogony 886 says Zeus made Metis his first wife, and Wikidata lists her as a spouse.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Zeus, and none of his alternative names belong to another being.

links.reason: Eumolpus is son of Poseidon and Chione (Apollodorus 3.15.4; Pausanias); Dionysus is only a cult association with the Eleusinian mysteries, not a parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Thracian/Eleusinian Eumolpus, son of Poseidon and Chione; no other names to dispute.
The Wikidata match is the right Philoctetes, son of Poeas.

Wikidata's Tithonus is the Trojan prince, son of Laomedon and lover of Eos, so the match is right. The Wikidata father Cephalus and spouse Cissia do not appear in this book's tree and are not at issue.
Mycene, daughter of Inachus and wife of Arestor, eponym of Mycenae, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed.
Wikidata match is the wife of Amphiaraus, correct; no other names.
Python is the Delphic serpent born of Gaia (Earth), whom Apollo slew; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are involved.
Wikidata match Antigonus I Monophthalmus is correct.

links.reason: Selene is confused with Diana/Artemis; the editor has ruled Zeus is not her parent, and no tradition makes her his lover.
Editor decision: wrong everywhere.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus and given to Epimetheus; she was not Zeus's lover.
Pallas is a title of Athena (already listed) or a Titan or giant of that name, not a separate child of Zeus.
Nemesis is a daughter of Nyx (Hesiod); the editor ruled Themis is not her parent.
Sisyphus is a son of Aeolus, not Zeus.
Xanthus the river or horse is confused with another figure; the editor's decision about Midas as parent shows the name is ambiguous.
The Sibyl is a prophetess (Pausanias gives Lamia or Theodorus as parent); the link rests on a misreading.
Personified abstraction taken for a person; Truth has no firm tradition of descent from Zeus.
Personified abstraction; Fortune is a daughter of Oceanus or another parent, with a late, unsupported link to Zeus.
Personified abstraction, not a genuine child of Zeus.
A group of beings taken as a single person; only some nymphs are his daughters.
A group taken as a person; Naiads are not collectively Zeus's children.
Eetion is the father of Andromache and Iasion's name is confused with his; no tradition makes Zeus his father.
Hermus is a river god, not recognised as a son of Zeus.
Macar is a son of Helios or Aeolus, not Zeus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Zeus; Jove and Jupiter are the Roman names for the same god.
Celeus is the king of Eleusis, husband of Metanira. The Wikidata match is correct, and no other names are attached to him.

Wikidata match is Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, son of Hipponous, husband of Evadne and father of Sthenelus. The Wikidata father list also names Alector, an alternative tradition, but it is not a flagged link.

links.reason: Pausanias makes Hippocoon a rival of Tyndareus, a son of Oebalus by another mother (Batia in other sources); the book gives Gorgophone only Tyndareus.
Arene is the wife of Aphareus, a daughter of Oebalus in tradition, not a child of Gorgophone.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Gorgophone, daughter of Perseus.

links.reason: Selene is confused with Diana/Latona's line; editor ruled Zeus-Selene wrong everywhere.
Pandia is Zeus's daughter by Selene, a link ruled wrong; the Selene tie is rejected.
Hesiod makes Pandora a created woman, not Zeus's lover; Pandora married Epimetheus.
A group taken for a person; Hesiod only has Zeus father certain nymphs, not a single child.
A group taken for a person.
A group node duplicates the individual Muses; keep the individual links.
A group taken for a person; Aglaea, Euphrosyne, Thalia are the individuals.
Pausanias gives Lamia and others as parents; Zeus is not the Sibyl's father in this setting.
Thalia the Muse and Thalia the Grace are two beings; Zeus is father of both but the links must be separated by figure.
Sisyphus is son of Aeolus; Jove is not his father.
Macar is a son of Aeolus or Helios, not of Jove.
Personified abstraction without firm ancient source as Zeus's child.
Tyche is usually an Oceanid, not clearly Jove's child.
Kairos is a personification, not Zeus's child in any firm source.
Bellona is a Roman war goddess, not Jove's child in the tradition.
Hesiod makes Eris a child of Night.
Pallas the Titan or giant is confused with Pallas Athena; Pallas is not Jove's child.
Eetion is Iasion's alias; not clearly Jove's son.
Hermus is a river, unsupported as Jove's child.
Erato in the Aeneid is a Muse or a different Erato; Zeus is not her father there.
Editor ruled Inachus not Argus's father; the Argus of Pausanias differs, Zeus father is for Argus son of Niobe.
Editor rules Midas parent of Xanthus right only in Hesiod; Zeus link is a horse or river confusion.

identity.detail: Jupiter matches Jove; Zeus is the Greek counterpart, which the site merges, so no split is needed.
Auge is the Tegean priestess, daughter of Aleus and mother of Telephus by Heracles; the match is correct.
Thoas, son of Ornytion and prince of Corinth, matches the Wikidata entry. Pausanias supports both listed links.
Leda, wife of Tyndareus, is the right match. Thestius as her father is the common tradition (Apollodorus, Pausanias), and the flag only reflects different mothers and fathers in other traditions.
Mopsus the Lapith seer, son of Ampycus (Ampyx), is correctly matched; Ampycus is simply the Latin form of Ampyx.
Thalia in the Iliad is the Nereid listed in the catalogue of sea nymphs (Il. 18.39). Wikidata's Thaleia, Nereid daughter of Nereus and Doris, is the same being.
Wikidata match is Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus by Zeus. No other names are attached to her.

The match is Ascalaphus, king of the Minyans at Orchomenus and son of Ares, which fits the book. The Theoi parents Acheron and Gorgyra/Orphne belong to the other Ascalaphus, the Underworld figure, but the tree has no link from them, so nothing needs fixing.
Wikidata match is Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus; no other names to check.

Elephenor, king of the Abantes of Euboea, son of Chalcodon, matches the Wikidata entry. The Pausanias passage names Chalcodon as his father, so the flag about differing parents does not indicate an error.
The Wikidata match is Philoctetes, son of Poeas. Poeas and Poias are two spellings of the same father, so both links are right and need no change.
Helenus is the Trojan seer son of Priam and Hecuba, so the match is correct and he has no other names.

links.reason: The editor ruled this right in this book, but the Coroneus passage is spoken by a different Coronis, the crow who was once a maiden, daughter of Phocian king Coroneus. She is not Apollo's lover; the Thessalian Coronis is Phlegyas' daughter.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Thessalian Coronis, Apollo's lover and mother of Asclepius. The book also has a separate Coronis, the crow, so the Coroneus link belongs to her.

links.reason: Etias is not a child of Aeneas in the tradition Pausanias follows; the link is unsupported and sits oddly with Aeneas's known children (Ascanius, Silvius, Euryleon).
Thrasybulus is not a known son of Aeneas; the link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Aeneas; the epithets 'Anchises' son' refer to him.

links.reason: A group (the Peliades) is listed as one person; the daughters (Alcestis, Asteropea, Antinoe and others) should be named individually, not as one entry.

identity.detail: Pelias of Iolcus, son of Poseidon and Tyro, is correctly matched.
Erato here is the Arcadian nymph, wife of Arcas and prophetess of Pan, matching the Wikidata entry; not the Muse Erato.
Antiochus III the Great fits Pausanias' Antiochus, who was defeated by the Romans at Thermopylae in 191 BC.

links.reason: Pausanias' Clymenus (Chthonia's brother in Hermion, a cult title of Hades) is not a sibling of Demeter in Hesiod, who names only Hades as her brother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Demeter herself; Ceres, Deo and Doso are all her names.
Diomedes son of Tydeus, king of Argos, is the Trojan War hero; the Wikidata match is correct. Aegialia (Aegiale), daughter of Adrastus, is his wife in Apollodorus, so the spouse link stands.
Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle, the Argive Epigonus, matches Wikidata. Strabo's passage in the Hesiod fragment refers to the same son of Amphiaraus.
Strife is Eris, and the match is correct.
Maron, priest of Apollo at Ismarus and son of Euanthes in the Odyssey, is the right match. Other traditions name Dionysus, Silenus or Oenopion as his father, but the book follows Euanthes.
Perseis is the Oceanid wife of Helios, mother of Aeetes and Circe (Hesiod, Theogony 956-962); the Wikidata match Perse is correct.
Tyro daughter of Salmoneus is the correct match.
Lacedaemon, son of Zeus and Taygete, husband of Sparta, is the right match.
Lycomedes, king of the Dolopians on Scyros, is the right match. He is the father of Deidameia, and the book's sentence says so.

links.reason: Metamorphoses' Moon is Selene/Luna, not Apollo's sister; Diana is his twin, and the editor ruled Selene is no sibling or relative of his.
Hesiod's catalogue does not make Scylla his child; Scylla is the daughter of Phorcys/Crataeis or Phorbas/Hecate, and Apollo is not named a parent.
Hilaira is the Leucippid, daughter of Leucippus, wife of Castor; Pausanias does not make her Apollo's daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Apollo; the other names (Phoebus, Far-darter, Silverbow) are his epithets. Spouse Urania is a Wikidata oddity, not a marriage the book tells.

Idas son of Aphareus (Apollonius calls him Aphareus' son; Poseidon as divine father is a variant), brother of Lynceus, husband of Marpessa. The Wikidata match is correct and the other names are his epithets.
Venilia matches the Roman nymph/deity, mother of Canens by Janus in Ovid's Metamorphoses 14 and of Turnus by Daunus in Virgil's Aeneid 10, so the links are acceptable.

Wikidata's Admete is the daughter of Eurystheus and Antimache, matching Apollodorus's Admete, for whom Heracles fetched the belt of Hippolyta. The Wikidata mother field listing Admete beside Antimache looks like a data glitch, but it does not affect this book's link.

links.reason: Picus is Saturn's son in Roman tradition (Virgil, Ovid), but this is Pindar's Greek Kronos. Cronus and Saturn are different figures in the Roman context here, so the link is treated as a namesake mix-up.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Cronus; the names Kronos and Cronus are the same being.
Wikidata's Anteros is the god of requited love, the same being Pausanias describes at Athens and Elis. Aphrodite and Ares as parents agree with Theoi and the usual tradition.
Augeas of Elis is the right match; no other names are attached.

Amphion of Thebes, twin of Zethus, son of Zeus (Jove) and Antiope, husband of Niobe. The Wikidata match is correct. The two Niobe spouse links are duplicates of one real marriage, so nothing needs fixing.

Pausanias' Fortune (Tyche) matches Tyche; Hesiod Theogony 360 and Homeric Hymn to Demeter make her a daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, and Pausanias (4.30.4) follows Pindar in calling her a daughter of Zeus, which is a variant. Neither parent link is wrong.

links.reason: Pausanias' Polydectes is the Spartan king, son of Eunomus and father of Charillus; he is not the Seriphian king of Apollodorus, whose brother is Dictys.
Eunomus is father of the Spartan Polydectes in Pausanias; Apollodorus' Seriphian Polydectes is son of Magnes (or Poseidon) and Cerebia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Seriphian king, correct for Apollodorus; the Spartan Polydectes is a separate person.
Molossus is the son of Neoptolemus and Andromache. Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, so the tree's father link is correct and the Wikidata match fits.
Aerope, daughter of Catreus, is the right match. In Apollodorus she marries Plisthenes, who is Atreus's son in some versions, so the link matches the book's own text.
Micythus, son of Choerus, tyrant of Rhegium and Zancle, matches Pausanias' Micythus of Rhegium who dedicated offerings at Olympia.
Dolius is Penelope's gardener-slave in the Odyssey, and the Wikidata match is the same person.
Pisistratus is the Athenian tyrant, father of Hippias and Hipparchus, as Pausanias says; the match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Antiochus III only a 'descendant of Seleucus Nicator', not his son; he was a great-great-grandson, so the direct parent link is a misread.

links.link: Antiochus, father of Seleucus parent_of Seleucus
links.reason: Pausanias's 'Seleucus the son of Antiochus' is Seleucus II Callinicus, slain by Ptolemy (a Ptolemaic king in the passage), not Seleucus I Nicator; Seleucus I's father Antiochus is a different link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Seleucus I Nicator is right for the Seleucus Nicator named in Pausanias; the other Seleucus (son of Antiochus) is Seleucus II and should be kept apart.
Ganymede, son of Tros, is the Trojan cup-bearer; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Cretan king Idomeneus, son of Deucalion, so it is the right being. No other names are listed.
Wikidata's Chryseis is the daughter of Chryses in the Iliad, so the match is the right being. The name Astynome is a later writers' name for her, not someone else.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group taken for a person; the sons should be named individually.

identity.detail: Heracles is the right match; Alcides is a real patronymic name for him.

links.reason: Pausanias tells of Achilles and Helen united on the White Island after death, which is a posthumous union and not a marriage; under the editor's rule it counts as a lover.
Helen left Menelaus for Paris, her abductor or lover; her marriage was to Menelaus, and the editor's rule treats non-marriage links as lovers.
Theseus abducted the young Helen and she was rescued by her brothers; this was not a marriage.

links.link: Helen parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias says Helen bore Iphigenia to Theseus, but this link is a different tradition from the book's story, and Iphigenia is the daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra here.

identity.detail: Helen of Troy is the right match; Tyndarid is simply an epithet, not a separate person.
The match is the king of Phthia, son of Actor, who purified Peleus and gave him his daughter Antigone. No other names are attached.

links.reason: The quoted passage lists Tegean votive offerings (Callisto, Arcas, Elatus, Aphidas, Azan) and says nothing of a daughter Laodamia of Amyclas; Pausanias does not name her as Amyclas's child in that sentence.

identity.detail: Amyclas of Sparta, son of Lacedaemon and Sparta, is the right match.
Tyndareus, king of Sparta, husband of Leda, matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.
The Wikidata match is the Argo's builder, the son of Polybus or Arestor. This book's Argus is the son of Phrixus and Chalciope, who is a different person. The match should be removed or replaced.
Wikidata match is Lausus, son of Mezentius, in the Aeneid. The link Mezentius as father is right (Aeneid X, Mezentius laments 'My son!').
Wikidata's Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, matches the book's sacrificed daughter; the parent links are right.
Teucer, son of Telamon and half-brother of Ajax, is the right match. No other names are given.
Belus, king of Egypt and father of Aegyptus and Danaus, matches Wikidata. Poseidon and Libya as parents are the standard tradition.

links.reason: Anaxibia is Nestor's wife in some accounts (daughter of Cratieus/Atreus' sister in Apollodorus), but in Homeric tradition Antilochus' mother is Eurydice or Anaxibia; the link is a variant mother, not a confusion, so it should be kept.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Pylian prince Antilochus, son of Nestor.
Wikidata match is Orestes, son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Opheltes' father is Lycurgus of Nemea (king of Nemea), not the Arcadian son of Aleus or the Athenian orator.
Eucosmus' tomb at Argos/Nemea context belongs to a different Lycurgus (the Nemean king), not Aleus' son or the orator.
Ancaeus' father Lycurgus is the Arcadian son of Aleus, not the Athenian orator.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Lycurgus here is a mythical figure (Arcadian son of Aleus, Nemean father of Opheltes), not Lycurgus of Athens, the 4th-century BC orator. Several Lycurguses are merged under one name.
Wikidata 'siren' is the right group of beings; the Argonautica names Achelous and Terpsichore as their parents, as Theoi confirms.

links.reason: Pityocamptes (Sinis) is a different bandit, usually son of Polypemon by Sylea in some accounts, but in Pausanias Sinis is a separate figure; Wikidata mixes Procrustes with Polypemon, father of Sinis. Procrustes/Damastes is a different bandit from Sinis's father.

identity.detail: In Pausanias, Polypemon is the father of Sinis (Pityocamptes) and is not Procrustes; the Wikidata match merged them. Procrustes (Damastes) is a separate bandit; the alias Procrustes should be split off.

links.reason: Rhadamanthus married Alcmena after Amphitryon's death in Apollodorus and Hesiod's tradition, but the Iliad doesn't say this and the editor reads non-primary spouse links as lovers; he is not her husband in the Iliad.

identity.detail: x

The book names two Deucalions. The flood hero is the son of Prometheus and father of Hellen, with Pyrrha as wife. The Cretan Deucalion is the son of Minos and father of Idomeneus. Their relatives should be kept apart. The Wikidata match to the flood Deucalion is right for the first. Amphictyon and Orestheus follow the flood Deucalion in the sources and Molus belongs to the Cretan one.
Leches, son of Poseidon and Pirene and eponym of the Corinthian port Lechaeum, matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: A group taken for a person. Wikidata lists a naiad as mother, but Metamorphoses names no mother, and Euboea is the individual named in the tradition, not the Naiads as a class.

identity.detail: Glaucus of Anthedon, the sea-god, matches the Wikidata entry. Nothing in the data suggests another being.

links.reason: Medea married Aegeus at Athens (Apollodorus, Ovid) and bore Medus; the check flagged two spouses, but this is a second marriage, so it is not a lover link.
A group of children is taken for a person; her sons are already named individually (Mermerus, Pheres).
Eriopis is not a child of Medea in the sources; Pausanias' Eriopis belongs to another figure.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Colchian sorceress Medea; no other names are listed.

Peleus is the Phthian king, husband of Thetis and father of Achilles; the match is correct. Antigone (daughter of Eurytion) was his earlier wife per Apollodorus, so the second spouse is a genuine marriage and needs no change.

links.reason: Ancient sources make Oeagrus the son of Charops or Pierus and Methone, not Ares; Apollonius's Argonautica gives no father, and the Ares link rests on a Wikidata variant that no source in the book supports.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Thracian king Oeagrus, father of Orpheus.

links.reason: Narcissus is the son of the river god Cephisus and the nymph Liriope (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3); Selene is not his mother, and the editor already rules out Artemis as his mother.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the moon goddess Selene, and 'Moon' is simply her name in English.
The Wikidata match is the eponym of Cleonae, daughter of Asopus; the book names her as such, so the match is correct.
Wikidata match is Mausolus, the Carian satrap and husband of Artemisia II of Caria; this fits the book's sentence.

links.reason: This is a group, not a single person. The Peliades are already covered by the named daughters, such as Alcestis, Asteropea and Antinoe.

identity.detail: x

Wikidata's Idomeneus is the Cretan king of the Trojan War, which matches the Odyssey's Idomeneus. The parent link to Deucalion agrees with Wikidata and with the editor's accepted Minos-Deucalion link, so the flag about parents is not a real problem.
Actaeon, son of Aristaeus and Autonoë, grandson of Cadmus, is the hero Ovid names with the epithets Autonoëian hero and Hyantian youth. The match is correct.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Midas's mother is Cybele, whom the Metamorphoses identifies with the Phrygian Great Mother; this is a syncretic link, not a Hesiodic child of Rhea. The Argonautica's Idaean mother is Rhea herself, whose children are the Olympians, and Midas is not one of them.

identity.detail: Rhea matches the Titan Rhea; 'Idaean mother' is her Cretan/Phrygian cult title and refers to the same goddess in the Argonautica.
Wikidata match is the Corinthian hero Bellerophon; the alias 'Aiolid king' fits him as a descendant of Aeolus through Sisyphus and Glaukos.
Parthenopeus in Wikidata is the Arcadian Seven against Thebes hero, which matches this character.
Wikidata match is Arachne, the Lydian weaver of Ovid Metamorphoses 6; no other names are attached.
The Wikidata match is the Calydonian king Œneus; no other names look like different beings.

Wikidata's Tecmessa is the Phrygian princess, captive and wife of Ajax, and mother of Eurysaces. The book's lines say she was taken by Ajax's spear and then made his wife, so the spouse link is right. Wikipedia names her father as Teleutas, while Wikidata gives Teuthras. Sophocles' Ajax names her father as Teleutas, and Teuthras is a variant. This is a naming variant, not a different person.

links.reason: Apollonius Rhodius 3.1036 makes Hecate daughter of Perses; Zeus as father appears only in a scholiast citing Musaeus, and the book does not tell it.

identity.detail: Hecate matches; Brimo and Crataeis are her epithets, not other persons.
Wikidata match is Cerberus, the hound of Hades. Both parent links (Echidna and Typhaon/Typhoeus) are right, so no fix is needed.

links.reason: Hesiod's Catalogue (Eugammon's Telegony) has Telegonus, Odysseus' son by Circe, marry Penelope after Odysseus' death. It is a marriage, but only in the Hesiod tradition, and Ovid's Metamorphoses does not tell it, so it should not be kept in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Penelope, wife of Odysseus and daughter of Icarius, is the right match.
Brontes is one of the Cyclopes who work at Vulcan's forge in the Aeneid (8.425). The Hesiodic Brontes is a son of Uranus and Gaia, so the match and the links are correct.
Polybus of Corinth is the king who raised Oedipus, and the match is correct. The book names his wife Merope, one of the traditional names Wikipedia lists.
Opheltes, called Archemorus, son of Lycurgus of Nemea, is the right match. Pausanias names Lycurgus as his father, which agrees with Wikidata, so the parent flag is no problem.
Wikidata match is Agave, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, mother of Pentheus. No other names are listed, so nothing needs splitting.
Cayster is the river god of the Lydian river, and Caystrus is the same being.

Erinyes/Eumenides/Furies is the same group of goddesses. Pausanias (1.28.6, 2.11.4, 8.34) calls them Semnai Theai or Eumenides and gives Night, or Earth and Ouranos, as parents; both links have ancient support.
Asopus is the river god, son of Oceanus and Tethys; the match is fine.
Asteria, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, sister of Leto, mother of Hecate by Perses, matches Wikidata.

Ascanius, also called Iulus, is the son of Aeneas and Creusa in the Aeneid, and the Wikidata match is this same person. The Ilus name is a variant of Ascanius and does not refer to a different being. Wikidata's mother entry for Lavinia reflects a rival tradition (Livy) and does not affect this book's links.
Nemesis (Rhamnousia) is the right being; no other names are listed. Both parentages (Nyx per Hesiod, Oceanus per Pausanias) are attested, so both links stay.

The Wikidata match is Tantalus son of Thyestes, but most of this book's links concern the Lydian Tantalus, father of Pelops, Niobe and Broteas. Pausanias names the son of Thyestes as a separate person, Clytemnestra's first husband.

Wikidata match is Augustus himself. The alias Cæsar is a title he used, and in Ovid it refers to him and to Julius Cæsar by context. The book's sentence calls Julius his father in the adoptive sense, which is fine for this book, so the parent link is kept.
Myron of Eleutherae, the sculptor, is the right match. Lycius was his son, as Pausanias says.

links.reason: Metamorphoses' Moon is Luna/Selene taken for Diana; the editor ruled Selene unrelated to Apollo.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, not of Apollo; no source gives Apollo as her father.

identity.detail: Wikidata Apollo is the right god. Kyrene and Cyrene appear as separate lover links, which is a duplicate spelling and not a different being.

Polydorus son of Cadmus and Harmonia, king of Thebes, father of Labdacus, is the right match. Pausanias' Eurycrates is a different tradition (a Spartan king, son of Anaxandrus), but Pausanias does list Polydorus as Eurycrates' ancestor? No, keep as given.
Memnon, king of Aethiopia and son of Tithonus and Eos, is the right match. Aurora is Eos in Pausanias. Wikidata's mother Cissia is a variant tradition, not a problem.
Panopeus, son of Phocus and twin of Crisus, is the right match. Hesiod mentions Panopeus as father of Epeius and Aegle (Theseus's lover), consistent with Wikidata.

links.reason: Ovid's Moon is Selene/Luna, not Diana; the editor ruled Selene is not Apollo's sibling or relative.
Scylla is usually daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis (Hesiod's attribution to Apollo is unsupported); likely confused with another Scylla.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, wife of Castor; not Apollo's child.
Lycomedes is not Apollo's son in Pausanias; likely confusion with another Lycomedes.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Apollo; the aliases Far-Darter, Phoebus and Lycian Apollo are all epithets of him.
Wikidata's Pentheus is the Theban king, son of Echion and Agave, as in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

links.reason: Hesione was a Trojan captive given to Telamon as war prize (concubine), mother of Teucer in some accounts; not a wife by the editor's rule.

identity.detail: Telamon, son of Aeacus and father of Ajax and Teucer, matches Wikidata.
Nereids as a group of sea nymphs, the daughters of Nereus and Doris, matches Wikidata. No other names are attached.
Wikidata Hyllus is the son of Heracles and Deianira; match is correct.
Aglaophon is the Thasian painter, father of Polygnotus, as Pausanias says; the Wikidata match fits.

links.reason: A chorus is a group in Aeschylus' play, not a person; the individual Oceanids are his children.
Hesiod makes Theia a Titan sister who marries Hyperion; she is also listed as an Oceanid, but never as Oceanus' wife. His wife is Tethys.
The river Xanthus (Scamander) is a Trojan river god. The editor's Midas parent of Xanthus note concerns a different Xanthus, so the link may confuse two figures.
Passalus is a Cercopes figure, and the link looks like a confusion with Oceanus' children. Hesiod does not make him Oceanus' son.
Acmon is a Cercopes name or a Dactyl. The link looks like a confusion with the Oceanid in Hesiod.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Oceanus. No other names are listed.
Hesione, daughter of Laomedon of Troy, is the right match. Telamon takes her as war prize and later wife/concubine; Podarces (Priam) is her brother per Apollodorus.
Mezentius is the Etruscan king and father of Lausus in the Aeneid. The Wikidata match is correct and he has no other names.
Wikidata match is the Titan Atlas, son of Iapetus; no other names to separate. Note the Libyan or Arcadian Atlas is not confused here.

Megara is the Theban princess, daughter of Creon and wife of Heracles; the Wikidata match is correct. Kreon is the same person as Creon, so the parent link agrees with Wikidata. Iolaus as a later spouse is a tradition (Megara given to Iolaus after Heracles), not an error.

links.reason: Pausanias' Ætolus son of Oxylus (brother of Laias) is a different, later Ætolus from Endymion's son, the eponym of Aetolia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Endymion's son Aetolus; the Oxylus link belongs to a separate namesake, not an alternate name.

Philammon, son of Apollo and Chione (Ovid Met. 11), is the right Wikidata match. The tree has Philammon as the father of Thamyris from Pausanias, which is consistent with the tradition. Nothing needs changing.
The Wikidata match is the eponym Epidaurus, and he has no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Dipoinos and Skyllis pupils of Daedalus (Cretan tradition), not his sons; Dipoinos is not his child in Metamorphoses or the Theoi listing.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian craftsman Daedalus; Dædalus is just the Latin spelling, no wrong names.
Wikidata's Giants is the race of Gigantes, which fits Hesiod's Theogony (185), where they are born from Earth and the blood of Uranus. The link Earth parent_of Giants is correct, so it is not listed.

Wikidata's Anaxagoras is the king of Argos, son of Megapenthes (or of his son Argeus), the figure Pausanias 2.18.4 mentions. The philosopher Anaxagoras is a different person, but nothing here confuses the two.
The match is correct: Amythaon, son of Cretheus and Tyro, father of Melampus and Bias. No other names are listed.
Wikidata's Oenone is the nymph wife of Paris, daughter of the river god Cebren; the match is correct.

links.link: Uranus parent_of Chorus of the Furies
links.reason: The Chorus is a group, not a person. The individual Furies (Tisiphone, Allecto, Megaera) are already linked as Uranus's children.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the primordial sky god Uranus, and 'Heaven' is only his name in translation.
Salamis is the nymph, daughter of Asopus and Metope, who bore Cychreus to Poseidon. The Wikidata match is correct and she has no other names that belong to someone else.
Wikidata match is Patroclus, son of Menoetius, companion of Achilles. Menoetius and Menoethius are spelling variants of the same father, so both links are right.

links.reason: Diomedes' father is Tydeus, son of Oeneus; Oeneus is his grandfather, so the parent link confuses generations.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Diomedes is the son of Tydeus and king of Argos, which matches this Diomede.

In Hesiod's Theogony the Cyclopes (Brontes, Steropes, Arges) are children of Heaven and Earth, which matches Wikidata and Theoi. The Wikidata match is the Cyclopes as a group, and the links are right.

Pausanias's Lelex, king of Laconia and later of Megara, is the son of Poseidon and Libye. The Wikidata match is the same being. 'Leleges' names the people he ancestors, not a separate person, but this is only a minor alias issue.
Pirithoüs is the Lapith king, son of Ixion (or Zeus), friend of Theseus; the match is correct.
Wikidata match is Hesiod the poet; no other names to question.
The match is the Nereid Galatea, beloved of Acis and pursued by Polyphemus, which is who Ovid describes. She is not the post-antiquity statue of Pygmalion.

links.reason: Hermus is a river, a son of Okeanos and Tethys in Hesiod, not a child of Zeus.
Eetion in Hesiod is Iasion's variant name, not a son of Zeus; here it confuses the two.
Pausanias gives the Sibyl as a daughter of Zeus and Lamia in some accounts, but the editor accepts the Lamia and Theodorus parentage only in pausanias, so it should not be in this book.
Opportunity (Kairos) as son of Zeus is only a Pausanias personification and is not used in Pindar.
Macar is the Lesbian or Rhodian king, a son of Helios or Aiolos, not of Zeus.
Duplicate of Athena, the same goddess under a variant spelling.
A group taken for a person.
A group taken for a person.
A group taken for a person; the individual Muses are listed separately.
Personification in Pindar's praise, not a genealogy.
Personification in Pindar's praise, not a genealogy.
Hesiod's Theogony makes Themis Zeus's second wife and Wikidata lists her as spouse; should be spouse not lover.
Pandora was a gift to Epimetheus; Hesiod does not make her Zeus's lover.
Vulcan is the Roman Hephaistos; this is a Roman-name duplicate.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match joins Zeus with Jupiter, a Roman equivalent; Jove is Jupiter and Aitnaian, Nemeaian and Kronian are cult epithets of Zeus. Kronidai is a plural patronymic and does not name Zeus alone.
The Wikidata match is Hippothoon, the Attic eponymous hero and son of Poseidon and Alope. No other names are listed.

links.link: Danaus parent_of Chorus of the Danaids
links.reason: The Chorus of the Danaids in Aeschylus is a group of the daughters, not a person; the individual daughters are already linked.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Danaus is the king of Libya and Argos, the same being as in Apollodorus.

Wikidata's Orestes is the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, which matches Pindar's Orestes. All the links are standard: Tisamenus is his son by Hermione, Penthilus is his son by Erigone, and Hermione is his wife.
Wikidata match is Cerberus, the hound of Hades; no other names listed. Parents Typhon and Echidna are confirmed by Hesiod and Theoi.

links.reason: The Pausanias sentence lists Adrastus son of Talaus as an associate of Polynices on the expedition; it does not make Polynices his father. Talaus is his father.

identity.detail: Adrastus, king of Argos and leader of the Seven, son of Talaus, is the right match.

links.reason: The book's Hesiod passage makes Anaxibia a child of Pleisthenes and Cleolla, so she is Atreus's granddaughter. The Wikidata link skips a generation (the other tradition, in which Anaxibia is Atreus's daughter, is not told in this book).

identity.detail: Wikidata's Atreus is the king of Mycenae, son of Pelops, and is the right match.
Wikidata's Antilochus is Nestor's son, the Pylian prince at Troy, and the book's Antilochus is the same person. The Nestor link is stated in the book itself.
Hypermnestra is the Danaid who spared her husband Lynceus, and the Wikidata match is this same person. She has no other names that need splitting.
Coön, eldest son of Antenor and Theano, wounded Agamemnon and was killed by him; this matches Pausanias' mention of Coon in the Trojan context. Both parent links are correct.

Crantor, son of Amyntor, is the squire of Peleus killed by Peleus's friend Ovid's centaur Pedasus? In Metamorphoses 12 Crantor is Peleus's armor-bearer, killed by Demoleon, and he was given as a hostage to Peleus by Amyntor, so the match is right.
Galaxaura is the Oceanid in Hesiod's Theogony catalogue, and the Wikidata match is the same being. Her parents Ocean and Tethys are correct.

Wikidata's Tydeus is the Aetolian hero, son of Oeneus and father of Diomedes. Pausanias calls him son of Oeneus, which agrees. The tree's other links (Deipyle as wife, Gorge as mother) are standard and come from Apollodorus and Wikidata.

Athamas is the Boeotian king, son of Aeolus, husband of Nephele, Ino and Themisto. Wikidata's father list (Minyas, Aeolus) reflects variant traditions, not a different being. The two flagged spouses (Ino and Themisto) are both wives in Apollodorus and Pausanias, so no change.

links.reason: Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon; Pausanias names Hyperion as a son of Aegisthus's era? No: he is a son of Orestes' line or a Titan namesake, so the link confuses two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the king of Mycenae, Agamemnon; no other names to dispute.
Hesione is the Trojan princess, daughter of Laomedon, who was given to Telamon and had Teucer by him. The match is correct and no other names are attached.
Nereids is a group of sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus and Doris, and the Wikidata match is the same group.

links.reason: A group label, not a person; Pausanias names Medeus and Eriopis (Cinaethon) and Mermerus and Pheres elsewhere, so the collective link is redundant.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason; no other names to question.

links.link: Aegyptus parent_of Chorus of the Danaids
links.reason: The Chorus of the Danaids are the daughters of Danaus, not of Aegyptus; Aegyptus fathered the fifty sons who pursued them.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Aegyptus, son of Belus and brother of Danaus.

Orion the hunter of myth is the being meant here, even though the Wikipedia description covers the constellation. The Hesiod fragment names Euryale and Poseidon as his parents, which matches the tradition.
Althaea, daughter of Thestius and wife of Oeneus, is the right match; no other names are involved.
The Wikidata match is the right being: Polemocrates, son of Machaon, worshipped at Eua. He has no other names.

pausanias/artemis.name: Artemis
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Hegemone, Artemis

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Hegemone, one of the two Athenian Charites, which is not the goddess Artemis. Hegemone is also a cult title of Artemis at Athens, but this entry is a different being. The match should be replaced with the goddess Artemis. The cult epithets (Alphean, Dictynna, Agrotera, Euclea, Hymnia, Limnas, Limnatis, Coccoca, Apanchomene) are all titles of Artemis and need no split.

links.reason: Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived. Pausanias' Erythea (a Hesperid nymph) is not his child, and Theoi lists no such child for Geryon.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Geryon is the giant of Erytheia, as the Aeneid names him.

links.reason: Pausanias' Polydamas, son of Nicias, is the huge Thessalian athlete of Skotoussa, not a child of the Athenian general Nicias, so the link belongs to a different Nicias.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Nicias is the otherwise unknown father of the athlete Polydamas of Skotoussa. The Wikidata match, the Athenian general of the Peloponnesian War, is a different person.
Wikidata's Neoptolemus is this very being, the son of Achilles and Deidameia. Pyrrhus is his own other name, not a different person.
Cimon is the Athenian general, son of Miltiades, as Pausanias states; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Metra is the daughter of Erysichthon, wife of Autolycus' namesake line? Actually no source gives Autolycus a wife Metra; Metamorphoses has no such marriage, so the link is a misread.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Autolycus, son of Hermes and Chione, the thief of Parnassus and grandfather of Odysseus; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is the right Philoctetes, son of Poeas. Poeas and Poias are spelling variants of the same father, so both links are fine.
Wikidata match is Iris, the rainbow goddess and messenger; Thaumas is her father in Hesiod and the Iliad's tradition, so the link is right.

links.reason: Endeis, mother of Peleus and wife of Aiakos, was daughter of Cheiron, not a Nereid; the Pausanias link confuses her with a Nereid sister of Thetis, and Theoi lists her as no Nereid.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Nereid Thetis, mother of Achilles. Neptune as a spouse in Wikidata is a Roman-equation oddity, but it does not affect this book's tree.
Wikidata match is Menoetius the Titan, son of Iapetus; no other names are listed. The Themis mother link in Wikidata is already ruled wrong by the editor and is not in this tree.
Wikidata match is the right Aegisthus, son of Thyestes; the links are fine. Erigone as his daughter follows Pausanias and the usual tradition, so it stays.
Lysander, the Spartan admiral, son of Aristocritus, is the right match; the book's sentences confirm the father.
Inachus is the river god and first king of Argos, son of Oceanus and Tethys. The Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Pisus in Pausanias is a different figure (son of Perieres of Elis-line tradition); Apollodorus does not give Perieres this son, and Pausanias' Pisus is a separate figure.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Messenian king Perieres, son of Aeolus and husband of Gorgophone.

links.reason: Nicostratus is the son of Menelaus by a slave woman (Pieris the Aetolian or Tereis), not Helen; Apollodorus' Epitome gives Helen only Hermione, and in Hesiod Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus by another mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the son of Menelaus; fine.
Mardonius is the Persian general, son of Gobryas, who fought at Plataea; the match is correct and he has no other names.
Thrasymedes is Nestor's son from Pylos, and the Wikidata match is correct.

Wikidata's Medusa is the Gorgon. In Pausanias, the rationalized account of a Libyan queen, daughter of Phorcus, who fought Perseus, is this book's own telling of the same figure, so it is not a separate being.
Orchamus is Ovid's Persian king, father of Leucothoë; the Wikidata match fits and no other names are listed.
Wikidata's Lampetia is the same being. Odyssey 12 names Hyperion as the sun-god, which here is an epithet for Helios, so Hyperion as parent is right for this book. Neaera as mother is also right.

links.link: Hercules sibling_of Iphiclus, son of Amphitryon
links.reason: Duplicate of Iphicles, Hercules' half-brother, already linked under that name; the 'Iphiclus' form is a variant spelling of the same person.
Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, who is already linked from the book's own sentence.
Misspelled duplicate of Tlepolemus.
Spelling duplicate of Tlepolemus.
Statius' Chromis is a Theban warrior and not a son of Hercules in Apollodorus; unsupported.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group taken for a person; the sons are Therimachus, Creontiades and Deicoon.

identity.detail: Heracles is the correct match; Alcides and Hercules are the same hero.

Demonice, daughter of Agenor and Epicaste, is the Aetolian princess who bore Ares sons including Evenus and Thestius (Apollodorus 1.7.7 and 1.7.4 give Agenor's children as Demonice and Porthaon). The Wikidata match is the same being.
Anaxias/Anaxis, son of Castor and Hilaeira, matches Pausanias' Anaxis; the Castor link is correct.

links.reason: In Hesiod's Theogony, Eros arises on his own beside Earth and Tartarus; Chaos is not his parent. Theoi's note does not support this link in this book.
Hesiod (Theogony 116) has Chaos come first, with no parents. Chronos as parent is from the Orphic tradition, which this book does not follow.

identity.detail: Chaos matches the primordial being; no problem with the match or the names.

links.reason: Paris took Helen to Troy; the editor's rule reads every spouse link other than the marriage to Menelaus as a lover, and Menelaus is her husband.
Theseus abducted Helen as a girl (Pausanias, Apollodorus), but this was never a marriage, so it is a lover link.
The union with Achilles on the White Island is a post-death tradition (Pausanias), not a marriage, so it is a lover link.

identity.detail: Helen of Troy is the right match.

links.reason: Lucina is a title of Juno (or Diana) as birth goddess, not a daughter of Ops; the link rests on a cult title taken for a person.

identity.detail: Ops is the Roman goddess, consort of Saturn; the match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias (Hermione) calls Clymenus a Hermionian, a son of Phoroneus or Foroneus who founded a Demeter cult. He is not a sibling of Demeter, so this confuses a cult title or founder with a god. Hades as Clymenus is a separate epithet, so the link is unsupported.

Despoina is the Arcadian cult title of Persephone, so Despœna is the same being as Persephone and not a second child. Pausanias (8.37) says she is Demeter's daughter by Poseidon, which makes her a separate cult figure there. She duplicates the Persephone link.

identity.detail: Ceres is the Roman Demeter. The match is acceptable for this being.

The Wikidata match is Acusilaus of Argos, the 6th-century BC logographer, son of Cabas. The book's Acusilaus is the mythical son of Odysseus and Penelope in the Telegony, so the two are different beings.

links.reason: In the Aeneid Pilumnus is Turnus's grandsire (his ancestor), not Venilia's husband. Virgil names Daunus as Turnus's father (10.616). Pilumnus is also Daunus's ancestor, so this link confuses the generations.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses (14.332) Canens is the daughter of Janus and Venilia. The Aeneid says nothing of this, and the link is from another book and shouldn't be here.

identity.detail: Venilia matches the nymph, mother of Turnus. The Wikipedia blurb mixes her with the sea deity.
Mopsus the Lapith seer, son of Ampycus (Ampyx), is the right match. In the Thebaid he is the Argive seer, son of Ampycus, so the Wikidata match fits.

links.reason: In Aeneid 10.76 Venilia is Turnus's mother and the wife of Daunus, not of Pilumnus. Pilumnus is Turnus's ancestor (Aeneid 9.4, 10.619), so the link confuses him with Daunus.

identity.detail: Wikidata's spouse Danaë comes from a confusion with Pilumnus, the Italian founder of Ardea. In Servius, Danaë was said to have come to Italy and married Pilumnus. The Roman nature deity Pilumnus and the Aeneid's ancestor of Turnus are likely the same being, but the Danaë link is not in Virgil.

The Wikidata match is Antimachus of Colophon, a poet of about 400 BC. Pausanias' Antimachus is a mythical Argive, the grandfather of Oetylus' eponym (Oitylos), son of Amphianax. These are different people, so the match should be dropped.
Wikidata's Peitho is the personification of persuasion, which is the same being. Pausanias mentions her cult at Athens and Megara, with no sign of a different person under the name.
Eleusis is the eponymous hero of the town; the Wikidata match is this being.
Aleus, king of Tegea and son of Aphidas, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the king of Chios; no other names to dispute.
Manto, daughter of Tiresias, is the right match and has no mismatched names.
Wikidata match is Amphitryon, son of Alcaeus and husband of Alcmena; all links fit this one being.
Philistus of Syracuse, the Sicilian historian, son of Archomenides (Archomenidas), matches the book's sentence.
Wikidata match is Thespia, daughter of Asopus and Metope, eponym of Thespiae; Pausanias' sentence agrees.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses 14, Vertumnus, disguised as an old woman, persuades Pomona and then wins her; they are united as a couple, and Wikidata lists him as her spouse. The quoted sentence only shows his rivalry as a suitor.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Roman fruit goddess Pomona, the same being as in the book.

links.reason: Apollodorus 3.6.4 means the Lycurgus king of Nemea, husband of Eurydice, not the Thracian king; Opheltes belongs to the Nemean Lycurgus.
Aleus's son Lycurgus is the Arcadian of Tegea, not the Thracian king; the editor holds it right for this book, so it belongs to the Arcadian Lycurgus.
Apollodorus 3.9.2 gives Iasus to the Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus, not the Thracian.
Apollodorus 3.9.2 gives Amphidamas to the Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus, not the Thracian.

identity.detail: In this book the name Lycurgus covers three men: the Arcadian son of Aleus (father of Ancaeus, Epochus, Amphidamas, Iasus), the Nemean king husband of Eurydice (father of Opheltes), and the Thracian Edonian king, the Wikidata match, son of Dryas. Only the Thracian fits the match.
Wikidata match is Neoptolemus, son of Achilles and Deidamia; Hermione as his wife is the standard tradition (Pausanias, Euripides), so all links stand.
Wikidata's Atalanta joins the Arcadian and Boeotian huntresses, but Pausanias tells of her as a single figure and notes Schoeneus's Arcadian connection. The match is acceptable.
Wikidata's Laius is the Theban king, father of Oedipus and son of Labdacus; no other names to doubt.

links.link: Cephalus spouse_of Clymene, daughter of Minyas
links.reason: Pausanias gives Clymene as the mother of Iphiclus, but Procris is Cephalus's wife in Ovid; under the editor's rule, a spouse other than the marriage is read as a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Cephalus, son of Deion and Diomede. Ovid's 'son of Æolus' is a variant, not a different person.

links.reason: Lucifer is the morning star, son of Aurora/Cephalus or Astraeus in tradition; Iapetus is not his father, and the editor already ruled Atlas not his father either.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Iapetos is the Titan; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Idas is the Messenian son of Aphareus (or Poseidon) and Arene, the right being; no other names are attached.
Wikidata match is the eponymous queen Sparta, daughter of Eurotas, wife of Lacedaemon; no problem.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemos to Achilles on Skyros but was not his wife in the main tradition; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lover.
Helen and Achilles joined only in the afterlife on Leuke (Pausanias); this was no marriage on earth, so lover is the fit.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the son of Peleus and Thetis; no other names are in doubt.

links.reason: In the Thebaid Mars addresses Mercury as 'brother' only in a loose sense; Mercury is son of Jove and Maia, Mars son of Jove and Juno, so a full sibling link is not supported, and the line is just a courteous address.
Hesiod's Homeric Hymn tradition has Hermes lie with Dryops' daughter; no marriage, so per editor's rule this is a lover.
Pindar's 'Fame' is a personified abstraction, not a child of Hermes.
Faunus is the Roman woodland god, son of Picus; the Hermes-Pan/Faunus link rests on a conflation of Faunus with Pan.

identity.detail: Mercury matches Hermes; the epithets Cyllenian, Maenalian and Tegean are his cult titles, so the names are fine.
Wikidata match is the Cretan judge Rhadamanthus. The Hephaestus entry as father is odd, but that is a Wikidata matter and not a name confusion.
Wikidata's Polybus is the Trojan son of Antenor and Theano, a brother of Acamas, Agenor and others. The Iliad mentions him among Antenor's sons (11.59), so the match is right.
Mopsus the seer of Clarus, son of Manto, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Mopsus the Lapith seer, son of Ampycus (Ampyx), is the Argonaut seer. Ampycus is the same person as Ampyx, so the link is correct.

The Wikipedia description supplied is about Greek flood myths (the floods of Ogyges, Deucalion and Dardanus), not Megarus. Pausanias' Megarus, son of Zeus and a Sithnidian nymph who escaped Deucalion's flood on Mount Gerania, is the Megarian eponym. The Zeus parentage is right, but the description is a poor match and the link should be checked.
Ischys son of Elatus is the Arcadian lover of Coronis; the Wikidata match is the same being.
Amycus is the centaur, son of Ophion, at the Lapith wedding in Ovid's Metamorphoses 12; the match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Cretan prince Althaemenes, son of Catreus; no other names are involved.
Capys, son of Assaracus and father of Anchises, is the Dardanian Capys. The Aeneid's Trojan Capys, companion of Aeneas, is a different man, but nothing in this entry mixes them up.

Wikidata's Neleus is the king of Pylos, son of Tyro and Poseidon, father of Nestor. Nothing indicates a mismatch. Wikidata also lists Hippocoon and Cretheus as fathers, but these are alternative traditions and not errors in the Neleus match.
Wikidata match is the Phoenician princess Astypalaea, mother of Ancaeus by Poseidon in Apollonius; this is the same being.

Wikidata match is Ariadne, daughter of Minos, and no other names are listed, so nothing to fix. Her children Oenopion, Thoas and Ceramus (by Dionysus or Theseus) and her sister Phaedra are all standard tradition.
Atreus matches the king of Mycenae, son of Pelops and Hippodamia.

links.reason: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, is a different figure; Dione is her mother only in a Hyginus-type tradition that is not the Iliad's, and it is a later confusion (Dione as Atlantid) that this book does not tell.

identity.detail: Dione the Titaness matches Wikidata. The Iliad's parents are not stated; Oceanus and Tethys is one Theoi tradition, Uranus and Gaia is the other, so both are acceptable.

links.reason: Pasithea is the wife of Hypnos (Sleep) in Homer (Iliad 14) and Nonnus; Pausanias' line calls her only his beloved, but the tradition makes her his wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Grace Pasithea; no other names.

links.reason: Sicyon is the son of Marathon (Pausanias 2.6.5) or Metion's line in some accounts; Hesiod's Sicyon link is not as a child of Erechtheus. Pausanias also gives Sicyon's father as Erechtheus' descendant in a variant, but the main tradition does not make him Erechtheus' son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian king Erechtheus; no other names are listed.

Wikidata's Tithonus is the Trojan prince, son of Laomedon and lover of Eos, so the match is right. Cephalus as a father is a variant tradition that comes from Wikidata, not from this book, and it is not a link in this tree.
Belus is the Egyptian king, son of Poseidon (Neptune) and Libya, father of Danaus and Aegyptus. Wikidata's match is the same being, and the parent difference is only a Wikidata mother listing.

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, not a person; their eponym Dolion was a son of Silene or Poseidon, not the group itself.

links.link: Poseidon parent_of Phocus, son of Ornytion
links.reason: Phocus son of Ornytion is a different being from the Poseidon-linked Phocus, and Ornytion is his father.

identity.detail: Poseidon matches Wikidata correctly and Neptune is his Roman name.

links.reason: Mercury (Hermes) is a half-brother, son of Maia; the book gives no sibling link to Apollo, so the full-sibling link is a misread of shared father Jupiter.
Book's Moon is Diana/Luna as Apollo's sister, but the editor says Selene is not Apollo's child; the link confuses Selene with Diana.
Apis son of Apollo in Aeschylus is a seer of Argos, not connected to this book's tradition; likely a different Apis, but unconfirmed by Theoi.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus (wife of Castor), not Apollo's child.
Pycimede is Ileus's daughter-line figure, not Apollo's child in the cited tradition.

identity.detail: Match is correct. The names Delian God, Delphian God, Phoebus, Pythius, Paean and Smintheus are epithets of Apollo; Titan in the book refers to the Sun, not Apollo.

Wikidata match is Lachesis, the Moira. Pindar (Olympian 1, Fragment) has Themis as mother of the Moirai by Zeus, and Hesiod's Theogony gives both parentages (Nyx and Zeus with Themis). The Themis link is attested, so keep it.

links.reason: A group node duplicating the individual daughters; Pausanias names Asteropea and Antinoe individually.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Pelias, king of Iolcus, correct.

links.link: Peleus sibling_of Phocus, son of Æacus
links.reason: Pausanias says Phocus was the son of Endeis's sister Thetis (a Nereid-like namesake), so Phocus is Peleus's half-brother only via Aeacus; Pausanias states Phocus was son of Aeacus and Peleus and Telamon were sons of Endeis, so the sibling link is consistent with the book—keep.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Peleus, king of Phthia.
Harpina, daughter of Asopus and Metope, mother of Oenomaus by Ares, matches the Wikidata entry.

Picus, king of Latium, son of Saturn per Ovid's Metamorphoses 14, is the right match. Wikidata's father Mars is a variant tradition, and the book's own line (Saturn) is right for this book. Canens as wife is also right.

links.reason: Erytheia is the island where Geryon lived (Hesiod: 'Erytheia'), not his child; the other book's Erythea as a daughter appears to confuse the place or a nymph of that name with a child of Geryon.

identity.detail: Geryon is the correct match for Geryones, the three-headed son of Chrysaor and Callirrhoe.
Alcidamea is the mother of Bunus by Hermes, as Pausanias (citing Eumelus) states; the Wikidata match is the same being.

links.reason: Themistinoe is wife of Cycnus son of Ares in Hesiod's tradition (or other Cycnus); Pausanias' Cycnus of Colonae married Proclea then Phylonome.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Cycnus is the Poseidon-son king of Colonae, father of Tennes and Hemithea, not the Cycnus son of Ares (killed by Heracles) matched by Wikidata. Ares/Pyrene/Pelopeia parentage belongs to the other Cycnus.
Aesacus is Priam's son who loved Hesperia (daughter of Cebren) and became a seabird; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon; no other names are attached.

Wikidata match is Chrysaor, son of Poseidon and Medusa, father of Geryon. All links are fine; Callirrhoe as his partner and mother of Geryon follows Hesiod (Theogony 287-294), and it stays as a lover link.
Apis is the Sicyonian king, son of Telchis in Pausanias. He is not the Egyptian bull god or the Argive Apis, and no other names are attached to him.
Helisson is the Arcadian son of Lycaon, eponym of the town and river Helisson; the Wikidata match is the same being.
Epopeus of Sicyon (son of Aloeus or Poseidon and Canace) is the match; Apollodorus' Epopeus is the Sicyonian king who took Antiope, so no change.
Amythaon, son of Cretheus and Tyro, father of Melampus and Bias, matches Wikidata.

Wikidata's Megaera is the Fury Megaera, one of the Erinyes. Apollodorus (1.1.4) says the Erinyes Alecto, Megaera and Tisiphone were born from Earth and the blood of Sky's castration, so the links to Earth and Sky fit the book.

links.reason: Pausanias' Amyntas, an Ephesian pancratiast, is the son of a different Hellanicus, not the historian of Mytilene or the boxer son of Alcaenetus.
The boy boxer Hellanicus, son of Alcaenetus, in the 89th Olympiad is a different man from the historian Hellanicus of Mytilene.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Hellanicus is a boy boxer, or the father of an Ephesian pancratiast, not Hellanicus of Mytilene the historian. The Wikidata match is a namesake. The book has two distinct Hellanicuses (the boxer and the father of Amyntas) that should be split.
Polyxo, wife of Tlepolemus and queen of Rhodes, matches Pausanias' account of Helen at Rhodes; no other names are mixed in.

Sthenelus, son of Perseus and Andromeda, king of Mycenae and father of Eurystheus, matches Wikidata. Apollodorus has other Sthenelus figures (e.g. the Argive son of Capaneus), but none are joined here.
Phemonoe, the first Pythia at Delphi, is the same being as the Wikidata match; Apollo as her father is a tradition Pausanias can follow, so no change.

Wikidata's Aeacus is the king of Aegina, son of Zeus and Aegina, father of Peleus and Telamon. The Theoi entry listing Zeus and Europa is a different tradition, from the Hesiodic Catalogues, which is about Aeacus's brother Rhadamanthus or Minos, not Aeacus. No other names are mixed in.
Wikidata match is Pittheus, king of Troezen, son of Pelops and Hippodamia and father of Aethra. The links to Aethra, Pelops and Troezen are all supported by the tradition.
The Wikidata match is Thyestes, son of Pelops and brother of Atreus, so it is the right being. He has no other names that belong to someone else.
Wikidata's Tisiphone is this Fury. Erinys is the generic name for the Furies and is acceptable as an alias here.
Wikidata's Antenor is the Trojan counselor, husband of Theano, and matches this being.
Wikidata's Neoptolemus is the same being as Pyrrhus, son of Achilles and Deidamia; the names Neoptolemus and Pyrrhus are the same person.

links.reason: A chorus is a group, not a single person; the individual Oceanids are already listed as her children.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Tethys, wife of Oceanus; no other names involved.
Mimas is the Giant born of Gaia from Uranus' blood; the Wikidata match is correct and he has no other names.
Adonis is the right match. In Metamorphoses 10 he is the son of Myrrha and Cinyras, and Venus loves him.
Wikidata match is Thyestes, son of Pelops and Hippodamia, brother of Atreus and father of Aegisthus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Apollodorus 1.3.2 says Calliope bore Orpheus to Oeagrus 'or, nominally, to Apollo'; it names no marriage, and the editor's rule reads any non-marriage spouse link as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope; no other names are in doubt.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Hyperion king of Megara and 'son of Agamemnon', but this is a different Agamemnon (a Megarian king), not the Mycenaean.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Mycenaean king Agamemnon; no other names.
Wikidata match is the right Pelops.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros, but the tradition describes a union, not a marriage; editor rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lover.
Pausanias reports the afterlife union of Achilles and Helen on Leuke, not a marriage; editor rule reads it as lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan War hero Achilles; no other names are involved. Neoptolemos, Neoptolemus and Pyrrhus should be one son.

links.reason: Boreas carried Orithyia off by force (Apollodorus 3.15.2), and the editor's rule reads any spouse link other than a marriage as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata matches the Athenian princess Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Hadrian was Trajan's ward and kinsman, adopted on his deathbed (per the tradition), not his biological son; Wikidata's parent link is unsupported by Pausanias, who calls Hadrian Trajan's successor.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the emperor Trajan; no other names are involved.
Hippomedon of the Seven against Thebes matches Wikidata. Talaus as father is one tradition and Aristomachus another, and Pausanias (2.36.8) mentions his house at Lerna without contradicting either.

Graces are the Charites, a group of goddesses, and the Wikidata match is appropriate. Pausanias follows the tradition that they are daughters of Zeus, and Aphrodite as mother is an accepted variant that is not contradicted here.

links.reason: Direction reversed: Pandora is Pyrrha's mother, not her daughter (Apollodorus 1.7.2 makes Pyrrha the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora).
Thyia, mother of Magnes and Macedon by Zeus in Hesiod's Catalogue, is the daughter of Deucalion, not of Pyrrha; the Wikidata link confuses her with another figure.

identity.detail: Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion, matches Wikidata.
Wikidata's Urania is the Muse, the right being. She has no other names, so nothing needs splitting.
Priapus matches the Wikidata entry; Bacchus and Venus as parents agree with Pausanias and Diodorus Siculus, and no other names are involved.

links.reason: Amphissos by Apollo belongs to Dryope daughter of Eurytus/Dryops in Ovid; here the hymn's Dryops' daughter is Pan's mother by Hermes, a different Dryope.
Andraemon married Ovid's Dryope, Iole's half-sister; this is not Hermes' bride in the Hymn to Pan.
Iole is half-sister of Ovid's Dryope (daughter of Eurytus), not the nymph bride of Hermes.

identity.detail: The book's Dryops' daughter (Hermes' wife, mother of Pan) is merged with Dryope, mother of Amphissus by Apollo and wife of Andraemon. Keep the Wikidata match only for the Dryope of Metamorphoses; split Amphissos, Andraemon and Iole to her.
Acrisius, king of Argos, son of Abas, matches Wikidata. No other names are attached.
Anticlea, wife of Laertes and mother of Odysseus, is the right match; no other names need splitting.
Wikidata match is Adrastus, king of Argos and leader of the Seven against Thebes, son of Talaus. This is the same being as in Apollodorus.

links.reason: Iambe's usual parentage is Pan and Echo in some sources (Pan and Echo), but Hesiod doesn't mention this and Iambe is a Demeter-hymn servant; however the Pan–Echo tradition does exist, so this is uncertain.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the oread Echo; no other names to question.
Palamedes, son of Nauplius, who is the Greek hero betrayed by Ulysses, is the right match. The Aeneid mentions him (Book 2) as falsely accused and killed. No other names are listed.

links.reason: The Hesiod (Catalogue of Women) Antiope is a daughter of the son of Nauboius (Phocian line, mother of Iolea, Minyan context), not the Amazon Antiope, daughter of Ares.
A character cannot be their own sibling; this is a self-link from merging two Antiopes' entries.
Ares fathered the Amazon Antiope (Pausanias, Theoi), but Hesiod's Antiope is the daughter of Nauboius's grandson/son, so the link belongs to the Amazon.

identity.detail: Hesiod's Antiope, mother of Iolea and daughter of the son of Nauboius, is not the Amazon Antiope (Ares' daughter, wife/lover of Theseus). Wikidata's match is the Amazon; the book's Antiope should be unmatched or matched to the correct Antiope.
Automate is a Danaid, daughter of Danaus. Pausanias says she married Architeles, and the Wikidata match fits. The Wikipedia note about Busiris is another tradition, not a different person.

Wikidata's Theano is Antenor's wife, the priestess of Athena at Troy, daughter of Cisseus (Iliad 6.299). The links agree with that. Cisses is a spelling variant of Cisseus, and Antenor is her husband. Her children Glaucus, Agenor and Eurymachus fit the tradition.

links.reason: Erigone is the daughter of Icarus of Attica, whom Dionysus taught winemaking (Apollodorus 3.14.7). Daedalus' son Icarus, who fell into the sea, had no children. The link comes from a different Icarus in Metamorphoses.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Daedalus' son Icarus, who is the right being. He has no other names to question.
Silvius, son of Aeneas and Lavinia in Aeneid 6, matches the Wikidata entry for Silvius Postumus. Wikidata also lists Ascanius as a father, which is the variant tradition, so the match is not wrong.

Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and wife of Perseus, matches Wikidata. Apollodorus names Cepheus as her father, and Cassiopeia as mother is consistent with tradition, so the flag is not a real conflict.
The match is Laius of Thebes, son of Labdacus, husband of Jocasta and father of Oedipus. All three links agree with the book and the tradition.

links.reason: Astraea as Helen's mother confuses a namesake; the standard mothers are Leda or Nemesis, not Astraea.
Theseus abducted Helen as a girl; no marriage, so lover per editor's rule.
Achilles and Helen's union on the White Island is a late afterlife tale, not a marriage; treat as lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Helen of Troy is correct.
Myles matches the Laconian king, son of Lelex and brother of Polycaon. Pausanias names Lelex as father and does not name the mother, so Wikidata's Cleocharia is a harmless addition.

Steropes is the Hesiodic Cyclops, a son of Uranus and Gaia (Theogony), so the Wikidata match is correct. The tree's link from Earth is right. The flag only means the tree lacks Uranus as father, which is no error.

links.reason: Ixion's father is usually Phlegyas (also Antion, Peision, or Leonteus in other sources); Ares as father is an unsupported outlier from Wikidata, not stated in Aeschylus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lapith king Ixion; no other names involved.
Psamathe the Nereid, mother of Phocus by Aeacus, matches Wikidata. Wikidata lists Proteus as spouse, but that is not a link in this tree, so nothing needs fixing.
Wikidata match is Persephone, daughter of Zeus and Demeter and wife of Hades (Pluto). Kore is her own name for the maiden. Nothing to fix.
The Wikidata match is the Trojan seer Helenus, son of Priam and Hecuba, and he has no other names to question.
Melampus the seer of Pylos and Argos, son of Amythaon and brother of Bias, is the right match.

links.reason: Dryope was Hermes' lover (mother of Pan in the Homeric Hymn); the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
Pindar's Hermes has no child Fame; this is a personification misread, not a son of Hermes.

identity.detail: Mercury matches Hermes, the Roman form of the same god; the alias names are correct.
Wikidata match is the Titan Epimetheus, brother of Prometheus; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; no other names to check.
Anthas, son of Poseidon and Alcyone, brother of Hyperes, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

links.reason: The book says Cycnus is son of Ares and Pyrene, not Cyrene; Cyrene is a misreading of Pyrene.
Themistonoe belongs to a different Cycnus, the Hesiodic one is the son of Ares; the Themistonoe link is to the Cycnus of Colonae, so this is a namesake.
Hemithea and Tennes are children of Cycnus king of Colonae (son of Poseidon), not Ares' son killed by Heracles.
Tennes is the son of Cycnus of Tenedos/Colonae, a different man from Ares' son.
Phylonome is the wife of Cycnus of Colonae in Pausanias, not Ares' son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the son of Ares; the Pausanias relatives belong to the Cycnus of Colonae, handled by the link removals.
Chloris, wife of Neleus and mother of Nestor, matches Wikidata. Melibœa is her alternate name in the Niobid tradition, so no split is needed.
Diomedes son of Tydeus matches the Wikidata hero; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Pirithous was son of Ixion (or Zeus) and Dia; Aethra is Theseus' mother, and Apollodorus gives Pirithous no link to her.
