Apollodorus says Aegeus lay with Aethra at Troezen on a single night, which is a union and not a marriage; the editor's rule reads non-marriages as lovers.
Pausanias' Aethra wife of Phalanthus of Taras is a different woman, not Theseus' mother; Apollodorus does not mention this.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Theseus' mother, Aethra daughter of Pittheus; the Phalanthus link belongs to a namesake.
Wikidata match is the hero Perseus, son of Zeus and Danaë; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Hebe is the goddess of youth, cupbearer of the gods and wife of Heracles. This matches the book's Hebe.
Nereids as a group of sea nymphs matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Morpheus, son of Sleep (Somnus/Hypnos) in Ovid Metamorphoses 11; no other names to dispute.

The Wikidata match is the Lycian archer Pandarus, son of Lycaon, from the Iliad. The Aeneid's Pandarus, a Trojan gatekeeper and brother of Bitias, is a different person (son of Alcanor). Vergil's Pandarus and Homer's are separate, so the match should be removed or split.
Erato is the Muse, daughter of Zeus (Jove) and Mnemosyne; the Wikidata match is correct. In the Aeneid (7.37) she is invoked as a Muse.
Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy; no other names to question.
Briareos and Aegaeon are one Hundred-Hander in the tradition; the Wikidata match is fine. Eumelus's sea-dwelling Aegaeon is a variant of the same being.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives no parentage for Nephele; the Oceanid parentage is not stated in this book, and the Wikipedia entry notes two Nepheles, so this is not clearly attached to the Athamas wife. Not contradicted by a source, though, so cautious removal is not warranted.
Nessus the centaur is the son of Ixion and the cloud Nephele (the Ixion cloud). Apollodorus' Nephele, mother of Phrixus and Helle, is the other figure, so the link joins two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata merges two Nepheles: the cloud made by Zeus in Hera's likeness for Ixion (mother of the centaurs, Nessus) and Athamas' wife, mother of Phrixus and Helle. Apollodorus' Nephele here is Athamas' wife, so the Nessus link belongs to the Ixion cloud.

Iris is the right match for the rainbow messenger. In the Aeneid (5.604ff) Iris takes the form of Beroe, a Trojan woman, to incite the women to burn the ships. Beroe is a separate mortal Trojan woman (wife of Doryclus) whom Iris only impersonates, so the alias Beroe should not be treated as another name for Iris.
The Wikidata match is the emperor Nero, which is the right being.
Wikidata match is Ismene, daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta, sister of Antigone; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Eupeithes of Ithaca, father of Antinous; no other names to question.

Teucer, son of Telamon and Hesione, half-brother of Ajax, founder of Salamis on Cyprus; the match is correct. Apollodorus says Telamon had Teucer by Hesione, and Ajax is Telamon's son by Periboea, so the sibling link is right as a half-brother.
Wikidata match is the West Wind god Zephyrus; the alias Zephyr is the same being.
Melite is the Naiad daughter of Aegaeus who bore Hyllus to Heracles in Apollonius' Argonautica (4.538-541), matching the Wikidata entry.
Chione, daughter of Boreas and Orithyia, mother of Eumolpus by Poseidon, matches Apollodorus 3.15.4.

links.reason: The Iliad's Chryses is the Trojan priest of Apollo. Minos was the father of a different Chryses, the son of Minos and Paria, who appears in the Parian/Cretan tradition. Wikidata's father list (Ardys, Minos) shows the two are mixed up.

identity.detail: Wikidata's parents (Minos, Ardys, Paria) belong to a different Chryses, the son of Minos on Paros. The Iliad's priest of Apollo at Chryse, father of Chryseis, is a separate person, so the family data was merged wrongly.
Aegina, daughter of Asopus, nymph of the island once called Œnone; the match is correct. Œnone is the island's old name here, not a different person.

links.reason: Mariandynus is usually a son of Cimmerius or Phrixus/Phineus is a rare attribution; the Argonautica never names him as Phineus' son and the link is a weak cross-book guess.

identity.detail: The Metamorphoses Phineus, Cepheus' brother and Andromeda's rival suitor, is a different person from the Thracian seer. Cassiopea as mother and the Cepheus sibling link belong more to the Ethiopian/Andromeda figure or a mixed tradition.
Wikidata match is Pittheus, king of Troezen, son of Pelops and Hippodamia; no other names are listed.
Eurybia, daughter of Pontus and Gaia, wife of Crius, matches Wikidata; Apollodorus gives her as mother of Astraeus, Pallas and Perses by Crius. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Ovid's Leucothoë is daughter of Eurynome, wife of Orchamus's Persian line, a different Eurynome from the Oceanid mother of the Graces.
The Hesiod passage (Catalogue) about Bellerophon names Eurynome, daughter of Nisus and wife of Glaucus, not the Oceanid.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Oceanid; the Bellerophon-mother Eurynome (Nisus's daughter) and Ophion's wife are other figures, so the Poseidon link belongs elsewhere.
Actaeon, son of Aristaeus and Autonoe, is the Theban hunter torn apart by his hounds. The Wikidata match is correct.

Molus is the bastard son of Deucalion, son of Minos, and father of Meriones, as Apollodorus 3.3.1 says. The Wikidata match is right; its alternate father Minos is a variant tradition, so the flag is not an error.

links.reason: The Eustathius fragment (Catalogue of Women/Nestor's daughter) says Polycaste was joined to Telemachus and bore Persepolis; tradition treats her as his wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the son of Odysseus and Penelope; no misattributed names.
Wikidata match is the sea monster Charybdis; no other names are listed. Poseidon and Gaia as parents are standard (Theoi lists both Pontos and Poseidon as fathers), so both links are fine.
Wikidata's Cnossia is the same figure: the nymph or slave who bore Xenodamus to Menelaus. The link to Xenodamus is right, and nothing else is flagged.

links.reason: Telegonus, Odysseus' son by Circe, marries Penelope after Odysseus' death in the Telegony tradition (Hesiod's Catalogue); it is a real marriage, so the link stays a spouse link but belongs to that tradition, not Apollodorus' own account.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Penelope, wife of Odysseus, daughter of Icarius; the parents Icarius and Periboea agree with Apollodorus.
Wikidata's Roxana is Alexander the Great's Bactrian wife, the same person Pausanias mentions (9.7), so the match is right and she has no other names.

links.reason: Hesiod (ll. 378-382) says only that Eos bore Astraeus the winds, 'a goddess mating in love with a god'; no marriage is stated, and the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Astraeus, son of Crius and Eurybia, and no other names are attached.

links.reason: Piras appears only in Pausanias's story of a Styx-related figure; Apollodorus gives Pallas as Styx's partner, so this is a different tradition and not supported here.

identity.detail: Styx the goddess and river is the correct match.

Wikidata match is the Moira Lachesis. Hesiod's Theogony gives the Fates as daughters of Night (line 217) and also of Zeus and Themis (line 904). The Night link is right for this book, so nothing needs fixing.
Philyra is the Oceanid mother of Chiron by Cronus; the Wikidata match is the same being and she has no other names.
Nicostratus, son of Menelaus, matches Wikidata and the Hesiod fragment; both parent links are right.
Ilus son of Tros, founder of Ilion, matches Wikidata. The Iliad's lines on Tros's sons and on Ilus begetting Laomedon support both links.

links.reason: The quoted sentence is Oedipus speaking of Laius; it does not name Polydore as Labdacus's father. Still, in the tradition Labdacus is Polydorus's son, so this link is plausibly right.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Polydorus, son of Cadmus; the name is fine.
Melanthus is the Athenian king, son of Andropompus and father of Codrus; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Phineus is Cepheus's brother, Andromeda's uncle and fiancé in Ovid, not Cassiope's son; the Hesiod-derived link appears to confuse him with another Phineus.

identity.detail: Cassiope is Cassiopeia, queen of Aethiopia and wife of Cepheus; the match is correct.
Larissa, daughter of Pelasgus, is the eponym of the Argive citadel. The Wikipedia text says two figures share the name, but the Wikidata match fits this Larissa.
Cylarabes is the Argive king, son of Sthenelus son of Capaneus; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are listed.
Wikidata match is Phrixus son of Athamas; Iophossa is Chalciope's alternate name, so no issue.

links.reason: Glaucon the Athenian victor is son of Eteocles of Athens/Orchomenos (Andreus's son), not the Theban son of Oedipus.
Pausanias's Eteocles son of Andreus (Orchomenian, said son of Cephisus) is a different man from the Theban son of Oedipus.

identity.detail: Pausanias has two Eteocles: the Theban son of Oedipus (father of Laodamas) and the Orchomenian son of Andreus/Cephisus (father of Glaucon). Wikidata match fits only the Theban.

Procles, twin son of Aristodemus and Argia, Spartan Heraclid, matches Wikidata. The links to Sous (Procles' son, per Pausanias and Plutarch) and Eurysthenes are consistent. Leogorus as another son is also attested in the tradition (Pausanias lists Soos as father of Eurypon; Leogorus is in Eurypontid lines).
Wikidata's Laomedon is the Trojan king, son of Ilus and father of Priam, so the match is correct. He has no other names to check.
Wikidata match is the seer Amphiaraus, son of Oicles; no other names to question.

links.reason: Phialo, mother of Aechmis by Heracles, was the daughter of the Arcadian Alcimedon in Pausanias. Ovid's Alcimedon is a different man, a sailor in Acoetes' crew in Metamorphoses 3.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Myrmidon son of Laerces from the Iliad. Ovid's Alcimedon is a sailor on the ship that carried Bacchus, so the match is a different man.
Wikidata match is the Muse Melpomene; no other names to question. Apollodorus (1.3.4) gives Melpomene as mother of the Sirens by Achelous, so the link is right.
Statius' Arcadian huntress, mother of Parthenopaeus, matches the Wikidata Atalanta; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Tydeus is the Aetolian hero, son of Oeneus and father of Diomedes, who fought among the Seven against Thebes. The match is correct and there are no other names.
Aratus of Sicyon, son of Clinias, is the right match.

links.reason: Neither Theoi nor Wikidata names Iapetus as Lucifer's father. The tradition gives Astraeus or Cephalus with Eos (Aurora), and Iapetus is Atlas's father, so this looks like a confusion with Atlas.

identity.detail: Lucifer is the Latin Morning Star, matching Phosphorus/Eosphorus. Hesperus is the same star seen in the evening, so the alias is acceptable.
Wikidata match is Hecuba, wife of Priam; no other names to question.

links.reason: Pausanias (1.5.2) has Scyrius, not Œolycus, as the rumored father of Ægeus; the standard line is Pandion II, so this link cannot be confirmed and likely confuses Ægeus with another figure. Pandion is the usual father.
Aethra lay with Ægeus (and Poseidon) in one night at Troezen; she was not his wife in the tradition, so mark as lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata Aegeus matches the Athenian king; no other names to dispute.
The Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy, which is correct.
Capys, son of Assaracus and father of Anchises (Apollodorus 3.12.2), is the Dardanian king. The Wikidata match is this being.
Wikidata's Itys is the son of Tereus and Procne, the same being Apollodorus names. Both parent links are correct.

The match is the Athenian general Iphicrates. Historically his father was Timotheus (a shoemaker's son per tradition), but the book's sentence calls him 'son of Timotheus', and the link follows that sentence. Note that Iphicrates' famous son was Menestheus; his father Timotheus is not the general Timotheus son of Conon, so the link should not be confused with that figure.

links.reason: Laestrygon as Poseidon's son is a tradition only in Hesiod's lost fragments; hard to support, but Telepylus founder Lamus is the usual source. Weak, but not contradicted.
Machaon is son of Asclepius, not Poseidon.
Podaleirius is son of Asclepius, not Poseidon.
Nireus is son of Charopus and Aglaea in the Iliad; no source makes Poseidon his father.
Kleatos is a Molione son of Actor, not Poseidon, though Molionids are sometimes called Poseidon's sons.

identity.detail: Nereus is a separate sea-god, a son of Pontus and Gaia, not Neptune; Saturn's son is an epithet. Neptune matches Poseidon.

Icarius, father of Penelope, is the Spartan brother of Tyndareus, which fits the Wikidata match (Spartan prince). The Wikipedia text calls him son of Perieres, which is a variant tradition, but the match is still the same person.
Democoon, bastard son of Priam in the Iliad, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are involved.
Busiris is the Egyptian king killed by Heracles, so the Wikidata match is correct. He has no other names to check.

links.reason: Megarian Alcathous is son of Pelops and Hippodamia (Pausanias 1.41, Wikidata); Porthaon's son Alcathous is a different man, so the link mixes two namesakes.

Pyrgo is a different person from the Megarian Alcathous' wife in Pausanias; per the editor's rule, a spouse link outside real marriages is read as a lover. Wikidata lists her, but Pausanias does not call her a wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Megarian Alcathous, son of Pelops; the Porthaon parentage belongs to a namesake.

links.reason: Hermione is the Ovidian/Metamorphoses name-variant for Harmonia (Hermione, Cadmus' wife, is a different figure from Menelaus' daughter); Harmonia is already linked as spouse, so this is a duplicate/confused entry.

Pausanias mentions Electra's gate at Thebes, named for a sister of Kadmos in some accounts, but the link confuses her with the Pleiad Electra; the tradition does not support her as Kadmos' sister in the standard genealogy.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban founder Cadmus; the name Kadmos is correct.

links.reason: Iliad 20.223 says Boreas took the form of a stallion and fathered horses on Erichthonius' mares; Erichthonius is the father of the mares' owner, not Boreas's lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Boreas the north wind; the parents differ only because the Iliad names none, and Astraeus and Eos are the standard parents.
Pelias, king of Iolcus, son of Tyro and Poseidon (Neptune), is the right match.
Wikidata match is the seer Amphiaraus; the name Amphiaraus is only a spelling variant.

links.reason: The editor ruled this link right only in the Metamorphoses, so it does not hold in Aeschylus; the book names no mother for Atlas.

identity.detail: Atlas the Titan matches; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Apollodorus (3.10.6) makes Thespius son of Agenor's line (Thestius, son of Ares' descendant Agenor, father of Althaea and Leda), not Erechtheus and Praxithea; Wikidata confuses him with another Thespius.

Apollodorus has Thespius (father of fifty daughters, host of Heracles) as son of Erechtheus' descendant Eratus? no: Thespius of Thespiae is son of Erechtheus only in a variant tradition; this book does not state it.

identity.detail: Apollodorus has two figures: Thestius of Pleuron (father of Leda, Althaea) and Thespius of Thespiae (fifty daughters). The Wikidata match mixes Thespiae king with Erechtheus's son; check which is meant.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony (886-900) says Zeus made Metis his first wife; the editor's rule only reads non-Hera marriages as lovers by default, but Hesiod states the marriage.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Oceanid Metis; the alias Thought is just the meaning of her name.
Mantius, son of Melampus and father of Oicles, Cleitus and Polypheides, matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Pausanias' story has Alpheus pursuing Artemis (Alphaea/Arethusa tradition), but Diana never yielded; in Statius Alpheus is a river, and no sentence in the Thebaid makes him her lover.

identity.detail: Diana matches the Wikidata entry; Artemis, Cynthia, Dictynna, Latonia and Trivia are all names for the same goddess.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, is the Trojan prophetess; the match is correct.
Wikidata's Erigone, daughter of Icarius of Athens, is the same being as the Erigone of Metamorphoses.
Wikidata match is Neleus king of Pylos. The Wikidata father Hippocoon looks like a stray entry, but that is not a link in the tree.

links.reason: Cadmus's wife is Harmonia (Hermione is a variant spelling in Metamorphoses); this is not Menelaus' daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Menelaus and Helen's daughter Hermione; the Cadmus link comes from a different figure (Harmonia).

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links, so any other spouse link is read as a lover. Andromache was Helenus' wife after Neoptolemus in Virgil and Pausanias, but the Iliad does not say so, and the editor's rule governs the link type.

identity.detail: Helenus, the Trojan seer and son of Priam, is the right match.
Wikidata match is Menelaus, king of Sparta, son of Atreus and Aerope; no other names to doubt.

links.link: Cephalus spouse_of Clymene, daughter of Minyas
links.reason: Clymene is Pausanias' tradition (Phylacus' son Iphiclus); Apollodorus gives Cephalus only Procris as wife.
Editor's decision: right only in Pausanias. In Apollodorus, Phaethon is Tithonus' son.

identity.detail: Apollodorus has two Cephaluses: the son of Hermes and Herse (Dawn's lover) and the son of Deion (husband of Procris). The Wikidata match is Deion's son, so split the Hermes/Herse/Dawn/Tithonus links from the Procris link.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children, not a person.

identity.detail: Hercules matches; Alcides and Amphitryon's child are epithets of Heracles, and Heracles is the same hero.

links.reason: 'Pandareus' daughters' is a group label, not a person; the real daughters (Camiro, Clytie) are already linked individually.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Pandareus, son of Merops, whose daughters Homer and Pausanias (Polygnotus' painting) mention.

Melia, Oceanus' daughter and Apollo's consort at Thebes, mother of Tenerus and Ismenus, is the right being. Wikidata's spouse Inachus belongs to a different Melia, the Argive one, who is not in this book's tree. No link here depends on it.
Milo of Croton the wrestler is correct; Pausanias names him as son of Diotimus, a native of Croton, and the only link listed is supported by the book.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 901) calls Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule reads only Hera/Juno as Zeus's marriages, but Themis is not listed there, so lover is too weak; she is a wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Themis is the Titaness, so the match is right and there are no other names.
The Wikidata match is Lynceus, the Messenian Argonaut and son of Aphareus and Arene. No other names are attached to him.
Pluto is Hades, ruler of the underworld, and the Wikidata match is correct. Saturn is the Latin name for Cronos, so the parent difference is only a naming difference.
Metabus, king of the Volsci and father of Camilla, matches Wikidata. He has no other names.
Wikidata match is King Numitor of Alba Longa, son of Proca, and the only link listed (Proca as father) is correct.

links.reason: Editor's decision: Aratus is Asklepios's child only in pausanias (where he is a mortal son of Clinias and Aristodama in Sicyon), so the link does not hold for this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Asclepius, the god of medicine; the name is correct.
Autonoe is the Theban daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon. The Wikidata match is correct.
The Wikidata match is Calypso, the nymph of Ogygia, daughter of Atlas, which is correct.
Bacchus matches Dionysus; the alternate names (Liber, Lyaeus, Euhius, Thyoneus, Bromian) are all epithets of the same god.
Wikidata match is the Argive king Talaus, son of Bias and Pero; no confusion.
Wikidata's Niobe, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, is the right being. She has no other names that need splitting.

links.reason: Eetion of Thebe, Andromache's father, is not Zeus's son; the Hesiodic Eetion (Iasion, Demeter's lover, in Hesiod's Theogony) is a different man of the same name.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Eetion, king of Cilician Thebe, father of Andromache and Podes; this is the right being.

links.reason: In Pausanias, Alpheus pursued Artemis but never won her. She is a virgin goddess, so he is not her lover; she escaped him (Arethusa's story is a separate myth). Oedipus the King does not mention it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Artemis. The alias Diana is the Roman equivalent, so it is acceptable. The Theoi listing of Demeter as her mother is a variant (Aeschylus), and the book follows Zeus and Leto.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Arcas as Callisto's son and never names her as Pan's mother. The editor has ruled that Dryops' daughter is Pan's mother, and only in Hesiod.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Callisto, the Arcadian nymph or daughter of Lycaon, which is the right being.

links.reason: Apollodorus lists Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix and Cilix as the children of Agenor and Telephassa; Thasus is not among them, and the book elsewhere treats him as a son or companion of Cilix or Phoenix.
Apollodorus names Phineus as a son of Agenor (or Poseidon) in a different passage, not by Telephassa; the book lists only four children of Telephassa.

identity.detail: Telephassa is the wife of Agenor and mother of Cadmus and Europa; the Wikidata match fits.
Leis, daughter of Orus and mother of Althepus by Poseidon, matches the book (Pausanias 2.30.5). Both family links are correct.
Perses, brother of Aeëtes and son of Helios and Perse, is the right being. In Metamorphoses 7 Ovid calls Hecate 'Perses' daughter', which is the same Perses, so the book's link is right.
Minerva is the Roman name used in this translation for Athena, so the match and the alternate names (Athena, Pallas, Trito-born) all refer to the same goddess.

The Wikipedia description is of Evander the Arcadian founder of Pallantium in Italy, son of Mercury and Carmentis. The Wikidata match, Evander of Pallene, is a different Evander, so the match should be corrected to the Arcadian Evander.
Deiphontes son of Antimachus, husband of Hyrnetho, is the right being.
Wikidata match is the Argive Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle; no misattributed names.

links.reason: Nero was Claudius's stepson and adoptive son, not his biological child; Claudius's children were Octavia and Britannicus, and Nero's father was Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the emperor Claudius, which fits Pausanias's mentions of him.
Myrtoessa is the Arcadian nymph who nursed Zeus, and the Wikidata match is correct. She has no other names that could belong to someone else.

links.link: Hermione spouse_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, so this duplicates the Neoptolemus link; keep one marriage and drop the duplicate node.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Hermione, daughter of Menelaus and Helen; no other names to split.

links.link: Lysimachus parent_of Alexander, son of Cassander
links.reason: Pausanias says Alexander was Lysimachus' son by Odrysiades; Alexander son of Cassander is a different man, so the link confuses two people.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Lysimachus, king of Thrace and Macedon, and this fits the book's Lysimachus.
Ocypete is one of the Harpies, daughter of Thaumas and Electra. Ocypode and Ocythoe are variant names for the same Harpy, so the match is right.
Wikidata's Syllis is the Sicyonian nymph, mother of Zeuxippus by Apollo, as Pausanias says. The match is correct.
Ischys son of Elatus is the right being; Pausanias (2.26) names him as Coronis's lover, which the tree records correctly.
The Wikidata match is Astyanax, son of Hector and Andromache. He has no other names that belong to someone else.
Wikidata's Elara is the daughter of Orchomenus and mother of Tityos by Zeus, which fits the Hesiod fragment. Wikidata's alternate father Minyas is a known variant, not an error.

links.reason: Ascanius is Aeneas's son by Creusa (Metamorphoses 14 calls him Iulus, son of Aeneas); Lavinia is his stepmother. Her son was Silvius in some traditions (Virgil, Aeneid 6).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Lavinia, daughter of Latinus and wife of Aeneas; no other names to question.
Pamphylus, the Dorian hero and son of Aegimius, matches Wikidata. Apollodorus (2.8.3) names him as a son of Aegimius, and Pausanias gives Orsobia as his wife.
Wikidata match is Iris, the rainbow goddess and messenger, daughter of Thaumas. No other names to check.
The Wikidata match is Phaethon, son of Helios, the one Apollonius Rhodius (4.598) describes falling into the Eridanus. No other names are attached to him.

Wikidata's Scylla is the sea monster of the strait opposite Charybdis, which is the being Apollonius Rhodius describes. The book gives Hecate (called Crataeis) and Phorcys as her parents, matching Theoi's Apollonius 4.828 entry.
Minerva is the Roman name of Athena, so the Wikidata match and the alternate names (Athena, Jove's daughter, Trito-born) all refer to the same goddess.

links.reason: Editor ruled Cronus parent of Crius wrong everywhere; Crius was Cronus's brother, a Titan.
Picus is the Latin king of Virgil and Ovid, son of Saturn in Latin tradition. Theoi's Cronos listing does not make him a child of the Greek Cronos in Pausanias.
Hesiod gives the Moirai as daughters of Night (Theogony 217), and in other versions of Zeus and Themis. Cronus is not their father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Cronus is correct.
Wikidata match is Cacus the fire-breathing giant, son of Vulcan; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Iphicles, Heracles' half-twin brother and father of Iolaus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Pausanias (Hermione) makes Clymenus a Chthonian god or an Argive figure honoured as Hades, and a local Hermionean tradition makes him Demeter's brother-in-cult. In Pindar the family is Kronos and Rhea's children, so he is not a sibling here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Demeter; no other names.

links.reason: In the Iliad Hera only promises Hypnos that Pasithea will be his wife; she is not Hera's daughter. Pausanias gives Pasithea as a Charis or a daughter of Aegle, and Theoi's listing does not make her Hera's child.

identity.detail: Hera matches Hera; Juno is her Roman counterpart, which is fine.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses the Iole who is sister of Dryope (daughter of Dryops) is the wife of Thoas, a different woman from Eurytus' daughter Iole of Oechalia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Eurytus' daughter Iole, who married Hyllus after Heracles' sack of Oechalia. Ioleia is just a variant spelling.

links.reason: Andromeda's mother is Cassiopeia, wife of Cepheus, queen of Aethiopia. Hesiod's Cassiopea is the wife of Phoenix and mother of Phineus, so the Andromeda link belongs to the other Cassiopeia.

identity.detail: Hesiod's Cassiopea, wife of Phoenix son of Agenor and mother of Phineus, is not the Wikidata Cassiopeia, queen of Aethiopia and wife of Cepheus. The Wikidata match and spouse Cepheus belong to a different woman of the same name.

links.reason: Iole is daughter of Eurytus of Oechalia, but Pausanias' Eurytus is the Molionid son of Actor (father of Thalpius), a different man.
Antioche is the wife of Eurytus of Oechalia in Hesiod; Pausanias gives this Eurytus wife Theraphone.

identity.detail: Pausanias mentions two Eurytuses: the Oechalian son of Melaneus (father of Iole, wife Antioche) and the Molionid son of Actor with Theraphone and Thalpius. Thalpius and Theraphone belong to the Actor-son Eurytus; Melaneus, Iole and Antioche belong to the Oechalian one.
Apsyrtus is Absyrtus, Medea's brother, so the Wikidata match is correct. In Apollodorus (1.9.23) his mother is Asterodeia (or Hecate/Idyia in other versions), which is consistent with the links.

links.reason: Hesiod makes Theia a Titan sister who bore Helios, Selene and Eos to Hyperion; Ocean's wife is Tethys.
A chorus is a group, not a person; the Oceanids are already linked individually.
Triptolemus is son of Celeus and Metaneira (or Eleusis); the Ocean/Gaia parentage is a rare variant not found in this book.
The Cercopes are a pair of brigands, a group, not an individual child; the Ocean parentage is unsupported.
Acmon is a Titan figure in Hesiod's tradition and not truly Ocean's child; the link is an unsupported guess.

identity.detail: Ocean is Oceanus, the Titan; the match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Muse Euterpe; no other names.

links.reason: Euryphaessa is Hyperion's wife (a variant of Theia) in the tradition, not his sister as a separate sibling link; the sibling link double counts the relationship.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Hyperion; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Chrysorthe, daughter of Orthopolis of Sicyon and mother of Coronus, matches Pausanias' Chrysorthe. She has no other names.
Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Laius, king of Thebes, father of Oedipus; no other names to question.
Pero, daughter of Neleus and Chloris, wife of Bias and mother of Talaus, is the right match.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace (Charis) in Hesiod, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome; the Iliad's Hera only promises Hypnos a Grace as a bride, so she is not Pasithea's mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Hera herself; Juno is her Roman counterpart and Hera Acraea is a cult title, but neither is a different being.

links.reason: Thespius is Apollodorus' king of Thespiae, father of the fifty daughters, not a son of Erechtheus; Wikidata mixes him up with another figure.

Hesiod's Sicyon is a son of Erechtheus only in a rare tradition (Pausanias says Marathon's son; Sicyon is eponym of Sicyon, son of Metion in Pausanias); not in Apollodorus' list of Erechtheus' children.
Orneus is son of Erechtheus in Pausanias, but Apollodorus lists Cecrops, Pandorus and Metion as sons; Orneus is better read as a link from Pausanias' tradition, a variant not in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Erechtheus, king of Athens; no other names are confused.

links.reason: Hesiod's Dryops' daughter bore Pan to Hermes but was not a wife; only marriages count as spouse, so read as a lover.
Pindar's Fame (Angelia, a personification) is not a child of Hermes in Pausanias; this is a misread of the herald's role.

identity.detail: Hermes matches. Mercury is the Roman equivalent, a standard identification. The epithets are cult titles of the same god.
Briareus and Aegaeon are the same Hundred-Hander; in Iliad 1.396-406 Homer says gods call him Briareus and men Aegaeon, whose father is Poseidon-linked in Iliad 1.403. The Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the goddess Eos; the names Dawn and Erigenia are epithets of the same being.

links.reason: Apollodorus 1.2.7 says the Nereids were born to Nereus and Doris, so Doris is his wife and not his child. The link reverses the relationship, and the spouse link already covers it.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the sea-god Nereus, son of Pontus and Gaia, and he has no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Acastus, son of Pelias and Argonaut; the book's sentence confirms Pelias as father. No other names to question.
Wikidata Alkmene is this Alcmena; Alcmene is only a spelling variant.
Iris, daughter of Thaumas and Electra, messenger goddess and rainbow personification, matches Wikidata's Iris. No other names are listed.
Tenerus is the Theban seer, son of Apollo and Melia, as Pausanias says; the Wikidata match is correct.
Phorcus in Pausanias is the sea god Phorcys; the Medusa passage is a rationalizing tradition that the book tells in its own words, so it is right for this book.
Glaucus of Carystus, boxer, son of Demylus, matches Wikidata; the flag is only a spelling difference (Demylus vs Demylus of Carystus), so the link is right.

links.reason: Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus (by a slave woman in Odyssey/Pausanias tradition), not Helen's; Odyssey and Pausanias give Helen only Hermione.
Pausanias says Theseus married Helen, but in the tradition she was abducted as a girl and rescued by her brothers, so only a lover under the editor's rule.
Afterlife union on Leuce reported by a visionary, not a marriage; treated as a lover under the editor's rule.

identity.detail: Match to Helen of Troy is correct; no other names to separate.

Alphenor is Ovid's name for a Niobid, son of Amphion and Niobe (Metamorphoses 6). The Wikidata match is acceptable, since Wikipedia treats him as perhaps the same as Archenor/Acheinor. Both parent links are right.
Leucippus son of Perieres of Messenia is the right match. The Boeotian town of Leuctra in the Wikipedia blurb is a side detail and does not make the match wrong.

links.reason: Most sources (Homeric Hymn 19, Herodotus, Apollodorus, Plato) make Hermes Pan's father; Zeus as father is a rare variant that the book's text does not state.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the god Pan. 'Crag-walker' is an epithet of Pan, not another being.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, bore Polypoetes to Odysseus after his return (Eugammon's Telegony) and is not a marriage like Penelope's; under the editor's rule that only marriages count, a second spouse is read as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Homeric Odysseus; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Pausanias (5.7.4, 6.22.9) tells of Alpheus pursuing Artemis, who tricked him, so no lover relationship. Artemis was a virgin goddess and Alpheus's love for Arethusa is the better-known tale.

identity.detail: Artemis matches the Wikidata entry; Diana is her Roman equivalent, which is acceptable.
Argyra is the sea-nymph who loved Selemnus in Pausanias (7.23). The Wikidata match, a Naiad of a well, is consistent with her, and no other names are attached.

links.reason: Doris is Nereus' wife and the mother of his daughters; Apollodorus lists her among the Oceanids, daughters of Oceanus and Tethys, not of Nereus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea-god Nereus, son of Pontus and Gaia.

links.reason: Cyanippus was the son of Aegialeus's sister Deipyle and Tydeus's... no: Cyanippus was son of Aegialeus per Pausanias only, while Apollodorus makes Cyanippus son of Aegeus's... he is son of Adrastus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the son of Adrastus who died at Thebes in the Epigoni war; no confusion of names.
Leucippus, Messenian prince, son of Perieres and Gorgophone, father of Arsinoe, Hilaeira and Phoebe, brother of Aphareus, is the right being. No other names are given.
Autonoë daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon, is the same being Pausanias names.

links.reason: Apollodorus 3.5.6 names Amphion's wife Niobe as daughter of Tantalus, a different Niobe from Phoroneus' daughter; Amphion and her children belong to the Theban Niobe.
Chloris, daughter of Amphion and Niobe, belongs to the Theban Niobe, not Phoroneus' daughter.

identity.detail: The tree joins two women named Niobe: Phoroneus' daughter (mother of Argus and Pelasgus by Zeus) and Tantalus' daughter (wife of Amphion, mother of Chloris and the Niobids). The Wikidata match fits only the Argive Niobe.

links.reason: Hesiod makes the Graces daughters of Zeus and Eurynome; Pindar does not name Aphrodite as their mother.
Iliad has Zeus as father of both, but Ares' mother is Hera and Aphrodite's is Dione, so they are half-siblings at best; the link is misleading and the usual tradition makes them lovers.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct; Cyprian queen and Cyprus-born are epithets of Aphrodite.

links.reason: Hesiod's Clymene, wife of Phylacus (mother of Iphiclus), is a daughter of Minyas, not Ovid's Clymene, mother of Phaëton and wife of Merops.

links.link: Clymene parent_of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus
links.reason: Iphiclus's mother in Hesiod is the Minyan Clymene, a different woman from the Oceanid who is Phaëton's mother.
Iapetus's wife is the Oceanid Clymene of Hesiod, but Ovid's Clymene is Phaëton's mother, married to Merops. The two are conflated under one name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Oceanid Clymene, wife of Iapetus, but Ovid's Clymene is Phaëton's mother, wife of Merops. Ovid does call her an Oceanid's daughter in some tellings, yet the Phylacus and Iapetus links belong to other women of the same name.
Aeacus, king of Aegina, is the right match.
Androgeos son of Minos matches the Wikidata entry; the book's sentences confirm Minos as his father. No other names to split.
Palamedes, son of Nauplius, matches the Wikidata entry. In Metamorphoses he is mentioned only in passing (13, Ulysses' speech), and no other names are involved.

Miletus is the eponymous founder of Miletus, son of Apollo (by Areia or Acacallis) and father of Byblis and Caunus. Pausanias also gives Anactoria as the old name of Miletus, a city and region, though the site may treat it as an alias; this alias is an ancient name, not another person, so it can stay.
Wikidata match Cadmus, founder of Thebes, is correct.
Wikidata match is the Andromeda daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, wife of Perseus; no other names to question.
Alipherus, son of Lycaon and eponym of Alipheira in Arcadia, matches Wikidata; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Doris is Nereus's wife, not his daughter; Hesiod makes her daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, and she is the mother of the Nereids by Nereus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea-god Nereus, the Old Man of the Sea; no other names to question.
Psamathe the Nereid, mother of Phocus by Aeacus, is correctly matched. Wikidata's spouse Proteus is a different story and is not a link in this tree.

links.reason: Aethra lay with Aegeus (and Poseidon) the same night; per the editor's rule only marriages count as spouse, so this is a lover link.
Pausanias' Oeolycus is an ancestor of the Aegeidae of Sparta, a different Aegeus; Athenian Aegeus is the son of Pandion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian king Aegeus, father of Theseus.
Wikidata's Juturna is the same Italic water nymph, sister of Turnus in the Aeneid. Her parents Daunus and Venilia fit Virgil (Aeneid 10.76, 12.139), and Janus as her spouse is not contradicted.
Wikidata's Hecuba is the same Hecuba, queen of Troy and wife of Priam. Hekabe is the Greek form of her name.

links.reason: Pausanias (7.4) gives Ancaeus and Samia the children Perilaus, Enudus, Samos, Alitherses and Parthenope. However, this Parthenope is Ancaeus' daughter, mother of Lycomedes by Apollo; the link fits only if it is this Parthenope, so it is likely correct and should be kept.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Samia is the Maeander's daughter and Ancaeus' wife, matching Pausanias.
Wikidata's Orestes is the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, which is the right being. He has no other names to check.
Wikidata match is Epimetheus, brother of Prometheus and son of Iapetus; no other names are attached to him.
Wikidata match is the goddess Hecate; no other names to question.

links.reason: Harmonia was Ares' daughter by Aphrodite, and married Cadmus; Ares was only a lover of Aphrodite, and the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lover links.
Iliad makes Aphrodite daughter of Zeus and Dione, not Hera, so she is only half-sister at most; the standard tradition makes her Ares' lover, not sibling.
Hermes is a half-brother only via Zeus, which is a loose kinship from Statius; the sibling link is unsupported by the tree's own parents.
Ixion is son of Phlegyas (or Antion), not of Ares; Ares is only Phlegyas' father.
Enyalios is a cult title or epithet of Ares, not a separate son.

links.link: Ares parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
links.reason: Pausanias names a Melanippus only as a son of Ares in a minor tale; the entry looks like a placeholder-named figure and cannot be confirmed.
Panic is a personification, not a person; Phobos and Deimos are the sons.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Ares; no foreign names.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros, but the tradition (Hesiod, Apollodorus) treats this as a union without formal marriage, so it is read as a lover per the editor's rule.
Achilles and Helen as a pair belong to the afterlife tradition on Leuke (Pausanias), not a marriage in this book; read as lover.

links.link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, so this duplicates the Neoptolemus link; it should be merged into one entry, not kept as a separate child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles; Hæmonian Achilles is just an epithet (Thessalian), not another person.

links.reason: In Metamorphoses 12 Chromis is a centaur killed by Caeneus/Theseus-era Lapith fight at Pirithous' wedding, not a son of Hercules; the Statius Thebaid Chromis is a different person (a son of Hercules, charioteer in Thebaid).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the centaur Chromis, which fits Metamorphoses; the Hercules parentage comes from a different Chromis in the Thebaid.
Wikidata's Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, is the Iphigenia Pausanias names; no other names are involved.
Match is the god Dionysus. The alternate names are cult epithets of the same god.
The Glaucus here is the Lycian captain, son of Hippolochus and cousin of Sarpedon, and the Wikidata match is the same person.
Moirae/Fates is the right match. Night as mother is supported by Hesiod Theogony 217 and Orphic Hymn 59, so the link stays even though Wikidata differs.

Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus. Oeager is Oeagrus, a spelling variant. Eurydice as Orpheus' wife is standard (Apollodorus, Ovid, Pausanias), so the two flagged spouse links are duplicates of the same correct marriage.
Wikidata's Penthesilea is the Amazon queen, daughter of Ares and Otrera, killed by Achilles at Troy; this matches the character.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 326-327) makes Orthos and Chimaera the parents of the Nemean lion (Phix and the lion). Typhoeus as father comes from Apollodorus, not Hesiod, so it does not belong in this book's tree.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Nemean lion itself. The Wikidata parents Typhon and Echidna differ from Hesiod's, but that is a variant tradition and not a wrong match.
Codrus, last king of Athens, son of Melanthus, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

Enarete, daughter of Deimachus and wife of Aeolus, mother of Cretheus, Sisyphus, Athamas, Salmoneus, Perieres, Canace, Alcyone, Pisidice, Calyce and Perimede (Apollodorus 1.7.3). The Wikidata match is correct.
Steropes is the Cyclops son of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) in Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.1.2) and Hesiod; the Wikidata match is the same being.
Wikidata match is Enyo the war-goddess, and the tree gives her no other names. Zeus and Hera as parents agree with Theoi and Wikidata.
Jocasta is Epicaste, wife of Laius and mother and wife of Oedipus (Pausanias 9.5.10-11 follows Homer's Epicaste). The Wikidata match is correct and the names are the same person.

links.reason: In the Aeneid Misenus is the son of Aeolus, a Trojan, not the keeper of the winds, Hippotes' son; these are different men named Aeolus.
Minyas' father in the Argonautica tradition is a different Aeolus, not Hippotes' son the wind-keeper (Minyas is usually son of Orchomenus, Poseidon or Chryses).

identity.detail: The name Aeolus covers several figures: the wind-keeper son of Hippotes (Odyssey), the son of Hellen and ancestor of the Aeolians (father of Minyas in some accounts), and the Trojan father of Misenus. Wikidata's Poseidon/Arne parentage belongs to the son of Hellen/Poseidon figure, not the Hippotes one.
Thaleia the Muse in Hesiod's Theogony (77) is the Muse Thalia, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne. The Wikidata match is correct. She is not the Grace Thalia, who is a different being.
Sandocus, son of Astynous (son of Phaethon), matches the Wikipedia description; the link to Astynous is consistent.
Idas son of Aphareus (Messenian Argonaut, brother of Lynceus, husband of Marpessa) matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Lathria belongs to a different Aristodemus in Pausanias (the Messenian king, or another namesake), not the Heraclid husband of Argia.
Anaxandra is a wife of another Aristodemus in Pausanias (the Messenian king's circle), not the Heraclid.
The daughter belongs to the Messenian king Aristodemus (sacrificed daughter), not the Heraclid, whose children are Eurysthenes and Procles.
Duplicate of the Messenian Aristodemus's daughter; not the Heraclid's child.
Artylas is father of a different Aristodemus; Apollodorus and Wikidata make Aristomachus the Heraclid's father.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Heraclid son of Aristomachus; the extra links from Pausanias come from namesakes, which is handled by the removals above.
Sicyon, eponym of Sicyon, is the right being. Pausanias 2.6.5 makes Marathon his father (son of Epopeus, in other accounts Erechtheus' or Metion's son), so the link is the book's own.

links.reason: Telemachus marries Circe in the Telegony epic cycle. Hesiod's Theogony 1011-16 and the Odyssey do not say so; the book lists only a lover relationship with Odysseus. The Wikidata spouse is the Telegony version. The editor's rule reads spouse links as lovers, so keep it as a lover link.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Circe, the daughter of Helios and Perse. Aeaean Circe is the same being.
Deidamia of Scyros, daughter of Lycomedes and mother of Neoptolemus by Achilles, matches Wikidata. The book's text says Achilles married her.
Iphicles, half-twin of Heracles and son of Amphitryon and Alcmena, is correctly matched. Iolaus is his son in Apollodorus too, so that link is fine.

Phaethon is the son of Helios in the Wikidata match. Pausanias 1.3.1 also gives a Phaethon son of Cephalus, a different tradition. The editor has ruled that Cephalus link right for this book, so no change is needed.
Wikidata match is the Argive king Triopas, son of Phorbas; matches the book.
Combe, daughter of Asopus, is the right match; she is the mother of the Curetes in Ovid's tradition (Met. 7.382), and no other names are mixed in.
The Wikidata match is Hector's wife Andromache, daughter of Eetion; no other names are involved.
Proserpine is the Roman Persephone, daughter of Jupiter and Ceres, wife of Pluto. The Wikidata match is correct. The alternate names Persephone and Proserpina are the same goddess.
Wikidata's Eriphyle is the wife of Amphiaraus and mother of Alcmaeon, which fits the book.
Orestes, son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, is the right match; no other names are attached.

links.reason: A group node duplicating the individual sons Polynices and Eteocles, who are already linked as his children.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Oedipus; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; no other names.
Wikidata match is the Trojan princess and priestess Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba; no other names to question.

links.reason: Lucina is a cult title of Juno (or Diana), not a separate daughter of Ops; Ovid's Ilithyia is Juno's birth-goddess aspect, whose mother would be Rhea/Ops only as Juno's mother, so the link confuses a title with a person.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Lucina is an epithet of Juno or Diana, not a distinct being. In Metamorphoses she is Juno as birth-goddess, and Ilithyia (Greek Eileithyia) is the same function, so the entry should be merged with Juno or Eileithyia rather than given its own parents.
Wikidata's Euthymus of Locri is the same boxer Pausanias describes.
Wikidata match is Aidos, the personification of shame or modesty. No other names are listed, so nothing needs splitting.

links.reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night, so Earth and Uranus (Hesiod's tradition) are not this book's parentage.
Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.453 makes the Furies daughters of Night, so Earth and Uranus (Hesiod's tradition) are not this book's parentage.

identity.detail: Eumenides and Furies are both names for the Erinyes, so the Wikidata match is correct.

Wikidata match is the sea goddess Amphitrite. Apollodorus makes her a daughter of Ocean, and Theoi cites Apollodorus 1.8 for Okeanos and Tethys. Wikidata's Nereus and Doris is the other tradition, so the parent links are right for this book.

links.reason: Pausanias' Aratus is the Sicyonian statesman, son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor's decision), not a child of Asclepius.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Asclepius is correct; Aesculapius is the Roman name for the same god.

links.reason: In Metamorphoses, 'Pallas' and 'Tritonia' here is Minerva (Athena), daughter of Jupiter; the Wikidata Pallas is the friend of Athena, daughter of Triton, so the Jupiter link is right only for the goddess.
The Pallas who is father of Clytus and Butes is the Athenian Pallas, brother of Aegeus (Metamorphoses 7), not the goddess or Triton's daughter.
The Pallas who is father of Clytus and Butes is the Athenian Pallas, brother of Aegeus (Metamorphoses 7), not the goddess or Triton's daughter.

identity.detail: Three beings share the name: Minerva/Athena (called Pallas and Tritonia in Ovid, daughter of Jupiter), the Pallas who was Athena's friend (daughter of Triton, the Wikidata match), and the Athenian Pallas, father of Clytus and Butes. The Wikidata match is wrong for the goddess Minerva and for the Athenian Pallas.
Iamos in Pindar's Olympian 6 is Iamus, son of Apollo and Euadne, so the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: The book's sentence names Artemisia, wife of Mausolus, who is Artemisia II of Caria (4th century BC). The Wikidata match is Artemisia I, fl. 480 BC, daughter of Lygdamis I, so the link belongs to a different woman.

identity.detail: The book's Artemisia is the wife of Mausolus (Artemisia II, Mausolus' sister-wife), not Artemisia I of Caria, who fought at Salamis. Her brother is described in the book as 'a Carian of Halicarnassus', so the match is likely confused; rematch to Artemisia II or treat the two as separate people.
Wikidata match is Pelops, son of Tantalos; no misattached names.
The Wikidata match is the Thessalian nymph Orseis, wife of Hellen and mother of Dorus, Xuthus and Aeolus.

links.reason: Dido's brother in the Aeneid is Pygmalion of Tyre, the king who murdered Sychaeus; Ovid's Pygmalion is a sculptor-king of Cyprus, a different person.

identity.detail: The match to Pygmalion of Cyprus is correct for Ovid's sculptor. Galatea is a post-antique name for the statue, which Ovid leaves unnamed.
Wikidata match is the Amazon queen Hippolyta, and Pausanias's Hippolyta, sister of Antiope, fits.

links.link: Arcas parent_of Pelasgus, son of Arcas
links.reason: Pausanias makes Pelasgus the father of Lycaon and so Arcas's ancestor, not his son; the link confuses two figures, and the name 'son of Arcas' looks like a misread.

identity.detail: Arcas is the Arcadian eponym, son of Zeus and Callisto, and Bootes is a normal alternate name for him as the constellation (or Arctophylax). Wikidata's father Lycaon is a variant, not an identity problem.

links.reason: Pausanias' Aratus is the Sicyonian statesman, son of Clinias and Aristodama (editor's decision), not a child of Asclepius.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god/hero Asclepius; no other names to doubt.
Acamas, son of Theseus, hero at Troy, matches Wikidata; Quintus Smyrnaeus calls him Theseus' son, so the link is right.

links.reason: In the Aeneid, Alcanor of Mount Ida is the father of the Trojan brothers Pandarus and Bitias, who are a different Pandarus. The Iliad's Pandarus is the Lycian archer, son of Lycaon.
Bitias is the brother of the Aeneid's Pandarus, son of Alcanor. The Iliad's Pandarus, son of Lycaon, has no such brother.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Iliad's Lycian archer, son of Lycaon. The Aeneid's Pandarus, son of Alcanor, is a separate character, which is why the two links above were removed.
Wikidata's Alcestis, daughter of Pelias and wife of Admetus, is the same being as the Alcestis in Pausanias.
Wikidata match is the Muse Terpsichore, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne; the book's Apollonius text calls her mother of the Sirens by Achelous, consistent with the tradition.
Pammon is the Trojan prince, son of Priam, killed by Neoptolemus. The match is correct and he has no other names.
Preugenes, son of Agenor son of Areus and father of Patreus, matches Wikidata and Pausanias; the flag on parents is not a real conflict.

links.reason: A chorus is a group, not a person; the Oceanids are already her daughters individually.
The river Xanthus in Hesiod's list is a son of Ocean and Tethys; the Midas-related Xanthus is another figure, but the editor's decision on Midas stands.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Tethys; no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias (2.16.1) makes Sthenelus the son of Crotopus's descendant line, not of Crotopus; in Pausanias Crotopus's son is Sthenelas per some accounts, but Statius's Thebaid (1.557-668) names only Psamathe and Linus as his children, so this link is an unsupported import.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argive king Crotopus, father of Psamathe in Statius; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Oeneus is the Calydonian king, son of Porthaon; the Pausanias link is not supported as a child of Pandion in the Athenian line.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian king Pandion, which is acceptable for the father of Procne and Philomela, though Wikipedia leaves open which of Pandion I or II.
Wikidata match is the Boeotian naiad Liriope, mother of Narcissus; no other names to check.
Polynices matches the son of Oedipus and brother of Eteocles. Antigone, Argia, Euryganeia (a variant mother with Wikidata and Wikipedia support) and Thersander (his son) are all standard.
Menestheus is the Athenian king at Troy, son of Peteos (Peteus). The link matches Wikidata's father, so nothing needs fixing.
Asopus is the river-god, son of Poseidon and Celusa in Pausanias. Wikidata's match is fine.

Creon of Thebes, son of Menoeceus and brother of Jocasta, is the right match. Pausanias' Creon is the same king, who ruled as guardian of Laodamas. The flagged parent difference is not a problem: Menoeceus is Creon's father in Wikidata and in the tradition.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 225) makes Night alone bear Strife, with no father; Erebus is not named as her parent in this book.

identity.detail: Eris is the right match; Strife and Eris are the same goddess.
Hesione, Oceanus' daughter and Prometheus' wife in Prometheus Bound, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are listed.
Thucydides son of Olorus, the Athenian historian, matches Wikidata; Pausanias names his father Olorus.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace; in Homer (Iliad 14) Hera promises her to Sleep as a bride, and she is not Hera's daughter. Theoi's listing is not a good basis, and the editor rejects other parentage for her.
Enyo is Ares' companion; in the Iliad she is a war goddess, and her parentage as Hera's daughter is a late, unsupported guess here.

identity.detail: Juno matches Hera as the book's queen of the gods; no other names are misattributed.

links.reason: Pausanias' Electra daughter of Atlas (the Pleiad, mother of Dardanus) is a different person from Agamemnon's daughter; the tree mixes two Electras.
Electra sister of Cadmus (Electran gate at Thebes) is a different person from Agamemnon's daughter.

identity.detail: The book's Electra is used for three women: Agamemnon's daughter (wife of Pylades, sister of Orestes), Electra daughter of Atlas (the Pleiad), and Electra sister of Cadmus. Only the Agamemnon links belong to the Wikidata match, which is correct for her.
Wikidata's Ornytion is Sisyphus' son, matching Pausanias; no other names are in play.
Miltiades the Younger, the Athenian general of Marathon, is the right match. Pausanias calls Cimon his son, which agrees with the tradition.
Agapenor, the Arcadian leader at Troy and son of Ancaeus, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

links.reason: Iliad 11.248 makes Coon Antenor's son, but not Theano's; Homer gives a different mother (Coon is Antenor's son by a different woman in tradition), so the Wikidata link is unsupported.
Helicaon is Antenor's son (Iliad 3.123) by Laodice's marriage, not Theano's; the Wikidata link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Theano, wife of Antenor and priestess of Athena; Cisses and Cisseus are spelling variants of her father's name.
Assaracus, king of Dardania, son of Tros and father of Capys, matches Wikidata (Iliad 20.232-239). Nothing to fix.

links.reason: Typhoeus is the Greek monster; Wikidata's Egyptian father is Seth (whom Greeks equated with Typhon), but Metamorphoses never makes Typhoeus Anubis's father, so this is a misidentified namesake link.
Io (as Isis) is not Anubis's mother in Ovid; Egyptian tradition gives Nephthys, and Io is only identified with Isis, so this confuses two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Egyptian god Anubis; no other names are involved.
The Wikidata match is the same Cretan princess Acacallis (Acalle in the Bibliotheca).

links.reason: Aethra is Theseus' mother; Pirithous' mother is Dia (wife of Ixion), so this confuses him with his friend Theseus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lapith king Pirithous; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Polynices, son of Oedipus and brother of Eteocles. Wikidata's spouse Argea is the same person as Apollodorus' Argia. All links are consistent with Apollodorus.

links.reason: Ceryx is the son of Hermes and Agraulus, daughter of Cecrops (Pausanias), not Cecrops' wife, the daughter of Actaeus.
Apollodorus 3.14.2 makes Cecrops' daughter Agraulus a different person from his wife Agraulus, daughter of Actaeus.

identity.detail: The node joins two beings: Agraulus, wife of Cecrops and daughter of Actaeus (the Wikidata match), and Agraulus, daughter of Cecrops and Agraulus, who is the mother of Ceryx. The Cecrops-parent and Ceryx links belong to the daughter.
Acamas son of Theseus (and Phaedra) is the Trojan War hero; the Wikidata match fits.
Wikidata match is Paroreus son of Tricolonus, the founder of Paroria in Arcadia. This agrees with Pausanias, and no other names are involved.

Taras is the eponymous hero of Taras (Tarentum), son of Poseidon, and the Wikidata match is the same being. No other names are listed. Satyrion as mother is a nymph tied to the place, which fits Pausanias's 'local Nymph'.
Wikidata match is correct: Amphitryon of Tiryns/Thebes, son of Alcaeus.
Wikidata's Atalanta is the same heroine. Her parentage varies by tradition (Iasus and Clymene, Schoeneus, Maenalus), and the links brought in from Apollodorus fit the Arcadian Argonaut version.

links.reason: Ovid's Metamorphoses has Nyctimene as daughter of Epopeus of Lesbos, not Nycteus; the tradition giving Nycteus a daughter Nyctimene is a different one and is not what Pausanias says.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban regent Nycteus, brother of Lycus; no other names to check.
Wikidata's Abas, king of Argos, is the same being as the book's Abas.

Teuthras is the king of Mysia, eponym of Teuthrania, and the Wikidata match is correct. Auge as his wife (in some versions adopted as his daughter) is well attested in Apollodorus and Pausanias, so the link is kept.

Cleonymus, son of Cleomenes II (Agiad), is the right match. Pausanias's 'Cleomenes, son of Cleombrotus' is Cleomenes II, who had sons Acrotatus and Cleonymus, so the flagged parent difference is only a naming variation. The book's sentence supports the link.
Maia the Pleiad, mother of Hermes, matches Wikidata. The Roman goddess Maia is a separate figure identified with her, but no other names are given here.

links.reason: Epimedes is one of the Idaean Dactyls named in Pausanias (5.7.6), not a sibling; the link treats a member of the group as a separate sibling.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Curetes, Dactyls is a merged entry. The Curetes are often distinguished from the Dactyls, but the sources treat them as interchangeable here, so no change.
Wikidata's Ganymede is the Trojan cup-bearer of Jupiter, which matches Ovid's Ganymede.
Wikidata match is the Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Poseidon and Thoosa; no other names confused.
Wikidata's Phigalus, the Arcadian son of Lycaon and eponym of Phigalia, is the same being Pausanias means.
Wikidata match is the poet Hesiod; no other names to question.

Wikidata's Turnus is the Rutulian king of the Aeneid, who also appears in Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 14). The parents Daunus and Venilia and the sister Juturna are the Virgilian tradition, so all three links are fine.
Astydamia, wife of Acastus of Iolcus and daughter of Cretheus, matches Astydameia; the alternate name Hippolyta is the same woman in the tradition. Nothing to fix.
Dorus, son of Hellen and Orseis and eponym of the Dorians, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Corcyra (Asopus' daughter) was mother of Phaeax by Poseidon in some accounts and is linked to Nausithous's line only through confusion; no source in Argonautica gives her as Alcinous' mother.
Arete is Alcinous' wife and niece (daughter of his brother Rhexenor), not his sibling; the Argonautica calls her his wife.
Pausanias' Troilus is not a son of Alcinous of Phaeacia; this link comes from a namesake or misreading.
Alcetus belongs to a different Alcinous in Pausanias, not the Phaeacian king.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Phaeacian king Alcinous, husband of Arete.
Steropes is one of the Hesiodic Cyclopes (Brontes, Steropes, Arges), children of Uranus and Gaia. The Wikidata match is this being and he has no other names.

links.reason: Galanthis is Alcmene's servant in Metamorphoses 9, not Tiresias's daughter; Pausanias does not make her his child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban prophet Tiresias; no other names.

links.reason: Iphigenia's mother is Clytemnestra (Wikidata, Aeschylus, Euripides); Helen is Clytemnestra's sister and Hermione's mother. Only a rare tradition (Stesichorus, in Pausanias) makes Helen the mother, and this book does not tell it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the daughter of Agamemnon; no other names.
Aeëtes of Colchis, son of Helios and Perse, father of Medea, Chalciope and Apsyrtus, brother of Circe. The match is correct.

links.reason: Dirce was the wife of Lycus, not Antiope's child; she was Antiope's tormentor, so this link is a mistake.
This is the Amazon Antiope, sister of Hippolyta, taken by Theseus; the Theban Antiope is a different person.
Hippolyta's sister is the Amazon Antiope, not the Theban daughter of Nycteus or Asopus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Theban Antiope. In this book the Amazon Antiope is a separate namesake, so the Theseus and Hippolyta links belong to her.
Salmoneus, son of Aeolus and Enarete, father of Tyro, is the correct match; no other names to check.

links.reason: No ancient source makes Hecate the mother of Janus; Metamorphoses 14 only gives Janus as father of Canens by Venilia, and the Wikidata mother is a doubtful later guess.

Wikidata's Caelus is the Roman Uranus, but the book never says this, and Janus's parents are given elsewhere as Caelus and Hecate or as Saturn, so the link is a doubtful identification, not the book's own tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Roman god Janus; the book calls him the Ionian Janus, which is the same god.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Sisyphus 'the son of Aeolus'; Zeus is not his father in the book or in the tradition (Aeolus and Enarete).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Corinthian king Sisyphus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Aidos is not Prometheus' child in Hesiod; Theoi's confirmation seems to stem from a misread. Hesiod has Aidos only as a personified goddess without that parentage.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus; no other names.
Wikidata match is Aethusa, daughter of Poseidon and Alcyone, mother of Linus by Apollo; the book's sentences agree.
Tlepolemus, son of Heracles and Astyoche, leader of the Rhodians at Troy, matches Wikidata. Polyxo as his wife is attested by Pausanias (3.19.10), so that link is fine.

The Wikidata match is the Corinthian hero Bellerophon. The parent difference is only the Glaucus vs Poseidon tradition. The Iliad (6.154) gives Glaucus as father and the editor's decision on the Glaucus link is final, so the Poseidon link is a variant rather than an error.

Tithonus, son of Laomedon and lover of Eos, is the right match. The Wikidata father Cephalus is a variant tradition (Cephalus is sometimes called Tithonus' father in other sources), but Laomedon is correct for Hesiod and Homeric tradition.
Wikidata match is Alcmaeon son of Amphiaraus, the Epigonus; the name variant is just spelling.
The Pierides here are the nine daughters of Pierus and Evippe who competed with the Muses in Ovid. The Wikidata match is the same group. The alternative name Emathides (Emathian sisters) is correct.
Hypseus, Lapith king and father of Cyrene, is the right being. Pindar's Pythian 9 calls Cyrene his daughter, and the tradition gives Peneus and Creusa as his parents, so all three links hold.
Diomedes, son of Tydeus, king of Argos and Aetolian hero, matches the Wikidata entry. The epithet 'Ætolian hero' fits him through his father's Calydonian descent.

links.reason: Selene is not Apollo's sister. The editor ruled that Selene-Apollo links are wrong; Diana is the sister, and the Moon here is a confusion (Metamorphoses).
Scylla's parentage is Phorcys/Crataeis or Triton, not Apollo; this is an unsupported guess, and Hesiod is dubious here.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, not Apollo; she was a Leucippid, wife of Castor.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the god Apollo; all other names (Phoebus, Paean, Delian, Thymbraean, Cirrhaean father) are his epithets.

links.reason: Hesiod's Phaethon, son of Eos and Cephalus, is a different being from Ovid's Phaethon, son of Clymene and the Sun; the editor ruled Cephalus as parent only right in Pausanias.

identity.detail: Aurora is the Roman Eos; the match is right.

links.reason: Pausanias 10.6 has Poseidon's intrigue with Thyia, but that is a different Thyia (Cephissus' daughter, in Pausanias' Delphic context, mother of Chloris' circle); the link mixes two namesakes. Actually the Poseidon passage in 9.36 concerns Chloris and Neleus, not Deucalion's daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Thyia is Deucalion's daughter, mother of Magnes and Makednos by Zeus. Pausanias' Thyia is the Autochthon Castalius' daughter, the first priestess of Dionysus, with Apollo as father of Delphus. These are two different women, so the Wikidata match is wrong for this book's Castalius/Apollo links.
Wikidata match is Peleus, son of Aeacus and father of Achilles; no stray names.
Phorbas, sixth king of Argos and father of Triopas, matches the book's Phorbas. Wikidata's fathers Argus and Criasus are alternate genealogies, not an error.
Alalcomenia, daughter of Ogygus (Ogyges), eponym of Alalcomenae, matches Wikidata. Pausanias's 'Ogygus' is the same person as Ogyges, so the parent flag is only a spelling difference.
Wikidata's Ganymede is the Trojan cup-bearer of Zeus, which matches the character in Pindar. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Harmonia is Ares' daughter. The Argonautica link misreads the family, and Harmonia married Cadmus.
Duplicate of the Penthesileia node, which is the same Amazon queen.
Thestius is the son of Agenor or Ares in some sources; Theoi lists him as Ares' son but other sources make him a son of Ares only in rare traditions. This may not be the same Thestius the book names.
Melanippe is an Amazon, usually the daughter of Ares only in some sources, and the Argonautica reading is a guess at a different Melanippe.

identity.detail: Wikidata matches the god Ares. Mars is his Roman counterpart, and Aphneus, Gynaecothoenas and Theritas are his cult epithets, so the names are acceptable.

Azeus is the Minyan son of Clymenus of Orchomenus and father of Astyoche; the Wikidata match is correct. The parent flag is not a real conflict: the book names Clymenus as father and does not name a mother, so Wikidata's mother Bouzyge does not contradict it.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony makes Echidna Typhon's mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse. This is a union, not a casual affair.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the monster Typhon (Typhoeus). No other names are listed.

links.reason: The Iliad (13.450-452) makes Deucalion his father and Minos his grandfather; Minos as father comes from Pausanias and conflicts with this book's tree, since Minos parent of Deucalion is the editor's accepted link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Cretan king Idomeneus; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is the sea god Phorcys, son of Pontus and Gaia, husband of Ceto; no other names to question.
Wikidata Aeëtes is the Colchian king of the Argonautica; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Paris carried Helen off to Troy and the editor reads any non-marriage 'spouse' link as a lover. The Iliad does treat her as his wife at Troy, but the editor's rule is final.
Pausanias tells of a posthumous union on Leuke, which is not a marriage; at most a lover.
Theseus abducted the young Helen; there was no marriage, so he counts as a lover.

identity.detail: Helen of Troy is the correct match.
Adrian and Emperor Adrian are Pausanias' names for the emperor Hadrian, so the Wikidata match is right.
Wikidata match is Thyestes, son of Pelops and brother of Atreus; this is the same being.

links.reason: Wikidata lists Selene as Endymion's spouse, and in the tradition she bore him fifty daughters (Pausanias 5.1.4), so she is more than a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Endymion, and he has no other names.
Cyllarus is the centaur of Ovid's Metamorphoses, beloved and husband of Hylonome; the Wikidata match is the same being.

links.reason: Duplicate spelling of Tleptolemus, the same son; keep only the book's Tleptolemus form.
Duplicate spelling of Tleptolemus, the same son.
Aventinus is a Roman tradition from the Aeneid, not Pausanias; a different tradition but not contradicted, though the link is off-topic here.
Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, already linked.

links.link: Hercules sibling_of Iphiclus, son of Amphitryon
links.reason: Duplicate spelling of Iphicles, already linked.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group taken for a person; the sons by Megara are not a single individual.

identity.detail: Heracles is the right match; the epithets are all Hercules.

Neleus, king of Pylos, son of Tyro and Poseidon, brother of Pelias, matches. Wikidata lists Hippocoon and Cretheus as fathers, but Cretheus is only the stepfather and Hippocoon is a different person; this does not affect the match.

Pausanias' Alcimedon is the Arcadian of Phigalia, father of Phialo (Heracles' lover, Pausanias 8.12). The Wikidata match is the Myrmidon leader at Troy, son of Laerces, in Homer's Iliad. They are namesakes, so the match and the father Laerces should not be applied to this character.

Wikidata match is Eurystheus, king of Tiryns/Mycenae, son of Sthenelus; the tree is consistent. Wikidata lists Admete as a spouse, but the book gives her as his daughter, and that link is already right.
Acacus, son of Lycaon and founder of Acacesium in Arcadia, matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata match is Procne, daughter of Pandion and wife of Tereus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Helen and Achilles were united only after death on Leuke (Pausanias, Ptolemy Hephaestion); the editor's rule reads any spouse other than a marriage as a lover.

links.link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus is another name of Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, already listed; the entry for the later king of Epirus is a different person and duplicates the link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis.

Libya, daughter of Epaphus, is the right match. In Aeschylus's Suppliants she is Epaphus's descendant and the land named for her. Her son Belus by Poseidon is standard, and Epaphus as her father is also standard.
Phylacides, son of Apollo and Acacallis and brother of Philander, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Agesipolis and Cleombrotus were sons of King Pausanias, son of Pleistoanax and exiled c. 395 BC, not of the regent of Plataea who was Pleistoanax's father.

identity.detail: The regent Pausanias (victor of Plataea, son of Cleombrotus) is merged with his grandson, King Pausanias (son of Pleistoanax, father of Agesipolis and Cleombrotus). The Wikidata match fits the regent only.

links.reason: Oenopion is son of Dionysus and Ariadne (Apollodorus Epitome); Wikidata's Theseus link is a confusion with Ariadne's children by Theseus in some traditions, not in this book.
Hesiod (via Plutarch) names Aegle as Theseus's passion for whom he abandoned Ariadne; a lover, not a wife.
Hippolyte is the Amazon, equated with Antiope; Apollodorus has Theseus carry off an Amazon, mother of Hippolytus, not marry her formally. Treated as a lover.
Helen was abducted by Theseus as a girl and never wed to him; at most a lover.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias's Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus and Helen, is a minor tradition and is not named in Apollodorus; she is not Agamemnon's Iphigenia.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias-only figure, not in Apollodorus, easily confused with other Melanippi.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Theseus; no other names listed.
Wikidata match is the Cretan judge Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa. Wikidata lists Hephaestus as a second father, which looks like a data error, but it is not a link in this tree.

links.reason: Apollodorus 3.14.2 names Agraulus as Cecrops' wife and also as a daughter; the daughter link imported from Pausanias duplicates the daughter Aglauros, already linked from Metamorphoses, and splits one daughter into two entries.

identity.detail: Cecrops I is the right match; Apollodorus' earth-born king of Attica.

links.reason: Hesiod: Gaia bore children to Pontus, but only Uranus is her husband; read as a lover per the editor's rule.
Aeschylus's Argus is not Earth's child here; Apollodorus gives Argus Panoptes as son of Arestor or as earth-born, a different being.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Roman Tellus/Terra, a different figure from Greek Gaia; Aether, Dies and Caelus data come from Roman Terra. Match to Gaia instead.
Melobosis is an Oceanid, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys; the Wikidata match is the same being.

Muses match the Wikidata Muse entry. Aliases Kalliope and Kleio are individual Muses, not the group, but they are listed as names of the group in this book; this is acceptable and not a clear mismatch.
Wikidata match is Nyctimus, the youngest son of Lycaon who survived Zeus's thunderbolts in Apollodorus. The spouse listed there is not in this book's tree, and nothing else needs fixing.
The Wikidata match is the Corinthian spring nymph Pirene. Wikidata's father Asopus and mother Metope are another tradition, and Pausanias does not follow them.

links.reason: Midas is the Phrygian king in Ovid's Metamorphoses, not a child of the Titan Rhea (possibly confused with Cybele); Hesiod never says this.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Rhea; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Epaphus, son of Zeus and Io; Apis and Munantius are alternate names for him.
Wikidata match is the sea goddess Amphitrite, wife of Poseidon; no other names to split.
Teuthras is the king of Mysia and eponym of Teuthrania. Pausanias's sentence says he married Auge, so the spouse link is right and nothing needs fixing.
Wikidata match is Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, the right being.

links.reason: In the Odyssey, Nestor's wife is a different Eurydice (daughter of Clymenus), not Orpheus' wife the nymph.
Apollodorus 3.6.4 names Opheltes' mother as Eurydice, wife of Lycurgus of Nemea, a different person from Orpheus' wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Orpheus' wife; the book's other Eurydice (wife of Lycurgus) and Nestor's wife are namesakes, handled via link removal.
Wikidata match is the right Ceyx, husband of Alcyone. No other names are listed.

Wikidata match is Pan the goat-god; no other names listed. Mercury as father and Callisto as mother are attested traditions (Scholiast ad Theocritus 1.3), and the Statius links to Eurymedon and Crenaeus are confirmed by Theoi.
Peratus (Eratus), king of Sicyon, son of Poseidon and Chalcinia, is the right match.

links.reason: The book has Aethra say Aegeus wedded her, but the editor's rule reads any spouse link beyond marriages as a lover; Aethra's union with Aegeus was a single night in Troezen, so it is better recorded as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian king Aegeus; no other names to dispute.
Wikidata match is the Titan Hyperion; Euryphaessa is a variant name for his wife (Theia in Hesiod), not a separate problem.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, is the Trojan prophetess; the match is correct.
Broteas son of Tantalus is the Broteas of Pausanias, who says he carved the Mother of the Gods image on Coddinus rock near Sipylus. The parent link to Tantalus is right and agrees with Wikidata.

links.reason: In the Aeneid Hyrtacus is the father of Nisus. Hippocoon son of Hyrtacus is a Trojan in the Aeneid's Sicilian games (Hippocoon, Hyrtacides, Aen. 5.492), so the link is likely right, though Hyrtacus of Arisbe is a different person from the Trojan in the Iliad.

identity.detail: Hyrtacus is the Trojan father of Nisus; the Wikidata match is plausible, and Arisbe as wife comes from the Iliad tradition.
Thalia is the Charis, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome (Hesiod Theogony 907-909); this matches the Wikidata entry.
Hypermnestra, daughter of Danaus and wife of Lynceus, is the right match in Apollodorus.

links.reason: Endeis, wife of Aeacus and mother of Peleus, is a daughter of Chiron (or Skiron), not a Nereid. She is no sister of Thetis; the link likely confuses her with Peleus's family.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Thetis is the Nereid mother of Achilles. Its spouse Neptune is a wrongly listed lover and the tree does not use it.
Wikidata match is Rhesus of Thrace, the same being as the Iliad's king; no wrong other names.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Demophon, the child nursed by Demeter, is the son of Metanira and Celeus of Eleusis. He is not the Thracian king of Elaeus in the Wikipedia description, and the match should be fixed, but this parent link is right for the book's Demophon.
Theseus' son Demophon (Phaedra's son, Acamas' brother) is a different person from Celeus' son at Eleusis. The link comes from other books, not this one's Demophon.
