Wikidata matches Aegina, the daughter of Asopus and mother of Aeacus, which is right. But 'Œnopia' is the old name of the island, which Ovid says Aeacus renamed after his mother. It is not a separate person and is not another name for the nymph. Keep it as a place name, not as a name for her.
Wikidata match is the Trojan prince Hector, son of Priam and Hecuba, husband of Andromache. No other names are attached to him.

links.reason: Aeschylus' Argus is the herdsman, called earth-born in some tellings, but the editor rules Inachus wrong and Aristor right only in Metamorphoses; Earth is not his parent in Hesiod.
Charybdis is daughter of Poseidon and Earth only in later scholia; the cited books do not state Earth as her mother.
Duplicate of Coeus, a variant spelling to be merged, not a separate child.
Duplicate of Phoebe, a variant spelling.
Duplicate of Antaeus, a variant spelling.
Hesiod makes Ceto a child of Pontus and Earth, so Earth is a parent; unsupported duplication aside, this holds.
Arion is the horse of Poseidon and Demeter; Earth only in a loose reading, not Hesiod.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Terra/Tellus is the Roman goddess; Hesiod's Gaia is the Greek Earth, a counterpart but a different cult figure.
Wikidata's Daphne is the nymph loved by Apollo; the alternative fathers Ladon and Amyclas are variant traditions, not another being.
Gobryas, father of Mardonius and Darius I's lance-bearer, matches the Persian noble in Pausanias, who calls Mardonius 'son of Gobryas'.

links.reason: In the standard tradition Ascanius (Iulus) is the son of Aeneas and Creusa; Lavinia is his stepmother (in Livy she bears Silvius, and in some versions Ascanius is her son, but Ovid's Metamorphoses does not say so).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct; Iülus is the same being as Ascanius.
Myrtilus, charioteer of Oenomaus and son of Hermes, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.
Cilix, son of Agenor and Telephassa, brother of Cadmus and Europa in Apollodorus, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names.

Persephone matches the daughter of Zeus and Demeter, queen of the underworld. Aïdoneus is Hades, so the spouse link is right. Styx as a mother comes from a minor tradition (Zeus & Styx) and is not in this tree.
The Wikidata match is the seer Amphiaraus. The duplicate Alcmaon node is a spelling variant of Alcmaeon, not a different being.

links.reason: Alpheus' pursuit of Artemis is told by Pausanias, not by Hesiod's hymn; Artemis stayed a virgin and the book states no such link, so it is a guess carried over from another book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus and Leto; Demeter as mother is an Aeschylean variant, not a problem here.
Wikidata match is Chiron the centaur; no other names are listed.
Deiphobus is the Trojan prince, son of Priam and Hecuba; the Wikidata match is correct.
Cisus, son of Temenus and king of Argos, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Glauce (Creusa) was the Corinthian princess Jason was to marry, but the tree has her as spouse; Medea is the wife. Per editor's rule, only marriages count, and Jason's marriage to Glauce never took place in most accounts (Euripides), so she is a betrothed/lover.
A group of children is taken for a person; the sons are named separately (Mermerus, Pheres, Thessalus, etc.), so this generic node is redundant.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason; the name Iason is the Greek form of the same person.

links.reason: A group label, not a person; the sons are already Mermerus and Pheres in this book.
Pausanias does not give Medea a daughter Eriopis; Eriopis is a different figure (Jason's mother or Alcathous' daughter), so this is a namesake confusion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Medea, daughter of Aeetes; no other names are in question.
The match is the river god Alpheus; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Aethlius is the first king of Elis, husband of Calyce and son of Protogeneia. In Apollodorus he is the son of Zeus and Protogeneia, daughter of Deucalion, which agrees.
Wikidata match is the Theban Harmonia, wife of Cadmus and daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. The Zeus and Electra parentage is the Samothracian variant and does not apply here.
Wikidata match is the Phaeacian king Alcinous, son of Nausithous; no other names are listed.

Muses matches the Muse group. In Metamorphoses they are the daughters of Jupiter (Zeus) and Mnemosyne, as Theoi and Wikidata also say. The Pierides are a separate group, and the book treats them that way.
Philyra the Oceanid, mother of Cheiron by Kronos, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.
Wikidata Auge, daughter of Aleus and mother of Telephus by Heracles, matches.

links.reason: Doris is Nereus's wife and the mother of the Nereids (Hesiod, Theogony); she is the daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, so this link confuses her with someone else.
The Nereids are a group, not a single person; the link should be to the individual daughters (Thetis, Glauce, Galatea, Psamathe) rather than a collective node.

identity.detail: Nereus the sea-god is correctly matched.

links.reason: Hesiod's Nestor, son of Neleus, is a different figure; Jocasta's father is Menoeceus, and Nestor is not her father in Apollodorus or the Theban tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct; Epicasta is the same person as Jocasta (Homer's Odyssey calls her Epicaste).
Eurypylus, son of Telephus and Astyoche, is the Mysian leader in Quintus Smyrnaeus' Fall of Troy; the Wikidata match and the alternate names (Telephus' son) fit him.

links.reason: Doris is an Oceanid, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys (Hesiod), and Nereus' wife; Apollodorus gives her as his spouse, not his daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea-god Nereus; no stray names.
Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas and mother of Asclepius, matches Wikidata.
Telchis is the Sicyonian king, son of Europs and father of Apis, as Pausanias says. The Wikidata match fits.
Wikidata match is the king Tantalus; no other names to question.
Phrynichus the tragedian, son of Polyphradmon, matches Wikidata and Pausanias's own words; the parent link agrees with Wikidata, so the flag is a false alarm.

links.reason: Selene as mother comes from a tradition about another Nemea, the daughter of Zeus and Selene. Pausanias gives only Asopus as her father and names no mother.

identity.detail: Nemea, nymph of Nemea and daughter of Asopus, is the right match.

links.reason: The Icarus in Ovid's Erigone passage is the Athenian Icarius, father of Erigone, who received wine from Dionysus. He is not Daedalus's son who fell into the sea, so this link confuses two people of the same name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Daedalus's son Icarus, so the identity is correct.

links.reason: Ares is Aphrodite's lover (Odyssey 8) and son of Zeus and Hera; the Iliad treats them as separate beings, not siblings, and the sibling link contradicts the lover link.

identity.detail: Aphrodite and Venus are the same being; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Ganymede of Troy, the cupbearer of Zeus; this is the same being, and no other names are listed.

links.reason: In Hesiod, Theia is Oceanus's sister and the wife of Hyperion, and Oceanus's wife is Tethys. Theia is also an Oceanid in the Homeric Hymn tradition, so the link confuses the two.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Oceanus; no other names are listed.
Callirhoe, daughter of Achelous and wife of Alcmaeon, matches Wikidata; Pausanias says so explicitly.

links.reason: Boreas is son of Astraeus and Eos in Hesiod (Theogony 378-380), but Theoi lists him as child of Astraios and Eos; this is actually right, so keep is warranted.

identity.detail: Eos is the right match; Morn is just a translation of her name.
Wikidata's Thasus is the Phoenician prince who sailed in search of Europa. Pausanias 5.25.12 calls him the son of Agenor, which matches the link.
Leto matches Latona, the mother of Apollo and Artemis/Diana. The Wikidata match is correct and her other name is the same being.
Iphis, child of Ligdus and Telethusa in Crete (Ovid, Metamorphoses 9), is correctly matched. No other names are involved.
Wikidata's Cleisidice is the Eleusinian princess, daughter of Celeus and Metaneira. The only link, Celeus as her father, matches the Homeric Hymn to Demeter tradition, so it is kept.
Ammon is the Egyptian god Amun, whom Pausanias equates with Zeus Ammon; the match is fine.
Wikidata's Ino is the Theban princess, daughter of Cadmus, who became Leucothea; the alias is the same being.

links.reason: In Pausanias and tradition Aglaurus is Cecrops' daughter, not his wife; the spouse link from Apollodorus confuses her with Cecrops' wife Agraulos, daughter of Actaeus.

identity.detail: Wikidata Aglaurus is a fitting match for Cecrops' daughter; the Wikipedia blurb mentions Actaeus' daughter (Cecrops' wife), but the book's Aglaurus is the daughter of Cecrops.
The Wikidata match is Pandora, the first woman, and no other names are listed. The Pyrrha link is right, since Apollodorus calls Pyrrha the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora.
Wikidata match is the Calydonian king Oeneus; no other names are listed.

Apis, king of Argos and son of Phoroneus, is a different being from Sarapis, the Hellenistic Egyptian god. In Apollodorus the Argive Apis is said to have been called Sarapis (Egyptian Apis/Epaphus tradition), so this alias is a conflation. Sarapis should be split off from Apis of Argos.
Wikidata match is the Spartan king Tyndareus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Euryale, mother of Orion by Poseidon, is called Minos's daughter in some sources (Hesiod/Apollodorus), but this link is flagged as variable parentage and is not stated in the Odyssey; the tree's note shows it is unsupported for this book.

identity.detail: Minos of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, matches. Note that the grandfather Minos (father of Lycastus) is a different being, but nothing here confuses them.

Glaukos in Pindar's Olympian 13 and Pythian odes can be the Lycian ally of Troy, son of Hippolochus (Iliad), matching Wikidata. Pindar's Glaukos of Corinth, son of Sisyphus, is a different person, but no link here confuses the two.

links.link: Cleombrotus parent_of Cleomenes, son of Cleombrotus
links.reason: Pausanias speaks of two Cleombrotuses: the son of Anaxandridas II (brother of Leonidas) and a later Agiad king, father of Agesipolis and Cleomenes (Cleomenes II). The sons belong to the later king, not the regent.
Agesipolis is the son of the later king Cleombrotus I (d. 371 BC), not of the regent. The book's other Agesipolis is the son of Pausanias.
This sentence concerns the sons of Pausanias (king, exiled), Agesipolis and a young Cleombrotus, a different man from the regent.

links.link: Cleombrotus parent_of Cleomenes III, son of Leonidas
links.reason: The sentence names Cleomenes the younger son of the later Cleombrotus, i.e. Cleomenes II. Cleomenes III, son of Leonidas II, is unrelated.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the regent, brother of Leonidas and son of Anaxandridas II. The book's Cleombrotus also covers the later king, father of Agesipolis and Cleomenes, and Pausanias's son Cleombrotus. These should be separate people.

links.reason: Silenus as a son of Pan/Hermes belongs to the Greek Pan or satyr tradition, not the Roman Faunus of the Aeneid; the link comes from a Greek-name equation.
Callisto is the mother of Arcas, and in some sources of Pan (Arcadian), not Faunus. The Aeneid makes Faunus the son of Picus.
In Ovid, Acis is the son of Faunus and the nymph Symaethis, but this is another Faunus (a Sicilian faun), and the Aeneid's Faunus is the king-god of Latium, son of Picus.
Statius' Eurymedon and Crenaeus are sons of a faun/Faunus figure, meaning a Greek-style faun in Thebes, not the Latin god Faunus.
Crenaeus in Statius is a son of a river-god, not Faunus the god of Latium; this is a different being of similar name.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Faunus is the right being; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Dirce, wife of Lycus, is not a child of Helios in Apollodorus. Wikidata's list of fathers (Helios, Achelous, Ismenus) looks like a muddle of different traditions, and the book names no father for her.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Dirce, wife of Lycus and queen of Thebes, which is the right being. She has no other names.
Simoeis is the river god of the Trojan plain, so the match is correct. Hesiod (Theogony 342) lists him among the children of Oceanus and Tethys. The sibling link to Xanthus (Scamander) is fine.
The Wikidata match is the king of Sparta, which is correct.
The Wikidata match is correct: Epaphus, son of Zeus and Io. Apis is an alternative name for the same figure.

links.reason: Scylla is not Triton's child in any tradition; the Argonautica link is an unsupported guess, and the usual Scylla parentage (Phorcys, Crataeis, Trienus and others) names other parents.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the sea god Triton. Pausanias also mentions Triton as a river and as a Tanagran figure, but these are not separate names here.

Pandion matches the Athenian king; Apollodorus tells of both Pandion I (father of Procne and Philomela, Erechtheus and Butes) and Pandion II (father of Aegeus, Pallas, Nisus and Lycus), and the Wikidata match is acceptable for this name.

links.reason: Phokos is the same son as Phocus, only spelled differently; the link duplicates the Apollodorus link and does not belong as a separate person.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Nereid Psamathe, daughter of Nereus, mother of Phocus by Aeacus. Proteus as spouse is a different tradition (Euripides' Helen) and not in this book.
The Wikidata match is Phrixus, son of Athamas and Nephele. No other names are listed, so nothing needs splitting.
The Wikidata match is the right one: Tisamenus, son of Orestes and Hermione, king of Argos, Mycenae and Sparta.
Wikidata match is Electra the Pleiad, mother of Dardanus by Zeus; the book's lines on the Pleiad hiding after Troy's fall fit her. All links are fine.
Wikidata's Antimache is the wife of Eurystheus, queen of Tiryns, which matches Apollodorus. Her father Amphidamas agrees with the book, so the parents flag is not a real conflict.
Wikidata's Thaumas is the sea god, son of Pontus and Gaia, as in Hesiod's Theogony. No other names are attached.

links.reason: Moon here is Selene, whom the editor ruled out as Apollo's relative; Artemis is the sister, and Ovid's Diana/Luna is a confusion.
Scylla is the daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis, not Apollo; this is a namesake (Scylla daughter of Nisus) or a misreading.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, not Apollo; this is a misreading of Pausanias.
This is a duplicate of the Cyrene link under another spelling.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the god Apollo. The other names are all epithets of the same being.
Wikidata match is Pylades, son of Strophius, the friend of Orestes.

Phocus, the Corinthian prince and eponym of Phocis, son of Ornytion (or Poseidon) and Pronoe, is the Wikidata match. Antiope as his wife is the Pausanias tradition. Hesiod's Phocus, son of Aeacus, is a different being, so this match may belong to another character, but nothing here shows that.

The Wikidata match and its Wikipedia description are for the Oceanid Argia, mother of Phoroneus. Statius' Argia is the daughter of Adrastus and wife of Polynices, so this is a different person. Her links in the book are correct.

Calybe here is the nymph, wife (or mate) of Laomedon and mother of Bucolion (Apollodorus 3.12.3). The Wikipedia page is a disambiguation that also lists a Dionysian follower, but the Wikidata match is the nymph, so it is the same being.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group taken for a person; the children of Heracles and Megara are not a single individual.

identity.detail: Hercules is Heracles; the names Hercules and Heracles are the same being.

links.reason: Asterion here is the Minotaur's name or Asterius, Crete's king, not a child of Minos in Apollodorus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Minos, king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa; no other names to dispute.

links.reason: Virgil's Aeneid makes Ocnus (founder of Mantua) the son of Manto, a Tuscan nymph or Theban seer in Virgil's telling. The tree has joined this to Tiresias' daughter, which is a different tradition and does not fit Hesiod's Manto, who is the mother of Mopsus.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Manto, daughter of Tiresias, is the same figure as this book's Manto.

links.reason: Apollodorus 1.2.3 gives Asia as Iapetus' wife and mother of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius; Clymene as his wife is Hesiod's tradition, not this book's.
Buphagus as a son of Iapetus comes from Pausanias; Apollodorus does not say it, and this Buphagus is a different figure (an Arcadian hero).

links.link: Iapetus parent_of Menoetius, son of Iapetus
links.reason: Duplicate of the Iapetus parent_of Menoetius link, with the child's name garbled; Apollodorus 1.2.3 already supports a single link.

identity.detail: Iapetos is the correct Titan; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Picus as a son of Saturn comes from Roman sources (Aeneid, Metamorphoses). Apollodorus does not give Cronus this child, and the Roman Saturn is a different tradition.
Apollodorus makes the Fates daughters of Zeus and Themis (1.3.1). The Wikidata link is a variant from Hesiod's other tradition, not this book's.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Cronus the Titan, which is correct.
Praxiteles of Athens, the sculptor, is the right match. The Phryne link as lover is supported by Pausanias, so it is kept.
Euros is the east wind Eurus, and Aurora is the Roman name for Eos, so the parent link matches Wikidata and Theoi (Astraeus and Eos). The flag is only a naming difference, not an error.

links.reason: Selene (Moon) is not Apollo's sister; the editor ruled Selene taken for Diana. Artemis is the sister.
Duplicate of Cyrene, same person under a Pindar spelling; keep one entry only.
Pausanias' Lycomedes is not Apollo's son; unsupported by Theoi.
Hilaira is a daughter of Leucippus, wife of Castor; not Apollo's child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Apollo; no other names are involved. Urania is a spouse only in Wikidata, not reliably, and treated as a lover.
Ischys son of Elatus, Koronis' lover in Pindar's Pythian 3, matches the Wikidata entry.
Molione, wife of Actor and mother of the Moliones (Cteatus and Eurytus), matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.
Hebe matches the goddess; Ganymeda is a Phliasian cult name for the same goddess, as Pausanias says, so it is not a separate being.
Lycaon, king of Arcadia and son of Pelasgus, is the right match; no other names are involved.

links.reason: The Lycaon son of Priam (Iliad) is a different person from Lycaon of Arcadia; the editor's note ties the Arcadian Lycaon to Pelasgus, so this link mixes up two men of the same name. Actually Iliad's Lycaon is Priam's son, so keep.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy; no other names.

links.reason: Iliad only makes both children of Zeus in a loose sense; tradition treats Ares as Aphrodite's lover, and Pausanias gives no sibling link.
Duplicate entry of the same Aphrodite-Harmonia link, which should be listed only once.

identity.detail: Celestial Aphrodite (daughter of Uranus) and Aphrodite Pandemos/daughter of Zeus and Dione are distinct in Pausanias; other epithets are cult titles of the same goddess.
Wikidata's Laertes is Odysseus' father, king of the Cephallenians, and matches the Iliad's "son of Laertes". The link Laertes parent_of Ulysses is right.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Dirce the wife of Lycus and names no divine father. Helios is not her father in the tradition; the Wikidata parent list (Helios, Achelous, Ismenus) looks like a muddle of different figures.
Pausanias says Dirce defamed Antiope and was killed by Antiope's sons, so Antiope is her victim and enemy, not her mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban queen Dirce, wife of Lycus; the spring and river named after her are the same figure.
Arion is the divine horse of Adrastus, and the Wikidata match is the same being. He has no other names.
Argea (Argia), daughter of Adrastus and wife of Polynices, matches the Wikidata entry; the alternate name Argeia is only a spelling variant.
Wikidata's Echo is the Oread of Cithaeron, the same being.

links.reason: Pausanias mentions Electra as a Theban gate name, a daughter of Atlas; she is not a sister of Cadmus in the standard tradition (Agenor's children: Cadmus, Phoenix, Cilix, Europa).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban founder, son of Agenor and Telephassa; the 'Agenor's son' epithet is correct.

links.reason: Libya, daughter of Epaphus, bore Belus and Agenor to Poseidon in the usual tradition (Apollodorus 2.1.4), so the parent link to Agenor is right; keeping it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the daughter of Epaphus, the eponym of Libya; no other names to correct.

links.reason: Pan is not Calisto's son in Ovid; the editor limits Dryops' daughter as Pan's mother to Hesiod, and Callisto's only child here is Arcas.
Ovid gives Calisto only Arcas; Faunus is a Roman Pan-figure with no tie to Calisto, an unsupported guess from the Pan confusion.

identity.detail: Callisto the Arcadian nymph, daughter of Lycaon, is the right match.
Acamas, son of Theseus, hero of the Trojan War, matches; the book's 'Sons of Theseus' are Acamas and Demophon.

links.reason: Iliad 11.221-226: Iphidamas is son of Antenor and Theano's sister? No: Cisses raised him as his mother's father, so his mother is Theano's sister, not Theano.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Theano, wife of Antenor and priestess of Athena.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace, daughter of Dionysus and Aegle per Pausanias's tradition (editor: Aegle is her mother here); Homer's Hera only promises her to Hypnos, so she is not Hera's child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Hera; the epithets (Argive, Samian, Child-goddess, Widow etc.) are cult titles of the same goddess.

links.reason: Pindar's Hermes fathers Angelos (Herald/Message) personified; 'Fame' is a misreading, not a known child of Hermes.
Statius treats both as sons of Jupiter loosely, but Mars is son of Juno (Hera) and Mercury of Maia; they are only half-brothers at best, not a standard sibling link.
Hesiod's Hymn and tradition give a nymph union with Hermes (Pan's mother); not a marriage, so lover.

identity.detail: Mercury matches Hermes as the Roman equivalent; no name belongs to someone else.
Wikidata match is Cranaus, the second king of Athens; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Theban-war hero Capaneus, husband of Evadne and father of Sthenelus; no other names to split.

Tityos is the right match: the giant slain by Apollo and Artemis for assaulting Leto, as in Odyssey 11. Both parentage traditions (Zeus by Elara, or Gaia) are attested, so Jove and Earth are both acceptable.

links.reason: Pindar's Hippolyte is Hippolyta, daughter of Cretheus and wife of Acastus, who is not the Amazon queen in Apollodorus.
Cretheus' daughter Hippolyta (Pindar) is a different woman; Apollodorus' Amazon is a daughter of Ares and not of Cretheus.
In Apollodorus, Theseus carries off the Amazon (Antiope or Hippolyte) and has Hippolytus by her; the link comes from Statius, and by the editor's rule non-marriage links are read as lovers.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is ambiguous: Hippolyte the Amazon queen and Hippolyta daughter of Cretheus (wife of Acastus) are two different women; the Cretheus and Acastus links belong to the latter.

links.reason: Themis is Zeus's second wife in Hesiod (Theogony 901) and Wikidata; Apollodorus 1.3.1 says Zeus married Themis, who bore the Hours and Fates.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis; no other names involved.
The Wikidata match is the Arcadian king Lycaon, who was turned into a wolf; this is the right figure.
Wikidata match is Pittheus, king of Troezen, son of Pelops and Hippodamia and father of Aethra. All three links are standard tradition (Pausanias, Plutarch's Life of Theseus), so none needs a fix.
Wikidata match is the Trojan prince Ganymede, cupbearer of Zeus; the name Ganymedes is the same being.
Athena, also called Pallas and Minerva, is the same goddess as the Wikidata match. In Oedipus the King the chorus's 'Pallas' is Athena, who is named as Zeus's child.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Antigone who married Peleus is the daughter of Eurytion (or of Actor), not Oedipus' daughter; the Thebaid's Antigone is Oedipus' child and unmarried.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Oedipus' daughter Antigone; the Peleus link comes from a namesake in Apollodorus.

links.reason: Pandora was made by Hephaestus, not Zeus's lover.
Hermus is a river, with no clear parentage by Zeus in this book.
Eetion is Iasion's alternate name; the link duplicates or confuses it.
Pindar's Truth as daughter of Zeus is a personification; keep only if desired, but not a person in this book.
Pallas the Titan is son of Crius and Eurybia; the link confuses namesakes.
Pausanias gives the Sibyl's parents as Lamia and Theodorus, as the editor decided; Zeus is not her father.
Sisyphus is a son of Aeolus.
Macar is usually a son of Helios or Aeolus; the link is unsupported.
Personification; Ion makes Opportunity the youngest child of Zeus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Zeus himself. The epithets are cult titles of the same god.
Wikidata match is Telegone, daughter of Pharis, wife of Alpheus and mother of Orsilochus (Ortilochus); all links agree with Pausanias.

links.reason: Pausanias' Polydamas son of Nicias is the Scotussan athlete, a different man from Hector's friend (son of Panthous).
Leocritus son of Polydamas, killed by Odysseus, is a different Polydamas (a Trojan named in the Delphi painting by Polygnotus), not the son of Panthous.

identity.detail: The book's Polydamas son of Nicias is the athlete of Scotussa, not Hector's companion. The Wikidata match to the Trojan Polydamas fits only the Trojan; the athlete should be a separate character.
Wikidata match is Chrysaor, son of Poseidon and Medusa, father of Geryon by Callirrhoe. No other names are given, so nothing needs splitting.
Porphyrion is the Giant, and the Wikidata match is correct. Apollodorus 1.34 makes Earth and Sky his parents, so both links stand.
Wikidata match is the king of Tiryns/Argos, Eurystheus; no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias (1.43.5) makes Manto a daughter of Polyidus, but she is the daughter of Polyidus of Megara, a descendant of the Corinthian seer, so this is a different person; Apollodorus gives no such link.
Pausanias (1.43.5) names Astycratea and Manto as daughters of Polyidus of Megara, not the Corinthian seer, son of Coeranus, in Apollodorus.

identity.detail: Wikidata Polyeidos is the Corinthian seer, son of Coeranus; the match is correct.
Eurotas is the Laconian king, son of Myles (or Lelex in some accounts), and father of Sparta; the match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Gorgon Medusa, daughter of Phorcys and Ceto, mother of Pegasos and Chrysaor by Poseidon; no other names to question.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Phineus is Andromeda's uncle, brother of Cepheus, and is a different Phineus from the Thracian seer. Hesiod makes the seer a son of Phoenix and Cassiopea, so Cepheus is not his brother here.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Thracian seer Phineus, who is the one Hesiod's fragments describe.

links.reason: Tantalus is son of Zeus (or Tmolus the Lydian king in some accounts per Apollodorus/Pausanias variants), but in Metamorphoses Tmolus is the mountain god judging Pan and Apollo; no sentence makes him Tantalus's father.
Omphale's husband is Tmolus the Lydian king (Apollodorus); Ovid's Tmolus is the mountain god who judges the contest, a different being.

identity.detail: Wikidata match merges two figures: the Lydian king, husband of Omphale (son of Ares and Theogone), and the mountain god who judges Apollo and Pan in Ovid. This book's Tmolus is the mountain god, so the parents, spouse and child links belong to the king.

links.link: Hermione spouse_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Duplicate of Neoptolemus Pyrrhus; the quoted sentence says he had no son by Hermione, but she was still his wife. It is the same person as the Neoptolemus link, so this separate entry is redundant.
Cadmus's wife Harmonia (Hermione in some forms) in Metamorphoses is a different person from Menelaus' daughter; Pausanias does not give this.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Menelaus' daughter; no other names to check.
Wikidata's Melicertes is the right being: the son of Athamas and Ino, later the sea-god Palaemon. The two names belong to one person.
Deiphontes, Heracleid husband of Hyrnetho, is the right match.
Rhadamanthys, son of Zeus and Europa, judge in Hades; the Wikidata match is correct. The Wikidata father Hephaestus looks like a stray entry, but no tree link uses it.
Abderus, the companion of Heracles killed by the mares of Diomedes, matches Wikidata; Apollodorus names Hermes as father and lists no other names.
Wikidata's Helenus is the Trojan seer, son of Priam and Hecuba. No other names are listed, so nothing needs splitting.

links.reason: Iphidamas son of Antenor in the Iliad; the Trojan Agenor (son of Antenor) is a different man from the Phoenician king.
Echeclus son of Agenor is the Trojan killed by Achilles (Iliad 20), not the Phoenician king.
This is the Spartan Agenor, descended from Lacedaemon, a different man.

links.link: Theopompus, father of Agenor parent_of Agenor
links.reason: Phocian Agenor, son of Theopompus, is a different man from the Phoenician king.
Demodoce daughter of Agenor is from Hesiod's tradition and attached to another Agenor (a Calydonian/Pleuron line), not the Phoenician king.

identity.detail: Pausanias names several Agenors (Phoenician king, Trojan Agenor, Phocian Agenor son of Theopompus, Spartan Agenor son of Areus). The Wikidata match is the Phoenician king only, so the others should be separated from it.

links.reason: Pittheus was a son of Pelops by tradition, but Hippodamia is not named his mother in the sources; Pittheus's mother is usually unnamed, and some versions make Pelops' wife Hippodamia his mother, so the link is unsupported here and in the book.

identity.detail: Hippodamia daughter of Oenomaus and wife of Pelops is the right match.
Phegeus of Psophis matches Wikidata.
Wikidata match is Phaethon, son of Eos; Hesiod's Phaethon is the same being, not the Helios' son.

links.reason: The daughters are a group node, not a person; the book's sentence supports the daughters, but the group link is better replaced by individual named daughters (Aedon, Cleothera in Odyssey 19 and 20).

identity.detail: Pandareus of Ephesus/Miletus, son of Merops, matches. Camiro and Clytie are his daughters per Pausanias (Polygnotus' painting), so those links are correct.

links.reason: Naiads as a group are not his children; Ovid has him as lover/father only of specific figures, and the group is taken for a person.

Apollodorus' Callirhoe, wife of Alcmaeon, is Achelous' daughter, but the duplicate with Pausanias' spelling is the same person; keep only one entry (the Pausanias-spelled duplicate is a duplicate name, not a different being).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the river god Achelous; Wikidata's spouses (Muses, Perimede, Sterope) are mostly lovers or mothers of the Sirens, not marriages, but no identity error.

links.reason: Jason abandoned Medea to marry Glauce (Creusa), but the marriage never took place; the editor's rule is that only marriages count as spouse, so this is read as lover.
This is a group, not a person; the sons are individually named (Mermerus, Pheres, Medeus), so it duplicates them.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Argonaut Jason, so there is nothing to fix. In the Odyssey he appears only briefly, as Hypsipyle's partner, so the book itself supports few of these links.
The match is Neleus of Pylos, the son of Tyro and father of Nestor. Wikidata lists Hippocoon as a father, which is doubtful, but that does not affect the book's links.
Wikidata's Meleager is the Calydonian hero, son of Oeneus and Althaea, which matches this book. Wikidata also lists Ares as a father, but that is a poetic variant and does not change the match.
Wikidata's Iris is the rainbow goddess, daughter of Thaumas and Electra, as Apollodorus says. No other names are attached to her.
Wikidata match is the Athenian princess Herse, daughter of Cecrops; no other names.
Peneus is the Thessalian river god, son of Oceanus and Tethys, and the Wikidata match is correct. His children Daphne, Andreus, Cyrene and Hypseus are supported by Theoi.
Wikidata's Daphne matches the nymph loved by Apollo. Pausanias makes her the daughter of Ladon, which agrees with Theoi's listing; Peneus and Amyclas are other traditions.
Wikidata's Perseus is the hero, son of Zeus and Danaë, and husband of Andromeda. No other names are listed.

Pleisthenes, son of Atreus and Aerope, father of Agamemnon and Menelaus in some accounts, matches the Wikidata entry. The Wikidata parents Pelops and Hippodamia belong to the other Pleisthenes, son of Pelops, but they are not linked here, so no change is needed.
Atë is the personification of delusion, daughter of Zeus (Iliad 19.91) or Eris (Hesiod Theogony 230). Both are ancient traditions, and the Wikidata match is correct.

Tereus is the Thracian king, husband of Procne and father of Itys; the Wikidata match is correct. Ovid calls him a descendant of Gradivus (Mars), which agrees with Ares as his father, so the parent flag is not a real conflict.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Dipoinos and Skyllis pupils of Daedalus (in some accounts sons), but Apollodorus does not make them his children; the link comes from another book and is unsupported here.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian craftsman Daedalus; no names are conflated.
Klotho is the Fate Clotho, and the Wikidata match is correct. In Pindar's tradition (Olympian 1, Hesiod Theogony 901) Themis is her mother, so the Themis link is right.
Wikidata match is the Cretan Ariadne, daughter of Minos and Pasiphae; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Mygdon is a Phrygian, son of Acmon or Poseidon in some accounts, and no ancient source cited here names Amycus as his brother. The Argonautica gives Amycus only Poseidon and Melie as parents and never mentions Mygdon.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Amycus, king of the Bebryces, is the same being as the book's Amycus. Its mother 'Bithynis' is a variant naming of the nymph Melie.
Echo the Oread nymph matches Wikidata; no other names listed. The link to Narcissus as an unrequited love is stated in Ovid's Metamorphoses.
Wikidata match is the Messenian king Aphareus, son of Perieres and Gorgophone, father of Idas and Lynceus; correct.

Wikidata match is Maera the hound of Erigone, but the Atlas link belongs to Maera the Pleiad (daughter of Atlas), a different being. Apollodorus's Maera as Atlas's daughter is the Pleiad; the hound is a namesake.

links.reason: The Catalogue of Women (Hesiod tradition) makes Polycaste Telemachus's wife, mother of Persepolis, so she was a wife and not just a lover; the editor's rule reads other spouse links as lovers, but this is an actual marriage.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Nestor's daughter Polycaste; she is the one who bathes Telemachus in Odyssey 3.
Wikidata's Crisus, son of Phocus and twin of Panopeus, is the same being.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony (1011-16) makes Latinus son of Odysseus and Circe; Pan as father appears only in a late Latin tradition (Servius, via Faunus), which confuses Faunus with Pan and is not found in this book.

identity.detail: The match is Latinus, the Hesiodic son of Odysseus and Circe; the Latin king of the Aeneid is a separate tradition, but the links brought from the Aeneid are right for him.

links.reason: Apollodorus 1.34 makes the Giants children of Earth and Uranus (Sky). Tartarus as father belongs to the Typhon tradition, not the Giants here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Giant Enceladus; no other names to dispute.
Wikidata match is Sisyphus, king of Ephyra (Corinth). In the Iliad (6.152-154) he is the son of Aeolus and father of Glaucus, so the links are consistent. No other names to question.

links.reason: Eteoclus son of Cephisus is a Boeotian Orchomenos tradition (Pausanias), a different river-god's local lore; Metamorphoses gives Cephisus only Narcissus, and this link is unsupported in this book, but it is not contradicted by a source I can cite, so it should be kept.}],

identity.detail: Eurycrates is the Agiad king of Sparta, son of Polydorus and father of Anaxander, as Pausanias states. The Wikidata match is correct and the flag is not an error.
Nycteus the king of Thebes, brother of Lycus and father of Antiope (in some versions) and of Nyctimene in the Lesbos tale, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are involved.

links.reason: Hesiod has Gaia bear Typhon to Tartarus, but the editor reads any non-marriage 'spouse' link as a lover.
Gaia and Uranus are the traditional pair, but under the editor's rule only listed marriages count, so this is read as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Terra/Gaia is the Greek Earth goddess, which is fine for this book. The Roman Tellus note is just a description; Gaia and Terra are the same goddess here.
Wikidata's Asteropaios is the Paeonian leader killed by Achilles in Iliad 21. Pelegon is his father in the book (Iliad 21.140-143), and Pelegon is the son of the river god Axios.
Wikidata's Io is the Argive princess loved by Zeus, so the match is correct. The spouse entry there is an odd extra but not a different being.

links.reason: A chorus is a group, not a person; the Oceanids are already covered by individual daughters.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Tethys; no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias names two Alcathoi: the Megarian king (son of Pelops, per Wikidata/Megarian tradition) and the unlucky suitor of Hippodamia killed by Oenomaus, son of Porthaon (Great Eoiae). Porthaon belongs to the suitor, not the Megarian king.

Asterius, king of Crete, married Europa and raised her sons by Zeus (Minos, Rhadamanthys, Sarpedon); no ancient source makes him father of a person named Crete. Apollodorus has no such child, and the link looks like a confusion with the island he ruled.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Cretan king Asterius, who is the foster-father of Minos and the husband of Europa, so it fits this book.
Hera matches Wikidata; Juno is her Roman equivalent, which is acceptable.

Telemus the prophet, son of Eurymus, who warned Polyphemus about Odysseus, is the same being as the Wikidata match. In Metamorphoses 13 Ovid has Polyphemus mention Telemus, son of Eurymus. No other names are listed.
Wikidata match is Hecamede, Arsinous' daughter and Nestor's captive. The book's text names Arsinous as her father, so the flag is a false alarm.
Wikidata match is the son of Heracles and Auge, the Mysian king; no issue with names.
Wikidata match Ptolemy II Philadelphus is correct; Pausanias' Ptolemy who married his sister Arsinoe II is this king.
Wikidata match is Ariadne, daughter of Minos; no other names to question.
Hesiod's Graces (Theogony 907-911) are the Charites, daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, so the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are mixed in.
Doris the Oceanid, wife of Nereus, matches Wikidata.
Wikidata match is the Theban Amphitryon, son of Alcaeus; no wrong names.

links.reason: Sinon as son of Sisyphus is only a late tradition (Virgil's Greek spy, said to be Sisyphus's son in post-Homeric sources); Hesiod does not say it, and it comes from an unsupported Wikidata import.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Corinthian king Sisyphus, son of Aeolus; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Hera herself; no other names.
In Pausanias, Victory is the Greek Nike, and Victoria is her Roman counterpart. Hesiod and Theoi name Pallas as her father, so the match is acceptable.
Wikidata's Aepytus is the Heraclid son of Cresphontes and Merope, which fits Apollodorus. No other names to check.
The Wikidata match is the Sirens as a group, which fits Pausanias's daughters of Achelous.
Wikidata's Niobe, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, is the Niobe of Ovid's Metamorphoses. No other names are listed.
Molione, mother of the Molionides (Cteatus and Eurytus) by Actor, is the right match; no other names to separate.

links.reason: Crius was a son of Uranus and Gaia (Hesiod, Theogony); the editor has ruled Cronus as parent of Crius wrong everywhere.
Pausanias' Crius, king of Euboea, is a different man from the Titan; his insolent son is not the Titan's child.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Kreios, but Pausanias' passage about Crius, king of Euboea, refers to a mortal namesake. Only the Titan links (Earth, Pallas, Astraeus) belong to the Titan.

links.reason: Pausanias' Laodice of Tegea, Agapenor's daughter who founded the Paphos-related temple, is a different woman from Priam's daughter Laodice.

identity.detail: Two Laodices are joined here: Priam's daughter (the wife of Helicaon) and Agapenor's daughter at Tegea. The Wikidata match is Priam's daughter, so Agapenor's daughter should be a separate character.

links.reason: Pausanias (9.10.3) makes Henioche and Pyrrha daughters of Creon, son of Menoikeus, but tradition (Pausanias) also names them as daughters of a different Creon, the Corinthian king's family is not involved; if not confirmed keep. Here they are accepted as Creon's daughters.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Creon of Thebes, son of Menoikeus, brother of Jocasta; no confusion.
Wikidata match is the Muse Terpsichore, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne per Hesiod Theogony 75. No other names are listed. The Achelous spouse link on Wikidata is not in this book's tree.

links.reason: Bellona is a separate Roman war goddess with no ancient source naming Juno as her mother; the Wikidata link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Juno matches Wikidata; Hera is her Greek equivalent, so the alias is fine.
Polites is the son of Priam and Hecuba, and the Wikidata match is this same being. He has no other names to question.
Cephalus son of Deion(eus) and Diomede, husband of Procris and Clymene, is the right being; Pausanias's Cephalus is the same. No misattached names.

links.reason: Cadmus's wife Harmonia (Hermione in some Latin texts such as Ovid's Metamorphoses) is a different being from Menelaus' daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Menelaus' daughter Hermione; Pyrrhus and Neoptolemus are the same man, so those two links should be merged, not dropped.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 901) makes Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule that only Hera and Juno count as Zeus's marriages is about 'spouse' links; this one is a wife, so it is not merely a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis; no other names.
Laomedon is the Trojan king, son of Ilus and father of Priam, Hesione and Podarces; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Machaon is Asclepius's son (Iliad); confused with Podaleirius, who is also Asclepius's son.
Podaleirius is Asclepius's son, not Poseidon's.
Agenor of Tyre and Phoenicia is Poseidon's son by Libya in Apollodorus; Oedipus the King has no such link, so the other Agenors are namesakes.
The Doliones are a people, a group taken for a person; Dolion was their eponym.

links.link: Poseidon parent_of Phocus, son of Ornytion
links.reason: Phocus is son of Ornytion, not Poseidon, in Pausanias.
Hera is Zeus's wife and sister, and is also a sibling of Poseidon as a daughter of Cronus and Rhea.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Poseidon; Neptune is his Roman name.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Erigone is the daughter of Icarius of Athens, not Icarus, the son of Daedalus. The Metamorphoses link confuses the similar names Icarius and Icarus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Erigone, daughter of Icarius of Athens, which is the right being.
Wikidata match is Oeax, son of Nauplius and Clymene, brother of Palamedes. The book says the same, so the parents agree and the flag is a false alarm.

links.link: Linus, son of Apollo parent_of Pierus
links.reason: Pierus of Emathia is the Macedonian king, son of Makedon in Wikidata's tradition; Linus as his father conflates him with another Pierus (father of Linus in some accounts, reversing the direction) and is not supported.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Macedonian king Pierus, eponym of Pieria. Oeager is just a variant of Oeagrus, not another person.

links.reason: Opheltes' mother in Apollodorus is Eurydice, wife of King Lycurgus of Nemea, not Orpheus' wife the nymph.
Nestor's wife Eurydice (daughter of Clymenus) in the Odyssey tradition is a different woman from Orpheus' wife.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Orpheus' wife; the Nestor and Opheltes links come from other women named Eurydice, so they were wrongly merged by name only.

links.reason: Pausanias's sentence 'Alexander was the son of Olympias the daughter of Neoptolemus' is about Alexander the Great, set against Pyrrhus. Alexander I of Epirus was her brother, not her son.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great.
Pandora matches the first woman, wife of Epimetheus; no other names to separate.
Smyrna is the same being as Myrrha, the mother of Adonis.
Wikidata match is Menelaus, king of Sparta, husband of Helen; no other names to question.

links.reason: Polybotes is a Giant, born of Earth (Gaia) from Uranus' blood or of Gaia alone, not Uranus' son in the usual tradition; Apollodorus makes Giants children of Earth.
Porphyrion is a Giant; Giants sprang from Uranus' blood falling on Earth, so Gaia is the parent, not Uranus directly.
Alcyoneus is a Giant born of Earth; not a son of Uranus directly.
Enceladus is a Giant born of Earth (Gaia) from Uranus' blood, not Uranus' child directly.
Anax is a Milesian eponym said to be a son of Earth (Pausanias 7.2.5), not of Uranus.
Hopladamus is a Giant son of Earth, not of Uranus.

identity.detail: Uranus matches the sky god; Heaven is his English name.

Wikidata's Panopeus, son of Phocus and twin of Crisus, is the same being. Panopeus is also the father of Epeus, the builder of the Trojan Horse, in Pausanias and Apollodorus' epitome, so the Epeus link is right.
Wikidata's Giants is the race of Gigantes who fought the Olympians, which is the group Ovid means in Metamorphoses 1. No other names to split.

Peleus matches the Wikidata entry: the king of Phthia, son of Aeacus and Endeis, and husband of Thetis and father of Achilles. Antigone, daughter of Eurytion (Apollodorus), was also his wife, so the 'spouse' flag is not a mistake.
Heleus, youngest son of Perseus and Andromeda, who founded Helos in Laconia, matches the Wikidata entry. The book's sentence supports the Perseus link.
Wikidata match is the Muse Urania; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Theban seer Tiresias; no other names to check.
Metanira is the wife of Celeus of Eleusis, and the Wikidata match is the same being. Celeus as her spouse is correct.
Cassandra, the Trojan priestess and daughter of Priam and Hecuba, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed.
Pausanias names Thespius, son of Erechtheus, as an Athenian eponym of Thespiae. This fits the Wikidata match, so nothing needs fixing.
Wikidata's Peteus is the Athenian son of Orneus, who was expelled by Aegeus. This matches Pausanias, and the character has no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias' Agraulus is the same as Aglauros, already listed as daughter; this duplicate comes from a name variant.

identity.detail: Cecrops I matches the Athenian king; no other names are mixed in.

links.reason: Orion's mother Euryale is the daughter of Minos (Hesiod, Catalogue); the Gorgon Euryale, daughter of Phorcys and Ceto, is a different being, so the link confuses two namesakes.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Gorgon Euryale, sister of Stheno and Medusa, which fits Pindar's Pythian 12.

links.reason: Apollodorus says Telamon received Hesione as a war prize and had Teucer by her; she was a captive concubine, not a wife. Per the editor's rule, non-marriage spouse links are read as lovers.

identity.detail: Wikidata matches Telamon, son of Aeacus and Endeis. Apollodorus has no other names for him.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; the alternative names Rhodopeïan bard and Thracian poet are epithets for the same being.

The match is Pleisthenes, son of Atreus and father of Agamemnon and Menelaus in Hesiod's tradition. Wikidata also lists Pelops and Hippodamia as parents, which belongs to a different Pleisthenes of the house of Tantalus, but the Atreus and Aerope links fit this book.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages stay spouse links; Perse (Oceanid) as Helios's wife is not a marriage in this tree, so read as lover.
Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse; Rhode (Rhodos) is a partner of Helios, so treat as lover.
Amalthea as Helios's child is a confusion with another figure of that name; the Argonautica does not say so and she is the nurse of Zeus.
Perses, brother of Aeetes, is the son of Helios and Perse in Apollodorus, but Perses in Metamorphoses is a different person; keep only the Colchian relation.

identity.detail: Helios matches the sun god; Sol is the Latin equivalent, so the names are fine.
Mimas is the Giant, born of Earth (Gaia) and Sky (Uranus) from his blood, as Apollodorus tells; the Wikidata match is correct.
Aeetes of the Odyssey is Aeëtes, king of Aea and brother of Circe; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Phocus son of Aeacus was Peleus's half-brother, not Thetis's son; Pausanias's Phocus is from Psamathe, and Thetis's only child is Achilles.
Endeis was daughter of Chiron (or Skiron) and wife of Aeacus, so she was Peleus's mother, not a sister of Thetis.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Thetis the Nereid is correct. Wikidata's spouse Neptune is not in the book (Poseidon was only a suitor in some versions).
Wikidata's Palamedes is the Euboean prince, son of Nauplius, which is the right being. He has no other names. The link to Nauplius as father is the standard tradition, so it is kept.
Wikidata match is the right Pasiphae, daughter of Helios and wife of Minos.

links.reason: Hades' mother is Rhea; Cybele is a Phrygian goddess later identified with Rhea, and Ovid's Metamorphoses gives no such parentage for Pluto here.

identity.detail: Pluto/Hades/Orcus is the same god. Wikidata's spouse Nox (Night) is dubious, but the Proserpina link is right.
Wikidata's Laertes is the Ithacan king, son of Arcesius and father of Odysseus (Ulysses); the match is correct.

links.reason: In Virgil's Aeneid and Ovid's Metamorphoses Picus is son of Saturn, the Italian god, and Saturn is only identified with Cronos. Hesiod's Cronos is not his father, and Theoi does not list Picus as his son.

identity.detail: Cronus is the right match. The name Saturn is the Roman god identified with him; the Picus link comes from that merge.

Pausanias calls him the son of Craugis, which matches Wikidata's father Craugis of Megalopolis. The flag appears to be a spurious mismatch. The Wikidata match to Philopoemen of Megalopolis is correct.
Bia is the personification of force, daughter of Pallas and Styx in Hesiod's Theogony; the Wikidata match and the alias Force are correct.

links.reason: Aigina's mother is Metope in some accounts (Asopus' daughters), but in Pindar's Olympian 6 Metope bears Thebe; Aigina is not named as her child in this book, though Theoi lists Aegina as Asopus' daughter by Metope, so this link is a tradition-supported one.

identity.detail: Metope the Arcadian naiad, daughter of Ladon, wife of Asopus, mother of Thebe; the match is correct.
Pedias, Lacedaemonian daughter of Mynes and wife of Cranaus, is the right being. Apollodorus 3.14.5 names her as Cranaus' wife, and Atthis as his daughter.

The Wikidata match Sphettos is the Attic deme/city. Pausanias's Sphettus is the eponymous hero, a son of Trœzen who gave his name to the township. The hero is a different being from the place, so the match should be corrected or flagged.
Pylas, king of Megara, son of Cleson (Pausanias) or Cteson, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are involved.
Machaon, son of Asclepius and brother of Podalirius, matches the Wikidata entry. Epione as mother is a Theoi-confirmed tradition, while Wikidata gives Coronis; both are valid.

links.reason: Pausanias says Polyxenus's son Amphimachus was named after the friend Amphimachus son of Cteatus, who died at Troy. The tree gives the Elean leader's son to the wrong man; Wikidata's parents Cteatus and Theronice belong to the Troy hero, and Polyxenus's son is a different, later Amphimachus (father of Eleus).

identity.detail: Two men named Amphimachus: the Troy leader, son of Cteatus (Wikidata's match), and Polyxenus's son, father of Eleus and named after him. The Polyxenus link belongs to the second one.
Aventinus, son of Hercules and the priestess Rhea in Aeneid 7, matches the Wikidata entry. He is not the Alban king Aventinus or the hill's namesake.
The Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy, and there are no other names to check.
Glaucus of Potniae/Corinth, son of Sisyphus, matches Wikidata; the Deliades link (Bellerophon's brother, Apollodorus) fits the same man.

links.reason: Niobe is the daughter of Tantalus, and some sources name Dione as her mother only as a Pleiad or Atlantid namesake; the Titaness Dione is not her mother in Hesiod.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titaness Dione, mother of Aphrodite; no other names to split.
Ida is the Cretan nurse of the infant Zeus, daughter of Melisseus in Apollodorus. The Wikidata match is the same being.

Melanion is the Arcadian husband of Atalanta, and the Wikidata match is correct. Wikidata gives his father as Amphidamas, which is one tradition. Pausanias does not contradict it, so the flag needs no change.
Wikidata match is Oenopion, king of Chios, son of Dionysus and Ariadne; no other names to separate.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links; Apollodorus gives Side as Orion's wife, but Hera cast her down, and she is not a marriage the editor accepts, so read as lover.
Metioche and Menippe are the daughters of Orion in Boeotian tradition (Antoninus Liberalis 25); this link is supported, not contradicted.

identity.detail: Wikidata Orion is the giant huntsman and Boeotian hero; no wrong names.

links.reason: The Teleclus and Alcamenes father-son link is about the Spartan king Alcamenes, not the sculptor.
Polydorus is the son of the Spartan king Alcamenes, not of the sculptor.

identity.detail: The book's Alcamenes includes the Spartan king (son of Teleclus, father of Polydorus) and the sculptor from Wikidata. They are two different people, so the family links belong to the king.

links.reason: In Hesiod's Theogony Earth (Gaia) comes from Chaos, not from Aether. The Wikidata link is unsupported by the book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the personified upper sky, Aether, so the match is correct.
Dius is Hesiod's father in the Certamen text; the Wikidata match is a disambiguation-style entry with no conflicting data, and no other names are attached.
Philammon the musician, son of Apollo and Chione (or Philonis), is the right match. He has no other names to check.

Arges is the Hesiodic Cyclops, son of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Heaven) in Hesiod's Theogony; the Wikidata match is correct. Earth and Heaven are the same beings as Gaia and Uranus, so both links are right.
Lycius the sculptor, son of Myron, matches Pausanias' text and the Wikipedia description.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Scylla as daughter of Phorcus and Hecate (or Crataeis/Trienus); the Argonautica link is not supported for Triton as her father, and it seems to confuse Triton with another figure.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea god Triton, son of Poseidon and Amphitrite.
Ocnus (Bianor), founder of Mantua and son of Manto, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed. The link Manto parent_of Ocnus is right (Aeneid, Wikidata).
Apemosyne, daughter of Catreus of Crete, matches Wikidata and the book; no other names are involved.
Wikidata's Pallas is the Giant flayed by Athena in the Gigantomachy (Apollodorus), born of Earth from Sky's blood, so the parent links are right.
Euphemus the Argonaut, son of Poseidon and Europe daughter of Tityos, matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: This is a group (Alcithoë, Leucippe, Arsinoë) treated as a single person. The individual daughters are the real links.

identity.detail: Minyas the founder of Orchomenus is the right match. Apollonius calls him son of Aeolus, which differs from Wikidata's Poseidon but is acceptable for this book.
Wikidata Cinyras is the Cyprian king, father of Myrrha and Adonis, which matches the book. No other names to check.
Harmonia, wife of Kadmos and daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, matches Wikidata. The Theoi entry for Zeus and Elektra refers to a different Harmonia of Samothrace, which is a variant tradition.
Phosphorus and Eosphorus are the same Morning Star god. Dawn-bringer is simply the translation of the name.

Enipeus is the Thessalian river god loved by Tyro (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6 and Homer, Odyssey 11). Oceanus and Tethys as parents follow the tradition that all rivers are their children (Hesiod, Theogony), so the match is correct.
Iolaos is the Theban hero, nephew and charioteer of Heracles, son of Iphicles. Hesiod's Shield calls him 'son of Iphiclus', which agrees.
Simois the river god of the Trojan plain matches Simoeis; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, is a spouse only in the post-Odyssey tradition (Apollodorus), where Odysseus marries her after returning; the editor's rule reads any spouse beyond Penelope as a lover, and the Aeneid never mentions her.

identity.detail: Ulysses is the Latin name of Odysseus, so the match is correct.
Wikidata match is Phaethon son of Eos, not Phaethon son of Helios, and no other names are listed.

Tenes of Tenedos matches Tennes. Pausanias names Cycnus as father, with Proclea as mother and Hemithea as sister. Wikidata's extra father Apollo is only an alternative tradition (Pindar, Scholiast), not an error in this book's tree.
Alkmene is the right match; Alcmena is just the Latin form of her name.
Wikidata's Mopsus is the seer, son of Manto and Rhacius, which matches Pausanias' sentence. Both links are right.
Wikidata match is Aeson, son of Cretheus and Tyro and father of Jason; no other names to question.

fall-of-troy/aphrodite.name: Aphrodite
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Cypris, Aphrodite

links.reason: The Iliad has Ares and Aphrodite as separate children of Zeus and Dione's circle only loosely; Ares is son of Zeus and Hera, so Aphrodite (daughter of Zeus and Dione) is a half-sibling at most. Elsewhere they are lovers, so a sibling link confuses the relationship.

identity.detail: Aphrodite, Cypris, Cytherea and Venus are the same goddess; the several Wikidata entries are all her.
Wikidata's Orneus is the Athenian son of Erechtheus, which matches the book.
Wikidata match is Leucothoë, daughter of Orchamus and Eurynome, lover of Helios; this fits Ovid's Metamorphoses. No other names to split.

Psamathe the Nereid, mother of Phocus by Aeacus, matches. Her other husband per Wikidata, Proteus, belongs to a different Psamathe tradition (Theoclymenus's mother is Eido/Idothea), but that does not affect this match.
Hylonome is the female centaur who dies with her husband Cyllarus in Ovid's Metamorphoses; the Wikidata match is correct and she has no other names.

Temenus, son of Aristomachus and Heraclid king of Argos, is the right match. His children are Hyrnetho, Agelaus, Eurypylus and Callias in Apollodorus, and Phalces, Cisus and Cerynes in Pausanias. These are all the same Temenus, and the differences are variants rather than errors.
Wikidata match is the Lemnian queen Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, mother of Euneos and Thoas by Jason; no other names to question.
Panthous, Trojan elder and father of Euphorbus, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names.
Wikidata match is Adrastus, king of Argos and leader of the Seven against Thebes. All four links are standard: Talaus is his father, and Argia, Deipyle and Aegialeus are his children.

links.reason: Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon in the Iliad or Theoi's listing; Pausanias mentions a different Hyperion, apparently a misread or namesake. Agamemnon's children are Iphigenia, Electra, Orestes, Chrysothemis, Laodike, Iphianassa.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (or Nestor's daughter, wife of Pelias or Strophius); Pausanias does not make her his daughter.

identity.detail: Agamemnon, son of Atreus, is the right match; the name 'Atreus' son' is a patronymic for him.

links.reason: Orthus is Echidna's son (Hesiod, Apollodorus), already linked as child; Hesiod's Theogony has Orthus bred by Echidna and Typhon, with no lover relation.
Typhon is Echidna's mate (Hesiod, Wikidata lists him as spouse), so treat as spouse.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Echidna is correct; Lernæan Echidna is an epithet for the Hydra-related monster, not a separate person.
Wikidata match is the river-god Inachus, father of Io and Phoroneus; no other names.
Tyche is the right match for Fortune.

Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths and father of Coronis, matches the Wikidata entry. The book's sentence names him as her father, and the parent links to Ares and Chryse come from other books and are supported by Pausanias and Pindar.
Idas son of Aphareus (or Poseidon) of Messenia, brother of Lynceus, husband of Marpessa; the match is correct. Pindar's 'sons of Aphareus' refers to Idas and Lynceus.
Menestheus of Athens, son of Peteos, is the right match. Peteos and Peteus are spelling variants of the same father, so the two links are duplicates and both are correct.
Crocale, Diana's nymph in Ovid's Metamorphoses 3, daughter of Ismenus per the book's text; Wikidata match is consistent.
Wikidata's Laius is the Theban king, father of Oedipus and son of Labdacus. The links all fit, and the marriage to Jocasta is a real one.

Cranaus is the second king of Athens after Cecrops, so the Wikidata match is correct. The Atthis link is right: Apollodorus 3.14.5 gives Cranaus daughters Cranae, Cranaechme and Atthis, and says Atthis died a maiden.

links.reason: Statius' Thebaid gives Pan sons among Arcadians, but these are Statius' own inventions and not in Pausanias.
Crenaeus is a Statius Thebaid Arcadian figure with no support in Pausanias.

identity.detail: Pan matches the Wikidata god; the alternate names are cult epithets of the same god (Nomius, Deliverer, Scolitas, Œnois).

links.reason: No ancient source gives Poseidon as Eurynome's lover; the Oceanid is Zeus's partner, mother of the Charites (Hesiod Theogony 907-911), and Poseidon is confused with another figure.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Leucothoë's mother is Eurynome, a Persian queen, who is a different person from the Oceanid.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Oceanid. The spouse Ophion is the Titan partner from Apollonius Rhodius and belongs to the same Eurynome, so no change.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony never mentions Buphagus; the link was imported from Pausanias, where it concerns a different tradition, and Hesiod gives Iapetus only the sons Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus and Epimetheus.

identity.detail: Iapetos is the Titan Iapetus; the match is correct.

links.reason: Mulciber is Vulcan/Hephaestus; Rhadamanthus is son of Zeus and Europa (Apollodorus, Homer's Iliad). Wikidata's Hephaestus father is a confusion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the judge of the dead, son of Zeus and Europa; no other names.
Wikidata Iolaos is the Theban hero, Heracles' nephew and charioteer; no mismatch.

links.reason: Pausanias' Lycus son of Pandion is the Athenian Lycus, not the Theban regent of Statius, who is a son of Chthonius or Hyrieus and brother of Nycteus.
Thrasybulus as a son of Lycus comes from Pausanias' account of a different Lycus, not Statius' Theban Lycus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Theban regent Lycus, which is correct for Statius.
Apollodorus follows the Arcadian Atalanta, daughter of Iasus and Clymene, and the match is acceptable. Wikidata mixes in Schoeneus (Boeotian version), but the book names Iasus.

links.reason: The cited sentence is about Ares and the Amazons, not a marriage. The Akmonian-wood nymph Harmonia was only Ares' lover and mother of the Amazons, so per the editor's rule it is a lover link.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Amazons' mother, the Akmonian nymph. Argonautica names Harmonia only in passing, and the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite who married Cadmus is a different figure, so the tree should not merge them.
Podes son of Eetion, Hector's friend in the Iliad (17.575), matches Wikidata. Eetion as his father is consistent with the tradition that he was Andromache's brother.

links.reason: Poseidon's son Chryses (father of Minyas, from Chrysogeneia, Pausanias) is a different Chryses from the Trojan priest of Apollo in the Iliad, who is not Poseidon's son; the link confuses two namesakes.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Chryses is the Trojan priest of Apollo, but Wikidata's parents Ardys, Minos and Paria suggest a confusion with other Chryses figures (Paria's son and Minos' son). The book's Chryses needs checking, since Apollodorus mentions several. Relatives should not be merged across these namesakes.
Wikidata's Scylla is the sea monster of the strait opposite Charybdis, which is the Scylla of the Odyssey. No other names are listed.

links.reason: Erigone's father is Icarius of Athens, who received Dionysus; Ovid's Metamorphoses has Icarius, and the link confuses him with Daedalus' son Icarus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Daedalus' son Icarus; no other names are involved.

links.link: Telephus parent_of Eurypylus, son of Telephus
links.reason: Duplicate of the Eurypylus link; the book's Eurypylus is the son of Telephus, so the separate node 'Eurypylus, son of Telephus' only repeats it.

identity.detail: Telephus, son of Heracles and Auge, matches Wikidata.

Wikidata match is Pylades, son of Strophius, cousin and friend of Orestes. Both links agree with Pausanias and the Wikidata data. Wikidata lists several mothers, but that is not an error in this book's links.
Wikidata's Hermaphroditus is the right being. Ovid's Mercury and Venus (the 'Cytherean Goddess') match Hermes and Aphrodite, so the parent links agree with Wikidata and Theoi.
The Wikidata match is Neleus, king of Pylos, the father of Nestor, and the book's usage fits this being.
Polygnotus of Thasos is the painter Pausanias describes, son of Aglaophon; the match is correct.
Herse, daughter of Cecrops of Athens, is the right match; Ovid's Metamorphoses has her loved by Mercury, and no other names are attached.

links.reason: Orthus is Echidna's son, not her mate. In Theogony 326 the line is read as Echidna 'subject in love to Orthus', but Hesiod names Orthus as her offspring (line 309), and the Sphinx and Nemean lion are born of Orthus and Chimaera in the usual reading.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Echidna. Parentage varies by tradition: Phorcys and Ceto in Hesiod, Tartarus and Gaia in other sources.
Abas, king of Argos, son of Lynceus and Hypermnestra, is the right match. Pausanias's links all agree with the Argive Abas.
Cytissorus, son of Phrixus and Chalciope and founder of Cytorus, is the same being as the Wikidata match, so the match is right and no other names are mixed in.
Learchus is the son of Athamas and Ino and brother of Melicertes. The Wikidata match is the same being.
Hippolochus is Bellerophon's son and Glaucus's father in the Iliad, which matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata's Andromache is the wife of Hector, so the match is correct.

links.reason: Pausanias names Agesilaus son of Doryssus, the early Agiad/Eurypontid king of Sparta, who is a different man from Agesilaus II, son of Archidamus II.
The sentence 'the son of Agesilaus was Archelaus' concerns the early king Agesilaus son of Doryssus, not Agesilaus II.

identity.detail: The book has two Agesilaus: the early king, son of Doryssus and father of Archelaus, and Agesilaus II, son of Archidamus II and father of Archidamus III. The Wikidata match to Agesilaus II is right only for the latter; the Doryssus and Archelaus links belong to the first.

links.reason: Pandora is Pyrrha's mother; Hesiod has no Pyrrha-mother-of-Pandora link, so the direction is reversed.
Duplicate spelling of Deucalion; the same marriage is already kept under Deucalion, so this link is redundant. Merge with Deucalion.

identity.detail: Wikidata Pyrrha is the wife of Deucalion and daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora; matches. Deukalion and Deucalion are spelling variants of one person.

The match is Acrisius, king of Argos, son of Abas and husband of Eurydice, daughter of Lacedaemon. Pausanias says this directly. The two Eurydice spouse links are the same marriage, so there is no wrong link. The flag on 2 spouses comes from a duplicate entry.
Athena (Minerva as Roman equivalent) matches the Wikidata entry for the goddess Athena; no other being is mixed in.
Wikidata match is Sisyphus, king of Ephyra; no other names to question.
Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths/Phlegyans and father of Coronis, is the right match. Pausanias names Ares and Chryse as his parents, which agrees with Wikidata.

links.reason: Hesiod's Eurynome is the mother of the Graces by Zeus. Neptune is not her lover; the link appears to confuse her with another figure.
In Ovid, Leucothoë's mother is the Persian Eurynome, wife of Orchamus. She is a different woman from the Oceanid.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Oceanid who sheltered Hephaestus in Iliad 18. Ophion as her spouse comes from the Argonautica, a different tradition.

links.reason: The passage (Pausanias 2.10.3) is about a different Agasicles, the Sicyonian son of Nicagora and Echetimus, not the Spartan king. The Spartan Agesicles was the son of Archidamus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Spartan king Agasicles, son of Archidamus. The Sicyonian Agasicles in the Nicagora passage is a different man, which is handled in the link.
The Wikidata match is the Thracian Eumolpus, son of Poseidon and Chione. Wikidata's listing of Dionysus as a father is a minor oddity, not an identity problem.

links.reason: Pausanias (8.5) has the elder Aristocrates, son of Aechmis, and the later Aristocrates (4.17, son of Icetas) as two rulers of Orchomenus; Aechmis belongs to the elder one.

identity.detail: Two Arcadian kings of Orchomenus named Aristocrates are merged. The elder, son of Aechmis, is the impious king of Pausanias 8.5. The younger, son of Hicetas, was bribed in the Messenian war. Wikidata's match is a single entry, so it should be split.

links.reason: Pausanias names two Ancaei: the Samian/Lelegian king, son of Poseidon and Astypalaea, and the Argonaut killed by the Calydonian boar, son of Lycurgus. The Lycurgus link belongs to the Arcadian Ancaeus.

identity.detail: The tree joins two beings under one name. The Samian king (son of Poseidon, husband of Samia) is distinct from the Arcadian Argonaut, son of Lycurgus, who died at Calydon. Wikidata's Ancaeus is the Samian one, so the Lycurgus link and the Calydonian boar passages belong to the Arcadian.

Ascalaphus son of Acheron, witness against Persephone in Hades, is the right being. Apollodorus names Gorgyra as mother; Orphne is the variant in other sources. The Iliad's Ascalaphus, son of Ares and Astyoche, is a different person and is not linked here.

Wikidata match is Capaneus, the Argive hero among the Seven against Thebes, struck down by Jupiter's thunderbolt at the walls of Thebes. Wikidata also lists Alector as a father, but the links above are fine; no other names are in play.

Wikidata's Buphagus is the Arcadian hero, son of Iapetus and Thornax, which matches Pausanias. The flagged parent difference is not a real conflict: Pausanias names the same parents, Iapetus and Thornax. This Iapetus is an Arcadian figure, not the Titan, so the links are best read as that Iapetus.

Wikidata's Acrisius is the king of Argos, father of Danaë. The two Eurydice spouse links are the same marriage to Eurydice, daughter of Lacedemon, which Hesiod and Pausanias both support, so they are not a conflict.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony (116-122) names Eros as born at the start alongside Chaos, Gaia and Tartarus, with no parent. Chaos as his father comes from Oppian and Orphic-style sources, not Hesiod.
Hesiod does not make Night the mother of Eros. In the Theogony (123-125) Night is born of Chaos, and her children are listed separately without Eros. The Night parentage is from Aristophanes' Birds.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Eros is the right god. The name Love is just a translation and does not refer to anyone else.

links.reason: Editor ruled Zeus parent of Selene wrong; Selene (Moon) is not a Jupiter lover here, confused with Diana.
Editor ruled Artemis parent of Pandia wrong; Pandia as Zeus and Selene's daughter rests on the Selene confusion.
Argus here is the many-eyed son of Aristor (editor: right in this book); Apollodorus's Argus son of Zeus and Niobe is another Argus.
A group taken for a person; the individual Graces Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia are already listed.
A group taken for a person.
A group taken for a person; the individual Muses are listed.
Opportunity (Kairos) is a personification and cult figure, not a child of Zeus in Ovid; Pausanias has Kairos as a cult statue.
Pindar's allegory; Truth is a personification, not a figure in Metamorphoses.
Editor ruled Lamia and Theodorus parents of Sibyl in Pausanias; Ovid's Sibyl is mortal, daughter of neither Jupiter.
Eetion is Iasion's alternative name; Iasion and Eetion are the same being, so a duplicate.
Not in Ovid for Jupiter alone; Mars is son of Juno and Jupiter in Hesiod, but parentage here is unsupported by the book.
Pallas here is Minerva's epithet or a Titan Pallas, not Jupiter's own child apart from Minerva.

identity.detail: Zeus and Jupiter is the same being; the aliases Jove, Saturnian Jupiter and Panomphaean Thunderer are all him.

links.reason: Mars is Venus's lover in Metamorphoses, not her brother; Iliad has Ares as son of Zeus and Hera, Aphrodite as daughter of Zeus and Dione, so they are half-siblings only at most, a misreading.

identity.detail: Venus/Aphrodite match is correct; Erycina and Cytherea are her epithets, not other beings.

links.reason: Ares and Aphrodite are lovers, not siblings; in the Iliad Aphrodite is Zeus' daughter by Dione, Ares is Zeus' son by Hera, so half-siblings at most, but the tradition treats them as lovers.
Duplicate of Penthesileia, same Amazon queen; keep one spelling only.
Thestius is son of Ares in Apollodorus? Pausanias and Apollodorus make him son of Agenor/Parthaon's line, not Ares; unsupported.

links.link: Mars parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
links.reason: This is a stray entry for a Melanippus labeled only by his father; likely confused with another Melanippus.

identity.detail: Mars is matched to Ares, the Greek counterpart, which is standard for this site.

links.link: Pyrrhus, king of Epirus parent_of Pergamus
links.reason: Pausanias' Pyrrhus here is Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, who is the same person as Pergamus' father; a separate Pyrrhus of Epirus node duplicates the Neoptolemus link and should be merged or dropped (the king of Epirus Pyrrhus lived much later).

identity.detail: Pergamus, son of Neoptolemus and Andromache, matches Wikidata; no wrong names.

links.reason: Pausanias' Asterion the son of Minos is the Minotaur, who is the child of Pasiphae by the bull, not of Minos; the text names him as Minos' son only loosely, but Theseus killed the Minotaur, which is Asterion, so the link confuses Minos' son with the Minotaur's name. Keep only if the book states it; here it does, so this is a misreading risk.

identity.detail: Wikidata Minos is the king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa; this matches. Wikidata lists Crete as a spouse, which is a bad entry but not an identity issue.

links.reason: Scylla's parentage is Phorcys and Crataeis, or Phorbas/Trienus/Hecate etc. in some versions; Triton is never her father, and Argonautica gives no such link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the sea god Triton, son of Poseidon/Neptune and Amphitrite, which fits Ovid's conch-blowing Triton.
Wikidata match is Auge, daughter of Aleus and priestess of Athena Alea, mother of Telephus; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Romulus is the legendary founder of Rome, the same being as in the Aeneid. Mars as father is right, and Hersilia as wife is the tradition in Ovid's Metamorphoses and Livy.
Metanira, wife of Celeus of Eleusis, matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Cadmus' wife was Harmonia (Hermione is a variant spelling in Metamorphoses), not Menelaus' daughter.
Pausanias names Tisamenus as the son of Orestes and Hermione in one tradition, but other accounts make Erigone his mother; the link is unsupported in Hesiod.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Hermione, daughter of Menelaus and Helen; the Cadmus link comes from Harmonia confused with Hermione.

links.reason: Apollodorus' Antigone who married Peleus is the daughter of Eurytion of Phthia, not Oedipus' daughter; the two are confused.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Oedipus' daughter Antigone; the Peleus link comes from a different Antigone, daughter of Eurytion.
Arges is the Hesiodic Cyclops, son of Sky (Uranus) and Earth (Gaia) in Apollodorus 1.1.2. The Wikidata match is correct.
Pausanias (Sicyonian genealogy) makes Thelxion son of Apis and father of Ægyrus, matching Wikidata's Thelxion. The Wikipedia note about two figures of this name is not a conflict for this book.

links.reason: Epicasta as Nestor's daughter appears only in the Hesiodic tradition (Catalogue of Women, mother of Homer), which the editor limits to hesiod; Pindar does not say it.

identity.detail: Wikidata Nestor of Pylos matches; no other names involved.
Erginus, king of Minyan Orchomenus, son of Clymenus, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Hesiod (ll. 240-264) makes Doris the daughter of Ocean and Nereus's wife, so she cannot also be his daughter. The link comes from Apollodorus, who confuses her with a Nereid of the same name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Nereus, the Old Man of the Sea. No other names are attached.
Wikidata match is Artaphernes, satrap of Lydia and brother of Darius I; his father Hystaspes is correct, so nothing needs fixing.

links.reason: Machaon is son of Asclepius; Poseidon is not his father in Homer or Hesiod.
Podaleirius is son of Asclepius, brother of Machaon.
The Doliones are a people, not a person.
The Moliones are twins, a group; their father is Actor or Poseidon by Molione (variant in Iliad scholia), but a group is not a single person.
Kleatos is not a child of Poseidon; the Moliones' father is Actor.
Phorcys is a sea god, son of Pontus and Gaia, not of Poseidon.

links.link: Poseidon parent_of Phocus, son of Ornytion
links.reason: Phocus son of Ornytion is son of Ornytion (or Poseidon in a variant by Pausanias); no firm contradiction.

identity.detail: Poseidon matches; Neptune is the Roman equivalent and Genethlius is a cult epithet.
