Wikidata match is Iasion, the Samothracian lover of Demeter; no other names are mixed in.

links.reason: Apollodorus and Wikidata give Side as Orion's wife, but the editor's rule reads any spouse link as a lover. Side was a mythic consort whom Hera cast into Hades, so it is best recorded as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Orion is the giant huntsman of the Odyssey. The father differs only because traditions vary: Poseidon and Euryale (Hesiod, Apollodorus) versus Hyrieus (Parthenius). Poseidon and Euryale are well attested.

links.reason: Hesiod's nymph, daughter of Dryops, bore Pan to Hermes, but she was no wife. The editor reads non-marriages as lover links.
Pindar does not make Fame a child of Hermes; this looks like a misreading of a Pindar passage.

identity.detail: Mercury is the Roman form of Hermes, and 'Cyllene's god' is the same god. The match is correct.
Wikidata match is the sea-goddess Amphitrite, wife of Poseidon (Neptune in Ovid); no other names to split.
Wikidata match is Ismene, daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta and sister of Antigone; this is the same being as in the Thebaid. No other names are given.
Aerope daughter of Cepheus of Tegea, lover of Ares, mother of Aeropus; matches Wikidata and Pausanias (8.44.7-8).
Wikidata match is the Boeotian youth Narcissus, son of Cephisus and Liriope, as in Ovid. The Theoi listing of Endymion and Selene as parents refers to a different tradition and is not in this book.
The Wikidata match is Jason the Argonaut, son of Aeson. No other names are in play.

Andropompus, father of Melanthus of Athens, descendant of Neleus, is the right being. Wikidata lists two fathers (Penthilus and Borus), but Borus is a variant tradition and does not make the match wrong.
Scamander is the same river god as Xanthus; the names are two names for one being.

argonautica/cypris.name: Cypris
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Cypris, Aphrodite

links.reason: Ares is Zeus and Hera's son. Aphrodite's lover Ares is no sibling, and the Iliad's Dione/Zeus parentage does not make them siblings.

identity.detail: Cypris is Aphrodite, with Cytherea as a standard epithet; the match is correct. The several Wikidata entries are only variants of the same goddess.

links.reason: The cited sentence names only Antiphus as his son killed by the Cyclops; Odyssey 2.21-24 says Aegyptius had three other sons, Eurynomus being one of the suitors' companions, but the book's sentence does not support this link as written. Eurynomus is named as a different son, not in that sentence.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the elderly Ithacan Aegyptius; no other names.

links.reason: In the Iliad (20.219-229) Boreas, as a stallion, sired the horses of Erichthonius's herd, not Erichthonius himself; he is not Boreas's lover.
Theoi gives Astraios and Eos as parents; Morn is a vague, unsupported variant of Eos and does not fit as a separate parent.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the north wind god Boreas; no other names to question.
Erechtheus, king of Athens, is the right match. The Hesiod fragment names him as father of Sicyon, which is a variant that suits this book. The other links are standard Athenian tradition.

links.reason: Dido's father is Belus (Virgil) or Mattan I (Belus in Aeneid); Agenor is the Phoenician king, father of Cadmus and Europa, and does not fit as Dido's father in Virgil's tradition.

identity.detail: Dido is the Carthaginian queen; 'Sidonian' is a fitting epithet for her as a Phoenician.

links.reason: Antiope (or Hippolyte) is the Amazon Theseus married and the mother of Hippolytus; Wikidata lists her as a spouse.
Theseus abducted the young Helen but did not marry her; she was rescued by the Dioscuri, so she was a lover at most.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
links.reason: Not supported by this book. Melanippus here is a different person (Hesiod's Theseus line has no such son).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Theseus; no other names are listed.

The Wikidata match is Ialmenus, son of Ares (Mars) and Astyoche, twin of Ascalaphus, the Orchomenian leader. The book's Ialmenus (a Theban fighter in Statius) may be a different man, but nothing flagged contradicts the match.

links.reason: Hesione is the sister of Podarces, the original name of Priam, who was Laomedon's son. Wikipedia's Podarces is the Phylacian brother of Protesilaus.
Laomedon fathered Podarces, the Trojan who became Priam. The Phylacian Podarces is the son of Iphiclus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Thessalian Podarces, son of Iphiclus and brother of Protesilaus. The book's links (Laomedon, Hesione) belong to the Trojan Podarces, who is Priam. Keep them apart.

Euros is the east wind god, matching the Aeneid's Eurus. Aurora is the Roman name for Eos, so the parent link agrees with Wikidata and Theoi (Astraeus and Eos), and the flag is a naming difference only.
Onchestus, the Boeotian eponym and son of Poseidon, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names to question.

Megapenthes son of Proetus, king of Argos, matches Wikidata. Proetus as father is supported by the book. Anaxagoras as his son is the traditional Argive line (Bibliotheca / Pausanias on Anaxagoras succeeding Megapenthes), so it is fine.

links.reason: Pausanias gives Laodamas as Eteocles' son; Glaucon is Eteocles' son only in a minor tradition, and in Pausanias the Glaucon is a different person (Sisyphus' son), so the link confuses two men.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Eteocles, son of Oedipus; no other names to question.
Canens matches the nymph of Latium, daughter of Janus and Venilia and wife of Picus; no other names are involved.

metamorphoses/diana.name: Diana
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Diana, Dictynna

links.reason: In Pausanias, Alpheus pursued Artemis (Alpheiaa) at Letrini, but she was never his lover and escaped him. Metamorphoses has no such link, and Alpheus's love there is for Arethusa, a nymph of Diana's train.

identity.detail: Dictynna is a Cretan goddess, sometimes the nymph Britomartis, later identified with Artemis. Metamorphoses does not use the name for Diana, and the double Wikidata match is ambiguous. The other names (Cynthia, Phoebe, Trivia, Delian Goddess, Titanian Goddess) are epithets of Diana. 'Ortygian Goddess' in the quoted line is Diana as well.
Wikidata match is Panthous, the Trojan elder, son of Othrys and father of Euphorbus, Polydamas and Hyperenor. No other names are attached.

links.reason: A placeholder 'Crius's son' imported from Pausanias is not a named person; Hesiod names Astraeus, Pallas and Perses as Crius's sons (Theogony 375-377).

identity.detail: Kreios matches the Titan Crius; no other names to doubt.
Asia is the Oceanid wife of Iapetus and mother of Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus and Epimetheus; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata's Phidias is the sculptor Pausanias describes; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Metamorphoses 8 calls her the daughter of Erisichthon and wife of Autolycus' namesake context is unclear; but she is Mestra, wife of Autolycus in other tradition, not in the book's cited sentence

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Autolycus, son of Hermes and Chione.
Wikidata match is Arete of Scheria, wife of Alcinous; no confusion.
The match is Manto, daughter of Tiresias, and no other name is attached to her.
Wikidata's Iris is the rainbow goddess and messenger, daughter of Thaumas. Ovid's Iris in Metamorphoses is the same being, and the book gives no other names.
Conon is the Athenian general, and Pausanias names him as the father of Timotheus, which matches.

links.reason: Oeagrus is not an attested husband; the editor's rule reads any non-marriage spouse link as a lover, and the tradition names Oeagrus as Orpheus' father (or Apollo), without a marriage.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope; no other names to check.
Wikidata match is the right Mantius, son of Melampus; no other names.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony names Themis as Zeus's second wife, mother of the Horae and Moirai. Wikidata also lists Zeus as her spouse, and the editor's rule reserves marriage only for Hera, so this link should be read per the editor's decision as a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis. Her names are consistent.
Wikidata's Enyo is the Greek war-goddess, the same being; Theoi also lists Zeus and Hera as her parents.
Phyleus, son of Augeas of Elis and father of Meges, matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Ovid (Metamorphoses 14.613-615) lists Epytus, then Capetus and Capys as successive kings, with Capys named first; it does not call Epytus Capetus's father. Livy and Wikidata make Capys his father.

identity.detail: Capetus Silvius, king of Alba Longa, is the right match.

Memnon, king of Aethiopia, son of Tithonus and Eos (Aurora), is the same being as the Wikidata match. Ovid's Metamorphoses 13 tells of his death at Achilles' hands and his mother Aurora's grief. The Cissia listed as a mother is a variant tradition, not a second being.
Wikidata's Eurycleia is Odysseus' nurse, the daughter of Ops son of Peisenor, as the book states. No other names are in play.
Priam, king of Troy, is the correct match.
Phoenix, son of Amyntor and tutor of Achilles, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed. The one link, Amyntor as father, agrees with the Iliad and Wikidata.

links.reason: Bellona is not Juno's daughter in Roman tradition; she is usually a war goddess associated with Mars as sister, wife or companion, and no source names Juno and Jupiter as her parents. Metamorphoses gives no such parentage either.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Roman war goddess Bellona; no other names to question.

links.reason: Midas's mother is Cybele (Plutarch, Hyginus Fabulae 191), a Phrygian goddess; Pausanias gives only Gordias as father, so a link to Rhea from Metamorphoses conflates Cybele with Rhea and is not supported here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Phrygian king Midas son of Gordias; no other names are attached.
Boreas, the north wind god, matches; Thracian Boreas is the same being.
Barsine, daughter of Artabazus and mistress of Alexander the Great, mother of Heracles, matches Wikidata; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Hermione is Cadmus's wife Harmonia under a variant name (Ovid's Latin form Hermione); the book's passage about the exile does not name a separate spouse, and Harmonia is already linked as his wife, so this duplicate link should go.
Pausanias's Electra is a different person (the Pleiad, Cadmus's mother's namesake or Harmonia's mother); Cadmus's sisters are Europa, with Phoenix and Cilix as brothers, not Electra.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match to Cadmus is correct, but 'Sidonian stranger' is only a descriptive epithet for him and not a separate being; the alias 'Hermione' is Harmonia, his wife, not him.
Wikidata's Enyo is the Greek war-goddess who appears in the Iliad (5.333, 592). Parentage by Zeus and Hera follows Theoi and Wikidata, so the parent links stand.
Didaeon matches the Oechalian prince, son of Eurytus; no other names to question.
Horkos is Oath, the personified spirit of the oath, son of Eris in Hesiod. The match and the alias Horcus are correct.

links.reason: Duplicate of Priam parent_of Cassandra (same daughter under a variant spelling); the tree should keep only the one Cassandra node.

identity.detail: Wikidata Priam is the king of Troy. The only issue is the duplicate Cassandra/Kassandra node.

links.reason: Wikidata names Enyo, not Rhea, as mother; Rhea is probably a confusion with Rhea Silvia, mother of Mars's sons, or another Rhea. No source makes Rhea his mother.

identity.detail: Enyalius matches the war god Enyalius, an aspect of or companion to Ares; the match is sound.
Amphion, twin of Zethus, son of Zeus and Antiope, husband of Niobe, is the right Wikidata match. The two Niobe spouse links are the same marriage listed twice, and it is correct.

links.reason: In Pausanias 1.14.3 Cercyon is Triptolemus' brother in a version; but in Metamorphoses Cercyon is the Eleusinian wrestler killed by Theseus, and Ovid never makes him Triptolemus' sibling. Pausanias gives Cercyon as Triptolemus' father or kin of Eleusis, not a clear sibling tie for this book's character.The link is unsupported here.}],
Pausanias (2.30.7) makes Saron a king of Troezen, not a son of Althepus; this appears to be an unsupported Wikidata guess, and the book gives no such link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Troezenian king Althepus, son of Poseidon and Leis.
Hippolytus, son of Theseus, who is revived by Asclepius and becomes Virbius in Ovid; the match and the name Virbius are correct.
Wikidata match is Actaeon, son of Aristaeus and Autonoë; the Pausanias passage names him as Aristaeus' son. Nothing to correct.
Alecto is the correct match for this Fury. No other names are listed that belong to someone else.
Paris and Alexander are the same being, and the Wikidata match is correct.

aeschylus/cypris.name: Cypris
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Cypris, Aphrodite

links.reason: Ares is Zeus and Hera's son; the Iliad makes Aphrodite a daughter of Zeus and Dione, so they are not siblings. Aeschylus calls Ares the partner of her bed, so lover.

identity.detail: Cypris, Aphrodite and Cytherea are the same goddess. The two Wikidata entries are one being, and the flag comes from the duplicate match.

links.reason: This is Podarces, son of Iphiclus and brother of Protesilaus. The Laomedon link belongs to the Trojan Podarces, who is Priam's original name; Apollodorus gives him as Laomedon's son.
Hesione is the sister of the Trojan Podarces (Priam), not of the Thessalian Podarces.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Thessalian Podarces, son of Iphiclus, and it fits. The links from Apollodorus come from the other Podarces, who is Priam.
Deinomenes, father of Hieron I and Gelon of Syracuse, matches the Wikidata entry. The book's verse about the house of Deinomenes fits.
Xenophon of Athens, father of Gryllus who died at Mantinea; the match is correct.
The match is correct: Epimetheus the Titan, brother of Prometheus.
Wikidata match is the sea goddess Amphitrite, wife of Poseidon; no misattributed names.
Wikidata match is Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon; no other names to question.

links.reason: The cited sentence names only Europs and Argus, the son of Phoroneus' daughter. It does not mention Niobe as a child of Phoroneus in this passage; Niobe is his daughter in other sources, but this sentence does not support the link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argive Phoroneus, son of Inachus; no issues.

Amphion, twin of Zethus and son of Zeus and Antiope, husband of Niobe, matches the Wikidata entry. The flagged 'two spouses' is just the Niobe link duplicated across Apollodorus and Ovid's Metamorphoses, so there is no second wife.

Wikidata's Castalia is the Delphic spring nymph, which matches the book. Pausanias cites Panyasis for Achelous as her father. Wikidata also lists Cephissus as a father, which is a variant tradition and not an error.

In Quintus Smyrnaeus' Fall of Troy, Tisiphone is the Fury (Erinys) who appears at Troy. The Wikidata match is Alcmaeon's daughter, a different being. The Alcmaeon parent link comes from Apollodorus and belongs to that namesake, but it is not listed as flagged here.
Wikidata match is Procris, daughter of Erechtheus and wife of Cephalus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Duplicate spelling of Tlepolemos, son of Herakles; the same person should not be listed twice.

links.link: Herakles parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children taken as one person; the sons by Megara are not a single individual.
Chromis in Statius is a different figure than a child of Herakles; unsupported.

links.link: Herakles sibling_of Iphiclus, son of Amphitryon
links.reason: Duplicate of Iphikles, the twin brother of Herakles.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Heracles; the alternative names are all his.
Paeon, son of Endymion, matches the Elean prince and eponym of Paeonia; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is Amphoterus, son of Alcmaeon and Callirrhoe, brother of Acarnan; this is the same being. No other names are in play.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links. Apollodorus has Omphale as Iardanes' daughter, and Tmolus as her husband in some accounts, but nothing in Pausanias supports a marriage. Tmolus's role as her spouse is also disputed, so this is not a clear marriage.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Omphale of Lydia, the same being.

Wikidata match is Illyrius, son of Cadmus and Harmonia, the eponym of the Illyrians, which matches Apollodorus. Wikidata also lists Polyphemus and Galatea as parents. That is the other Illyrius tradition (Galatea's son), not this book's, but it adds no link to this tree.

Wikidata match is the Sinon of the Trojan Horse story. Sisyphus as father is a known later tradition (Virgil's Aeneid and its commentators, with Aesimus as another named father), and nothing contradicts it, so the link stays.
Ulysses is the Latin name for Odysseus, so the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Perseus, the Argive hero, son of Zeus and Danae; no other names to question.

links.reason: Apollodorus has Plisthenes as Aerope's son or as Atreus's son by her, not her husband; she married Atreus (a husband is a different person from the son).

identity.detail: Aerope, daughter of Catreus, is the right match; no other names to question.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace, daughter of Dionysus (Bromius) and Aegle per Pausanias; the Iliad's Hera only promises her to Sleep, so she is not Hera's child (Theoi's confirmation is doubtful).

identity.detail: Juno and Hera are the same goddess by Roman-Greek equation; the Wikidata match is fine.
Wikidata match is the Titaness Mnemosyne, mother of the Muses. Zeus as her father is already ruled wrong by the editor.

Phoenix, son of Agenor and Telephassa and eponym of Phoenicia, matches the Wikidata entry. Apollodorus 3.1.1 gives him as Agenor's son, and his children vary by tradition (Phineus, Thasus, Astypalaea), so nothing needs changing.
Anchises of Dardania, son of Capys and Themiste, father of Aeneas by Aphrodite; the Wikidata match is correct.
Palaechthon is the earth-born father of Pelasgus in Aeschylus' Suppliants; the Wikidata match is the same being.

links.reason: A group label, not a person; the sons Eteocles and Polynices are already linked individually.
Euryganeia is Oedipus's second wife in the epic Oedipodea tradition (cited by Pausanias), and Wikidata lists her as a spouse; this book does not mention her, but she was a wife, not a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Oedipus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Pausanias' Cleogenes, son of Silenus, is an Elean horse-race victor with a human father named Silenus, not the satyr-tutor of Dionysus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the satyr Silenus, tutor of Dionysus, and he has no other names to check.

The book's Zeuxidamus is the son of Leotychides II and father of Archidamus II (Eurypontid, 5th century BC). The Wikipedia description (10th king of the Eurypontid dynasty, with Archidamus as father per Wikidata) points to an earlier namesake, so the match is a different person. The book's links themselves are right.

Proserpina is the Roman name of Persephone, the Proserpine of the Thebaid. Jove and Demeter (Ceres) as parents and Dis (Pluto) as husband are standard. Wikidata's spouse list also names Liber and Hercyna, but those are not in this book's tree.

links.reason: The editor's rule reads any spouse link other than the listed marriages as a lover. Aphrodite/Venus with Hephaestus/Vulcan is among the listed marriages, so this one is correct and the make_lover fix is not needed; in the Iliad, though, Charis is his wife.

identity.detail: Vulcan is Hephaestus in this book; the match and the names Crook-foot and Hephaestus are fine.

Wikidata match is the Fate Clotho. In Hesiod's Theogony (217-222) Night bears the Fates, so the book's link is right. Wikidata also lists Zeus and Themis as parents, which is the other Hesiodic tradition (Theogony 904).
The Wikidata match is Critolaus, son of Hicetaon. This matches Pausanias' Critolaus, and the book gives no other names for him.

links.reason: In Iliad 20 Boreas, as a stallion, sired horses on Erichthonius' mares; Erichthonius was no lover of Boreas.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the north wind god Boreas; no other names are given.
Mausolus is the Carian satrap, husband and brother of Artemisia II; the Wikidata match is correct.
Epopeus of Sicyon is the right match. Pausanias (2.1.1) gives Marathon as his son and Aloeus as his father, citing Eumelus, and Wikidata agrees.
Eteoclus son of Iphis, one of the Seven against Thebes, matches Pausanias' passage and Wikidata.
Wikidata match is the West Wind god Zephyrus; no other names to separate.

links.reason: Aegle was a lover for whom Theseus abandoned Ariadne (Hesiod), not a wife.
Antiope (or Hippolyte) is the Amazon who bore Hippolytus, and she is commonly treated as Theseus' wife; the Amazon is one figure with Hippolyte.
Theseus abducted the child Helen; she was never his wife, and Pausanias gives Iphigenia as their daughter.
Statius gives Hippolyte as Theseus' wife; she is the Amazon mother of Hippolytus, identical to Antiope in other versions, so the duplicate should be merged.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian hero Theseus; no other names.
Alcippe, daughter of Ares and Agraulus (Aglaurus), matches the book and Wikidata.
Wikidata match is the Argive king Adrastus; 'Persean hero' is an epithet, not a separate person.
Norax, son of Hermes and Erythea, founder of Nora in Sardinia, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names.
Iapetos the Titan, son of Uranus and Gaia, is the right match; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Erigone is the daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra in some accounts, not of Clytemnestra and Agamemnon; however Wikidata lists her as child of Orestes in other traditions, and Pausanias does not make her Clytemnestra's daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Clytemnestra; the spelling Clytæmnestra is just a variant.
Wikidata match is Anogon, son of Castor and Hilaeira, who is also called Anaxias. Apollodorus says Castor had Anogon by Hilaira, so the link is right.
Xerxes I is the right match; the Persians treats him as son of Darius and Atossa.
Nessus the centaur who killed Heracles matches. Wikipedia's 'son of Centauros' and Wikidata's Ixion and Nephele are both accepted centaur genealogies. The link to Nephele is acceptable.
Harpies as a group matches the Wikidata entry. In Hesiod (Theogony 265-269) Thaumas and Electra are the parents of Iris and the two Harpies Aello and Ocypete, so the link is right.
Wikidata's Kratos is the personification of strength, son of Pallas and Styx, which matches Hesiod's Cratos (Strength). The alternate name Strength is a translation of the same name.
The Wikidata match is Tereus, the Thracian king, husband of Procne. Pausanias' Tereus (the husband of Procne who wronged Philomela) is the same being.
Wikidata match is Nestor of Pylos; no other names to question.

Idmon the Argonaut seer matches the Wikidata entry. Statius's Thebaid has a different Idmon, the Theban seer Amphiaraus's follower, but the link here, Apollo as father, is traditional for the Argonaut seer, so I keep it.
Wikidata match is the Phoenician princess Astypalaea, daughter of Phoenix, sister of Europa, mother of Eurypylus and Ancaeus by Poseidon.
Tros, son of Erichthonius and Astyoche, king of Troy, is the right match. No other names are involved.
Acarnan, son of Alcmaeon and Callirrhoe and brother of Amphoterus, is correctly matched. The Alcmaeon link is right as listed.
Wikidata match is the right Amphitryon; no other names to split.
Wikidata's Polyxena is the daughter of Priam and Hecuba, sacrificed at Achilles' tomb; this matches Pausanias' Polyxena. No other names are involved.
Belus, king of Egypt, son of Poseidon and Libya, father of Danaus and Aegyptus, is the right match.

Wikidata's Aventinus is the son of Hercules and Rhea from Virgil's Aeneid vii; that matches Aventinus in Metamorphoses xiv, who is also a Latin king of Alban line? No: Ovid's Aventinus Silvius is an Alban king, but the Hercules link is not contradicted by the book, so no change.
Axius is the Paeonian river god (Axios), father of Pelegon in Iliad 21; the Wikidata match is correct. Pelegon is the same as Pelagon in other sources, a spelling variant.
Wikidata Tantalus is the right being; no other names are confused.
Heleus, son of Perseus and Andromeda in Apollodorus, matches the Mycenaean prince; no other names to split.
Wikidata's Agave, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, is the Theban princess and mother of Pentheus, so the match is correct.
Medus, son of Aegeus and Medea, matches the Wikidata entry.
Telethusa is the Cretan mother of Iphis and wife of Ligdus in Ovid; the Wikidata match is correct.
Ino and Leucothea are the same being, since Ino became the sea goddess Leucothea. The Wikidata match is correct.

links.link: Hercules sibling_of Iphiclus, son of Amphitryon
links.reason: Duplicate of Iphicles under a variant name; the Iphiclus here is a different person in other books, so this link likely belongs to the namesake. Keep only one Iphicles link.

links.link: Hercules parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children is taken for a single person.

identity.detail: Wikidata Heracles is the right being; Hercules and Heracles are the same hero.

links.reason: Hesiod's Dryope, mother of Pan by Hermes, is a different nymph; Ovid's Dryope bore Amphissus to Apollo and married Andraemon.

identity.detail: Wikidata Dryope matches Ovid's daughter of Eurytus, the half-sister of Iole, who was loved by Apollo. The Hesiodic Dryope, mother of Pan, is a different figure.

links.reason: Statius' Thebaid (11.47, 12.557) makes Megaera a daughter of Hades (Dis) and the Furies are Night's children; the Gaia/Uranus lineage is Hesiod's (the blood of Uranus), not Statius'.
Statius' Thebaid (11.47, 12.557) makes Megaera a daughter of Hades (Dis) and the Furies are Night's children; the Gaia/Uranus lineage is Hesiod's (the blood of Uranus), not Statius'.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Fury Megaera; no other names involved.
The Wikidata match is the right Andromache, wife of Hector. Her other name is not in question.

links.reason: The editor ruled this right only in Pausanias, where Argus is Epidaurus' father. It does not belong in Apollodorus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Pelops, son of Tantalus. The Wikidata mother and the spouses Danais and Axioche are variant traditions, not another person.
Thamyris is the Thracian singer, son of Philammon and the nymph Argiope; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Misenus in the Aeneid is the son of Aeolus, a Trojan, not the wind-king; a different Aeolus.
Cephalus, husband of Procris, is the son of Deioneus (or Hermes/Pandion); the Æolus named in Ovid is the Thessalian Aeolus, son of Hellen, not the wind-king, grandson of Hippotas.

identity.detail: Book has two Aeolus figures: the wind-king (grandson of Hippotas) and the father of Halcyone, which Ovid treats as the Thessalian Aeolus, so the Wikidata Aeolus (son of Hippotes) fits only partly.

links.reason: Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon in the tradition; Pausanias' Agamemnon had Iphigenia, Electra, Orestes, Chrysothemis (and Hermione is Menelaus' daughter). Likely a confusion with the Titan Hyperion or a misread.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (Atreus' daughter) in Pausanias' account, or a wife of Nestor; she is not his child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct; 'Atreus' son' is a patronymic for the same Agamemnon.
Athis is the Indian youth of Metamorphoses V. Limnate (Limnaee) is the same nymph under a variant spelling, so the flagged parent difference is only a name variant and the link is right.
Dionysus matches; Bacchus is the same god.
Python is the Delphic serpent born of Gaia (Earth), and the Wikidata match is the same being.
Chrysippus is the illegitimate son of Pelops, abducted by Laius, and the Wikidata match is this same being. No other names are listed, so none is wrongly attached.
Wikidata match is Thersites the Greek soldier at Troy, son of Agrius of Calydon per tradition (Apollodorus, Epitome). No other names are attached to him.
Wikidata match is Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene. Theoi lists the Ouranos & Gaia and Karystos parentages as variant traditions, not a different being.
Hippias is the Athenian tyrant, son of Pisistratus and brother of Hipparchus; the Wikidata match is correct.
Lais of Corinth is the hetaira Pausanias describes, so the match is correct. Pausanias says she went to Thessaly for love of Hippostratus, so the lover link is right.

links.reason: Hesiod does not give Poseidon as Eurynome's lover; the link likely confuses her with another Eurynome (the mother of Bellerophon by Glaucus' line or Poseidon's other partners).
In Ovid, Leucothoë's mother is Eurynome, wife of Orchamus of Persia, a different woman from the Oceanid.

identity.detail: The Oceanid Eurynome matches. Pausanias also notes the Phigalian Artemis title, which is not a separate person.

The Wikidata entry Asopichus is a disambiguation-style match covering two men: Asopichus of Orchomenus, the Olympic boys' runner who was the son of Cleodamus, and Asopichus, the father of the Athenian general Phormio. Pausanias' Asopichus is the father of Phormio, so the Orchomenian runner would be the wrong person. The Phormio link is right for this book.
Wikidata match is Ladon, the dragon of the Hesperides' garden. No other names are attached to him, so nothing is confused.
Wikidata match is Orestes, son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra; no other names to question.
Hektor is the Trojan prince Hector, son of Priam and Hecuba; the Wikidata match is correct and there are no other names to separate.
Wikidata match is Paris, son of Priam and Hecuba; no other names are listed.

Megara is Creon's daughter of Thebes and Heracles' first wife; the Wikidata match is correct. Wikidata also lists Iolaos as a spouse. The tradition that Heracles gave Megara to Iolaus is Euripides/Apollodorus-adjacent, and it is not in this book's tree, so nothing needs fixing.

links.reason: Idas's brother Lynceus is the Messenian Lynceus, son of Aphareus; this Lynceus, husband of Hypermnestra, is the son of Aegyptus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argive Lynceus, son of Aegyptus and husband of Hypermnestra; no other names to question.
Persepolis (Perseptolis) is the son of Telemachus; Hesiod, per Eustathius, gave Polycaste, Nestor's daughter, as his mother, so both links fit the Hesiodic tradition.
Amphitrite is correctly matched to the sea goddess, wife of Poseidon, with no other names to question.

links.reason: Icarius, father of Penelope, was the son of Oebalus (or Perieres in some versions), but Pausanias calls Tyndareus the uterine brother of Aphareus and names Perieres' sons as Aphareus, Leucippus and Pisus; the Wikidata link is a variant not found in this book, and it conflates Perieres with Oebalus' line.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Messenian king Perieres, son of Aiolos; no problem with names.

pausanias/apollo.name: Apollo
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Pythios, Apollo

links.reason: Aeschylus' Apis is the Argive healer-seer, son of Apollo in Suppliants, but Pausanias' Apis is a different figure (Argive king, son of Phoroneus/Zeus), so the link does not belong in this book.
Wikidata lists Amphissa as a spouse, but Pausanias says only that she was beloved by Apollo, so she remains a lover under the editor's marriage rule.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match 'Pythios, Apollo' is the cult epithet entry, not the god himself; the god is Apollo. Cult names such as Agyieus, Boedromius, Maleates and Pythius are epithets of this same god, so they stay as his names.
Paris and Alexander are the same Trojan prince.
Wikidata match is the Corinthian hero Bellerophon, son of Poseidon (Hesiod) and fostered or fathered by Glaucus; no stray names.
Wikidata's Erinyes is the right being. In Hesiod's Theogony (176-185) they are born of Earth from the blood of Ouranos's severed genitals, so both links agree with the book and Theoi.

links.reason: Hesiod's Homeric-style tale has Hermes lie with the nymph, daughter of Dryops, and father Pan; this was a union, not a marriage, per the editor's rule on spouses.
Pindar's mention of Hermes and Fame is a poetic image (Hermes bringing renown), not a parentage; Theoi lists no such child.

identity.detail: Wikidata Hermes is the god; no other names to separate.

links.reason: Hesione was given to Telamon as war prize after Heracles sacked Troy (Apollodorus), so she was a concubine, not a wife; Teucer's mother, per the editor's rule that non-marriages are lovers.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Telamon, the son of Aeacus and the Argonaut; the Aeacus and Endeis links fit. Actaeus and Glauce on Wikidata are alternative traditions (Telamon's maternal line in some sources), not errors.
Wikidata's Aristodama is the 3rd-century BCE poet of Smyrna. Pausanias' Aristodama is the mythical mother of Aratus of Sicyon, so the two are different people.

Melanion and Hippomenes are the same figure, Atalanta's husband in the race myth; the Wikidata match is acceptable. Apollodorus's own father for him differs, but the Megareus link comes from Ovid's tradition.

links.reason: Per Apollodorus and Pausanias, Rhadamanthys married Alcmena after Amphitryon's death in Boeotia; the editor's rule treats any non-marriage as a lover, but this was a marriage, so it stays a spouse link.

identity.detail: Rhadamanthys matches Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa; no other names to question.

links.reason: Chaos is a primordial being, not Cronus's child; the Theogony has Chaos arising first, and Cronus is a child of Uranus and Gaia.
Ops is the Roman counterpart of Rhea; the book's wife is Rhea, so a second spouse duplicates her (the flag). Keep Rhea.

Rhea is Cronus's sister in Hesiod, but the same tree lists her as his spouse; the Iliad has Rhea bearing his sons, so the marriage is the link this book follows. Sibling is also correct in myth, but it is a duplicate of the Rhaea spelling variant, so it is dropped.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct: Saturn and Cronus are merged as one being, which is the book's Romanized rendering and fits the site.
Eleusis is the eponymous hero of the town; the Wikidata match is correct.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, is the Trojan prophetess; the match is correct. Apollo as her lover or suitor fits Apollodorus's account, so no change is needed.
Wikidata match is Pylades, son of Strophius, friend and cousin of Orestes. Wikidata lists several mothers (Cyndragora, Anaxibia, Astyoche), but those are traditional variants, not a different being.
Telephus, son of Heracles and Auge, king of Mysia, is the right match. Corythus as a father in Wikidata is a variant, not an error here.

links.reason: Erythrus is not a known child of Alcmena; she bore Heracles, Iphicles and Laonome. Unsupported by Pausanias or Theoi.

identity.detail: Alkmene is the right match; Alcmena and Alcmene are the same being.

links.reason: Apollodorus's Eurytus son of Actor is the Molionid Eurytus, not Eurytus of Oechalia; Hesiod gives Stratonica as mother.
Pausanias's Thalpius is the son of Eurytus the Molionid (Actor's son), not the Oechalian archer.
Theraphone's husband in Pausanias is another Eurytus, not the Oechalian king.
Dryops' daughter is the mother of Pan by Hermes in the editor's decision; she is not a child of Eurytus.

identity.detail: The match is Eurytus of Oechalia; Wikidata's parents differ from Hesiod's but are an accepted variant.
Wikidata's Aepytus matches Æpytus, son of Cresphontes and Merope, king of Messenia. No other names are attached to him.
Tiasa is the Laconian river nymph, daughter of Eurotas; the match is correct. The book names only Eurotas as her father, so the flag about parents is not a problem.

links.reason: Æsimides, son of the Athenian archon Æschylus (the Medontid, c. 750s BC), belongs to a different Æschylus, not the tragedian.
Symmachus the Elean wrestler is the son of a different Æschylus, an Elean, not the Athenian tragedian.

identity.detail: The name Æschylus covers three men in Pausanias: the tragedian, son of Euphorion; the Athenian archon, father of Æsimides; and the Elean father of Symmachus. The Wikidata match fits only the tragedian.
Wikidata match is the right Eurystheus, king of Tiryns/Mycenae, son of Sthenelus.

links.reason: Pausanias (7.4) means Procles, the Epidaurian king of Samos, not the Spartan son of Aristodemus; the two are different men with the same name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Spartan Procles, son of Aristodemus and twin of Eurysthenes. The Samian Procles is a different man, handled by removing the Leogorus link.

links.reason: Pausanias (1.35.6) makes Anax the son of Earth alone, called Autochthon; the book names no father, and Uranus as father is an unsupported Wikidata addition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Anax who was king of Anactoria (Miletus), son of Earth and father of Asterius.
Podalirius is the son of Asclepius (Æsculapius) and brother of Machaon; the Wikidata match is correct.

Pausanias' Polydectes is the Spartan Eurypontid king, son of Eunomus and father of Charillus. The Wikidata match is the mythic king of Seriphos, son of Magnes or Poseidon and Cerebia. The tree's links are right for the Spartan, but the Wikidata parents belong to the Seriphian king, so the match should be dropped.

links.reason: A chorus is a group, not a person; the individual Oceanids are already linked.

identity.detail: Match is the Titan Tethys.
Aristogiton is the Athenian tyrannicide, so the Wikidata match is correct. The link to Leaena as his mistress follows Pausanias's own sentence.

Wikidata's Peleus is the right being, the Phthian king, son of Aeacus and father of Achilles. Antigone, daughter of Eurytion, is a real tradition as his first wife (Apollodorus), so the two spouses are not an error.
The Wikidata match is Deiphobus, son of Priam and Hecuba, who married Helen after Paris died. The links are correct.

links.reason: Apollodorus 3.11.1 names Menelaus' son Megapenthes by a slave woman (Pieris or Tereis), a different person from Proetus' son, the king of Argos; the Proetus link belongs to the king and the Menelaus link to the namesake.

identity.detail: Two Megapentheses are joined under one name: the king of Argos, son of Proetus and Stheneboea, and the son of Menelaus by a slave woman. Wikidata's match fits only the Argive king; Menelaus' son should be a separate person.

The Wikidata match and Wikipedia description point to Cleite, the Danaid who killed Cleitus, or the maenad. This Cleite is the wife of King Cyzicus in Apollonius' Argonautica, daughter of Merops of Percote, who hanged herself after his death. She is a different being.

links.reason: Athena is a virgin goddess; in Metamorphoses Clytus is not her child, so this is a misread or unsupported link.
Athena is a virgin goddess with no children; Butes is a mortal (e.g. an Argonaut or son of Boreas or Pandion) and not hers.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Pallas, the companion of Athena (her friend, with Triton as father), not the goddess Athena. The Athene in Pindar is the daughter of Zeus (born from his head), so the match should be to the goddess Athena. Pallas is only an epithet of her, so it should not be a separate identity.
Glauce (Creusa), daughter of Creon of Corinth and Jason's bride, matches the Wikidata entry. Pausanias also mentions other Glauces, but nothing in this tree conflates them.

links.reason: Duplicate of the book's own link; Glaucus son of Sisyphus is already given by Pausanias, so this extra Glaucus node should be merged with it, not kept separately.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Corinthian hero Bellerophon; no alternate names to question.

links.reason: Hesiod makes Aegle a woman Theseus loved (Ariadne was left for her); no marriage, so she is a lover.
Theseus abducted the child Helen, but no marriage followed (Pausanias); she is a lover at most.
Demophoon is a duplicate spelling of Demophon, the son of Theseus; it duplicates the Demophon link and should be merged, not kept as a separate person.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias mentions a daughter of Theseus and Helen named Iphigenia, but she is a different person from Agamemnon's daughter; this is a separate mention and should be a distinct entity, not a Theseus child of the main Iphigenia.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias names a Melanippus son of Theseus only in a passing mention; this appears to be a mismatch with a different Melanippus entry, and nothing in Statius supports it.
Antiope (or Hippolyte, in some traditions) is the Amazon wife of Theseus and mother of Hippolytus; many sources treat her as his wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Theseus; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Timandra was Echemus's wife and a daughter of Tyndareus and Leda in Pausanias 8.5.1 and the Hesiod fragment, but Apollodorus 3.10.6 mentions her only as Echemus's wife, so the link is supported only by other books. This is a tradition other books tell, not a misread. Keep it as an outside link, not a wrong one.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Leda is this Aetolian princess, the daughter of Thestius and wife of Tyndareus. Wikidata gives her mother as Deidamia, a variant of Eurythemis, which does not affect the match.
Wikidata's Leto, the Titan daughter of Coeus and Phoebe and mother of Apollo and Artemis, is the same being as Pausanias' Leto.
Wikidata match is the Giant Enceladus, opponent of Athena; no other names are mixed in.

links.reason: Arne is the mother of Aeolus's children by Poseidon (Boeotus) in the tradition, not Hellen's mother; Hellen's mother is Pyrrha (Theoi, Apollodorus).

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the eponymous Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha.
Pyrrhus is the birth name of Neoptolemus, son of Achilles and Deidamia; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Astraea is the daughter of Astraeus and Eos (Aratus; Hyginus), not Themis; in Metamorphoses she is the Justice goddess who leaves earth, with no mother named.
Hesiod's Theogony (Theoi, Wikidata) has Themis as Zeus's second wife, so she is a wife rather than a mere lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Themis; no other names listed.
Wikidata match is Maia the Pleiad, mother of Hermes/Mercury; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Aegisthus, son of Thyestes and Pelopeia, who lived with Clytaemnestra and helped kill Agamemnon; this fits the Hesiod passage.
Glauce (Creusa), daughter of Creon of Corinth, is the right match. Apollodorus says Creon betrothed her to Jason, who married her.
Wikidata's Coronis is the Thessalian princess, daughter of Phlegyas and lover of Apollo, who bore Asclepius. This matches the book.
Wikidata matches Hippomenes, the Boeotian son of Megareus who wed Atalanta. The other Hippomenes, father of Leimone, is a separate person and is not merged here.
Acastus, son of Pelias, Argonaut and Calydonian hunter, matches the Wikidata entry.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Damasias (Damasius) Penthilus' son, brother of Tisamenus in one sentence, but this conflicts with the other sentence, which makes Agorius son of Damasius, son of Penthilus; Damasias as Penthilus' son is not contradicted, so keep is more apt.

identity.detail: Penthilus matches the son of Orestes and Erigone.
Wikidata match is the Dardanus who founded Dardania, son of Zeus and Electra. The other names are not in dispute.

links.reason: In Hesiod's Theogony (211-225), Strife (Eris) is a child of Night alone, and Sleep likewise; Erebus is not named as their father.
Hesiod's Theogony (211-212) makes Sleep a child of Night alone, with no father named.

identity.detail: Erebos is the right match for this being. The Wikidata mother Caligo is a Latin variant tradition (Hyginus), not an error here.

links.reason: Duplicate of Androgeus (same son, Greek spelling variant); the tree has two nodes for one person, so this is a split-names issue, not a different child.
Asterion is the Minotaur's name, or Minos's stepfather (Asterion of Crete), not a son of Minos.

identity.detail: Minos of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, is correctly matched. Androgeus and Androgeos are the same person under two spellings, and should be merged.
Wikidata match is the god Dionysus (Bacchus); no other names are mixed in.
Lynceus the Messenian Argonaut, son of Aphareus and Arene, brother of Idas' cousin line; the Wikidata match is correct and there are no other names to separate.
Proteus the sea god, Poseidon's son, matches Wikidata; the Odyssey's Old Man of the Sea is the same being. The parent flag is only Neptune/Poseidon naming, and Theoi confirms Poseidon.

links.reason: Oeagrus is traditionally her partner (Apollodorus, Argonautica), but under the editor's rule only marriages count as spouse links, so this is read as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope; no other names to question.
Saron, king of Troezen and eponym of the Saronic Gulf, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are attached to him.

links.reason: This is the Amazon Antiope, mother of Hippolytus, not the Theban Antiope.
Hippolyta is sister of the Amazon Antiope, not the Theban one.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban Antiope; the Amazon Antiope's links are a separate being.

links.reason: Ptolemy Philometor's mother was Cleopatra I of Egypt, a historical queen, not Meleager's wife, the daughter of Idas.

links.link: Cleopatra parent_of Alexander, son of Cleopatra
links.reason: This Alexander is the son of a different Cleopatra, the Ptolemaic queen mentioned by Pausanias, not Idas' daughter.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is correct: Cleopatra (Alcyone), daughter of Idas and Marpessa and wife of Meleager.
Callipatira (Pherenice) is Kallipateira of Rhodes, daughter of Diagoras. Pausanias names her as the mother of Eucles and Pisirodus, so the match is correct.
Charites is the correct match: the Graces as a group of goddesses.

links.reason: Hyperion is not a child of Agamemnon in the Theoi listing or in Pausanias' usual account; the link looks like a confusion with the Titan Hyperion or a misread name.
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (or in some accounts Nestor's daughter), not his daughter, so this looks like a misreading of Pausanias.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the king of Mycenae and there are no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias' Duris is the father of Scaeus, a Samian boxer's father whose statue stood at Olympia, not Duris of Samos the historian and tyrant; the book gives no sign that the two are the same man.

identity.detail: Pausanias' Duris is only named as the father of the boxer Scaeus. The Wikidata match, Duris of Samos the historian, is a different and later person (4th-3rd century BC), so the match is not safe.
The Wikidata match is the king of Psophis, which is correct.
Labdacus, son of Polydorus and grandson of Cadmus, king of Thebes and father of Laius, matches Wikidata. Pausanias also calls him the son of Polydorus.

links.reason: Hesiod does not make Aidos a child of Prometheus; the link looks like a misreading, and Theoi's confirmation does not support it.
Pausanias' Cabiri Prometheus is a different figure from the Titan, so this link belongs to that namesake.

identity.detail: The Cabiri Prometheus in Pausanias at Thebes is a separate being from the Titan, so the Ætnæus link should be split off from the Titan.
Wikidata's Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, is the being the book names.
Wikidata match is the Rhodian leader Tlepolemus, son of Heracles; in Metamorphoses he is addressed as Hercules' son, which fits. Polyxo is his wife in Pausanias, so the spouse link stands.

links.reason: Oenone was Paris's first wife, a nymph of Mount Ida, per Apollodorus and Quintus of Smyrna; the Iliad does not mention her, but the link is not wrong, so I did not remove it. Under the editor's rule, only marriages count as spouse links. Oenone is traditionally a wife, so this stays a spouse link.

identity.detail: Paris, also called Alexander or Alexandrus, is the Trojan prince, son of Priam and Hecuba. The Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Hesione was Telamon's war captive from Troy (mother of Teucer in Metamorphoses and other sources), not his wife; per the editor's rule non-marriage links become lover.
Duplicate of Ajax under a spelling variant; the Ajax link is already stated by the book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Telamon, son of Aeacus.
In Apollodorus the Cyclopes (Arges, Steropes, Brontes) are the sons of Sky and Earth, which matches the Wikidata match. The Wikidata item covers the general creature type, but it fits this book.

links.reason: Pausanias' sentence concerns a different Euphorbus, an Eretrian traitor and son of Alcimachus, not the Trojan son of Panthous.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Trojan hero. The Pausanias passage about the Eretrian Euphorbus is a namesake, but it does not change the match.
Wikidata's Lycaon is the Trojan son of Priam and Laothoe, matching the Iliad's Lycaon killed by Achilles; no other names are attached.
Wikidata match is the right Andromache, wife of Hector and daughter of Eetion; no other names are given.
Wikidata match is Io, the Argive princess loved by Zeus; no other names to question.

Memnon, king of the Aethiopians and son of Tithonus and Eos, fits the Wikidata match; no other names are listed. Cissia as a second mother is a variant tradition (Cissia as his mother appears in some sources) and is not a book link.

The book's Hippolyte is the wife of Akastos and daughter of Kretheus (Astydameia in other sources), who tried to seduce Peleus. The Wikidata match is a different Hippolyte: the Amazon queen, or possibly the Hesperid. The match should be corrected to the wife of Akastos.

Wikidata match is Nausicaa, Homer's Phaeacian princess, daughter of Alcinous and Arete. The book's sentence names Alcinous as her father, so the link is right. Wikidata lists Telemachus as her spouse, which is a late tradition (Eustathius, citing Aristotle), but the tree has no such link.

links.reason: "Oedipus's sons" is a group placeholder, not a person; the sons Polynices and Eteocles are already linked individually.
In the Oedipodea tradition Euryganeia was Oedipus's second wife and mother of his children; the editor reads non-primary spouses as lovers, so this link is kept as is.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Oedipus; no other names to question.
Plutus the god of wealth, son of Demeter and Iasion, matches Wikidata. No other names to question.

links.reason: The quoted line (Hymn to Aphrodite) calls Anchises 'son of Dardanus' only as a patronymic for the Dardanian line. Anchises' actual father is Capys, son of Assaracus, so Dardanus is a remote ancestor.

identity.detail: The match is the founder Dardanus, son of Zeus and Electra. No other names are listed.
Wikidata match is the daughter of Temenus and wife of Deiphontes; no other names.
Wikidata match is the sea goddess Amphitrite, wife of Poseidon; Hesiod (Theogony 243, 930) makes her a Nereid, daughter of Nereus and Doris, and the links are consistent with this.

links.reason: Naiads are a group, not a person; in Metamorphoses they are only nymphs who feast Theseus, not a stated child group of Achelous.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the river god Achelous; Ocean and Tethys follow Hesiod, and Apollodorus gives Ocean and Tethys or Gaia.
Dione the Titaness is the right match; Apollodorus names her as Zeus's partner and Aphrodite's mother.
Alkyoneus is the Giant killed by Heracles, and the Wikidata match fits. Theoi confirms Gaia and Ouranos as his parents.

links.reason: The book's sentence (3.1.2) is about Minos's son Glaucus, who drowned in a honey jar. This Glaucus is the son of Sisyphus, so the link joins two namesakes.

identity.detail: x

links.reason: Iambe is the daughter of Pan and Echo in some late sources, but Theoi does not list her and the Wikidata link is unsupported; in Hesiod's corpus Iambe is the servant of Metaneira, a different figure.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Pan the goat-footed god; no other names to question.
Ilithyia is Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, so the Wikidata match is correct. She has no other names that need splitting.

Vesta is the Roman goddess identified with Greek Hestia. Pausanias' Vesta is Hestia, daughter of Cronos and Rhea, which matches Saturn and Ops in Wikidata as the Roman equivalents. The flagged parent difference is only a Greek/Roman naming difference.
Wikidata match is Aeson, king of Iolcus and father of Jason; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Troilus is the Trojan prince, son of Priam (or Apollo) and Hecuba. The link to Priam is the standard tradition, so it stays.
Wikidata match is the hound of Hades; 'Echidnean dog' is Ovid's epithet for Cerberus (son of Echidna), so the name is correct.
Wikidata's Amalthea is the nurse of Zeus, so the match is right.

Amphissa, daughter of Macareus (Macar, son of Aeolus) and beloved of Apollo, eponym of Amphissa in Locris, matches the Wikidata entry. Macar and Macareus are the same person. The Wikidata 'spouse' Apollo is correctly a lover here.
Wikidata's Zethos is the Theban twin, brother of Amphion. Aëdon is his wife in the tradition, and no other name is mixed in.
The Wikidata match is Hector, son of Priam, and no other names are listed.

links.reason: Boreas snatched her away (Argonautica 1.211-223); per the editor's rule, only marriages stay as spouse, and this abduction is read as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, is the same being as the book's Oreithyia.

links.reason: Iphicrates was the son of Timotheus in the book's sentence only through a misreading: historically Iphicrates (the general) was son of a shoemaker, and Timotheus was his friend; the Pausanias passage names a different 'Iphicrates son of Timotheus' as read, but the famous Iphicrates is not Timotheus's son.

identity.detail: Timotheus son of Conon is the Athenian general; the match is correct.
Wikidata's Tityos is the giant killed after assaulting Leto; no other names are attached to him.

links.reason: Ptolemy Philometor was the son of the Ptolemaic queen Cleopatra I, not Meleager's wife in the Iliad.

links.link: Cleopatra parent_of Alexander, son of Cleopatra
links.reason: This is Alexander of Epirus, son of Philip II's daughter Cleopatra of Macedon, not the Iliad's Cleopatra.

links.link: Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas parent_of Cleopatra
links.reason: Philip II's daughter Cleopatra of Macedon is a different person; the Iliad's Cleopatra is the daughter of Idas and Marpessa.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is correct: Cleopatra, also called Alcyone, daughter of Idas and Marpessa and wife of Meleager. The links from Pausanias belong to Macedonian and Ptolemaic namesakes.
Wikidata match is Salmoneus, king of Salmone and father of Tyro; no other names are attached.

links.reason: Pausanias' Micon is the father of Onatas of Aegina, a different man from Micon the Athenian painter and sculptor, so the link belongs to a namesake.

identity.detail: The book names Micon of Aegina, father of the sculptor Onatas. The Wikidata match is Micon the Younger of Athens, a painter, and not the same person. Pausanias does mention the Athenian painter elsewhere, so the name is shared by two men in the book.

links.reason: The book's Cercopes sentence says only that Theia and Ocean had sons, not that they married; Hesiod gives Hyperion as her husband, so under the editor's rule Ocean is read as a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Theia, and she has no other names listed.
Menestheus, the Athenian king and leader at Troy, is the right match. Peteos is the same person as Wikidata's Peteus, so the parent link is correct and the flag is only a spelling variant.

Wikidata's Aeacus, king of Aegina, son of Zeus and Aegina, father of Peleus, Telamon and Phocus, is the right match. Theoi's alternate listing of Zeus and Europa as parents belongs to Aeacus, the judge of the dead, which is a different tradition, not a different person, so no change.

links.reason: Ovid's Metamorphoses calls her 'daughter of Schœneus' (the Boeotian Atalanta); Iasus is the father of the Arcadian Atalanta, so this link comes from the other book's namesake.
Parthenopaeus is the son of the Arcadian Atalanta (with Melanion or Ares); Ovid's Boeotian Atalanta, who marries Hippomenes, is not given this son in the book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Atalanta; the book's version is the Boeotian daughter of Schoeneus, and the Arcadian relatives belong to the other Atalanta, but the identity match itself is acceptable.
Porphyrion is the Giant in Pindar (Pythian 8), matching Wikidata. Parents Ouranos and Gaia fit Hesiod and Apollodorus 1.34.
Wikidata's Ino is this Theban princess, and Leucothea is her own divine name after her transformation.
Miletus, son of Apollo and Deione (Areia/Acacallis in other versions), founder of Miletus, father of Byblis and Caunus, matches the Wikidata entry.

Clytie, the Oceanid in Ovid's Metamorphoses who loves Helios and turns into a heliotropic flower, matches the Wikidata Clytie. Her parentage as Oceanus and Tethys is the standard one for Oceanids, so nothing needs fixing.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony 901-906) makes Themis Zeus's second wife, and Wikidata lists Zeus as her spouse. The editor's rule reads only Hera and Juno as Zeus's marriages, but that rule does not make Themis a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Themis is the Titaness, so the match is correct.

links.reason: Hesiod's Eetion (Iasion), the lover of Demeter and son of Zeus and Electra, is a different man from Andromache's father, the king of Cilician Thebe.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Eetion, king of Cilician Thebe, which is the right being. The only problem is the Zeus link, which was brought over from the other Eetion in Hesiod.

links.reason: The Fall of Troy passage gives the Seasons (Horae) no moon-goddess mother; in Hesiod they are daughters of Zeus and Themis. Likely a misread or a confusion.

identity.detail: Selene matches the Moon goddess; the epithet 'Titanian goddess' fits her as Hyperion's daughter.
Cyrus in Aeschylus' Persians is Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire. The match is correct. Atossa as his daughter is the historical tradition (Herodotus), so the link is fine.
Glaucus the prophetic sea-god, the Argonauts' Glaucus Pontius, matches; the Scylla lover link is accepted as the same sea-god.
Plutus the god of wealth, son of Demeter and Iasion, matches Hesiod Theogony 969-974.
Porthaon, king of Calydon, father of Alcathous in Pausanias, matches the Wikidata entry.
Acacallis, daughter of Minos and Pasiphae, is the same being the book names; the Elyrus tradition of Phylacides and Philander is one of her accepted traditions.
Hyllus son of Heracles and Deianira, husband of Iole; the Wikidata match is correct. The book's mention of a river Hyllus is a river name, not a separate person.
Minerva matches the Roman Minerva (Athena); 'Tritonian maid' is her epithet (Tritonia), so it is the same being. Jove as her father is correct.
Paris, also called Alexander, son of Priam and Hecuba, is the correct match.
Sky, Heaven and Uranus are the same being. The Wikidata match to Uranus is correct.
Wikidata match is Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus. Thyone is her alternate name after deification, so it is not a different person.

Wikidata Nessus is the centaur killed by Heracles, which is the right being. Wikipedia says he was the son of Centauros, and Theoi lists Ixion and Nephele as his parents. Centauros was the son of Ixion and Nephele in the tradition where Centauros fathered the centaurs, so the two accounts agree in tracing the line to Ixion and Nephele. The parent links are acceptable.

links.reason: Idomeneus is son of Deucalion and thus grandson of Minos; Pausanias' loose phrasing aside, the Iliad and Odyssey make Deucalion his father, and the editor ruled Deucalion's link only for hesiod and odyssey.
Androgeos is the same person as Androgeus, so this duplicates the Androgeus link; the form should be merged rather than kept as a second child.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Minos the king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, fits. The Aeneid's judge of the dead is the same Minos. Wikidata's spouse Crete is odd but not a link here.
Wikidata match is Menelaus king of Sparta, correct.
Wikidata match is the Lemnian queen Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, who bore Euneus and Nebrophonus to Jason; no other names to check.
Astyanax and Scamandrius are the same child of Hector and Andromache, as in Iliad 6.402-403, and the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match Hebe is the cup-bearer goddess, daughter of Zeus and Hera, wife of Heracles; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Nereid Cymothoe, daughter of Nereus and Doris (Hesiod, Theogony; Homer, Iliad 18). No other names.
Euphrosyne is the Charis, daughter of Zeus and Eurynome (Hesiod Theogony 907); the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Hylas, the youth companion of Heracles. The book's sentence names Theiodamas as his father, consistent with Wikidata. No other names are involved.
Lycortas of Megalopolis, Achaean statesman and father of Polybius, matches Pausanias' Lycortas; the link to Polybius is correct.
Theoclymenus is the Argive seer of the Odyssey, son of Polypheides. The only parent link is Polypheides, which the book states and which matches Wikidata, so the flag has nothing to correct.
Molurus, son of Arisbas, killed by Hyettus per the Megalai Ehoiai; the Wikidata match is the same being and the Arisbas link agrees with Wikidata.
The Wikidata match is the Titan Atlas. No other names are given.
Wikidata match is Epaphus, son of Zeus (Jupiter) and Io, king of Egypt; Apis is a known alternative name.

Pausanias names Phormio son of Asopichus, matching the Athenian general (Thucydides calls his father Asopius). The parent link agrees with the book's text and with Wikidata's father, so no fix is needed.
Argus Panoptes is the right match; Ovid's Aristor is a variant of Arestor.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive concubine won in war, not a wife; under the editor's rule that only marriages count as spouse, she is read as a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Ajax the Great (son of Telamon) is correct. Eriboia is the same person as Periboea, so that link is a variant spelling and is fine.
Wikidata match is the Roman god Vertumnus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Hesione was given to Telamon as war prize after Heracles' sack of Troy (Ovid, Metamorphoses); a captive concubine, not a wife, so per editor rule only marriages count as spouse.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Argonaut Telamon, son of Aeacus; no foreign names attached.
Marpessa, daughter of Evenus and wife of Idas, mother of Cleopatra (wife of Meleager), matches the Wikidata entry.
Podaleirius matches Podalirius, son of Asclepius. The alias "Asclepius' son" is only a patronymic epithet, and it fits both Podaleirius and Machaon, but it is not a different person.

Wikidata's Daphnis is the Sicilian herdsman, son of Hermes (Mercury), as in Theocritus and Parthenius. Metamorphoses mentions Daphnis only briefly, so this is the same being. The Hermes link is confirmed, so the parentage flag needs no fix.

links.reason: Harmonia was wife of Cadmus; Ares was only her father (Apollodorus 3.4.2) or lover; editor rule treats non-marriage as lover. Her parentage is stated by the book itself.

Aphrodite is Ares' lover, not sibling; the book says she bedded with Ares. The Iliad calls her daughter of Zeus, but Ares is a son of Zeus and Hera, so a sibling link is only a half-sibling at most and conflicts with the lover link.
Duplicate of Penthesilea under a variant spelling; the same person, so the duplicate node should be merged.

links.link: Ares parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
links.reason: A garbled name label for a son of Ares; it is not a distinct character.
Thestius, father of Leda and Althaea, is son of Ares only in a rare Wikidata line; Apollodorus makes him son of Agenor and Epicaste.

identity.detail: Ares and Mars are treated as the same being, and the Wikidata match is Ares.

links.reason: Ares and Theogone are the parents of Tmolus the mountain god (Ovid, Metamorphoses 11), while Apollodorus's Tmolus is the Lydian king, husband of Omphale; the Wikidata entry merges the two.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match joins two figures: the Lydian king, husband of Omphale (Apollodorus 2.6.3), and the mountain god who judged the contest of Apollo and Pan. Only the king and the Omphale marriage belong to this book; the Ares/Theogone parentage belongs to the mountain god.
Peneus is the Thessalian river god, son of Oceanus and Tethys; the match is correct.
Alcyone the Pleiad, daughter of Atlas, mother of Hyperes and Anthas by Poseidon, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Anius, king of Delos, is son of Apollo and Rhoeo (Diodorus, Ovid); nothing in the Aeneid or Theoi makes Creusa his mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Aeneas' wife Creusa, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, so it is the same being.

links.reason: Ismenis is a daughter of Asopus and Metope; in Pausanias Caanthus is a son of Oceanus and Tethys, and Theoi lists no such child for him.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Caanthus, son of Oceanus and Tethys. Poseidon as father on Wikidata is not supported by Pausanias 9.10.5, which names Oceanus.
Pandia is the daughter of Zeus and Selene (Homeric Hymn to Selene), and the Wikidata match is the same being.
Nemesis (Rhamnousia) matches the goddess; Pausanias gives both Night and Oceanus as parents, each from a different tradition he cites, and all three links are right for this book.

The Wikipedia entry says Misenus names two individuals and describes the friend of Odysseus. The Aeneid's Misenus is the Trojan trumpeter, son of Aeolus, who served Hector and then Aeneas and is buried at Cape Misenum. The Wikidata match may be the Odysseus companion rather than this one.
Perseus the Argive hero, son of Zeus and Danae, is correctly matched; the epithet Gorgon-slayer is his.
Abas, king of Argos, son of Lynceus and Hypermnestra and father of Acrisius and Proetus, matches Wikidata. Metamorphoses 4.607 names him as Acrisius's father.
Wikidata match is the river god Alpheus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Menoitios son of Actor and Aegina is a different tradition from Apollodorus; in Apollodorus (1.9.16, 3.13.8) Menoetius is son of Actor and Aegina, so this is Menoetius the father of Patroclus, and the duplicate entry should be merged or removed.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the nymph Aegina, daughter of Asopus and Metope; no name problem.

links.reason: Janus is a Roman god with no tradition of Hecate as his mother; no ancient source supports this link, which confuses unrelated beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Hecate; no other names to question.
Xanthippus, the Athenian general at Mycale and father of Pericles, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.
The Wikidata match is the Boeotian king Athamas. Minyas as father is a variant genealogy, not a mismatch.
Wikidata's Phialo is the same Arcadian woman, daughter of Alcimedon and mother of Aechmagoras by Heracles. Her parentage matches Wikidata's father Alcimedon, so the flag is not a real conflict.
Eurymachus the Ithacan suitor, son of Polybus, matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.
Wikidata match is the Oceanid Pleione, mother of the Pleiades including Maia; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Theban son of Oedipus; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Ovid (Met. 9) makes Galanthis a servant of Alcmena, with no father named; Tiresias is not her father. Antoninus Liberalis gives Galinthias as daughter of Proetus of Thebes, and the link from Pausanias looks like a mix-up with Tiresias' daughter Manto.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Galanthis is the same being, Alcmena's maid turned into a weasel.
Wikidata match is the king of Tiryns/Mycenae, son of Sthenelus; no other names to question.
Perse (Perseis), Oceanid wife of Helios and mother of Circe and Aeetes, matches Wikidata.

links.reason: Pausanias' Anticlea at Pharae, daughter of Diocles and wife of Machaon, is a different woman from Odysseus' mother Anticlea, daughter of Autolycus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Odysseus' mother, wife of Laertes, which fits the Polygnotus painting passage. The Pharae Anticlea is a separate namesake, and only the Diocles link belongs to her.
Mermerus, son of Jason and Medea, matches Wikidata; no other names to dispute.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace, not Hera's child; Hera only promises her to Hypnos in the Iliad, and Theoi lists no such parentage.

identity.detail: Hera matches the goddess; Juno is her Roman equivalent.
Xuthus, son of Hellen, matches the Wikidata entry. Hesiod's Catalogue of Women gives him sons Achaeus and Ion by Creusa, so the links are consistent.
Wikidata match Chiron the centaur is correct; Chiron is just the Latin spelling of Cheiron.

Syleus, the Lydian vinedigger killed by Heracles, is the right match. Xenodoce as his daughter fits the tradition (Apollodorus 2.6.3). Wikidata's father Poseidon is a recognised tradition, and it is not a link in this book's tree.
Wikidata match is Anaxidamus, the Eurypontid king of Sparta, son of Zeuxidamus (Pausanias 3.7.6). The parent link agrees with Wikidata, so the flag does not point to an error.

links.reason: Hesiod does not make Aidos a child of Prometheus; Aidos (Shame) is a personification with no ancestry here, a misread of the Theoi listing.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus; no other names to question.

links.reason: The Iliad never mentions Alpheus pursuing Artemis; the story is a local Pausanias tale (Alpheus and Arethusa/Artemis Alpheiaia in Elis), a cult legend and not part of Homer's account.

identity.detail: Diana is the Roman name of Artemis, so the match and the alias are the same being.
Lilaea is the Naiad daughter of the river Cephissus, the one Pausanias names as the eponym of the town Lilaea in Phocis. Cephisus and Cephissus are the same river god, so the parent link is right.

links.reason: Athamas is son of Aeolus (Apollodorus, Pausanias); Minyas is not his father. Wikidata likely confuses with Orchomenus/Athamas lore; Pausanias makes Orchomenus his son and says nothing of Athamas as his son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the founder of Orchomenus, Boeotia; no other names to question.

Wikidata match is Atropos, the third Moira. In Hesiod's Theogony (217-219) the Moirai are daughters of Night, so the link Night parent_of Atropos is right for this book. Hesiod also names the Moirai as daughters of Zeus and Themis (904-906), so the Wikidata parents are also supported.
Wikidata match is the Spartan king Menelaus; no other names are listed.
Orestes son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra is the right match; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Hyperion is a Titan; Pausanias does not make him Agamemnon's child. Likely a misread, since Agamemnon's children are Orestes, Iphigenia, Electra, Chrysothemis and others (Hyperion is not among them).
Anaxibia is Agamemnon's sister (daughter of Atreus, wife of Strophius) in Pausanias, not his daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Agamemnon.

Proserpine is the Roman name of Persephone, so the Wikidata match is right. The name 'Preserver' is a stray epithet, though it may be a rendering of Soteira or Sosipolis. It is not a different person.

links.reason: Hesiod (Theogony) and Wikidata make Themis Zeus's second wife; the editor's rule limits marriages to Hera and Juno for Zeus, so this stays a lover link and no change is made.

identity.detail: Themis the Titan goddess matches.

links.reason: Iole's father is Eurytus of Oechalia, the archer. Pindar's Eurytos is the Argonaut son of Hermes, so the link belongs to the other man.
Iphitus is the son of Eurytus of Oechalia (Odyssey, Apollodorus), not of Hermes' son the Argonaut.
Antioche is the wife of Hermes' son Eurytus in Hesiod's tradition and belongs to the Oechalian family or another figure, not to Pindar's Argonaut.
Thalpius son of Eurytus is the Epeian (Actorione) of the Iliad, a different Eurytus.
Pausanias' Eurytus, husband of Theraphone, is the Actorione, not Hermes' son in Pindar.

identity.detail: Pindar's Eurytos is the Argonaut, son of Hermes and brother of Echion, from Pangaios. Wikidata's Eurytus of Oechalia (son of Melaneus, father of Iole and Iphitus) is a different man. The Actorione Eurytus (Thalpius, Theraphone) is a third.

links.reason: Apollodorus (Epitome 1.4) calls Sinis son of Polypemon and Sylea, but this Polypemon is the father of Sinis, not Procrustes; Polypemon is only a name of Procrustes elsewhere (Damastes), so the link confuses two beings.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Procrustes has Polypemon as an alias, but Apollodorus's Polypemon is Sinis's father (husband of Sylea), a different figure; Procrustes is a separate bandit killed by Theseus.

Cyrene the Thessalian huntress, mother of Aristaeus by Apollo, matches Wikidata. Her father is given as Hypseus in Pindar and as Peneus in some traditions, so the parent difference is a variant of the tradition, not a mismatch.
Wikidata match is Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis; no other names to doubt.

links.reason: Amalthea is the nurse of Zeus (a goat or nymph), not a child of Helios; likely a confusion with another figure.
Dirce is a Theban spring-nymph or queen, daughter of Ismenus or Asopus; no source makes her Helios' child.

identity.detail: Helios is the right match for Sun.
Telemus, the Cyclopes' seer, son of Eurymus in Odyssey 9, is the same figure as the Wikidata match. The book's text supports the link to Eurymus.
Wikidata match is Amymone the Danaid, daughter of Danaus; no other names to question.
Polites is Priam and Hecuba's son, killed by Pyrrhus before Priam in Aeneid 2. The Wikidata match is correct and he has no other names.
Wikidata match is Actaeon, son of Aristaeus and Autonoe; no confusion with other beings.

Thersander son of Polynices, one of the Epigoni, matches Wikidata. Pausanias gives his children Tisamenus, Lathria, Anaxandra, and the Haliartus/Coronus pair (Haliartus and Coronus are sons of Thersander, grandson of Sisyphus, in Pausanias 9.34.7). That could be a different Thersander, but I cannot confirm it, so I keep them.
Pheno, daughter of Clytius of Athens and wife of Lamedon, matches Pausanias; no other names to question.
Antenor the Trojan elder, counselor of Priam, husband of Theano, matches Wikidata; no other names to doubt.
Phaethusa is Helios' daughter, guardian of the cattle on Thrinacia. The Wikidata match is correct, and the book's Hyperion is the sun-god Helios under another name.

links.reason: In Statius' Thebaid, Argus is the Argive king, father of Deipyle and Argia (Adrastus's line), not the Argonaut son of Phrixus; the link belongs to the shipbuilder Argus of the Argonautica.
Chalciope's son Argus is the Argonautica figure who sailed with the Argonauts; he is not Statius' Argus, the Argive ancestor.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Argus the Argo-builder, but Statius' Argus is the Argive king/eponym (or the Argive hero), so the match is a namesake; Polybus is also not his father.
Bias, son of Amythaon and brother of Melampus, king of Argos, is the right match. The tree has no other names for him.

links.reason: Adrastus was king of Argos and Polynices' father-in-law, not his son; Pausanias gives Thersander as the son of Polynices and Argia, and Adrastus's descendants are separate.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban son of Oedipus; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Calydonian hero Meleager; the names Meleager and Oeneus' son are the same being.
Wikidata's Cassandra is the Trojan princess and priestess of Apollo, daughter of Priam, who appears in Aeschylus' Agamemnon. No other names are attached to her.

links.reason: Metamorphoses and Homer (Iliad) give Panthous as Euphorbus' father; Alcimachus is unsupported for him and likely a confusion with another figure.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Trojan hero Euphorbus, son of Panthous, who Pythagoras claims to have been in Ovid.

links.reason: Athamas is normally the son of Aeolus (Apollodorus, Theoi); Minyas is a Wikidata confusion. Pausanias does not make Minyas his father.

Schoeneus is usually son of Athamas only in some Boeotian traditions, but more commonly of Athamas via Themisto? Not in Pausanias or Theoi's main listing; Schoeneus is the father of Atalanta in Boeotian accounts, so this is a doubtful link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Boeotian king Athamas; no other names to split.
Thalia the Muse, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne, matches Wikidata; Apollodorus (1.3.1) lists her among the nine Muses.

links.reason: Apollodorus gives Meleager a child only by Atalanta (Parthenopaeus is sometimes so named); Polydora is Pausanias' tradition of a daughter, but Apollodorus (1.8.3) says Meleager married Cleopatra and has Polydora only as Protesilaus' wife in other traditions, so the link is unsupported in this book.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Calydonian hero Meleager; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the centaur Chiron; no other names listed.
Wikidata's Manto, daughter of Tiresias, is the right being.

links.reason: Anchises' father is Capys (Iliad 20.239: Dardanus, Erichthonius, Tros, Assaracus, Capys, Anchises); Dardanus is a remote ancestor, not his father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Anchises, father of Aeneas; no other names.

links.reason: This is Io, daughter of Inachus, confused with the Egyptian goddess Isis. In Pausanias Isis is the Egyptian goddess, though he mentions Io's identification with her in Egypt.
Zeus's lover was Io, not the Egyptian goddess Isis; the other books' link belongs to Io.
Peiren is a father of Io in Hesiod's tradition (Io as Isis), not of the Egyptian goddess.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Egyptian goddess Isis, which suits Pausanias. The Argive Io links came from other books that equated Io with Isis, and they should not attach to her.
Wikidata match is Hyrnetho, daughter of Temenus and wife of Deiphontes; no other names to question.
Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, matches the Wikidata entry. The Theoi listing of Ouranos & Gaia and of Karystos reflects variant traditions, not a different being.
Wikidata match is the Odyssey's maidservant Melantho, daughter of Dolius. Her sister Melantheus is a different person (Melanthius is her brother), but no other names are attached to her here.

links.reason: Leosthenes, the Athenian general of the Lamian War, was the son of an earlier Leosthenes (exiled 362/1 BC), not of any Hippocrates.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Athenian commander of the Lamian War, which fits Pausanias' Leosthenes.
Wikidata match is Eriphyle, wife of Amphiaraus; no other names.
