Eumaeus the swineherd of Odysseus matches Wikidata; the book names his father Ctesius son of Ormenus (Odyssey 15), and no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Penelope, wife of Odysseus; no other names to question.
Pegasus is the winged horse, son of Poseidon and Medusa; the Wikidata match is correct and the alternate name Pegasus Eleutherensis is just a local epithet, not a different being.
Euphemus, son of Poseidon, the Argonaut and ancestor of the Cyrene colonists, matches the Wikidata entry.
Polygonus, Thracian son of Proteus, matches Apollodorus' account of Heracles' wrestling match; no other names to split.
Wikidata's Dionysus is the god, and Bacchus is the same god under another name.

links.reason: Editor ruled Jove as parent of Pasithea wrong everywhere; Pasithea is a Grace in Iliad 14 given to Hypnos, and Hera is not her mother in the tradition (Pausanias gives Aegle).

identity.detail: Juno equals Hera in the Wikidata match; names Hera, Saturn's daughter, and Saturnian Juno all refer to the same goddess.

links.reason: Pausanias' Troilus, son of Alcinous, is a different figure; the Odyssey names Alcinous' sons as Laodamas, Halius and Clytoneus, and no Troilus is among them.
Pausanias' Alcetus, son of Alcinous, is a different figure; the Odyssey names Alcinous' sons as Laodamas, Halius and Clytoneus, and no Alcetus is among them.
The Odyssey's own text says Arete was the daughter of Rhexenor, Alcinous' brother, so she is his niece and wife, not his sister. The Hesiod link is misread.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Phaeacian king Alcinous, so the identity is correct.
Wikidata match is Cassander, king of Macedonia, son of Antipater. All links agree with Pausanias and the historical record. Plistarchus, Cassander's brother, is also attested.
The Wikidata match is the right Cinyras, king of Cyprus.
Wikidata match is Astyanax, son of Hector and Andromache; the book's passage on his being hurled from the towers fits.

links.reason: The quoted sentence only mentions the works of Ares; Harmonia was his lover by Aphrodite's union, not a wife. Per the editor, only listed marriages count, so this is a lover link.

links.link: Ares parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
links.reason: This is a garbled node name from Pausanias; the Melanippus is a different Theban figure, not a clear son of Ares.
Hermes is a son of Zeus and Maia, so a half-brother, not a full sibling; the sibling link is loose but not contradicted, however Statius uses it figuratively.
Aphrodite is Ares' lover, not his sister; the Iliad has Zeus calling Ares hateful, not Aphrodite his sibling.
Penthesileia duplicates Penthesilea, the same Amazon under a variant spelling; merge the two names.

identity.detail: Ares is correctly matched; Enyalius and Mars are accepted equivalents here (Mars the Roman counterpart).

links.link: Eurydice spouse_of Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas
links.reason: Pausanias calls Eurydice, daughter of Antipater, wife of Philip (a different Eurydice from Ptolemy's wife); the Philip link belongs to Philip's Eurydice, the Ptolemy link is right for Antipater's daughter.
Nestor's wife Eurydice in the Odyssey tradition is a different person, not Ptolemy's wife.
Pausanias: this Eurydice, daughter of Lacedaemon, is the wife of Acrisius, not Ptolemy's wife.
Acrisius' wife Eurydice is the daughter of Lacedaemon, a distinct person from Ptolemy's wife.
Orpheus' wife Eurydice is the mythic figure, unrelated to Ptolemy's wife.

identity.detail: The Pausanias name Eurydice covers several people: Ptolemy I's wife (Antipater's daughter, mother of Lysandra), Acrisius' wife (daughter of Lacedaemon), Orpheus' wife, Nestor's wife, and Philip's wife. The Wikidata match to Eurydice of Egypt fits only the Antipater-daughter links.

links.reason: Editor ruled Zeus-Selene links wrong; Selene (Moon) mixed with other Selene/Luna figures.
Editor decision: Zeus parent of Selene is wrong everywhere.
Pandia is tied to Selene; the Zeus-Selene link is ruled wrong, so this one rests on a namesake mix-up.
Pandora was made by Hephaestus; Zeus was not her lover. Hesiod's Pandora daughter of Deucalion is a different being.
A group taken for a person; Nymphs and Naiads are not a single child.
A group taken for a person.
A group node duplicates the individual Muses already listed.
A group node duplicates Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia.
Editor says Sibyl's parents are Lamia or Theodorus (Pausanias), not Zeus.
Editor decision.
Personification without a firm tradition; unsupported.
Unsupported guess for a personification.
Personification, unsupported.
Pallas is a Titan or giant, or an epithet of Athena, not Zeus's child.
Editor: Midas parent of Xanthus only in Hesiod; no Zeus link.
Hermus is a river, not Zeus's son.
Eetion father of Andromache is mortal, no Zeus parentage.
Hesiod makes Eris daughter of Night.
Hecate is daughter of Perses and Asteria.
Nemesis is daughter of Night, or Oceanus in some accounts; not Zeus.
Sisyphus is son of Aeolus.
Macar is son of Aeolus or Helios in tradition.
Apollodorus gives Pelasgus as a son of Zeus and Niobe, so keep it only through that tradition.
Cybele is conflated with Rhea or Ops, who is the mother.

identity.detail: Jove, Jupiter and Zeus are one being. But Jupiter Ammon (father of Iarbas) is a distinct Libyan form, and the Selene link comes from the namesake Selene; Pandora confusion also noted.
Pholus the centaur of Pholoe and Pelion matches; Apollodorus names Silenus and a Melian nymph as his parents, as Theoi confirms.
The Wikidata match is Androgeus, son of Minos and Pasiphaë, and no other names are attached to him.
x

links.reason: Theoi lists Okeanos and Tethys as parents of the Oceanids, but Nephele is not among them. Wikidata's Oceanus link belongs to the Ixion cloud-figure or is an unsupported guess, and this book gives Nephele no parents.

identity.detail: Wikipedia describes two cloud figures called Nephele, one in the Ixion story and one in the Phrixus and Helle story. In this book she is the mother of Phrixus and Helle, so the match is acceptable.
Iolaos is the right match: the Theban hero, nephew and charioteer of Heracles.

links.reason: Callirrhoe and Callirhoe are duplicate spellings of one name, and the daughter of Acheloüs (wife of Alcmaeon) is a different person from the Oceanid Callirhoe; the duplicate link should be merged into one.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the river god Acheloüs; the Wikidata mother Nais is a variant tradition and the names are fine.
Ocnus (Bianor), son of Manto, founder of Mantua, matches the book's Ocnus; Wikidata's two fathers (Auletes, Tiberinus) are a known variant.
Proetus, son of Abas and king of Argos and Tiryns, is the right match.
Wikidata Ino is the Theban princess Leucothea, the right being.

links.reason: Pausanias's sentence is cut off and says Dysponteus was the son of Œnomaus only as a Pisan/Dyspontii tradition; the text is not confirmed here as Œnomaus's own story, and Dysponteus is a founder figure of the Dyspontii. Actually the book states he was 'they state the son' of Œnomaus, so this is a book tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Oenomaus of Pisa is correct; the name Œnomaus is a spelling of Oenomaus.

links.reason: Glaucon is not a son of Eteocles in Apollodorus; Pausanias mentions a Glaucus as son of Sisyphus or Eteocles' line only in a different context, and Apollodorus names Laodamas as Eteocles' son.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban king Eteocles, son of Oedipus.

links.reason: Metamorphoses' Midas is the Phrygian king, son of Gordius and Cybele; Cybele was identified with Rhea but not in Pindar, and the link is not part of Rhea's Olympian family.
Enyalios is usually an epithet of Ares, son of Zeus and Hera; no ancient source makes Rhea his mother.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titaness Rhea; no other names are listed.
Autesion, king of Thebes and son of Tisamenus, is the right match and matches Pausanias.
Ladon the dragon of the Hesperides matches the Wikidata entry. Both parentages (Typhon and Echidna, or Phorcys and Ceto) are attested traditions, so the links are fine.

links.reason: Charillus son of Polydectes is the Spartan king, whose father Polydectes was a Eurypontid king of Sparta, not the Seriphian king.
Eunomus father of the Spartan Polydectes (Pausanias) is a different man; Seriphian Polydectes is son of Magnes (or Peristhenes/Poseidon) and Cerebia.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Seriphian king, correct for Hesiod; the Spartan Polydectes is a separate namesake whose links were imported from Pausanias.
Hyacinth is the right match, the Spartan hero of Amyclae.
The match is the Phocian or Athenian Cephalus, son of Deion and Diomede. Wikidata's father 'Deioneus' is a variant of Deion.

Wikidata match Ion son of Xuthus fits Apollodorus's Ion, son of Xuthus and Creusa. Apollo as father is a variant from Euripides, not a mistake. Helice as wife and Bura as daughter come from Pausanias (Ion's wife Helice, daughter of Selinus, and their daughter Bura) and are right.
Wikidata match is Pentheus, king of Thebes, son of Echion and Agave; no other names, so nothing to fix.
Wikidata match is the Agiad king Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias; Plistoanax is just a spelling variant.
Wikidata's Penthesilea is the Amazon queen who fought for Troy. Mars (Ares) as her father is confirmed by Theoi and Wikidata, so the flagged parent difference is only the missing mother Otrere.
Wikidata match is Aristias, the Phliasian dramatic poet and son of Pratinas, whose tomb Pausanias saw at Phlius; this fits the book's sentence.
The Wikidata match is the hero Perseus, son of Zeus and Danae. No other names are attached.
Wikidata match is Notus, the south wind, son of Astraeus and Eos (Hesiod Theogony 378); no other names to question.
Oeagrus is the Thracian king and father of Orpheus, so the Wikidata match is correct. No other names are attached to him.
Wikidata Acrisius, king of Argos, father of Danaë and son of Abas, is the right match. Eurydice of Argos is his wife per Apollodorus and Pausanias, so the two spouse links are fine.
Wikidata's Labdacus is the Theban king, son of Polydorus and father of Laius. This is the same being as in the book, and he has no other names to question.
Opheltes (Archemorus), son of Lycurgus of Nemea, matches Wikidata. The parent links match Wikidata and Apollodorus, who names Lycurgus and Eurydice.
Aïdoneus is Hades, the Aeschylean form of the name; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Athamas was a son of Aeolus, not of Minyas; the link confuses two figures (Athamas of Boeotia and Minyas of Orchomenus).
This is a group node for Alcithoë and her sisters, not a separate person; the individual daughter links already cover it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the founder of Orchomenus; the Wikidata parentage varies by tradition (Poseidon, Chryses), which is fine. The Orchomenus link is probably the eponymous son or Minyas's own city name, which is plausible.
Asclepius is the right match, and he has no other names to check.
Pontus is the personified Sea, so the Wikidata match is correct. Hesiod's Theogony 132 has Gaia bear him alone, which agrees with the Wikidata mother.

links.reason: Helen and Achilles are joined only in the afterlife tradition on Leuke (Pausanias); no marriage in this book, so it is read as a lover per the editor's rule.
Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros; the book gives no marriage, so per the editor's rule it is a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles; epithets Aeacid, Peleides, Aeacus' son are patronymics of him.

links.reason: Metamorphoses 2 only says Nyctimene defiled her father's bed and never names him; Theoi/Hyginus (Fab. 204) give Epopeus of Lesbos as the father, while Nycteus is Antiope's father in Thebes, so the link confuses two traditions.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Lesbian Nyctimene, daughter of Epopeus, turned into an owl; this is the right being.
Laomedon, Trojan king, son of Ilus, father of Priam, Hesione and Podarces; the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Thespian boy Cleostratus from Pausanias; no other names.
Wikidata's Tisiphone is the Fury of this name; no other names are listed.

Theras, son of Autesion, regent of Sparta and founder of Thera, matches Wikidata. Argonautica mentions him as ancestor of Euphemus' descendants (Theras, son of Autesion, leading Minyan descendants to Calliste), so the identity holds.

links.reason: Hesione as his wife comes from Aeschylus. Hesiod's Catalogue gives Pronoea as the mother of Deucalion, and the Theogony names no wife for Prometheus.
Aetnaeus comes from a Pausanias local tradition (Sicilian Aetna), not from Hesiod, and the Hesiod text does not support it.
Aidos as a child of Prometheus is a late or obscure tradition. Hesiod does not say so, and in his poems Aidos is not Prometheus's child.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus. No other names are involved.
Iarbas is the Libyan king, son of Jupiter Ammon and a Garamantian nymph in Virgil (Aeneid 4.198-199). The Wikidata match is correct, and Jove as father agrees with Wikidata's Zeus Ammon.

Poeas, king of Meliboea and father of Philoctetes, is the right being. Apollodorus names him as Philoctetes' father, and Wikidata's father Thaumacus and spouses Methone and Demonassa are consistent with the tradition.

Persephone matches the Wikidata entry. Proserpina is her Roman name. The Styx mother listed by Wikidata and Theoi is a rare variant, but the book follows Demeter, and no link for Styx appears in the tree.

links.reason: Pausanias' Chthonia, sister of Clymenus son of Phoroneus at Hermione, is a different person; the cult title Chthonia was merged into Demeter, so the sibling link is wrong.

identity.detail: The name Chthonia is shared with Chthonia, sister of Clymenus at Hermione, who is a separate mortal. It should be split from Demeter. The Wikidata match to Demeter is correct.

links.reason: Procris, wife of Cephalus, is not Arcesius's mother in the tradition. Ovid's Ulysses names only Jupiter as Arcesius's father, and in Ovid Procris's marriage to Cephalus is childless. The Wikidata mother is a confusion with another Cephalus line.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Ithacan king Arcesius, father of Laertes. No other names are attached.
Wikidata match is Ascalaphus son of Acheron, the one in Ovid's Metamorphoses who saw Proserpina eat the pomegranate seed. The Iliad's Ascalaphus, son of Ares, is a different person.
Wikidata match is the Euboean prince Palamedes, son of Nauplius. The book names Clymene as his mother, and Wikidata lists Clymene too (plus Hesione as a variant), so nothing needs fixing.
Marathon, son of Epopeus and father of Sicyon and Corinthus, is the Sicyonian/Corinthian figure in Pausanias; the Wikidata match is acceptable.
Wikidata match is Io, the Argive princess loved by Zeus; the spouse entry is only a minor record and no other names are involved.

links.reason: Athamas is the son of Aeolus (Apollodorus, Hesiod); Minyas is confused with him, though Minyas is a different figure, an Orchomenian king, and not Athamas's father.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Boeotian king Athamas, husband of Ino and father of Learchus and Melicerta (Palaemon). No names need splitting.
The Wikidata match is Persephone, daughter of Zeus and Demeter and wife of Hades. The alternate parentage from Zeus and Styx is a rarer tradition and does not change the identity.

links.reason: Scylla the monster is not Triton's daughter in the Aeneid; the Argonautica link doesn't carry over to this book's Triton, and Theoi's confirmation rests on a rare variant.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Triton, son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, is the sea god of the Aeneid. Neptune is the Roman name for Poseidon, so the parent link is right and the flag is only a naming difference.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, is the Trojan priestess; the match is correct.

links.reason: Tecmessa was a captive concubine won in war, not a wife; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.

identity.detail: Ajax the Great (son of Telamon) is the correct match; Eriboia is just another spelling of Periboea, so that link is right.
Vulcan matches Hephaestus and Mulciber, all the same god.
Wikidata match is Mnemosyne the Titaness; no problem with the name Memory. Wikidata's parent Zeus is wrong per the editor, and mother Clymene is a dubious mix-up.
Wikidata's Charon is the ferryman of the underworld. Pausanias's Charon is the same being, so the match is right. The Night link is supported by Theoi (Erebos and Nyx), and Wikidata agrees.

links.reason: Apollodorus (Library 2.5.4) calls Pholus the son of Silenus and a Melian nymph, but he is a centaur. Theoi lists this as a variant, though the link confuses the centaur Pholus with a satyr family; in Ovid's Metamorphoses Pholus is a centaur with no tie to Silenus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the same Silenus, the tutor of Dionysus; no other names to separate.
Wikidata match is the Cretan princess Ariadne, daughter of Minos; no other names listed.

Chloris, the Minyan daughter of Amphion and Niobe and wife of Neleus, is the right match. Wikidata's father Amphion agrees with the links brought from Pausanias. Apollodorus also names her as mother of Nestor, Pero and Periclymenus.
Wikidata match is Ariadne, daughter of Minos; no other names.

links.reason: The quoted sentence is about Eurytus son of Actor and Molione, one of the Moliones, not Eurytus of Oechalia, who is the father of Iole and Iphitus.
Pausanias' Theraphone, mother of Thalpius, belongs to the Eurytus son of Actor (Molione's line), not to Eurytus of Oechalia.
Thalpius is the son of Eurytus son of Actor, one of the Moliones, not of Eurytus of Oechalia.
Hesiod's Antioche is the wife of Eurytus of Oechalia, but the tradition is unclear. Given the namesake confusion and the editor's rule, the spouse link is unsupported in this book.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Eurytus of Oechalia, which is correct. The Actor parent link and the Thalpius/Theraphone links come from the other Eurytus, son of Actor, and need separating.
Wikidata match is the horse Arion; no other names to question.

links.reason: Leocritus is the son of Arisbas in the Odyssey and Iliad (Leocritus son of Euenor is a suitor in the Odyssey); Pausanias does not make him Polydamas's son, and the link seems to confuse namesakes.

identity.detail: Polydamas, son of Panthous and friend of Hector, matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata match is Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus (Bacchus/Liber); no other names to question.
Proetus, son of Abas and king of Argos and Tiryns, is correctly matched. Antea and Stheneboea are two names for the same wife, not two different women.
Tragasus/Cragasus is the same figure, father of Philonome, Cycnus's second wife (Pausanias 10.14.2); the link is correct.

Wikidata's Zephyrus is the West Wind, son of Astraeus and Eos (Aurora), which matches Ovid's Zephyrus. The flag on the parents is only because Theoi also lists Gaia (Aeschylus), a variant. The tree's links are fine.
Iliad 18 names Charis as the wife of Hephaestus (Vulcan), and the Wikidata match fits. The link is right, so nothing needs fixing.

The Muses, the group of goddesses, match Wikidata's Muse. Zeus and Mnemosyne are the standard parents (Hesiod, Homeric Hymns), and the other Theoi parentage listings are variants that don't conflict with them.
Chalciope, daughter of Aeetes and wife of Phrixus, matches Wikidata. Her alternate names Iophossa and Euenia are ancient variants for the same woman.

Evander of Pallene is a different figure, a son of Priam or an Evander of Pallene tied to a different tradition. The Aeneid's Evander is the Arcadian founder of Pallantium, son of Carmentis, so the match should be the Arcadian Evander of Rome.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony (116) has Chaos come into being first, with no parent; the Orphic Chronos (time) is a different figure from the Titan Cronus and is not Chaos's father in Hesiod.

identity.detail: Chronos the personification of time is a valid match. Hesiod himself does not mention this figure; it is easily confused with the Titan Cronus.
Ialmenus, son of Ares and Astyoche, twin of Ascalaphus, leader of the Orchomenians, matches the Iliad passage. Wikidata's extra mother Pernis is a variant tradition, not an error in the book's link.

Proserpina is the Roman name for Persephone, so the match is the right being and the two names are the same goddess. In the Odyssey she is queen of the dead, wife of Hades (Pluto). Hades as spouse, Jove (Zeus) as father and Ceres (Demeter) as mother are all standard.

links.reason: In the Iliad, Boreas sired the horses with the mares of Erichthonius, the Trojan king, son of Dardanus. That is not the Athenian Erichthonius, and Boreas was not his lover.

Apollodorus 3.12.2 gives the Trojan Erichthonius, son of Dardanus, who fathered Tros. The Athenian Erichthonius, son of Hephaestus, is a different being. Dardanus, Tros and Astyoche belong to the Trojan one.
Tros is the son of the Trojan Erichthonius (Apollodorus 3.12.2), not of the Athenian king.

identity.detail: Two Erichthoniuses are joined: the Athenian, born of Hephaestus and the earth (Apollodorus 3.14.6), and the Trojan, son of Dardanus and father of Tros. The Wikidata match is the Athenian king. The Trojan links (Dardanus, Tros, Astyoche, and Boreas with the mares) belong to the Trojan one.
The Wikidata match is Priam, king of Troy, son of Laomedon. Every link is a known child or spouse of Priam; Kassandra and Cassandra are one daughter written two ways.
Libya, daughter of Epaphus and Memphis, matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.
Endeis, wife of Aeacus and mother of Peleus and Telamon, matches Wikidata. Pausanias follows the Sciron-daughter tradition, which Wikidata also lists.
Wikidata match is the war-goddess Enyo, associated with Ares; no other names given.

The Odyssey's Deucalion is the Cretan son of Minos and father of Idomeneus (Od. 19.180), not the flood hero son of Prometheus. The Wikidata match is the flood Deucalion, so the Prometheus, Pyrrha, Hellen, Molus, Amphictyon and Orestheus links belong to that namesake and should be removed.

links.reason: Perses the Titan is son of Crius and Eurybia. Helios's son Perses (brother of Aeetes) is a different figure with the same name.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Titan Perses, father of Hecate by Asteria, so it is the right being.

links.reason: Anchises was son of Capys and grandson of Assaracus, not of Dardanus; the line runs Dardanus, Erichthonius, Tros, Assaracus, Capys, Anchises. Hesiod does not make Dardanus his father.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the founder Dardanus, son of Zeus and Electra.
Hyllus, son of Heracles and Deianira, husband of Iole, matches Wikidata. The flag about parents is likely because the book does not name Deianira as his mother, and the Hercules link is correct.
Wikidata match is the goddess Circe; 'Ææan Circe' is just an epithet (Aeaean).

links.reason: Pausanias says Araethyrea was Phlias's mother and not Chthonophyle, who was his wife.

identity.detail: Phlias (Phlius), son of Dionysus and husband of Chthonophyle, is the right being. Androdamas and Andromedas appear to be the same son under two spellings in the text.
Phaeno is an Oceanid, daughter of Oceanus; the Wikidata match fits and no other names are listed.

Attes is Attis, the Phrygian consort of Cybele; the match is right. Pausanias 7.17.8-12 gives two traditions, Calaus as father (Hermesianax) and the Sangarius/Nana story, and the editor has accepted both.

links.reason: The editor's rule is that only marriages count as spouse. Callidice is a Thesprotian queen whom the Telegony summary says he married, but the flagged spouse link is treated as a lover, not a wife, since Penelope is the wife.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the right Odysseus.
Styx the goddess and river matches Wikidata; no other names are involved.
Hestia matches the Wikidata entry; Vesta is her Roman counterpart, an acceptable alias.

links.reason: This Phoebe is the Messenian daughter of Leucippus; Earth (Gaia) is the mother of the Titaness Phoebe, who is a different being. Pausanias' link belongs to the Titan.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Messenian princess Phoebe, daughter of Leucippus and wife of Pollux, is the right match.
Wikidata match is Philyra the Oceanid, mother of Cheiron by Cronos; no other names to dispute.
Poltys, king of Aenus and brother of Sarpedon, son of Poseidon, is correctly matched.
Wikidata match is the seer Amphiaraus, son of Oicles; no other names to question.

Melampus the seer, son of Amythaon, brother of Bias; the Wikidata match is correct. Antiphates and Mantius are his descendants in the Odyssey (Antiphates, Mantius) and Pausanias, so those links stand.

links.reason: Opheltes (Archemorus) is the son of Lycurgus of Nemea, king of Nemea, not the Thracian Lycurgus of Iliad 6.
Iasus is a child of Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus; Apollodorus's Arcadian Lycurgus is not the Thracian king.
Amphidamas is a son of Arcadian Lycurgus, son of Aleus, so belongs to the other Lycurgus.

identity.detail: Lycurgus of Thrace matches Iliad 6 (son of Dryas, who opposed Dionysus). Other Lycurguses (Arcadian, Nemean) are separate, and only their children were wrongly attached here.

Echestratus is the Agiad king of Sparta, son of Agis I, and father of Labotas. The book's 'Agis, son of Eurysthenes' is Agis I, so the parent link matches Wikidata and the flag is not a real conflict.

links.reason: Pausanias names a different Thrasybulus, the Elean seer of the Iamidae, son of Æneas; the Athenian general is the son of Lycus.
Agathinus, son of Thrasybulus, is honored by the Achaeans of Pellene, so he is not the Athenian general's son and most likely belongs to another Thrasybulus.

identity.detail: The book has at least two men named Thrasybulus: the Athenian general (son of Lycus, matching Wikidata) and the Elean seer (son of Æneas). Agathinus's father is likely a third man from Pellene or the seer, not the general. Keep the Wikidata match for the Athenian only.

Idmon the Argonaut seer matches Wikidata's Idmon. Apollodorus (1.9.23) calls him a son of Apollo (and Asteria or Cyrene), with Abas as his mortal father in another tradition, so the Apollo link is right.

links.reason: Hesiod makes Theia the wife of Hyperion and sister of Oceanus; she is not his wife, and Tethys is his only marriage.
The Xanthus of the Trojan river is a river god and a son of Oceanus, but the Xanthus linked in other books is the horse or the Lycian figure; this link confuses namesakes.
Hesione the Oceanid wife of Prometheus is in Aeschylus, but Hesione daughter of Laomedon is the other Hesione; the link takes the wrong one.
Passalus was one of the Cercopes, not a child of Oceanus; the link is unsupported.

identity.detail: Oceanus matches the Titan correctly.

links.reason: Apollodorus 3.3.1 names a different Deucalion, son of Minos and father of Idomeneus, Crete and Molus, not the son of Prometheus.
Apollodorus 3.3.1 gives Molus to Deucalion son of Minos, not the flood hero.

identity.detail: The tree joins two Deucalions: the son of Prometheus (husband of Pyrrha) and the son of Minos (3.3.1). Idomeneus and Molus belong to the Minos one. The Wikidata match fits the son of Prometheus.
Wikidata match is the right Andromache, wife of Hector.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemos to Achilles on Skyros, but no source calls this a marriage; under the editor's rule it is a lover link.
The union with Helen on Leuke is an afterlife tradition (Pausanias) and not a marriage, so it is read as a lover link under the editor's rule.

links.link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, is the later historical king and not the son of Achilles. Pyrrhus is the mythical son's other name, Neoptolemos, which is already linked, so this is a duplicate.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis.
Sthenelus, son of Perseus and king of Mycenae, father of Eurystheus, is the right being. The Iliad passage (19.114-119) confirms this.

links.reason: Apollodorus (Epitome 3.25) says Achilles had a union with Deidamia on Scyros and she bore Pyrrhus; no marriage is told, and under the editor's rule a non-marriage is a lover link.

identity.detail: Deidamia, daughter of Lycomedes, mother of Pyrrhus/Neoptolemus, matches the Wikidata entry.
Dioscuri match Castor and Pollux; Leda as mother is confirmed by Theoi, and no other names are listed.

links.reason: Pausanias' Pisus (founder of Pisa in Elis) is not a son of Messenian Perieres in the usual tradition; Hesiod's Perieres has Aphareus and Leucippus, so this looks like a confusion.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Messenian king Perieres, son of Aeolus; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus and Clymene, wife of Aeson and mother of Jason, is the same person the Argonautica names.

Tityus matches Tityos, the giant punished in the underworld for assaulting Leto. Both Earth and Jupiter as parents are attested traditions (Gaia in Homer and Virgil; Zeus and Elara in Apollodorus), so both links are fine.
Wikidata match is Medusa the Gorgon; 'Gorgon' is an epithet for her, not a different being.

links.reason: The book's line (Catalogue of Ships-like passage) names Eurypylus as son of Mecisteus, so the link is stated by the book; but it is actually a mix-up: Euryalus is the son of Mecisteus, and the book's sentence gives Eurypylus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Mecisteus, son of Talaus and Lysimache; no issue.

Aletes, son of Hippotas (Hippotes) and descendant of Heracles, is the Dorian conqueror of Corinth; the Wikidata match is correct. The parent flag is only a spelling difference (Hippotas/Hippotes), and the book's sentence confirms the link.

links.reason: Hesiod makes Aegle a woman Theseus loved (he abandoned Ariadne for her); no marriage is attested.
Theseus abducted the child Helen, but she was never his wife; she was rescued by the Dioscuri and later married Menelaus.
Hippolyta/Antiope the Amazon is Theseus' captive partner and mother of Hippolytus; Statius treats her as wife, but only marriages count and the same figure is Antiope.
The book spells Demophon as Demophoon; this duplicates the Demophon link, so one person has two entries.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Theseus; no other names are listed.
Anaxander is the Agiad king of Sparta, son of Eurycrates, and the Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Gorgon Medusa; no other names are listed.
Wikidata match is Lagus of Eordaia, the father (putative) of Ptolemy I, as Pausanias says.

links.reason: Endeis is the daughter of Chiron (or Sciron) and Chariclo, wife of Aeacus; Thetis is a Nereid, daughter of Nereus and Doris, and was Peleus' wife, so she is no sibling of Endeis.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Endeïs, wife of Aeacus and mother of Peleus and Telamon, is the same being.
Wikidata's Eurysaces, son of Ajax the Great and Tecmessa, is the same being Pausanias names; both links are supported by his text.
Wikidata's Chione is Daedalion's daughter, who is also called Philonis. She bore Autolycus to Hermes and Philammon to Apollo. The Daedalion link matches Wikidata, so the flag is not a real conflict.
Heliades are the daughters of Helios (the Sun) and Clymene, mourners of Phaethon in Ovid; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, is a tradition from the Telegony (Odysseus's marriage to her after his wanderings); she is not his wife in Pausanias, and under the editor's rule any non-marriage spouse link is read as a lover.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Odysseus himself; no other names are involved.
Parthenopaeus the Arcadian, one of the Seven against Thebes, is the right match.
Wikidata match Leto is the Titan daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, mother of Apollo and Artemis; no other names to doubt.
Palamedes is the Euboean son of Nauplius, and the Wikidata match is correct. The only link listed, Nauplius as father, is right, so no changes are needed.

links.reason: Editor's rule reads any spouse link other than the listed marriages as a lover; Pausanias says Boreas 'married' her, but the editor's decision is final, so it is recorded as a lover link.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian princess Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Hermione is a variant name for Harmonia (Ovid sometimes), so this duplicates the Harmonia marriage; or confuses Menelaus' daughter Hermione with Harmonia. Cadmus's only wife is Harmonia.
Pausanias' Electra is a Theban gate-name/Atlas's daughter Electra, mother of Harmonia/Iasion in some accounts, not Agenor's child; Cadmus's sister is Europa.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban founder Cadmus; no other names to question.
Gryllus is Xenophon's son, who fought at Mantinea; the Wikidata match fits Pausanias' text.
Wikidata match is Epaminondas the Theban general, son of Polymnis, as Pausanias says; no other names to question.
Wikidata's Tiresias is the Theban seer, son of Everes and Chariclo; no other names are given.

Neoptolemus, son of Achilles and Deidamia, is correctly matched. Hermione is his wife in tradition (Pausanias, Euripides' Andromache), and Andromache was his concubine/captive, so the existing links are fine.

Wikidata's Tithonus is the right being, son of Laomedon and lover of Eos, and he has no other names listed. Cephalus appears in Wikidata as a father, which is a variant of the Eos tradition (Eos's son Phaethon by Cephalus), not Tithonus's parentage. It is not a link in this book's tree.
Triton matches the sea god, son of Poseidon and Amphitrite (Hesiod, Theogony 930-933). No other names are attached.

Rhea and Ops are conflated in Roman tradition, and Wikidata's parents Caelus and Terra are the Roman counterparts of Uranus and Gaia. Rhea is the mother of Juno and Neptune by Saturn (Cronus), so the match is acceptable.

links.reason: Vesta's mother is Ops (Rhea), Saturn's wife. Cybele is a distinct Phrygian goddess, though sometimes syncretized with Ops/Rhea; Metamorphoses does not make her Vesta's mother.

identity.detail: Vesta matches the Roman hearth goddess, the counterpart of Greek Hestia; no other names to question.

links.reason: Passalus is one of the Cercopes; in Hesiod's tradition and elsewhere he is not a child of Theia, so this link was misattached from another book.
Theia's husband is Hyperion (Hesiod, Theogony); Oceanus is the husband of Tethys, so this confuses the two Titan sisters.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titaness Theia; Euruphaessa is her own epithet, so no change is needed.
Wikidata's Eurypon is the Spartan king, son of Soos (Sous), matching Pausanias; the flag on parents is only a spelling difference (Sous/Soos).

links.reason: Epicasta as Nestor's daughter appears only in Hesiod's tradition (mother of Homer), which the editor limits to Hesiod; Pausanias does not tell it.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Nestor of Pylos, son of Neleus; no other names to dispute.
Pausanias 10.11.3 calls him Antiochus the Syracusan, son of Xenophanes, which matches the historian Antiochus of Syracuse. The Xenophanes parent link is right and needs no fix.
Amarynceus, the Elean chief and father of Diores (Iliad 2.622), matches the Wikidata entry. Wikidata's father Pyttius or Alector is a known genealogy variant and does not conflict with the link.

aeschylus/apollo.name: Apollo
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Loxias, Phoebus, Apollo

links.reason: Selene (Moon) is not Apollo's sister; Artemis is. The editor rules Selene links wrong; Ovid's Diana/Moon identification is not a sibling link for Selene.
Scylla is usually the daughter of Phorcys or Crataeis; the Apollo parentage rests on a rare Hesiodic fragment and is unsupported by Theoi.
Hilaeira was a daughter of Leucippus, not Apollo; this confuses her with a namesake.
Hymenaeus is more usually a son of Apollo, not a lover; the lover link is unsupported.
Ileus (Locrian Oileus) is not a known lover of Apollo; the fragment is dubious.

identity.detail: Apollo, Loxias and Phoebus are all the same god, so the multiple Wikidata match is acceptable. Spouse entries such as Urania and Amphissa are lovers, not marriages.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; no other names to question.

Hippomedon is the Argive, one of the Seven against Thebes; the Wikidata match is the same being. In Apollodorus (1.9.13, 3.6.3) he is a son of Talaus' line or of Aristomachus, both traditions attested, so the Talaus link is not contradicted.

links.reason: This is Cleopatra I of Egypt, mother of Ptolemy Philometor, not Idas' daughter, the wife of Meleager.

links.link: Cleopatra parent_of Alexander, son of Cleopatra
links.reason: This is the Ptolemaic queen Cleopatra, mother of Alexander (Ptolemy X), not the mythic Cleopatra.

links.link: Philip of Macedon, son of Amyntas parent_of Cleopatra
links.reason: Pausanias' Cleopatra daughter of Philip II is the historical Macedonian princess, sister of Alexander the Great, not Meleager's wife.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the mythic Cleopatra (Idas' daughter, wife of Meleager). The tree also merges the Macedonian princess Cleopatra (daughter of Philip) and the Ptolemaic queen Cleopatra (mother of Ptolemy Philometor and Alexander) under this name; they should be separate people.
Wikidata match is the hound of Hades; Typhon and Echidna are his standard parents (Hesiod Theogony 306-312), so all links are fine.
Talaus son of Bias and Pero, Argonaut and king of Argos, matches Wikidata. Adrastus is his well-attested son.

links.reason: Pausanias' Pandion is the Athenian king; Oeneus the Calydonian is son of Porthaon, as the Hesiod fragment says. Likely a namesake confusion with Oeneus son of Pandion of Athens.
Mothone is the daughter of the Athenian Oeneus in Pausanias, not the Calydonian Oeneus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Calydonian king Oeneus. The Athenian Oeneus, son of Pandion, is a different person and must stay apart.
Parthenopeus is Parthenopaeus, the Arcadian son of Atalanta who fought among the Seven against Thebes. No other names are listed.
Polybotes the Giant who fought Poseidon is the right match; no other names are listed. Pausanias 1.2.4 tells the story of Polybotes under Nisyros, which fits this being.
Wikidata match is Procris, daughter of Erechtheus, the same person Pausanias names.

Wikidata's Aetolus is the son of Endymion who slew Apis and fled to the Curetes; Apollodorus 1.7.6 agrees. The mother Selene on Wikidata is a variant tradition (Endymion's lover), but it is not a wrong match.
Wikidata match is Aegimius, the Dorian ancestor and king. Dorus as his father and Dymas and Pamphylus as his sons agree with the tradition (Apollodorus 2.8.3, Pindar), so nothing needs fixing.

links.reason: Pausanias (9.5.10-11) follows the Oedipodea: Euryganeia, daughter of Hyperphas, was Oedipus's wife and mother of his four children. Wikidata lists her as a spouse, so lover is wrong.
This is a group node that duplicates the individual sons Polynices and Eteocles, who are already linked.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Theban king Oedipus, and the alternate spelling Œdipus is the same being.
Wikidata's Hera is the Olympian queen, sister and wife of Zeus. Juno is her Roman counterpart, so that alias is fine.
Arion is the divine horse, and the Wikidata match is correct. The Areion spelling is the same horse.

links.reason: Charillus is the Spartan king of Pausanias, son of Polydectes of Sparta (Eunomid line), not the Seriphian king of Metamorphoses.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Seriphian king; the Spartan Polydectes is a separate person, only relevant to the Charillus link.
Wikidata's Atossa is the Achaemenid queen, daughter of Cyrus, wife of Darius and mother of Xerxes, which matches Aeschylus' Persians. 'Queen Mother' is her title in the play, not a different person.
The Wikidata match is the right Amphitryon, son of Alcaeus, and he has no other names.

links.link: Dexamenus parent_of Eurypylus, son of Euaemon
links.reason: Pausanias says some writers claim the chest went to a different Eurypylus, son of Dexamenus and king at Olenus, who came with Heracles. The Thessalian Eurypylus is son of Euaemon, so this link belongs to the Olenus namesake.

identity.detail: The match to the Thessalian king Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, is correct. Wikidata's father Evaemon is the same as Euaemon, so the parent flag is only a spelling difference.
Dercetis is the nymph who in Statius's Thebaid bore Alatreus to Lapithaon; the Wikidata match is the same nymph (Derceto/Atargatis is a separate, related figure but no confusion is shown here).

links.link: Thetis parent_of Phocus, son of Æacus
links.reason: Phocus son of Aeacus was born to Psamathe, a different Nereid, not Thetis; Thetis's son is Achilles by Peleus.
Endeis was the daughter of Chiron and wife of Aeacus, mother of Peleus; she is not Thetis's sister, since Thetis's parents are Nereus and Doris.

identity.detail: Thetis the Nereid matches. The Wikidata spouse Neptune is a faulty extra; Peleus is her husband.

Wikidata match is the Argive Hippomedon, one of the Seven against Thebes. No other names are listed. The parentage is a variant between Aristomachus (son of Talaus) and Talaus himself (Apollodorus gives him as son of Talaus's line, Statius calls him Argive/Lernaean), so keep.
Wikidata match is Orpheus, the Thracian bard and Argonaut. The alias 'Oeagrus' son' is only a patronymic for the same person.

links.reason: Aidos (Shame) is not a child of Prometheus in Hesiod or Theoi's listing; the link is a misreading, so it is unsupported in this tree.
Pausanias's Aetnaeus is a Sicilian epithet or cult figure linked to Zeus and Hephaestus, not a son of Prometheus; the link is an unsupported guess.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Prometheus, and no other names are given.
Wikidata match is Hecuba, queen of Troy and wife of Priam. No other names are attached.
Echemus is the Tegean king of Arcadia, son of Aeropus, who killed Hyllus. The Wikidata match is correct.
Deiphobus, son of Priam, who married Helen after Paris died, is the right match. No other names are in play.
Omphale of Lydia, daughter of Iardanes and widow of Tmolus, matches Wikidata; the book's parentage agrees with Wikidata's father Iardanus, so the flag is not a real conflict.
Wikidata's Hellen is the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha and the eponym of the Hellenes, which matches the book's Hellen.
Ceyx of Trachis, king and husband of Alcyone, is the right match. The Hesiodic passage names him as the father of Themistinoe, and nothing suggests the name covers another person.
Wikidata Aeëtes is the Colchian king, son of Helios, father of Medea; the name Aeetes is the same being.
Admete the Oceanid in Hesiod's Theogony (line 349) is the Wikidata Admete, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys. No other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Rhodos, the nymph of Rhodes and wife of Helios; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the centaur Cheiron, son of Cronos and Philyra; the name Chiron is just a spelling variant.

links.reason: Clytius is a son of Alcmaeon only in Pausanias' tradition (via Alphesiboea/Arsinoe); Apollodorus never says this, but this is unsupported in this book, so merely unconfirmed, not contradicted.... treated as keep-level.
Duplicate of Callirrhoe, daughter of Achelous, spelled differently; the Callirrhoe link already covers her.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Epigonus Alcmaeon, son of Amphiaraus; no other names to question.

links.reason: Atlas is father of a different Hesperus (the Hesperid-related, Atlantid Hesperus/Hesperis tradition); Argonautica's Hesperus is Eos's son, and the editor ruled Atlas parent of Lucifer wrong everywhere.
Aegle the Hesperid is daughter of Hesperus son of Atlas (or Nyx/Erebus), a different Hesperus from the Evening Star son of Eos.
Ovid's Metamorphoses makes Ceyx son of Lucifer (the Morning Star), not Hesperus the Evening Star; the editor's rule on Lucifer shows the confusion.

identity.detail: Hesperus son of Eos (Evening Star) is conflated with Hesperus son of Atlas, father of the Hesperides; and Hespere, a Hesperid nymph, is a different being. Wikidata match itself is fine.

links.reason: Neptune's mother is Rhea/Ops; Cybele is a conflation, and no source in the book supports her as his mother.
Duplicate of Ancaeus spelled differently; it is the same person, so the duplicate should be merged, not kept.
Nireus is the son of Charopus and Aglaia, not Poseidon, in the Iliad.
Eryx is son of Aphrodite and Butes (or Poseidon in some versions); the Neptune link is unsupported here.
The Doliones are a people, a group taken for a person.
The Moliones are a pair of brothers treated as one person; they are sons of Molione, and Poseidon is claimed as their father in some accounts. Not a single person.
Kleatos is a Molione brother, not a distinct child of Poseidon; the link duplicates the Moliones.
Despoina is a cult title of Persephone, taken for a person; Pausanias says Demeter bore her to Poseidon.

identity.detail: Neptune matches Poseidon; the identification is the standard Roman equivalence.
Wikidata match is the right Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and mother of Dionysus. Her alternate name Thyone belongs to her after her ascent, so it is not a separate being.

links.reason: In Aeschylus' Persians, Darius is the husband of Atossa and father of Xerxes, so the link is reversed. Wikidata's Xerxes I as father belongs to Darius, the crown prince, a different person.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the crown prince Darius, son of Xerxes I and Amestris. The book's Darius is Darius I the Great, husband of Atossa and father of Xerxes. The name 'Darian' is only a variant spelling.
Athena is correctly matched; Minerva, Pallas, and the Tritonian/Itonian epithets are all Athena (Pallas here is the goddess, not the Titan or giant).
Cassandra, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, Trojan prophetess; the match is correct.

links.reason: Theseus abducted Helen as a girl (Pausanias) but the union was not a marriage; the editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.
The Achilles and Helen union on the White Island is a late tale of an afterlife pairing (Pausanias), not a marriage.
Paris carried Helen off while she was still Menelaus' wife, so the Iliad treats her as his lover, not a lawful wife.

identity.detail: Helen of Troy matches this Helen.
The Wikidata match is the Titan Tethys, wife of Oceanus. No other names are in play.

Wikidata's Tros is the Trojan king, son of Erichthonius, father of Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymede, as Iliad 20 says. The flag about parents differing from Wikidata does not apply: the book names Erichthonius, matching Wikidata's father. Astyoche is not named in the book, which is no contradiction.
Wikidata match is Eteocles, son of Oedipus and king of Thebes; epithets (Agenorean chieftain, Echionian monarch/prince) are Theban titles for the same man.
Wikidata's Phryne is the Thespian hetaira (born Mnesarete) whom Pausanias mentions. The lover link to Praxiteles is correct and matches the book's text.

links.reason: Arcesius is the father of Laertes, son of Zeus or Cephalus in some accounts; Procris is not his mother. Ancient sources (Ovid, Apollodorus) have Procris childless, and Cephalus is sometimes named as Arcesius' father by Hyginus, not Procris.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Athenian Procris, daughter of Erechtheus and wife of Cephalus. Erectheus and Erechtheus are spelling variants of the same father.

links.reason: Pasithea is the wife of Hypnos (Sleep) in Iliad 14 (Hera promises her to him) and in Wikipedia and Wikidata; she was not merely a lover.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Charis Pasithea, wife of Hypnos; no other names are involved.
Wikidata match is Antilochus, son of Nestor, prince of Pylos. The Iliad's Antilochus is the same being, and there are no other names.

links.reason: Pausanias says Phlias was Chthonophyle's husband, not her son; his mother was Aræthyrea.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the daughter of Sicyon, so it is the same being.
Wikidata match is the Calydonian hero Meleager, son of Oeneus and Althaea. Ares as an alternative father is a variant tradition, not a confusion.

links.reason: In the Odyssey, Orsilochus son of Idomeneus is a Cretan whom Odysseus claims to have killed. That is a different figure from this tree's Idomeneus, and the Hesiod text names no son for him.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Cretan king Idomeneus, son of Deucalion and grandson of Minos, and this fits the Hesiod passage.

links.reason: In the Argonautica Poseidon's son is Triton (the Libyan god who speaks of 'my sire Poseidon'), not Phorcys, who is a son of Pontus and Gaia.
Pausanias makes Tritea the daughter of Triton (the sea god), so it belongs to Triton, not Phorcys.

identity.detail: Phorcys and Triton are two different beings merged under one name. Phorcys, father of Scylla, is the old sea god; Triton is Poseidon's son. The Wikidata match to Triton fits only the Triton part.

links.reason: Aegle was a lover for whom Theseus abandoned Ariadne (Hesiod via Plutarch), not a wife.
Duplicate spelling of Demophon, son of Theseus; the fall-of-troy spelling is the same person and should be merged with Demophon.
Theseus abducted the child Helen but did not marry her; she was rescued by the Dioscuri.
Hippolyta is the Amazon queen, a consort and not a wedded wife in the editor's rule; same figure as Antiope in some accounts.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias mentions Iphigenia as daughter of Theseus and Helen by one tradition, but she is not Agamemnon's Iphigenia; keep separate from the famous Iphigenia.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
links.reason: Melanippus is a different person; the attribution to Theseus is unsupported.

identity.detail: Wikidata Theseus is the right hero; Ægeus and Æthra spellings are the same beings as Aegeus and Aethra.

links.reason: Eumolpus is the son of Poseidon and Chione (Apollodorus); Dionysus as father rests on a Wikidata confusion and nothing in Hesiod supports it.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the god Dionysus; Bacchus, Heaven-born and Insewn are epithets of the same god.
Wikidata match is Catreus, son of Minos and king of Crete; no other names to question.
Lyrcus, illegitimate son of Abas of Argos, matches the Wikidata entry and the book's sentence; no other names are involved.
Keuthonymos is the same underworld spirit, father of Menoetes (Menoetius), the herdsman of Hades whom Heracles wrestled.
Wikidata's Myrrha (Smyrna), mother of Adonis, is the same being. Ovid names Cinyras as her father and the book names Cenchreïs as her mother, a variant of Wikidata's Metharme, so no fix is needed.
Polydorus is Priam and Hecuba's youngest son, killed by Polymestor in Metamorphoses 13. The Wikidata match is correct. The Hector sibling link is fine, since Hector is also a son of Priam and Hecuba.

Dis is Pluto/Hades, the underworld god, so the match to Dis Pater is fine. The Thebaid's Dis is the Roman Pluto, brother of Jove and Neptune, son of Saturn (Cronus) and Rhea, and husband of Proserpine.
Wikidata Pharis, son of Hermes and Phylodameia, founder of Pharae, matches the book's Pharis/Phares. All links are supported by Pausanias.

links.reason: Hesiod's Catalogue lists Polycaste as Nestor's daughter; Jocasta (Oedipus' mother, daughter of Menoeceus) is a different person, so this link confuses two figures.

identity.detail: Wikidata Nestor of Pylos, son of Neleus and Chloris, matches.

links.reason: Alcmena married Rhadamanthys in Boeotia after Amphitryon's death (Apollodorus; Pherecydes; Plutarch); it was a marriage, though listed under a spouse link from another book, so keep it as spouse.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Rhadamanthus is the son of Zeus and Europa. Wikidata's Hephaestus as a father is a doubtful extra, but the identity is correct.
Wikidata's Aegialeus is Adrastus's son, the Epigonoi leader who died at Glisas, which matches Pausanias. No other names are attached to him.

links.reason: In Virgil (Aeneid) and Ovid, Picus is the son of Saturn, the Roman god. That is not the Greek Cronus's son in this tradition and was merged through the Saturn/Cronus identification, so it is not supported for Aeschylus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan Cronus.
Phocus, son of Ornytion, grandson of Sisyphus, eponym of Phocis, matches Wikidata.
Coön, eldest son of Antenor and Theano, wounds Agamemnon and is killed by him in Iliad 11; the Wikidata match is correct.
Lysippos the sculptor is correctly matched. Pausanias mentions him as the sculptor, and his son Daippus was also a sculptor, so the link is fine.

links.reason: Editor's decision: Inachus as parent of Argus is wrong everywhere; Argus Panoptes is son of Aristor (or Arestor) and Argus of Argos descends from Zeus and Niobe.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the river god Inachus of Argos, son of Oceanus and Tethys; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Sicinus is the son of Thoas by the Naiad Oenoe (Oenoe's son), but in Apollodorus Sicinus is not Thoas' child; the link comes from Argonautica, not this book's tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata Thoas is the Lemnian king, son of Dionysus and Ariadne; this matches.
Amythaon, son of Cretheus and Tyro, father of Melampus and Bias, matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata match Itys is the son of Tereus and Procne; the book's links agree.

links.reason: Hesiod makes Aegle Theseus's lover, for whom he abandoned Ariadne; not a marriage.
Tradition (Pausanias, Plutarch) has Antiope bear Hippolytus to Theseus; Wikidata lists her as spouse. Sources differ, so the lover link is not clearly wrong.
Statius treats Hippolyte as Theseus's wife, same Amazon as Antiope/Hippolyta in other versions; link fine, but should be merged with Antiope.
Helen was abducted by Theseus as a girl and never married to him; she was only a captive or lover.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Iphigenia, daughter of Theseus
links.reason: Pausanias says this Iphigenia was Helen's daughter by Theseus, raised by Clytemnestra; she is not the daughter of Agamemnon, so a link to Theseus must not be confused with her.

links.link: Theseus parent_of Melanippus, son of Theseus
links.reason: Unsupported; Melanippus is not a recognized son of Theseus in the sources.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is correct; Cecropian is an epithet, not a different person.

Pausanias (5.10.6) names Sterope, wife of Oenomaus and daughter of Atlas, in the Olympia pediment. This matches the Pleiad Sterope, whom tradition also makes Oenomaus's wife (mother of Hippodamia), so the Wikidata match is acceptable.

links.reason: This is a placeholder, not a named person. Pausanias gives no son of Crius here, and Apollodorus names Astraeus, Pallas and Perses as his sons by Eurybia.

identity.detail: Kreios is the Titan Crius, son of Uranus and Gaia.
Pratinas of Phlius, tragic and satyr-play poet, father of Aristias (Pausanias 2.13.6); the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Per the Catalogue of Women and Wikidata, Polycaste, daughter of Nestor, married Telemachus; Pausanias gives no contrary tradition.

Telegonus tradition (Eugammon, Hesiod's Theogony ending) has Telemachus marry Circe, but the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers; Pausanias does not tell this, so keep it as lover only.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Odysseus' son Telemachus; no other names.
Argus son of Zeus and Niobe, king of Argos, is the right match.

links.reason: Cupid is son of Venus; Ovid does not make Mars his father, and the usual tradition (Hesiod, Homeric hymns) disagrees, though some late sources say Ares. Wikidata's claim is a minor variant.
Thestius, father of Leda and Althaea, is son of Ares only in a rare tradition; Apollodorus gives Agenor and Demonice as parents (Demonice was Ares' daughter, not the mother).
Ixion is the son of Phlegyas (or Antion), not Mars; Wikidata confuses the line.
Tmolus son of Ares and Theogone is a different figure from the Lydian mountain god in Ovid.
Harmonia is a daughter of Mars and Venus, but the label 'Cadmus's wife' duplicates the Harmonia node and is not a person.
Harmonia is Mars's daughter (with Venus), not his spouse; she married Cadmus.
Duplicate of Penthesilea under another spelling; keep one node.
Panic is a personification, not a person; Phobos and Deimos are Ares' sons, and Panic is a collective idea.

links.link: Mars parent_of Melanippus, son of Ares
links.reason: Descriptive title duplicating a person; the tie is unclear.
Venus is Mars's lover, not sister; she is Aphrodite, not a child of Juno and Jupiter.
Mercury is son of Jupiter and Maia, so only a half-brother; Statius uses loose language.

identity.detail: Mars is Ares as well; Gradivus and Mavors are epithets of the same god. Wikidata spouse is Venus or another; accept as lover.
Wikidata match is the Muse Calliope, mother of Orpheus; no misattributed names.

Wikidata's Aeacus is the king of Aegina, son of Zeus and Aegina and father of Peleus, Telamon and Phocus. The Æacus of Metamorphoses is the same being. The Theoi listing of Zeus and Europa is a different Aeacus tradition, not a mismatch.

links.reason: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Chaos is the primal unformed mass at the start (1.5-9), with no parent. Hesiod (Theogony 116) also gives Chaos no parent. Only the Orphic Rhapsodies make Chronos his father, and the book does not follow that tradition.

identity.detail: Chaos matches the primordial Chaos. Ovid uses it for the shapeless primal mass rather than a person.
The Wikidata match is the Titan Mnemosyne and no other names are attached.

links.reason: Pausanias gives Oeneus a different Pandion-line parentage (the Athenian Pandion belongs to another tradition); Thebaid and Iliad make Oeneus son of Porthaon (Portheus), so Pandion is unsupported here.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Calydonian king Oeneus; no other names involved.

Electra the Pleiad, daughter of Atlas, mother of Dardanus and Iasion by Zeus, matches Wikidata. The Wikidata spouse is probably Zeus, whom the editor's rule reads as a lover, but no spouse link is listed in this tree.
Wikidata match is the goddess Nemesis; 'Indignation' is her own name in Hesiod's gloss.

links.reason: Saturn's wife is Rhea (Ops); Cybele is often identified with Rhea, so she is the same wife under another name and not a separate spouse.
Cybele is a Phrygian goddess merged with Rhea; Rhea is Saturn's sister-wife, so this sibling link confuses Cybele with Rhea or is redundant.

identity.detail: Saturn/Cronus is the right being; Cybele is only a syncretic identification with Rhea, not a separate relative.

The Aeneid's Pallas is Evander's son, the young warrior killed by Turnus. The names Minerva, Tritonia and Tritonian maiden belong to the goddess Pallas Athena/Minerva, a different being, and should be split off. The Wikidata match 'Pallas' is the right person, though its father 'Evander of Pallene' may be a different Evander from the Arcadian king in the book.
Wikidata match is Eurysthenes, the Spartan king and Agiad founder, son of Aristodemus. This matches Pausanias.

links.reason: Endeis, Peleus' mother, was a daughter of Chiron or Sciron, not a Nereid. She is Thetis' mother-in-law, not her sister; the link comes from a confusion in Pausanias.
Phocus was the son of Aeacus and the Nereid Psamathe, and Peleus' half-brother. He is not Thetis' child; the link confuses Psamathe with Thetis.

identity.detail: Thetis the Nereid is the correct match. The alias 'Peleus' bride' refers to her as well. Wikidata's spouse Neptune is a Roman equivalent of Poseidon and is not used in this book.
Pandrosus is the daughter of Cecrops in Apollodorus; the Wikidata match is correct and no other names are involved.

links.reason: Glaucus loved the sea-monster Scylla (Ovid, Metamorphoses), not Nisus' daughter who betrayed Megara; Pausanias' Scylla is the Megarian princess.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Nisus' daughter, the Megarian Scylla, which fits Pausanias; the monster Scylla is a separate being, so the Glaucus link came from her.
Deidameia of Scyros, daughter of Lycomedes and mother of Neoptolemus by Achilles, matches Wikidata's Deidamia.
Wikidata's Iobates is the Lycian king, father of Philonoe and Antea (Stheneboea), so the match is correct and no other names need splitting.
Alope, daughter of Cercyon and mother of Hippothoon by Poseidon, matches Wikidata's Alope; the book's text agrees with Wikidata's father Cercyon of Eleusis.
Opheltes is the same being as Archemorus, the infant son of Lycurgus of Nemea and Eurydice, whom Statius calls Archemorus. No other name is wrongly attached.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemos to Achilles on Scyros, but no marriage is told; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lover.
Helen and Achilles are joined only in a late afterlife tradition (Pausanias); the Aeneid has no marriage, so under the editor's rule it is at most a lover link.

links.link: Achilles parent_of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus
links.reason: Pyrrhus of Epirus was a historical king descended from Neoptolemos; he is not Achilles' son. Neoptolemos (also called Pyrrhus) is Achilles' son.

identity.detail: Achilles matches the hero of the Trojan War. Pelides and Aeacides (descendant of Aeacus) are epithets for this same Achilles.
Demoleon, son of Antenor and Theano, is the Trojan killed by Achilles in Iliad 20; the Wikidata match is correct.
Celusa, nymph of Mount Celusa in Phliasia and mother of Asopus by Poseidon, matches Wikidata; no other names are listed.

Rhacius is the Cretan son of Lebes who married Manto and settled at Colophon. The Wikidata match is correct. The flag for 2 spouses is a duplicate of the same Manto link, supported by the book and by Pausanias, so no fix is needed.
Wikidata match is Labdacus, king of Thebes, son of Polydorus and Nycteis and father of Laius. This fits the book.
The Wikidata match is the Titan Atlas. The Odyssey's 'magician Atlas' is the same being.

links.reason: Hyrie is the mother of the other Cycnus, the son of Apollo and Hyrie, whose story Ovid tells in Book 7 (the Boeotian lake). The Cycnus who mourned Phaethon is the son of Sthenelus.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Ligurian king and friend of Phaethon, the son of Sthenelus, which fits this book.
Wikidata match is the god Hephaestus; no other names are listed.

links.reason: Hesiod's Homeric-style tale has Hermes loving Dryops' daughter, mother of Pan; she was not a wife. The editor reads non-marriage spouse links as lover links.
Pindar's 'Angelia' (Message) is a personification, not Fame (Pheme). Hermes' daughter here is a namesake confusion.
Eleusis as a son of Hermes is a pausanias variant; the editor limited Eleusis' parentage to Ogygus or Daira in pausanias, not Apollodorus.

identity.detail: Hermes matches the Olympian god; Mercury is his Roman equivalent and Argiphontes is his epithet.

links.reason: Pausanias calls Idomeneus a descendant of Minos and Pasiphae, not a son. His father was Deucalion, Minos's son, so Minos is his grandfather.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Cretan king Idomeneus, which is correct.
Carmanor is the Cretan priest who purified Apollo after the killing of Python. The Wikidata match is correct, and he has no other names.

Terpsichore is the Muse, daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne (Hesiod Theogony 75), and the Wikidata match is correct. Her link to the Sirens as their mother (via Achelous) is a tradition in Apollonius' Argonautica, and Theoi confirms it.

Wikidata match is Latinus, king of Latium. The Wikipedia blurb mentions the Odysseus/Telemachus tradition (Latinus as son of Odysseus and Circe), but that is a variant tradition. The Aeneid follows Faunus and Marica, so no fix is needed.
Wikidata match is the seer Amphiaraus, son of Oicles; no other names to question.
Iphigenia matches this Iphigeneia, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra; no other names are involved.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse; in the Odyssey Helen was Menelaus's wife, and Paris carried her off (she was his partner in Troy, not husband under the rule).
Theseus abducted Helen as a girl (Pausanias); not a marriage, so a lover per editor's rule.
Achilles and Helen on the White Island is a late tale, not a marriage; treat as a lover.
Nicostratus is Menelaus's son by a slave woman (Megapenthes' brother in some accounts); the Odyssey says Helen bore only Hermione.

identity.detail: Wikidata Helen of Troy is the right being.
Capys, son of Assaracus and father of Anchises (Iliad 20.239), is the right match. The mothers Hieromneme and Clytodora are alternative traditions and not a problem.
Wikidata match is Hades, god of the underworld; no other names to question.
Wikidata match is the Thracian bard Orpheus; no other names to question.
Wikidata Selene is the Moon goddess, daughter of Hyperion and Theia; 'Moon-goddess' is the same being.
Wikidata match is Hephaestus, the Greek god. Vulcan is his Roman counterpart, which is acceptable as an alias.

links.reason: Hesiod's Theogony and Apollodorus treat Echidna as Typhon's mate, and Wikidata lists her as his spouse. Under the editor's rule only marriages count as spouse, and this is a mating, so lover is acceptable; keep as is.

identity.detail: Typhoeus is Typhon (Typhaon, Typhos); the match is correct.

links.reason: Deidameia bore Neoptolemus to Achilles on Scyros but was not his wife in the usual tradition; the editor's rule reads non-marriage spouse links as lovers.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the hero Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis; no other names are attached.
Megapenthes is Menelaus' son by a slave woman, as the Odyssey says (Wikidata names her Pieris, which fits the tradition). The match is the same being.

links.reason: The Telemachus marriage is a Telegony tradition not told in Apollodorus; under the editor's rule a non-marriage spouse link is read as a lover link, and the book does not state a marriage.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Circe, daughter of Helios; no other names to split.

links.reason: Apollodorus makes Actor a different figure, the Elean Molione's father/Augeas's associate, not Augeas's brother; Augeas is son of Helios (or Phorbas, Poseidon) and Actor is not named as a sibling in any Theoi-listed source.

identity.detail: Augeias of Elis is the right match; Aegeus is a Wikipedia alias, not a separate being.

links.reason: Cadmus's wife is Harmonia; in Ovid's Metamorphoses "Hermione" is the same Harmonia under a variant name (or a confusion with Menelaus' daughter Hermione), not a second wife.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Theban founder Cadmus; no other names to fix.
Ceres is the Roman Demeter. The match is acceptable, and the parents Cronus/Saturn and Rhea/Ops agree with Theoi.
Thoas of Lemnos, son of Dionysus and Ariadne, father of Hypsipyle, matches Wikidata.

Wikidata match is Polynices, son of Oedipus, which fits the book. All the listed links are consistent with the tradition (Oedipus and Jocasta as parents, Eteocles and Antigone as siblings, Argia as wife, Thersander as son).

links.reason: Pausanias's Clymenus is a Argive/Hermionean cult figure, a title of Hades, not a separate brother; in Hermione Clymenus is a name of Hades, so this is a cult title taken as a person and duplicates Aidoneus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the goddess Demeter; no other names.
Benthesicyme is Poseidon and Amphitrite's daughter and Eumolpus's foster mother in Apollodorus. The Wikidata match is correct.
Wikidata match is Melanthius, son of Dolius, the disloyal goatherd of the Odyssey. The book's sentence names Dolius as his father, so the link is fine.
The Wikidata match is the Aetolian Leda, wife of Tyndareus. The Argonautica text itself says 'Aetolian Leda'.

Chloris is the Minyan daughter of Amphion of Orchomenus (son of Iasus) and Persephone, wife of Neleus and mother of Nestor and Periclymenus in Odyssey 11. The links all fit. Niobe as her mother is the Theban Niobe, wife of Amphion of Thebes, which is a different Amphion; this is a namesake error that Odyssey 11.281-286 does not support.

links.link: Arcas parent_of Pelasgus, son of Arcas
links.reason: Pausanias makes Pelasgus the father of Lycaon and an ancestor of Arcas, not his son. The link confuses the earlier Pelasgus with a later namesake.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Arcas is the son of Callisto and Zeus, which matches the book. Wikidata lists Lycaon and Parrhasius as fathers, but that does not change who this Arcas is.

links.reason: This is the Amazon Antiope (sister of Hippolyta), a different being from the Theban Antiope of Odyssey 11, mother of Amphion and Zethus.
Hippolyta is the sister of the Amazon Antiope, not of Asopus' daughter.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the Theban Antiope. The Amazon links (Theseus, Hippolyta) come from a different Antiope sharing the name, so they are removed rather than treated as a wrong match.

links.reason: Hesiod, Theogony 901: 'Next he married bright Themis'; Wikidata and the Wikipedia description also name her Zeus's wife. The editor's rule reads only Hera as Zeus's marriage, but Hesiod's text states this one is a marriage, so the lover label is a misread.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Titan goddess Themis; no other names listed.
Ianthe is an Oceanid listed in Hesiod's Theogony (349), daughter of Oceanus and Tethys. The Wikidata match is correct.
Aenetus, son of Deioneus (Deion) and Diomede, matches Wikidata; Deion is a variant spelling of Deioneus, so the link is fine.
Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, is the right being; Wikidata matches and no other names are attached.

Elephenor, son of Chalcodon and leader of the Abantes of Euboea, is the same being as the Wikidata match. The flagged parent difference is only that Wikidata also gives a mother, Melanippe, and the tree lists no mother, so Chalcodon as father agrees with Wikidata.

links.reason: The Naiads are a group, not a single person; Ovid's Metamorphoses calls the Echinades nymphs, not Achelous's children as a group.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is the river god Achelous. The Wikidata spouses (Muses, Perimede, Sterope) are not in Pausanias, but they are not a wrong identity.
Wikidata match is correct; Alexander is Paris's own second name.
Wikidata Europa is the Phoenician princess, daughter of Agenor, abducted by Jupiter; no confusion with the Titaness Europa or other namesakes.
Aphareus the Messenian king, son of Perieres and Gorgophone, husband of Arene, father of Idas and Lynceus. The match is correct.
Wikidata match is the Trojan prince Hector.
Wikidata match is the Aetolian Tydeus, father of Diomedes; no other names.

links.reason: In the Aeneid Latinus is the son of Faunus (and Marica). Faunus is the Roman counterpart of Pan, but the tradition is separate and the two are not the same being.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Pan the god, and he has no other names to question.
Absyrtus is the Colchian prince, son of Aeetes and Asterodeia in Apollonius, and Medea's half-brother. The match and the alternate name Absyrtus are correct.
Wikidata match is Odysseus himself; no other names to dispute.

links.link: Leonidas parent_of Cleomenes III, son of Leonidas
links.reason: Pausanias names two Leonidases: Leonidas I of Thermopylae, and Leonidas II, father of Cleomenes III and Epiclidas and son of Cleonymus. Those children belong to Leonidas II.
Epiclidas was a son of Leonidas II, the Hellenistic king, not of Leonidas I.

links.link: Cleonymus, father of Leonidas parent_of Leonidas
links.reason: Cleonymus was the father of Leonidas II, the grandfather of Cleomenes III, not of Leonidas I, whose father was Anaxandridas.

identity.detail: The name 'Leonidas' in Pausanias covers two kings: Leonidas I (Wikidata match; son of Anaxandridas, father of Plistarchus) and Leonidas II (son of Cleonymus, father of Cleomenes III and Epiclidas). Split the Leonidas II links to a separate character.
Creon of Thebes, son of Menoeceus and brother of Jocasta, is the right match; no other names are listed.
Wikidata's Polynices is the Theban son of Oedipus, which matches this character. The epithets (Aonian, Cadmean, Ismenian, Teumesian, Tyrian) all refer to him as a Theban exile.

pausanias/poseidon.name: Poseidon
flags: matched to several Wikidata entries: Poseidon, Taraxippus

links.reason: The Doliones are a people, a group taken for a person; their eponym Dolion was a different figure.
Laestrygon is the eponym of a people, and the link rests on a misread tradition in Hesiod.
Podaleirius is a son of Asclepius, not Poseidon.
Chios is an island or eponym, and no Poseidon parentage is stated in this book.
Sarpedon the Lycian is a son of Zeus; the Poseidon link is a rare namesake of the Thracian Sarpedon.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match to Poseidon Taraxippus is a cult epithet; the character should be matched to Poseidon himself. Cult titles such as Hippius, Isthmius and Asphalius are the same god, but Neptune is the Roman equivalent.
Wikidata match is Nestor of Pylos, son of Neleus; no other names are given.

Apame in Pausanias is the daughter of Antiochus son of Seleucus (Antiochus I Soter) and wife of Magas of Cyrene, which matches Apama II. The flag on parents is only because the book names the father alone; Wikidata's mother Stratonice does not conflict.
The Wikidata match is Aethlius, first king of Elis, which is the same being.
Europa the Phoenician princess, mother of Minos, is the right match; no other names are listed.
Arethusa the Syracusan spring nymph matches; no other names are given.
Diomedes son of Tydeus, king of Argos, matches the Wikidata entry. The alternate names Diomede and Tydeides refer to the same hero.
Halirrhothius, the Athenian son of Poseidon killed by Ares after the affair with Alcippe, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are listed that could belong to someone else.
Acaste is the Oceanid named in Hesiod's Theogony list of Oceanids, and the Wikidata match is the same being. Her parents Oceanus and Tethys are correct.
Wikidata match is Neoptolemus son of Achilles; no other names listed.

links.reason: In Pausanias, Alpheus was a river-god who pursued Artemis (or Arethusa) and failed, so he was never her lover. This isn't a relationship in Aeschylus.

identity.detail: Wikidata's Artemis is the right being. The names Artemis-Hecate and Diana are acceptable identifications, with Diana as the Roman counterpart. Aeschylus (via Pausanias 8.37.3) also gives a Demeter-daughter variant, but this book's own text names Leto.
Himeros is the winged love deity in Aphrodite's train, matching Hesiod's Himerus (Desire), who attends Aphrodite at her birth in the Theogony. 'Desire' is just the translation of his name.
Demaratus is the Eurypontid king of Sparta, son of Ariston (Aristo in Pausanias' text); the Wikidata match is correct and the parent flag is only a spelling difference.

links.reason: Pallas is a Titan son of Crius (Hesiod) or an epithet of Athena; Zeus is not his father.
Selene was confused with Diana/Pandia; Hesiod's Selene is a Titan's daughter, and the editor ruled Zeus parent of Selene wrong. Pandia is Zeus and Selene's daughter only in the Homeric Hymn.
Pandia comes from the Selene confusion, and the editor has ruled Artemis parent of Pandia wrong.
A group taken for a person; the Graces are already listed individually as Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia.
A group; the Muses are already listed individually.
A group, not a person.
Opportunity (Kairos) is an abstraction in Pausanias, and Zeus is not named as his father.
The Sibyl is called daughter of Zeus and Lamia only in Pausanias; here it is a cross-book link, and Zeus is not her parent in this book.
Truth is a personified abstraction in Pindar, not a daughter of Zeus here.
Apollodorus lists Justice among the Seasons, whom Zeus fathered with Themis; the link duplicates this as a separate person.
Iarbas is a son of Jupiter Ammon in Virgil, a different cult figure; this is a namesake.
Erato is a Muse; Zeus's paternity of the Muses is shown separately.
Macedon is Zeus's son only in Hesiod's catalogue, not in Apollodorus.
A cult-linked figure from Pausanias, not in Apollodorus; low confidence.
Arcesius is a son of Zeus in Ovid, but Apollodorus calls him a son of Cephalus.
Megarus is a son of Zeus only in Pausanias, not in Apollodorus.
Macar is a son of Aeolus in Apollodorus, with no father link to Zeus.
Ate is the personification of delusion, from other books only.
Eris is the personification of strife, from other books only; Hesiod makes her a daughter of Night.

identity.detail: Zeus is the right being; the alternate names (Jupiter, Jove) are Roman equivalents. Atabyrian Zeus and Saviour Zeus are cult titles.
The Wikidata match is the same Endymion, the shepherd or king beloved of Selene.

Wikidata's Procne is the Athenian princess, daughter of Pandion, wife of Tereus. The flag about parents is only a Pandion I versus Pandion naming difference, and Pausanias names Pandion as her father.

Wikidata's Sardus is the Sardinian eponymous hero in Pausanias (10.17). The book makes him the son of Maceris, whom Egyptians and Libyans call Hercules. Wikidata's father, Maceris of Libya, is that same person, so the parent link is right and the flag is only a naming difference.
Phrontis is the son of Phrixus and Chalciope, and the Wikidata match is the same being.
Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle, the Argive Epigonus, matches the Wikidata entry. No confusion with the namesake Amphilochus, son of Alcmaeon and Manto, is visible.

Wikidata's Hellen is the eponymous ancestor of the Hellenes, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, which matches Apollodorus. The book also says some name Zeus as his father, a variant that does not change who he is.
Wikidata match is the sea goddess Amphitrite, wife of Poseidon; no other names to split.
Zethos is the Theban twin of Amphion, son of Zeus and Antiope; the match is correct. Wikidata's spouse Aëdon is the traditional wife of Zethus (Odyssey 19), and Neis is his daughter in Pausanias.
Wikidata match is the Spartan princess Cynisca, daughter of Archidamus II; the book's sentences confirm this, and she has no other names.
Dymas the Phrygian king, father of Hecuba (Iliad 16.718; Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.761 calls her Dymantis), matches Wikidata. Hecuba as his daughter is a recognized tradition.

Tyche is the Oceanid of Hesiod Theogony 360, daughter of Ocean and Tethys. The Wikidata match is the same being. Other traditions, such as Zeus, Prometheus or Hermes as father, are not in this book's tree.

links.link: Hiero son of Hierocles parent_of Gelon
links.reason: Pausanias mentions a later Gelon, son of Hiero II of Syracuse, who married Nereis daughter of Pyrrhus. The links to Hiero son of Hierocles as parent and to Nereis belong to this later Gelon, not Gelon son of Deinomenes.
Nereis married Gelon the son of Hiero II, a different man from the tyrant Gelon son of Deinomenes (brother of Hiero I).

identity.detail: The tree joins two men named Gelon: the tyrant Gelon son of Dinomenes (brother of Hiero I), and Gelon son of Hiero II who married Nereis. Wikidata's match for the tyrant is correct. Hiero II (son of Hierocles) and Nereis belong to the second Gelon.
