Adrastus, king of Argos and leader of the Seven against Thebes, is the right match. The links to Talaus (father), Argia, Deipyle, Argea and Aegialeus (children) are all traditional.
The match is the river god Asopus; no names are confused.
The Wikidata match is the eponym of the Corybantes, son of Iasion and Cybele, so this is the right being.
Onatas of Aegina the sculptor is the right match; no other names.

Ancaeus of Samos, the Argonaut helmsman, matches Wikidata. Ovid (Metamorphoses 8) mentions him in the Calydonian boar hunt. Poseidon as father with Astypalaea as mother is a standard tradition, and the Samia marriage is also traditional (Pausanias). The flag only reflects a difference between the book's tree and Wikidata, not an error.
Brontes is one of the three Hesiodic Cyclopes (Brontes, Steropes, Arges), children of Sky and Earth in Apollodorus. The Wikidata match is correct.
Meges son of Phyleus, Epeian/Dulichian leader at Troy, matches Wikidata.
Gelanor, son of Sthenelas and king of Argos who yielded the throne to Danaus, is the Wikidata match (also called Pelasgus); no other names are confused.
Antilochus, son of Nestor, who died saving his father at Troy (Pindar, Pythian 6), matches the Wikidata entry.
Ptous matches the eponym of Mount Ptous. Pausanias follows Asius, who makes him son of Athamas and Themisto, which is one of the traditions the Wikipedia entry lists.
Iasus, king of Argos, son of Triopas and father of Io in Pausanias, matches the Wikidata entry. No other names are given.

links.reason: Pausanias does not make Laius the Sphinx's father; Statius's Sphinx is a monster of Hera/Typhon-Echidna lineage, and Laius's only child here is Oedipus.

identity.detail: Wikidata Laius is the Theban king, father of Oedipus; no other names to question.
Cestrinus is the son of Helenus and Andromache, and the Wikidata match is the same person.

Wikidata match is the Athenian princess Philomela, daughter of Pandion and sister of Procne. The flag only reflects that Wikidata also names the mother Zeuxippe, which does not contradict the father link. Nothing here needs fixing.

links.reason: Metra is the wife of Erysichthon in Ovid's Metamorphoses (Mestra); she is not Autolycus's wife. Ovid mentions Autolycus only as the son of Mercury and Chione, and Mestra's father is Erysichthon.
Neaera is not an established wife of Autolycus; his wife is Amphithea, mother of Anticlea (Odyssey 19). Neaera in Pausanias is a different woman.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the right Autolycus, son of Hermes and Chione, grandfather of Odysseus.
Haemon, son of Creon, killed by the Sphinx in the Oedipodea fragment, matches the Wikidata Haemon. No other names are involved.
Sinope, daughter of Asopus and eponym of the Black Sea city, is the right being. The Argonautica sentence names Asopus as her father.

links.reason: Pausanias says Cecrops married the daughter of Actaeus; Apollodorus names her Agraulos. Aglauros, Cecrops' daughter, is a different person, so the spouse link confuses mother and daughter.

identity.detail: Wikidata Cecrops I fits the first king; the Haliartus Cecrops son of Pandion is a separate later Cecrops.
Wikidata's Teucer is the son of Telamon and Hesione, brother of Ajax, and founder of Salamis on Cyprus. That is the Teucer Pausanias means, so the match is correct.
Wikidata's Pegasus is the winged horse born of Poseidon and Medusa, who is the Pegasos of Pindar's Odes (Olympian 13, Bellerophon). Nothing suggests a mismatch.
Gorgias of Leontinoi, the sophist and rhetorician, son of Carmantides, is the right match.

links.reason: Poseidon's son Cycnus is the Trojan king killed by Achilles, not Ares' son killed by Heracles in Hesiod's Shield.
Hemithea and Tennes are children of the Trojan Cycnus (Poseidon's son), per Pausanias, not Ares' son.
Tennes is the son of the Trojan Cycnus, not of Ares' son in Hesiod.
Phylonome is the wife of the Trojan Cycnus, son of Poseidon, not of Ares' son.

Themistinoe is Ceyx's daughter, and the Shield passage addresses Cycnus as Ceyx's son-in-law, but the sentence is Heracles' speech to Iolaus, the 'you' being the charioteer Iolaus. It does not say Cycnus is Themistinoe's husband; Iolaus is.

identity.detail: The match merges two Cycnuses: Ares' son killed by Heracles (Hesiod) and Poseidon's son killed by Achilles at Troy. Poseidon, Hemithea, Tennes and Phylonome belong to the Trojan one.

links.reason: Harmonia was Ares' lover (Aphrodite's daughter by Ares, married to Cadmus), not his wife; the editor's rule treats non-listed marriages as lovers.
Statius calls them as fellow gods only; Hermes is son of Zeus and Maia, so he is a half-brother at most, not a full sibling; unsupported sibling link.
Aphrodite (Cypris) is Ares' lover, not his sister; Iliad has her as Zeus's daughter by Dione, but no sibling link to Ares is stated in the Theoi parentage.
Ixion's father is Phlegyas (or Antion/Peision), not Ares; Ares is the father of Phlegyas, so Ixion is a grandson at most.
Parthenopaeus is the son of Atalanta by Melanion or Meleager; Ares is not his father in the main tradition.

identity.detail: Wikidata Ares is the Greek god; Mars is the Roman counterpart, and Penthesilea/Penthesileia are one person duplicated.

links.link: Heracles parent_of Hercules' sons by Megara
links.reason: A group of children treated as one person; the sons by Megara should be individual nodes.
Chromis in Statius' Thebaid is a different Chromis, not a son of Heracles.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is Heracles; Alcides and Amphitryon's son are epithets for him. Black-bottom (Melampygos) is also an epithet of Heracles.

links.reason: Latinus is son of Faunus the Italian king (son of Picus) in Aeneid and Metamorphoses, not Pan/Faunus of Statius's Arcadian god.
Silenus as son of Pan is a minor variant, but Statius's Faunus is Arcadian Pan; Silenus is usually a follower of Dionysus, so this link is an unsupported guess.
Ovid's Faunus is the Italian god, father of Acis in Metamorphoses; this is not Statius's Pan, though the Wikidata entry merges both.

identity.detail: Wikidata merges Greek Pan (son of Hermes) with Roman Faunus (son of Picus and Canens, father of Latinus). Statius's Faunus is Pan, so Latinus and Picus/Canens belong to the Italian Faunus.
Ceto, daughter of Pontus and Gaia, wife of Phorcys, is the correct match.
Wikidata match is the daughter of Aeolus and Enarete; no other names.

Pausanias' Clitomachus is the Theban athlete (pancratiast/boxer) whose statue at Olympia was set up by his father Hermocrates. The Wikidata match is the Carthaginian Academic philosopher Clitomachus, a different person, so the match should be removed.

links.reason: The passage is the Homeric Hymn/Hesiod-style fragment on Nireus and Telephus or other heroes; the 'Earth-Shaker' father of both gifts does not make Poseidon Machaon's father. Machaon's father is Asclepius (Iliad 2.731; Theoi), and the sentence names a different pair.

identity.detail: The Wikidata match is Machaon, son of Asclepius; no other names to question.
Calydon, eponym of the Aetolian city, son of Aetolus and Pronoe, is the same being as the Wikidata match. Apollodorus (1.7.7) gives his children as Epicaste and Protogeneia, so both links are right.
Nausinous is the son of Odysseus and Calypso in Hesiod's Theogony (lines 1017-18), and the Wikidata match fits.
Inachus, river god and first king of Argos, son of Oceanus and Tethys, matches Wikidata. Wikidata lists two unnamed spouse ids besides Melia, but no other names or identity problems are shown.

links.reason: Pasithea is a Grace/Sleep's wife in Iliad 14 (given by Hera as bride to Hypnos), not Hera's daughter; the editor ruled Pasithea parentage against Jove and Bromius, and Apollodorus does not name her as Hera's child.

identity.detail: Wikidata match Hera is correct; Juno is her Roman equivalent, and the editor treats Juno as Hera.
Zeuxippus, king of Sicyon and son of Apollo and the nymph Syllis, matches the Wikidata entry.
Wikidata's Polyphemus is the Cyclops son of Poseidon (Neptune) and Thoosa, the same being as in Aeneid 3. No other names are attached to him.

links.reason: Enyalius is a war-god epithet or title of Ares, not Rhea's son; no source supports Rhea as his mother.
Midas is a mortal Phrygian king, not a child of Rhea; Metamorphoses has him honoring Cybele/Bacchus, which was mistaken for parentage.
Corybas is a Corybantes figure, a group/attendant tradition (often son of Cybele/Rhea-Cybele); conflates Rhea with Cybele and is unsupported here.

identity.detail: Rhea matches the Titaness, wife and sister of Cronus.
Thamyris is the Thracian singer, son of Philammon and the nymph Argiope, as Pausanias says; the Wikidata match is correct.

links.reason: Editor's rule: only marriages count as spouse links. Glauce (Creusa) was Jason's betrothed or second wife, but she is not the wife Hesiod names (Medea), so she is read as a lover.
This is a group, not a person. The sons (Mermerus and Pheres) are named individually elsewhere, and Hesiod names only Medeus.

identity.detail: Jason matches the Wikidata entry; no other names are listed.

links.reason: In the Odyssey (13.260) Orsilochus is a son of Idomeneus only in the invented Cretan tale, where Odysseus claims to have killed him. Apollodorus has no such son, and the Odyssey's Orsilochus is a fictional character, so this is not a real child of Idomeneus.

identity.detail: Wikidata match is the Cretan king Idomeneus, son of Deucalion. The parents agree with Apollodorus (Deucalion), and Wikidata's added mother Cleopatra is not a conflict.
Diomed is Diomedes son of Tydeus, king of Argos, so the Wikidata match is right. The Iliad has no other names for him.

links.reason: Clytus and Butes are sons of the Giant/Athenian Pallas (Metamorphoses, Pallas of the Pallantids), not of Athena's friend or Tritonia.
Butes is a child of a different Pallas (Metamorphoses); the Thebaid's Pallas is Athena (Tritonia).

identity.detail: In the Thebaid, Pallas and Tritonia are epithets of the goddess Athena (Minerva), daughter of Jove. The Wikidata match is Athena's friend Pallas, daughter of Triton, a different being; match to Athena instead.
